case_summary.text: IT : Where a civil contractor did not produce salary and wage register and other evidences in support of expenses incurred, Assessing Officer was justified in estimating profit at 8 per cent of gross contract receipts

IT : Where assessee, a civil contractor, did not maintain proper books of account and, thus, Commissioner (Appeals) having regard to profit margin of earlier years, adopted profit rate of 5 per cent of contractual receipts, in absence of any discussion on merits, Tribunal could not enhance said profit rate to 8 per cent of gross turnover by invoking provisions of section 44AD
Lower authorities rightly adopted net profit at 4% from civil contracts considering profit of prior years: HC

CST & VAT: Where assessee was engaged in execution of civil works contracts and it had adopted standard rate of deduction provided under rule 6(4)(n)(v) and claimed standard deduction of 30 per cent on its contract receipt towards labour and like charges, in view of clear, express and unambiguous provisions of rule 6 of Karnataka Sales Tax Rules, 1957 and in particular Explanation II thereto, Assessing Authority was correct in allowing deduction of 27.44 per cent of gross profit on labour charge
7% net profit rate held reasonable for civil contractor as against AO's 15% estimate:ITAT

INCOME TAX: Where assessee, a civil contractor executing works for Government departments/PWD, had all contractual receipts through banking channels and declared net profit rate of 6.06% on turnover, which was higher than presumptive rate of 6% prescribed under section 44AD, estimation of net profit at 15% without proper basis was unjustified, and AO was to be directed to recompute income by applying net profit rate of 7%
IT: Profit of contractor depend upon various factors like place of execution of contract, accessibility of labour, raw material, etc. and would, therefore, vary from contractor to contractor
Net profit rate to be fixed on basis of past tax history of assessee, value of contract and price of raw materials

IT : Where there was difference in civil contract receipts shown by assessee in books of account and by contractee in form 26AS, net profit rate at rate of 8 per cent was to be applied to determine income embedded in said receipts

IT: Where assessee was fully engaged in labour oriented contract work and it had taken contracts from a construction company, which in turn had taken main contract from Government, Assessing Officer was directed to apply 5 per cent net profit on gross receipts of assessee

IT : Where in case of assessee, engaged in civil construction business, Tribunal applied a net profit rate of 7 per cent keeping in view previous history, local knowledge and circumstances pertaining to assessee, said order of Tribunal did not require any interference

CST & VAT: Where assessee was engaged in execution of civil works contracts and it had adopted standard rate of deduction provided under rule 6(4)(n)(v) and claimed standard deduction of 30 per cent on its contract receipt towards labour and like charges, in view of clear, express and unambiguous provisions of rule 6 of Karnataka Sales Tax Rules, 1957 and in particular Explanation II thereto, Assessing Authority was correct in allowing deduction of 27.44 per cent of gross profit on labour charges in addition to standard deduction at 30 per cent available towards labour and like charges

IT: Where in case of government contractor engaged in construction of roads books of account was rejected, Tribunal, relying upon profit rates of preceding three years, was justified in estimating profits earned by assessee during relevant years at 5 percent of gross receipts

IT: In case of civil sub-contract normal profit rate was about 5 per cent; where Assessing Officer worked out same to be 6.4 per cent in assessee's case, after scrutiny, said order could not be regarded as erroneous

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a civil contractor, who worked for State Government departments furnished income at 3 per cent turnover based on estimates and contended that volume of work was higher and there was heavy competition which resulted in his inability to get more profits, Tribunal was justified in upholding order of Commissioner (Appeals) in adopting net profit at 4 per cent from civil contracts in view of order passed in previous assessment years
IT: Where work carried out by assessee was not as a civil contractor but as a builder, provision of section 44AD could not be warranted to estimate gross profit at 8 per cent

IT: Where assessee, a civil contractor, declared net profit ratio of 5.64 per cent of gross contract receipts and Assessing Officer after rejecting book results determined total income by estimating net profit ratio of 15 per cent of gross receipts, income from contracting business be estimated by applying net profit ratio of 8 per cent of gross receipts
Revision u/s 263 quashed as AO rightly accepted civil contractor’s voluntary 6% profit estimate, no error found: ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a civil contractor, who worked for State government departments furnished income at 3 per cent turnover based on estimates and contended that volume of work was higher and there was heavy competition which resulted in his inability to get more profits, since in previous assessment years AO estimated its net profit at 3.5 per cent, AO could not estimate net profit at 8 per cent under section 44AD in relevant assessment year on ground that assessee should have kept accounting records

IT : Where assessee could not substantiate its claim of gross profit rate of 8.7 per cent declared by it as purchase cost and sale price were unverifiable, gross profit rate of 11 per cent determined by Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal was justified

INCOME TAX : Where assessee was engaged in construction work and Assessing Officer rejected book results and estimated net profit at rate of 4 per cent of total contractual receipts as against 1 per cent declared by assessee and Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed appeal ex parte, matter was to be remanded back to Commissioner (Appeals) to decide issue on merit

IT : Discretion to determine net profit rate vested in authorities must be exercised on basis of relevant factors which are past tax history of assessee, an appraisal of value of contract, price of raw material, labour etc.
IT : Where Assessing Officer had not cited any comparable case before applying ad hoc gross profit rate of 8 per cent which appeared to be on higher side, same was to be restricted to 7 per cent

INCOME TAX : Where assessee engaged in civil construction business failed to produce necessary bills and vouchers and Assessing Officer after rejecting books of account under section 145(3), adopted 5 per cent net profit on gross receipts but failed to bring on record any comparable case of similar nature, since assessee agreed for estimation of 3 per cent profit on gross receipts, reasonable profit of 3 per cent on total receipts would meet ends of justice
HC affirms deduction of 25% for labour charges for work contract in absence of any books of account
IT : Penalty under section 271(1)(c) cannot be imposed merely on ground that there were defects in account books of assessee and flat rate of profit is applied to arrive at gross profits of assessee

INCOME TAX : Where assessee carried on civil construction business and Assessing Officer rejected books of account as some of assessee’s purchases were not verifiable, working of income at rate of 8 per cent of contract receipts was justified

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a civil contractor with receipts exceeding Rs. 2 crores, did not maintain books of account and filed his return in ITR-2 estimating profit at 6 per cent of contract receipts, since assessee was not entitled to pay tax under section 44AD and Assessing Officer accepted said estimate after thorough analysis, Principal Commissioner could not invoke revisionary proceedings only on premise that income should be estimated at 8 per cent without citing any supporting
IT : Enhancement in profit rate was not justified where revenue failed to point any special circumstances for estimation of high profit
IT : Where assessee builder could not prove expenditure incurred with relevant books and vouchers, estimation of income at rate of 11 per cent was reasonable

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in business of freight transport by road, failed to substantiate genuineness of expenditure incurred, however incurrence of expenditure could not be doubted while achieving a high volume of turnover, profit of assessee was to be estimated at 10 per cent of gross receipts

INCOME TAX : Where assessee carried on civil construction business and Assessing Officer rejected books of account as some of assessee's purchases were not verifiable, working of income at rate of 8 per cent of contract receipts was justified

IT : Where Assessing Officer computed gross profit rate of assessee at 25 per cent of gross receipts without any justification, Tribunal was justified in adopting gross profit rate of 8 per cent as mentioned in section 44AD even though turnover of assessee was in excess of Rs. 40 lakh
AO can’t estimate 7% net profit without giving any comparative figures of sector of assessee's business: HC
If AO adopted GP rate on ad hoc basis for civil contractor, ITAT was correct in adopting presumptive tax rate
Order of AO wasn't erroneous if he had taken net profit rate of contractor above normal rate after scrutiny
AO’s action of determining income at 8% of contract receipts justified if purchases were not verifiable: HC

IT: Adoption of net profit rate of 9 per cent on gross receipt was justified where assessee did not produce supporting vouchers for expenses, details of purchases and stocks and copies of partners' bank accounts due to which Assessing Officer could not verify various details

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in business of freight transport by road, had generated gross receipts of Rs. 2.51 crores and had gotten his books of account audited under section 44AB read with provisions of section 44AE(7) showing profit and gains lower than, as envisaged under section 44AE, however as assessee had failed in substantiating genuineness of expenditure incurred, profit of assessee could be estimated at 10 per cent of gross receipts

INCOME-TAX : Where assessee engaged in civil construction business failed to produce necessary bills and vouchers and the AO has rejected books of accounts u/s.145(3) and resorted to best judgement assessment as per provisions of section 144 and he adopted 5 % net profit on gross receipts but failed to bring on record any comparable case of similar nature and reason for adopting such rate of profit,

INCOME TAX : Where revenue authorities in assessee's own case in earlier year had estimated net profit below rate of 1 per cent, there being no change of business during relevant assessment years, estimating net profit at rate of 8 per cent could not be justified
AO can’t apply Sec. 44AD if turnover exceeds threshold limit; ITAT uphelds 4% net profit of civil contractor
Profit rightly estimated on gross receipt as assessee failed to produce evidence in support of expenditures
IT : Estimation of net profit rate in case of contractor
IT : Profit at 3.5 per cent of total estimated turnover was held to be reasonable for a trader of farsan items

INCOME TAX : Where assessee was involved in execution of civil works and it had shown purchases from twelve parties even if assessee failed to produce said parties for verification, Assessing Officer could not have treated entire purchases as non-genuine purchases but only profit element on such purchases and thus, Appellate Authorities were justified in restricting addition by estimating profit of 12.5 per cent on total purchases

INCOME TAX: Where dispute was only with regard to rate of gross profit on income which was not disclosed by assessee, it could not be said that Assessing Officer erred in adopting gross profit at rate of 2 per cent on undisclosed income declared by assessee
CIT(A) not justified in applying 10% net profit rate when Co. declared NP at 2.5% in subsequent years: ITAT
No question of law arises if AO estimated gross profit at rate of 2% after rejecting books of account: HC
AO couldn’t take into account profit margin of principle-contractor to estimate profit of sub-contractor

HEADNOTE: Section 143, read with section 256, of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 33, read with section 66, of Indian Income tax Act, 1922] - Assessment - General - Assessment year 1924-25 - In respect of contracts spread over a number of years, assessee produced accounts but accounts for relevant accounting year could not be separated - ITO assessed profit at a standard rate without informing assessee of information or evidence on which rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal - Whether question of law arose out of order of ITO - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a contractor, was assessed to income-tax for the relevant assessment year in respect of certain contracts which commenced in 1922 and were finished some time in 1924. The assessee produced his accounts, but the accounts for the relevant accounting year could not be separated. The ITO considered the accounts to be unreliable. He, therefore, assumed profit at the standard rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of his assessment. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner concluded that in any case it was impossible to ascertain from the assessee’s accounts what the income had been for one year and, therefore, the only way of ascertaining it was to apply the usual rate of 10 per cent on the total payments received. On application under section 66(2) of the 1922 Act, the Commissioner declined to make any reference.

On application under section 66 (3) of the 1922 Act.

HELD: In the instant case the assessee did not allege that he derived no income at all from any contracts, nor did the assessment proceed definitely on the ground that the accounts were unreliable. The Assistant Commissioner adopted a standard rate for the assessment merely because no separate accounts were available for the accounting year. This was apparently due to the manner in which the accounting were kept. As the assessee failed to produce correct and complete accounts for the accounting year, it was open to the Income-tax Officer to make an assessment to the best of his judgment: vide section 23, read with section 11, of the 1922 Act. The Assistant Commissioner, however, gave no reasons for adopting what he called the usual rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of the assessment, and it was not known how that rate was arrived at. In the circumstances of the case, the point of law emerged for decision was whether in the case of a contract spread over a number of years when accounts for the year under assessment could not be separated, the ITO was legally justified in assessing profits at a flat rate without informing the assessee of the information or evidence on which the rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal.

Accordingly, the petition was accepted and the Commissioner was directed to state the case and refer the point of law to the High Court for decision.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Sardha Ram for the Assessee .

Jagan Nath Aggarwal for the Crown.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Valuation of stock - Assessment year 1959-60 - While completing assessment ITO did not accept assessee's reasons for low profits at rate of 9% in respect of a contract undertaken by him and applied flat rate of 12Â½% profit - On appeal assessee had not derived before AAC that full quantitative details were not available in respect of stores of value of Rs. 1,30,000 - For subsequent assessment year assessee declared a profit of 9.9% - Whether on facts provisions of section 13 were applicable to assessee's case and therefore, Tribunal was justified in upholding addition in assessee's income - Held, yes

FACT: The business of the assessee was execution of construction contracts. The assessee commenced its business from 25-1-1958, and the accounts were closed for the first time on 25-1-1959. During the accounting year the assessee undertook three contracts with respect to which it submitted separate profit and loss statements.

The accounts in respect of the first two contracts were accepted by the authorities under the Act in toto but with regard to the accounts relating to the third contract the ITO declined to accept the assessee's reasons for low profits at the rate of 9% in respect of that contract. He, therefore, applied a flat rate of 12Â½% profit and made certain addition to the assessee's income.

On appeal, the AAC had accepted the assessee's reasons for the low profit of 9% but had sustained an addition of Rs. 10,000 on the ground that the assessee's representative had not denied before him that full quantitative details might not be available in respect of the stores of the value of over Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of the contract. When the case came up before the Tribunal the addition of Rs. 10,000 was found to be excessive and was reduced to Rs. 6,000.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case there was material before the Tribunal on which its finding could be based: the assessee's representative had admitted before the AAC that full quantitative details in respect of the stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of that contract might not be available. In the circumstances, recourse to estimating the profits on the contract was inevitable. He, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 10,000 as against Rs. 26,434 added by the ITO. If the assessee wished to displace the AAC's estimate it was open to him to adduce evidence in support of its claim that the consumption of stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 was fully justified. This the assessee apparently did not do. For the subsequent year 1960-61 the assessee itself declared a net profit rate of 9.9% as against 9% declared in the assessment year in question. It could not be disputed that this was additional material which the Tribunal could take into consideration as it did. There was thus material before the Tribunal on which its estimate was based. The Tribunal's decision was, therefore, in conformity with the decision in the case of CIT v. Maharajadhiraj of Darbhanga [1933] 1 ITR 94 (P.C.).

The Tribunal was therefore justified in holding that the proviso to section 13 was applicable and there was material before it to sustain the aforesaid addition.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of revenue.

He, therefore, rejected the books of account and estimated the net profit at 8 per cent of gross contract receipt and estimated net profit.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) after considering submissions of assessee, restricted the net profit rate at the rate of 4 per cent of the gross contractual receipts.

On further appeal by the revenue: HELD: In the instant case the assessee as sub-contractor to execute the civil construction works awarded by the principals, which was a small part of the projects executed by the principals. On the contract receipts, the principals had also deducted the tax under section 194C. Besides, the assessee was also engaged in the business of trading of sarees. It was also a fact that the assessee filed duly audited profit and loss account and balance sheet along with its annexure. It also produced the audited books of account, bills/vouchers and bank statements before the Assessing Officer as admitted by him in the assessment order. Besides, it further produced all the details and explanations called for by the Assessing Officer from time to time. It also produced labour registers before the Assessing Officer. However, he was of the opinion that the said registers had not been maintained in a conventional manner and according to him, there were no signatures or thumb impressions of all the recipients. Because of the aforesaid observations, the Assessing Officer rejected the audited books of account of the assessee and estimated the net profit. The Assessing Officer gave the examples of net profit earned by three companies and, thereafter, he relied on the provisions of section 11AD and estimated the net profit at the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts. Now the assessee argued that the estimation of net profit at the rate of 8 per cent by relying on provisions of section 44AD was totally incorrect and without any basis for the reason that the assessee was sub-contractor and its profit margin was low in comparison to the contractors. Further, the Assessing officer had compared the profit of the assessee with the companies whose turnover and business paraphernalia was huge in comparison to the assessee. Further, the assessee had executed the part of work of civil construction for these companies and, therefore, it was not correct to compare the profit of those companies with the profit margin of the assessee. In fact the profit margin of those companies was also less than the margin which had been estimated by the Assessing Officer in the case of assessee. In the case of assessee as per audited books of account, the net profit margin for assessment years 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10 and 2010-11 was 1.94 per cent, 0.67 per cent, 0.20 per cent and 0.09 per cent respectively. Now, the assessee argued that the Assessing Officer had failed to appreciate that the profit margins of contractors and sub-contractors could not be same. In the assessment order he had worked out the average profit margins in the case of those three companies at 5.93 per cent, 6.15 per cent and 5.19 per cent respectively and in the case of assessee he had estimated the profit at the rate of 8 per cent, whereas, in the case of assessee the profit margin would be much less than in these companies being a sub-contractor of these companies. [Para 5]

In view of the above factual position and comparative figures given by assessee of its principal, wherein the net profit was ranging from 5.19 per cent to 6.15 per cent, it was held that definitely there would be lower profit in the case of sub-contractor, i.e., the assessee and, hence, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly estimated the net profit rate at 4 per cent. Accordingly, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) and this issue of revenue's appeal was dismissed. [Para 6]

A fair estimate of the income has to be made. Further, the Jurisdictional High Court held that Guesswork is inevitable; but, it cannot be wild guess; the guesswork should have a reasonable nexus to the available material and the circumstances of each case. [Para 10.3]

■ Now coming to the present facts of the case, it is found that the assessee is a civil contractor and the entire contract receipts were from government departments/PWD as can be verified from form 26AS and all the proceeds were received through proper banking channels on which the tax had been deducted at source. On perusal of the assessment order, we also noticed that in absence of any details/evidences filed by the assessee, the AO estimated the income @ 15% by holding that once the profit is determined on estimated basis, the assessee is not entitled to any further deduction as per provisions of section 30 to 43D and by holding that when the net profit rate to gross receipts is determined on estimation basis, no further deduction is to be allowed. The AO while applying the net profit @15% was guided by the provisions of section 44AD only & held that once the profit is determined on estimated basis, the assessee is not entitled to any further deduction as per provisions of section 30 to 43D as contained in section 44AD. It is the considered opinion that the AO estimated the profit of the assessee @15% without reference to any material gathered. The AO should not make his best judgment assessment on mere suspicion, impulsively or arbitrarily. The best judgment assessment must be based on the material on record which could be gathered by the AO on proper investigation. In the present case, the assessee's entire contractual receipts were from Government department & all proceeds were received through banking channel & thus the assessee's estimation of the net profit @ 6.06% of the turnover is higher than the rate of 6% prescribed u/s 44AD. It is viewed that flat 15% income on turnover is highly unjustified. However, it is the considered opinion that net profit rate of 7% in civil contract business especially when all the contract receipts were received through proper banking channel on which the tax has been deducted at source is a reasonable one and accordingly the AO is directed to recompute the net profit of the assessee @7% of the total turnover declared by the assessee i.e. Rs.17.40 crores. Accordingly, this ground of Appeal of the assessee is partly allowed. [Para 10.4]

Income-tax provisions nowhere either authorize the Assessing Officer or cast an obligation on the assessee to prove the negative result, i.e., to prove as to why he had failed to make a profit at a particular rate. The accounts may be rejected as unreliable if important entries and transactions are omitted therefrom or if proper particulars and vouchers, bills, etc., are not forthcoming or if they do not include entries relating to particular class of business transaction. Reasons for rejecting wages record as commented by the Assessing Officer related to full address of the labour, which was not given on the muster roll register. The wages record had been kept by the assessee as per regulation known as 'Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970. The addresses of the labourers to whom wages had been paid were not mentioned, since the labourers stayed in the Jhugi Jhoperies at a work site itself and to that effect the assessee had already replied to the Assessing Officer vide its letter dated 23-3-2001, through which site of construction where labourers resided was given which was, however, not taken notice of by the Assessing Officer and the same was sent to him by courier and was found to be duly received by the Assessing Officer. The Assessing Officer had also alleged that the actual date of payment was not mentioned by the payee receiving the wages. The date on which the entry had been made in the wages register was the actual date of payment. As per the nature of the contract work executed by the assessee, he had got a contract to carry out a particular job or a contract for which the material was supplied by the CPWD/DOT and the labour was provided by the assessee-contractor. The assessee used to make payments to the labourers on the basis of mandays put in by the labourers and not on the basis of work performed by them on each day. Therefore, there was no merit in the allegations of the Assessing Officer that work performed by the labour was not mentioned on the payment vouchers and in making them as basis for rejection of books of account. The payment to the assessee-contractor was also made on the basis of work completed which was measured by the department itself and not on the basis of what the labourer had done. The bills for such a contract were prepared, which were not verified by the engineers of contractee before making payments. On the basis of those bills which were finally approved by the Government engineers/contractee, the payment was given to the assessee-contractor after deducting TDS. Thus, it was humanly not possible to provide the details as to what work a particular labourer had done at the site. Further, the Assessing Officer had also not indicated any defect in the system of accounting regularly followed by the assessee, or its correctness, nor was there any change in the method of accounting during the year under consideration as compared to the earlier years to indicate any intention of the assessee to show low profit.

While examining the books of the assessee, the Assessing Officer has to consider the following aspects : (i) whether the assessee has regularly employed a method of accounting; (ii) even if regular adoption of a method of accounting is there, whether the annual profits can properly be deduced from the method employed; (iii ) whether the accounts have been correctly maintained; (iv) whether the accounts maintained are complete in the sense that there is no significant omission therein. If the answers to above four questions would be in the affirmative, then the assessee's profits would be computed on the basis of his accounts. In such cases, proviso to section 145(1) or section 145(2) cannot be invoked. On the perusal of the materials placed on record in the instant case, it was found that the answers to all the above four questions were in the affirmative. No finding had been recorded by either of the lower authorities as to the unacceptability of the method and to the irregularity of the accounts kept by the assessee. It is well-settled that in the absence of such a finding recorded by the authorities, the book results cannot be ignored or brushed aside.

Ltd. [2007] 294 ITR 451/ 162 Taxman 60 contended that the accounting standards prescribed by ICAI were required to be followed by the assessee. The revenue further referred to the decision of the Supreme Court in P.M. Mohammed Meerakhan v. CIT [1969] 73 ITR 735 to contend that income-tax authorities have power to estimate profits by treating unsold stock in trade and value it according to normal accountancy practice. HELD: The main case of the revenue was that the assessee should have disclosed profits on the receipts of contract on the basis of percentage completion method of accounting. As against that it was the case of the assessee that the initial price for which the contract was awarded was later on found to be unreliable as it was increased to 29 per cent, therefore, the percentage completion method was not applicable even according to the accounting standard AS-7.The assessee had never shown any profit out of the contract and the loss shown by the assessee was accepted by the lower authorities in the immediately preceding year and succeeding year. Thus, according to the accounts, the assessee had never earned profit from this contract. The accounts of the assessee were audited and it was not the case of the revenue that the assessee did not furnish details regarding accounts maintained by it. No defects whatsoever had been found in the account books maintained by the assessee. What can be assessed as income under the Act, is income. If there is an existence of income, then only it can be estimated. Therefore, not going into the controversy whether the accounting standard AS-7 was properly employed by the assessee or not, it would be considered that whether Assessing Officer was justified in assessing the net profit of the assessee from such contract at the rate of 10 per cent. There was no substance in the argument of the revenue that the assessee was under an obligation to maintain its account on the basis of the accounting standard AS-7, as the said accounting standard was not mandatory for the assessee for the year under consideration. Even if the percentage of completion method was held to be applicable to the case of the assessee, then the question would arise that what would be the basis for estimate. It is well-established law that the estimate made must be honest and fair. There must exist reasonable nexus between the available material and the estimate. Thus, the only question for determination arose whether there existed some material on the basis of which it could be said that application of net profit rate of 10 per cent was appropriate. It was the contention of the assessee that it had incurred losses while performing the contract. No material had been brought on record by the Assessing Officer that such contention of the assessee was contrary to the facts. Addition had been made without indicating any material or basis on which it could be decided that application of net profit rate of 10 per cent was appropriate. On the contrary, material was on the record to show that the assessee had incurred loss in performing such a contract. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was not justified in rejecting the books of account by invoking the provisions of section 145(3) without bringing on record any cogent reasons and infirmities in the maintenance of books of account of the assessee and further estimating the net profit. [Para 13]

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had decided the issue correctly.

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with Sections 29 and 32, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Profit rate) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether profit of a contractor would necessarily depend upon various factors like place of execution of contract, accessibility of labour, raw material, etc. and would, therefore, vary from contractor to contractor - Held, yes - Whether gross receipts to which net profit rate is to be applied shall be determined after giving allowance on account of depreciation - Held, yes - Assessee-firm, engaged in business of execution of government contract, executed works of laying optical fibre cables in a remote border area of Jammu and Kashmir - Assessing Officer made addition to income applying net profit rate of 12 per cent on gross receipt - However, both Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal scaled down net profit to 8 per cent and also reduced depreciation out of gross receipt - Whether no question of law arose from order of Tribunal - Held, yes [Paras 3 and 7] [In favour of assessee]IT: Profit of contractor depend upon various factors like place of execution of contract, accessibility of labour, raw material, etc. and would, therefore, vary from contractor to contractor

FACT: The assessee-firm was engaged in business of execution of government contract. It filed return of income which came on scrutiny. During assessment proceeding, while examining books of account, some discrepancies were found that expenditure claimed by assessee was very much on the higher side as the work executed by it. Consequently, the assessee was asked to produce proof of expenditure, incurred on wages and labour, wages register and also to correlate wages paid with the project executed.

Thereupon, the Assessing Officer, thus, applied 12 per cent rate on gross receipt after excluding cost of material supplied by the department and made addition accordingly.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reduced the net profit rate to 8 per cent as against 12 per cent on the contract receipt and allow depreciation and salary paid to partners as claimed.

On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On appeal:

HELD: There is no reason to interfere with the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals), affirmed by the Tribunal, scaling down the net profit to 8 per cent against 12 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer. The reasons assigned by the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal are clear and cogent and even otherwise no two contractors can have a similar rate of profit. The profit of a contractor would necessarily depend upon various factors like place of execution of the contract, the accessibility of labour, raw material etc. and would, therefore, vary from contractor to contractor. The assessee in the instant case, was admittedly laying optical fiber cables etc. in a remote border area of Jammu and Kashmir. [Para 3]

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income (In case of estimation of profit) - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessee was a contractor and assessee declared its income at an estimated 3 per cent of contract receipts - Search took place in assessee's premises and in view of seized materials Assessing Officer gave due opportunity to assessee to justify disclosed income and explain discrepancies noticed by special auditor - Assessee was also permitted to inspect seized documents - Despite that assessee could not explain said discrepancies - Accordingly Assessing Officer resorted to estimation of profits by adopting 11 per cent on gross contract receipts and initiated penalty proceedings - Whether there was gross or wilful negligence on part of assessee in failing to return correct income, penalty would be levied under section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of revenue]IT: Where assessee could not explain discrepancies noticed by special auditor and disclosed a lesser income than what it actually earned, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was to be levied

FACT: The assessee, a contractor undertaking projects of Indian Railways on turnkey basis, filed its return of income.

On the basis of the materials gathered by the income-tax authorities in the course of a search carried out in the assessee's premises as well as in the premises of the directors and trusted persons, the Assessing Officer referred the matter to a special audit in terms of section 142(2A). The special audit report, inter alia, reported that there were large number of transactions in which several discrepancies were noticed.

In response to the queries raised by the Assessing Officer on the basis of the special audit report the assessee could not give any proper explanation and wherever an explanation was sought to be given, it was found to be evasive. The assessee was also allowed inspection of the seized documents and was supplied photocopies of the seized records. Despite such opportunity, no convincing reason was given by the assessee.

The Assessing Officer proceeded to estimate the net profit of the assessee at 11 per cent of the gross receipts from the contracts. The Assessing Officer also found that some income from business activities was not included in the aforesaid receipts and the profit from such activity was taken at Rs.13.34 lakhs. Demands were accordingly raised.

Penalty proceedings were initiated by the Assessing Officer for concealment of income and after rejecting the assessee's explanation, a penalty was imposed for concealment of income under section 271(1)(c).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelled the penalty order on the ground that the Assessing Officer has not stated the basis of this estimate nor did he give an opportunity to the assessee to rebut the proposal to estimate the profits at 11 per cent of the gross receipts. He held that the assessee made a counter proposal which was a conditional offer as to the taxability of the profits and even if it is assumed that there was an agreement on the part of the assessee for being taxed at the rate of 11 per cent of the gross receipts, it does not follow automatically that the assessee concealed its income.

On second appeal by Revenue, the Tribunal dismissed it.

[Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts - Assessment years 1993-94 to 1997-98 - Assessee-firm was engaged in work of civil construction in Public Works Department (PWD) - Assessing Officer, after rejecting books of account, made assessment determining 8 per cent profit at flat rate - Commissioner (Appeals) reduced rate of profit from 8 per cent to 5 per cent on ground that since turnover of assessee exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs, it was bound to incur more expenses and rate of profit would be less - Further, Tribunal reduced profit rate to 4 per cent on ground that assessee was doing work for PWD and normally, profit rate was much less for work of PWD, as contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under supervision of PWD authorities - Whether rate of profit cannot be assumed, merely on assumptions or surmises and conjectures - Held, yes - Whether since Assessing Officer as well as Commissioner (Appeals) as also Tribunal had not recorded any finding based on any material and findings recorded were merely based on surmises and conjectures, findings of rate of profit could not be sustained and 
 matter deserved to be remanded to assessing authority for re-determination thereof - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm which was engaged in the work of civil construction in public works department, filed returns for the assessment years 1993-94 to 1997-98. The Assessing Officer on the analogy of section 44AD, after rejecting the books of account, made best judgment assessment determining 8 per cent profit at flat rate. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reduced the rate of profit from 8 per cent to 5 per cent, mainly on the ground that since the turnover of the assessee exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs, it was bound to incur more expenses and rate of profit would be less. On further appeal, the Tribunal reduced the rate of profit to 4 per cent on the ground that the assessee was doing the work for PWD and normally the net profit rate was much less for the work of PWD, as the contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under the supervision of the PWD authorities.

On appeal :

HELD: A bare perusal of the findings recorded by the Assessing Officer would indicate that he had applied the principles determining the profit vide section 44AD, whereas the aforesaid provision was not at all applicable in the case of assessee in the relevant assessment years. This factual position was not being disputed by either of the parties. That being so, the question arose as to what should be the profit rate for the purpose of determining the profit accrued or gained by the parties. Since the Assessing Officer, had not dealt with this question independent of section 44AD, the rate of profit could not be upheld. [Para 3]

So far as the determination of profit of 5 per cent by the Commissioner (Appeals) was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) had also not given any reason nor any material was placed before the Commissioner (Appeals), or for that matter before the Assessing Officer for arriving at a conclusion about the rate of profit. Merely on assumption that since the assessee was performing the work for the PWD and as the contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under supervision of the PWD authorities, the rate of profit would be low or merely because the turnover exceeded Rs. 10 lakhs, it would incur more expenses, the aforesaid rate of profits could not have been arrived at. Neither the Commissioner (Appeals) nor the Tribunal had taken into consideration the relevant material or facts which might be necessary for arriving at such a conclusion. [Para 4]

The rate of profit cannot be assumed merely on assumptions or surmises and conjectures. It is the first liability of the assessee to produce such records, evidence and material so as to substantiate his plea about the rate of profit that he claims and in case the books of account have been rejected , the onus shifts on to the Assessing Officer to determine the rate of profit on consideration of the material which may be brought before him or even on making such inquiry, which may be necessary and which may include the requirement of having any information from the assessee also during the course of determination of such rate of profit, namely, during the assessment proceedings. In no case, simply because the turnover was more than Rs. 40 lakhs or the assessee was performing civil construction work for Public Works Department, neither the rate of profits could be determined nor it could be taken to be less nor it could be reduced nor could be arrived at any presumptions. [Para 5]

It is thus, substance of the contract which matters and if, the agreement between the parties right from the beginning is that certain materials are to be supplied by the other party to the contract, that is, the Government department, or the authority concerned, then it is obvious that the contract was entered into on the footing that no profit would be made by the building contractor in respect of the supply of those materials. In the instant case, the contract between the parties, namely, the assessee and the railway authorities, was that cement and iron had to be supplied by the railway authorities for the execution of the work and no accounting of the cost of these materials was to be done while making out a bill in respect of the contract payment. Under these circumstances it must be held that since this particular contract falls in the first category where at the time of entering into the contract the quotation did not take into account the materials like iron and cement which were to be supplied by the railway authorities, all calculations at the time of entering into the contract were made on the footing that iron and cement were to be supplied by the railway authorities and it was obvious that these items could not be included in the total receipts of the assessee for the purpose of arriving at the figure of net profits by working out the percentages of that total figure.

The Tribunal fixed the figure of 10 per cent of the total receipts only in view of the fact that the cost of the materials supplied by the railway authorities was to be taken into consideration at the time of fixing the receipts. In the instant case, the ITO arrived at the figure on the basis of the receipts extending over three accounting year. He took the sum total of these receipts to be the base for the net income that had accrued to the assessee during the accounting year 1943-44 as the entire contract work had been completed during that year. Mere execution of the contract work will not necessarily entitle the contractor to make a demand for payment until it is ascertained that the works are up to the standard agreed upon between the parties. Some parts of such work may be wholly rejected and like bad debts in every earning may be ignored in computing the gains or profits. It might have been open to the ITO, in exercise of his discretion, to make an enquiry into whether and when the bills for payment became due to the assessee. Much depended upon the terms in the contract, and the manner of its performance. Even as a basis of guess work, which the Income-tax Officer was entitled to do, the basis could not be said to be in consonance with honest guess work. The ITO did not seem to have taken into consideration why the payments which, according to him, were due to the assessee in the accounting year were not fully paid till three years after. Sometimes the payments to the contractors are withheld on account of unsatisfactory execution and they are held entitled to payments only if and when they replace the rejected work by acceptable and accepted ones. The bare possibility of such contingency could not be wholly eliminated in the instant case. If the ITO, in arriving at the figure for assessment, left out these considerations, he certainly could not be said to have exercised his judgment which he was none the less called upon to do in making the assessment in cases of assessee's default under sections 23(4) and 13 proviso of the 1922 Act. Any method of accounting adopted by the ITO acting under the proviso of section 13 of 1922 Act can be rejected if the method in fact does not show the true income, profits and gains. In this view of the matter, the Appellate Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipt basis with regard to contracts carried out and completed during the year of accounting, there being every presumption that the incomes were paid as soon as they became due. At any rate, the Tribunal's decision might be upheld on the ground that when two methods of guess work are available for the purpose of assessment, the one which is more just to the assessee and which involves a much less margin of chance of uncertainty should be taken as the basis.

In the result, the Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipts basis with regard to contracts carried on and completed during the year of account.

As regards the reduction of flat rate, the Appellate Tribunal had arrived at the lesser flat rate on the basis of their decisions in similar cases in the district. Their opinions were not receivable evidence in the instant case. The decisions in different cases must have been based upon different facts and different inferences deducible from such facts. In this connection, it might be observed that the ITO had been very fair to the assessee bearing in mind the difference between the gross value and net value of the bills. The Appellate Tribunal, therefore, did commit a mistake of law in arriving at a finding for which there was no relevant evidence to support.

Therefore, the reduction of the estimated profit rate from 40 per cent adopted by the ITO to 30 per cent by the Tribunal on the ground that 30 per cent was the general rate adopted by it in the cases of other assessees doing the same kind of contract works during the same assessment year was not legal.

On reference : HELD: Contracts for building construction or of similar type can be divided into two broad categories. Category No. (1) will cover contracts where, at the time of entering into the contract, the contractor is told that some of the materials required for construction work will be supplied by the person or authority who entrusts the construction work to him and it is on that footing of such construction materials being supplied by the authorities or the other party to the contract, that the contractor enters into the contract for the construction quoting a particular figure for the entire contract. A sub-category of this first category of contract is the type of contract where, for notional purposes, a total figure is mentioned for the construction contract inclusive of materials and on the footing that the contractor is to supply all the materials for the construction work. However, at the time when the contract is entered into, it is clearly agreed between the contracting parties that some of the building materials will be supplied by the other party to the contract, that is, the person or authority entrusting the construction work to the contractor, and that credit will have to be given by the contractor for the materials, thus, received and the rates at which the credit is to be given is also agreed upon between the contractor and the other party to the contract. It was designated as a sub-category of category No. (1) because though notionally and on the face of it the contract has been entered into for a much larger amount and on the footing that the contractor is to supply all the materials, because of the clear agreement between the parties about the materials to be supplied by the other party to the contract and also about rates at which those materials are to be supplied, it is clear that in fact and in substance the parties have entered into the contract where certain specified materials are to be supplied not by the contractor but by the other party to the contract and the contractor right from the beginning enters into the contract on this footing and puts forward his quotation and ultimately gets the contract for the amount where he does not take into consideration supply of those particular materials or rates for those materials. Category No. (2) of contracts is the type where, right from the beginning, the contractor enters into the construction contract on the footing that he has to supply all the materials but while the contract is being executed, the other party to the contract supplies some of the materials and when the bill is finally paid, the other party to the contract claims credit for the price of the materials supplied to the building contractor. In that eventuality, it is really the total figure of the original contract or figure worked out in accordance with the terms of the original contract which will constitute the original receipts of the building contractor and the fact that, instead of going into the market and purchasing the materials for himself, the contractor gets these materials for himself, the party to the contract, does not enter into the picture so far as this aspect of the case is concerned. The question as to under which particular category, category No. (1) or category No. (2) set out above, a particular contract falls, will have to be decided looking to the substance of the transaction between the parties in each individual case. If the case falls under the first category, then it is obvious that the cost of the materials supplied by the other party to the contract cannot be taken into consideration in arriving at the figure of the total receipts of the contractor in respect of the particular contract for building construction. On the other hand, if the case falls, on the facts and circumstances of the particular case, in the second category, then the total receipts of the building contractor in respect of that particular contract will be the total amount of the contract notwithstanding the fact that the other party to the contract has supplied some of the materials required for building construction work.

It is, therefore, clear that in matters of this kind, when deciding whether a particular amount should or should not be considered to be trading receipt, it is the true nature and quality of the receipt, either actual or deemed, which has to be considered and not the outward form or the head under which the amount is entered in the account books of the assessee concerned.

It is thus, substance of the contract which matters and if, the agreement between the parties right from the beginning is that certain materials are to be supplied by the other party to the contract, that is, the Government department, or the authority concerned, then it is obvious that the contract was entered into on the footing that no profit would be made by the building contractor in respect of the supply of those materials.

On appeal :

HELD: Section 44AD clarifies that if the assessee's gross receipts are more than Rs. 1 crore and if the assessee did not maintain the books of account, then his profit has to be estimated at the rate of 8 per cent and depreciation should not be allowed. In the instant case, the assessee did not produce the books of account and also did not appear before the Assessing Officer, therefore the Assessing Officer was not able to verify the claim made in profit and loss account. As per section 144, if the assessee fails to comply with the terms of a notice issued under sub-section (1) of section 142 and if the assessee fails to provide the necessary information, the Assessing Officer had liberty to pass the order on the best judgment assessment. Secondly, if the assessee produced the books of account where the Assessing Officer is not satisfied about the correctness or completeness of the accounts of the assessee, or where the method of accounting provide standards as notified under sub-section (2), have not been regularly followed by the assessee, the Assessing Officer may make the assessment in the manner provide in section 145. On writ:

HELD: It is now well settled that while making a best judgment assessment, though there must necessarily be guess-work in the matter, it must not be arbitrary. In the instant case, the basis on which the computation was made was not disclosed in the order.

Having said, one has to examine, on facts and circumstances of the case whether the Assessing Officer was right in adopting net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts. There is no dispute with regard to the facts that the assessee is in the business of execution of works contracts. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee had disclosed 6.73 per cent to 7.44 per cent net profit, in the earlier period. For the assessment year 2007-08 in the scrutiny assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer has estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts for which the assessee has not preferred any appeal. Estimation of net profit from the business is one of the accepted method of determination of income from business. But, there is no hard and fast rule for estimation of income.

The department is following estimation of net profit on various rates depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. But, while estimating net profit from the business, there should be a basis for adopting a particular rate of net profit, either based on comparable cases of similar nature of business or assessee's own book results for earlier years. When there is no possibility of getting a comparable cases, and there is no possibility of reference to assessee's own book results for earlier periods, a reference to the provisions of section 44AD can be made, wherein the Act provides for estimation of net profit from the specified businesses subject to certain conditions. [Para 9]

The provisions of section 44AD provide for estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on gross receipts, in case where the assessees are involved in specified businesses and turnover from the business does not exceed specified limit. Although, the assessee's case does not fall within the ambit of the provisions of section 44AD of the Act, as its contract receipts exceed the specified limit, the analogy provided in the provisions of section 44AD can be adopted for estimation of net profit because of nature of business carried out by the assessee. The nature of business carried on by the assessee was squarely fit into the specified businesses referred to in the provisions of section 44AD of the Act. The presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD, reflects the legislative approved rate of net profit, which can be considered as fair and reasonable to estimate income from civil contract business, where the books of account are not found reliable by the Assessing Officer.

In this case, admittedly, the Assessing Officer had rejected books of account for the reason that the assessee has failed to produce supporting bills and vouchers in respect of expenditure. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee himself has admitted about 8 per cent net profit in the earlier period net of all deductions including depreciation. Therefore, considering the overall facts and circumstances of the case, the rate of net profit adopted by the Assessing Officer appears to be fair and reasonable. Hence, estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on total receipts net of all deductions including depreciation is upheld. [Para 10]

In so far as separate deductions towards depreciation is concerned, the assessee submitted that when estimation of net profit is made, separate deductions towards depreciation should be allowed, as depreciation is a notional deduction for normal wear and tear of the assets.

In this case, the assessee is involved in the business of execution of main works which carries more profit than sub-contract works and hence, the Assessing Officer has rightly adopted reasonable net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts and accordingly, further deductions towards depreciation is not allowed. Whether separate deductions can be allowed towards depreciation or not is a fact which is to be decided based on the facts and circumstances of each case and also based on the rate of net profit adopted for estimation of profit.

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with  section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounts - Estimation of income (Rate of profit) - Block period 2008 to 2010-11 - Assessee-company was a sub-contractor - In course of assessment proceedings assessee produced audited books of account, bills relevant vouchers, etc. - Assessing Officer observed that labour register had not been maintained in conventional manner - He rejected books of account and estimated net profit at 8 per cent of gross contract receipt - Whether it was not correct to compare profit of principal contractors with profit margin of sub-contractor - Held, yes - Whether since net profit rate of principal contractors was ranging from 5.19 per cent to 6.15 per cent, there would be lower profit in case of assessee sub-contractor and, therefore, Commissioner (Appeals) rightly estimated net profit rate at 4 per cent - Held, yes [Paras 5 and 6] [In favour of assessee]IT: On rejection of books of account under section 145, profit margin of assessee, a sub-contractor, is to be estimated at rate much less than average profit margin worked out by Assessing Officer of its principal (i.e., contractor)

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of executing work contracts of civil construction, supply of labour and trading in shares.

In response to a notice under section 153C, the assessee filed its return of income declaring certain income. The assessee also produced books of account, vouchers, invoices, bank statements, bank reconciliation and explained the credit entries.

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee failed to produce all the relevant vouchers, bills, invoices in support of the expenses. He further noted from the Labour Registers that it did not contain signature/thumb impression of all the recipients of the payment. He, therefore, rejected the books of account and estimated the net profit at 8 per cent of gross contract receipt and estimated net profit.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) after considering submissions of assessee, restricted the net profit rate at the rate of 4 per cent of the gross contractual receipts.

On further appeal by the revenue:

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits Assessment year 1964-65 - Assessee was a military contractor - Finding some irregularities in accounts, ITO assessed profits of assessee from military contracts by applying flat rate of 10 per cent on total receipts - Tribunal held that price of stores supplied by Government was to be excluded while applying flat rate to assessee's contract receipts - Whether order passed by Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a military contractor. During the relevant accounting period, the assessee took three military engineering service contracts. The ITO found that the expenditure of the assessee was not supported by vouchers and he detected some other mistakes also in the accounts. After applying the provisions of section 145(1), the ITO assessed the profit from these contracts by applying a flat rate of 10 per cent on the total receipts. The AAC allowed the appeal of the assessee and held that no rate of profit could be applied on the value of the stores supplied by the Government and this order was upheld by the Tribunal.

On reference, the Division Bench noticed the divergent views taken by the various High Courts and particularly because of the challenge laid to the correctness of the judgment in Brij Bhushan Lal v. CIT [1971] 81 ITR 497 (Punj.) and, thus, referred the matter for decision of the Full Bench.

HELD: The Supreme Court in Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524 (SC) reversed the said judgment of the High Court (supra) and held that the assessment was to be made excluding the cost of material and stores received for being used in the works undertaken by the contractor. Following, the aforesaid decision, it was to be held in the instant case that the Tribunal was justified in holding that price of stores supplied by Government was not to be included while applying the flat rate to the assessee's contract receipts.

Note : The decision was in favour of assessee.

The Assessing Officer further pointed out that there might be standard specification but it was difficult to arrive at a definite conclusion in the absence of specific formula for construction of roads of various thickness and it was further observed that in the absence of details, general statement would not support any measurement and it was not possible to arrive at the exact consumption of raw material. He therefore, made certain additions to income of the assessee on that account. As regards the payments made to the labourers, the assessee had submitted samples and muster rolls before the Assessing Officer. They were examined by the handwriting expert, which indicated that the thumbs’ impressions were not of different parties and the Assessing Officer observed that it could be easily deduced that the labour payments were excessive and inflated and, accordingly, made certain disallowance. However, the Assessing Officer allowed depreciation to the assessee as per profit and loss account. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee had not maintained verifiable accounts and as such, net profit rate should be applied. The consumption of the raw material claimed was within the parameters laid down by the laboratories for particular type of road construction. He also held that the Assessing Officer had not made out a fool-proof case for addition on account of bogus purchases and the road constructed by the assessee during the year was found up to the specification by the principals while making payment to the contractor and it could not be held that the assessee had not utilized grit and had not paid the wages for construction of roads. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) applied net profit rate of 10 per cent on the receipts as against 8 per cent applied in the immediately preceding year, keeping in view the discrepancy pointed out in the maintenance of the books of account. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) granted the depreciation after applying net profit rate as allowed by the Assessing Officer also.

On further appeal :

HELD: In the instant case, it was not disputed that during the year under consideration, the assessee had shown receipts from the business of construction of roads on different contracts. The Assessing Officer had also specifically mentioned that fact in the assessment order. The Assessing Officer had also mentioned in the assessment order that the books of account were examined by him. The assessee had also filed audit report under section 44AB. As regards the purchases, out of 17 parties, nine were rejected by the Assessing Officer along with the wages. The Assessing Officer had given reason that some parties were not produced. The parties were not having certificates. The payments though made by cheque, were obtained by other persons and the report of handwriting expert was not in dispute. Those reasons prompted the Assessing Officer to make addition on purchases of dalla grit. On the same reasons of handwriting expert’s report, wages were disallowed. However, it was noted that the Assessing Officer did not reject the books of account of the assessee. The Assessing Officer had also not pointed any mistake in the audit report. The Assessing Officer had merely observed that the transactions with the purchasing parties were not genuine as the onus cast on the assessee had not been discharged for the purposes of proving their genuineness. The Assessing Officer had not held that the purchases were bogus. The assessee had filed copy of the written submissions filed before the Commissioner (Appeals) stating therein that whosoever parties were available were produced before the Assessing Officer, but the Assessing Officer kept on insisting for personal production of the parties, which was neither required nor desirable. The assessee had given explanation that some of the parties were produced in person and for remaining, confirmatory letters and affidavits were filed and payments were made by cheque. It was also explained that the suppliers came to the site on truck loads, got the goods measured, negotiated the rates and then the challan/bills were given to the staff at the site for being filled. It was also explained that some of the parties were illiterate, semi-literate and therefore, took the assistance of the assessee in preparing the bills. It was also explained that the averment for the consumption of the grit was not clear from the formula on record which was also ill-quoted, as an average 1.35 times of grit is required for making a compact road, irrespective of the thickness. As far as the disallowance of labour payment was concerned, it was explained that the labourers were employed from the rural and backward areas at less rate simply to reduce the cost. The labourers were headed by the labourer called ‘Maith’ through whom the payments of the wages were made. The assessee pleaded before the Commissioner (Appeals) that the net profit rate should be fixed looking to the various conditions like past record, expenditure and underquoting of contract price, normal rates in comparable cases, etc. [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: Section 145(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment year 1991-92 - Assessee, carrying on construction business, declared net profit of 5 per cent on gross receipts - Assessing Officer applied rate of 7 per cent - Commissioner (Appeals) applied 10 per cent rate relying on a case purported to be comparable and by generalising that normal rate of profit in construction business was 10 per cent - In the preceding years rate of 6 per cent was applied in assessee’s own case - Whether history of assessee’s case itself was a guide in applying rate of profit and, therefore, Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in enhancing rate - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a registered firm carrying on construction business. It declared net profit of 5 per cent on gross receipts. The Assessing Officer applied the rate of 7 per cent subject to allowance of depreciation and interest on the basis of past history of assessee as well as the defective position of accounts. The Commissioner (Appeals) viewed that the normal rate of profit in construction business was 10 per cent and he, accordingly, applied 10 per cent rate relying on a case, purported to be a comparable case.

On second appeal :

HELD: There was no reason for the Commissioner (Appeals) to enhance the rate of profit to 10 per cent. The books of assessee, though defective, were not such which could not enable the assessing authorities to determine a fair rate of profit. Moreover, the assessee-firm itself also had its own history which could be a guide. Therefore, there was no reason for the Commissioner (Appeals) to rely on any other case and also to determine the rate by generalising that the normal rate of profit in construction business was 10 per cent.

Keeping the past history of assessee in view, it would be fair and meet the ends of justice if a net profit rate of 6 per cent, subject to depreciation and interest, was applied.

N.M. Ranka and J.K. Ranka for the Appellant. G.C. Bansal for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 254, read with section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 33(4), read with section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Appellate Tribunal - Order of - Assessment years 1943-44 to 1945-46 - Assessee-firm carried on business of aerodrome work, katcha building constructions etc. - On firm's failure to produce books of account for relevant assessment years, ITO took sum total of receipts of assessee for three accounting years and, thereupon adopted profit rate of 40 per cent in exercise of his power under section 13, read with section 23(4) of 1922 Act - Tribunal, however, opined that ITO should have applied rate of profit to annual receipts instead of total receipts and that by amalgamating receipts under one assessment ITO raised tax liability of assessee which was not fair - Besides, Tribunal also reduced profit rate from 40 per cent to 30 per cent - Whether Tribunal was right in asking ITO to assess assessee on receipt basis with regard to contracts carried out and completed during year of accounting, there being every presumption that incomes were paid as soon as they became due - Held, yes - Whether, however, as regards reduction of flat rate of profit, Tribunal did commit a mistake of law in arriving at said finding for which there was no relevant evidence to support - Held, yes

FACT: Two persons 'S' and B constituted an unregistered firm sharing the profits and losses in the proportion of 9-as and 7-as respectively. The business, of which the profits and gains were the subject of assessment, consisted of aerodrome work under the Central Public Works Department, certain katcha building constructions under the Military Engineering Service and small supply of potatoes to Garrison Engineer. During the accounting year 1942-43, the assessee received a sum of Rs. 2,92,256. During the next year, that is 1-4-1943 to 31-3-1944, they received a sum of Rs. 86,434 and during the following accounting year of 1-4-1944 to 31-3-1945, they received a sum of Rs. 25,703. Besides it appeared, there were certain estimated outstanding bills to the credit of the assessee which had been excluded from assessment. On firm's failure to produce, books of account, the ITO took the sum total of the above sums received in course of three years, that is Rs. 4,54,948, as the basis of his assessment. He deducted the income at Rs. 1,18,975, on the ratio of 40 per cent, a flat rate on the gross receipts. Deducting the excess profits tax of Rs. 1,13,317 the assessable income was set at Rs. 65,659 which was reduced by the AAC by a sum of Rs. 28,270 by way of rectification of an error in calculation of Rs. 24,270 and deducting the profits of Rs. 4,000 representing 40 per cent of the estimated outstanding bills. The AAC, on appeal, came to the conclusion that since it was a question of determination of that year's income, in the absence of account books and since this was the first assessment in the case, the proviso to section 13 came into operation and no question of cash basis could arise.

The Tribunal, however, thought that in the circumstances of the case, the ITO should have applied the rate of profit to the annual receipts instead of to the total receipts and that by amalgamating the receipts under one assessment the ITO raised the tax liability of the assessee which was not fair. The Tribunal, therefore, set aside the basis of the said assessment and remanded the case back to the ITO to assess the income on the basis of the receipts during each year.

On the question of the flat rate, the Tribunal reduced the estimate of 40 per cent to 30 per cent.

On reference :

HELD: The Tribunal's power of dealing with an order passed by an AAC is plenary and has been expressed as widely as can be conceived. According to the section, every order of assessment passed by an AAC either under section 28 or section 31 of 1922 Act, is appealable to the Tribunal. The latter can substitute its own order of assessment for the one passed by the appellate income-tax authority. This very widely expressed power, however, shall not be immune from such limitation to which ordinarily an appellate authority or tribunal is subject in the disposal of its duty.

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1964-65 and 1965-66 - Assessee manufactured sweets and other eatables and also sold confectionery articles which he purchased on wholesale from another merchant-Tribunal rejecting assessee’s books of account acting under section 145 and, on basis of data available, adopted flat rate for calculating profit - Whether, question relating to flat rate was pure question of fact and thus, no question of law arose from Tribunal’s order - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was carrying on business of manufacturing sweets and another eastables and selling confectionery articles which he purchased on wholesale from another merchant. He submitted his return for the year 1965-66, showing gross turnover in the sum of Rs. 2,34,576. According to the assessee the gross profit rate of the confectionery manufactured by him was 17.5 per cent and for the one that was purchased by him it was 8.5 per cent, yielding an average profit of 11.2 per cent. The ITO, not finding the books of account entirely, reliable estimated the turnover at Rs. 2,50,000 and calculated the average rate of profit at 17.5 per cent and taxed the assessee accordingly. The AAC reduced the gross turnover to Rs. 2,44,000 and reduced the average rate to 15 per cent profit. The Tribunal for the purposes of calculation firstly, reduced the total gross turnover to Rs. 2,40,000 and treating the portion relating to the confectionery manufactured by the assessee at Rs. 75,000, the profit rate assessed by the Tribunal was 20 per cent. Regarding the sale of the confectionery which was purchased by the assessee and sold by him, the turnover was taken at Rs. 1,65,000 and the rate applied to it was 10 per cent resulting in an average at 13.1 per cent. Similar rates of profit were applied by the Tribunal for the assessment year 1964-65. The Tribunal declined to make reference under section 256(1).

On application under section 256(2) :

HELD: Undisputably, the assessee placed before the taxation authorities its own account books and they were not found reliable and, therefore, the ITO, the AAC and the Tribunal had acted under the provisions of section 145(1) and the proviso thereto. The flat rate when it was calculated on the basic of available data, could not be called arbitrary or perverse. It had been said by the Tribunal that the firm, from whom the assessee bought manufactured confectionery and sold it made a profit of 19 per cent and the assessee made a profit of 10 per cent which had been charged by the Tribunal and against which there was no grievance. Therefore, at least up to 19 per cent there was clear evidence about the flat rate being just. If the Tribunal made it 20 per cent one could not say it capricious, conjectural or based on irrelevant or no evidence. A question relating to the flat rate was a pure question of fact. Although from the language of the questions which were asked to be referred to the High Court the grievance of enhancement was there yet it was not pressed. Therefore, it was not necessary to enter into the question whether the tax was enhanced because it was factually incorrect to say that the total liability of the assessee was increased. It was not necessary to enter into the argument whether the question arose from the order of the Tribunal or not because clearly no question of law arose in the instant case.

Note: The case was decided against the assessee.

The labourers were headed by the labourer called ‘Maith’ through whom the payments of the wages were made. The assessee pleaded before the Commissioner (Appeals) that the net profit rate should be fixed looking to the various conditions like past record, expenditure and underquoting of contract price, normal rates in comparable cases, etc. [Para 11] The report of research institute, in 1991, had given report of laboratory samples in respect of material data.
