HEADNOTE: III. Section  145  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 /  Section  276   of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Method of accounting  -  Rejection of accounts  (Net profit rate) - Assessment year  2010-11  - Assessee had filed no return of income - Assessing Officer on basis of information in his possession from Form No. 26AS of assessee that assessee had received contractual income of Rs. 4.37 crores from one, IGHPL, but, no return of income was filed by assessee, he rejected books of account of assessee and further estimated profits on said contractual receipts by applying rate of 12 per cent thereon - It was noted that no justification was given by Assessing Officer for rejecting assessee's rate of 8 per cent applied except a general dismissal of same stating that 12 per cent rate was justified - Whether therefore, Assessing Officer was not justified in applying net profit rate of 12 per cent on contractual receipts and same was to be set aside - Held, yes [Para 23] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company did not file its return for relevant assessment year.

■

Information in Form 26AS/ITS reflected contract receipts from IGHPL, on which tax had been deducted. Based on said information, Assessing Officer reopened assessment.

■

Further, the Assessing Officer observed that contractual income was not reflected in P&L account, though in response to notice under section 148, assessee offered income by estimating profit at 8 per cent.

■

The Assessing Officer rejected the books of accounts and estimated net profit at 12 per cent on the contract receipts, making addition over and above the 8% offered.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the application of 12 per cent net profit and the resultant addition.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

Coming to the aspect of the applicability of net profit rate for determining the profit earned from the contract receipts, while the assessee has applied rate of 8 per cent, the Assessing Officer has held a rate of 12 per cent to be justified. No justification has been given by the Assessing Officer for rejecting assessee’s rate of 8 per cent applied except a general dismissal of the same stating that 12 per cent rate is justified. In the light of the same, there is no reason to agree with the Assessing Officer that the net profit rate of 12 per cent on the contractual receipts was justified. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals), therefore, confirming the addition made to the income of the assessee on account of application of net profit made of 12 per cent to the contractual receipts is set aside and the application to 8 per cent rate to the contractual receipts, as claimed by the assessee, is held to be justified. The addition, therefore, made to the income of the assessee on account of application of net profit rate of 12 per cent to the extent of Rs. 17.51 lakhs is directed to be deleted. [Para 23]

1987-88, the assessee had filed its return of income declaring total income at Rs. 28,87,260. The assessment was completed by the Assessing Officer on a total income of Rs. 29,80,712. For the assessment year 1988-89, the assessee filed its return of income at Rs. 35,82,987 after taking into account the ‘on money’ of Rs. 40 lakhs offered to be assessed this year . It was found that the assessee had shown a profit of only 3 per cent on sale of flats and 3 per cent on work-contract taken. The Assessing Officer estimated the profits at 7.5 per cent after taking into consideration cases of other assessees engaged in construction business who had shown net profit from 7.5 per cent to 10 per cent. He, thus, added the difference of Rs. 5,09,600 to the income of the assessee over and above the profits as per the profit and loss account. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the view taken by the Assessing Officer for the assessment years 1986-87 and 1987-88. However, for the assessment years 1985-86 and 1988-89 he accepted that the assessments were to be completed on the basis of the project completion method.

HEADNOTE: Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits - Assessment year 1986-87 - Assessee was a labour contractor - Assessing Officer made certain additions as unexplained cash credits based on entries in cash book which were deleted on appeal - Whether since deposits as well as withdrawals of contract receipts were not properly reflected in books of account and as such, no reliance could be placed on bank accounts, order of Commissioner (Appeals) was valid in order - Held, yes - Whether considering that assessee was labour contractor, Commissioner (Appeals) was, however, not fair and reasonable to apply GP rate of 12.5 per cent against 10 per cent applied by Assessing Officer which was also agreed to by assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a labour contractor. For the assessment year 1986-87, the assessee agreed to the application of GP rate of 10 per cent. The Assessing Officer, however, noticed certain credits in the cash book which he filed to bank with bank withdrawals. The Assessing Officer ultimately concluded that Rs. 1,98,298 represented unexplained cash credits which he treated as income from undisclosed sources. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) holding that the books of account were not of any relevance, deleted the addition made by the Assessing Officer but applied the G.P. rate of 12.5 per cent. The revenue appealed against the deletion of addition of Rs. 1,98,298 and the assessee objected to the application of the rate of 12.5 per cent for calculating profits as against 10 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer.

On appeal:

HELD: As far the ground taken by the assessee in his cross objection regarding the application of the rate of 12.5 per cent by the Commissioner (Appeals) against the rate of 10 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer was concerned, looking to the fact that the assessee was a labour contractor, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not fair and reasonable to apply the GP rate of 12.5 per cent against the rate of 10 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer which was also agreed to by the assessee. Hence, it was fair and reasonable to apply a net rate of 10 per cent in the case of the assessee while calculating the profits.

As regards the addition of Rs. 1,98,295 made by the Assessing Officer by invoking the provisions of section 68, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) did not suffer from any illegality or infirmity regarding his conclusion that the deposits as well as withdrawals of contract receipts had not been properly reflected in the books of account and as such, no reliance could be placed on the bank account. Hence, the Commissioner (Appeals) was fully justified in deleting the addition of Rs. 1,98,298 made by the Assessing Officer.

Sudhir Sehgal for the Appellant. S.C. Pahwa for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: I. Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit (Net profit rate) - Assessment years 2012-13 to 2014-15 - Assessing Officer disallowed total expenses claimed in profit and loss account and sale consideration from immovable property and passed an ex parte order under section 144 - Commissioner (Appeals) based on his observation that purchase made by assessee in past were in dispute and genuineness of same had not been proved, computed net profit applying rate of 8 per cent on total revenue - However, it was found that net profit rate of 0.4 per cent had been accepted by this Tribunal in one of sister concern of assessee and even in scrutiny proceedings, revenue authorities in assessee's own case had estimated net profit below rate of 1 per cent - Whether therefore, looking to fact that there was no change of business during all these years, books of account were duly audited and no specific error had been pointed out by both lower authorities, estimating net profit at rate of 8 per cent could not be justified - Held, yes - Whether thus, application of net profit rate of 0.6 per cent on turnover of contract business during year would be proper - Held, yes [Paras 9.3 and 9.5] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where revenue authorities in assessee's own case in earlier year had estimated net profit below rate of 1 per cent, there being no change of business during relevant assessment years, estimating net profit at rate of 8 per cent could not be justified  INCOME TAX : Where business of earning commission from purchase and sale of land was being consistently carried out by assessee in previous year also and same was regularly entered in books of account and commission income earned from such transactions had been duly disclosed in financial statements and offered to tax, alleged amount of sale consideration of immovable property being just one of many transactions of sale of property executed by assessee on behalf of purchaser, could not be added to income of assessee  INCOME TAX : Where advances as appearing in audited financial statement were trade advances for execution of contract work which were transferred to sub-contractor and assessee was only conduit between work awarder and sub-contractor and transaction was made through banking channel, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in deleting addition made by Assessing Officer under section 68

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of construction of building bridges. It filed its return of income on 30-9-2012 declaring income of Rs. 35.09 lakhs. Notices under sections 143(2) and 142(1) were issued but there was no compliance. Since the Assessing Officer had not received necessary information pursuant to notices issued under sections 143(2) and 142(1), he disallowed the total expenses claimed in the profit and loss account and sale consideration from immovable property and passed an ex parte order under section 144.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) applied the net profit rate of eight per cent on the gross business turnover for the assessment year 2012-13 and set aside the finding of the Assessing Officer of denying the claim of total expenses incurred during the year.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: It is noted that the audited financial statements were available before the Assessing Officer but without disputing the sales turnover during the year he disallowed the total expenses including the purchase of material towards contract work undertaken by the assessee during the year. When the matter travelled before the Commissioner (Appeals) he observed in the impugned order that the net profit rate for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 disclosed by the assessee in its regular audited books of account is 0.22 per cent, 0.17 per cent and 0.25 per cent. Even during the course of scrutiny proceeding for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 net profit rate applied by the Assessing Officer was 0.16 per cent, 0.93 per cent and 0.18 per cent. Though the Commissioner (Appeals) appreciated the fact that undisputed revenue just could not have come without incurring an expenditure, but based on his observation that the purchase made by the assessee in the past were in dispute and genuineness of the same had not been proved, the Commissioner (Appeals) computed the net profit applying the rate of 8 per cent on the total revenue for the year of Rs. 87.46 crores.[Para 9]

The revenue has challenged the relief given by the Commissioner (Appeals) and the assessee is agitating for the higher net profit rate applied by the Commissioner (Appeals) and ignoring past net profit track of the assessee.[Para 9.1]

HEADNOTE: Section 28 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Assessee, carrying contract work under government departments, did not maintain proper account books - Whether net profit could be estimated at a flat rate on gross receipts including value of material supplied by government - Held, on facts, yes

FACT: The assessee, a firm of contractors, executed certain contracts given by the State Government during the assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74. For the assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74, the total gross receipts under the work contract respectively amounted to Rs. 19,41,472 and Rs. 22,86,353 out of which a sum of Rs. 1,27,215 and Rs. 4,82,527 was deducted, being the value of materials supplied by the Government. Since the assessee did not maintain proper account books or any stock book or material issue register, the ITO determined the net profit under the proviso to section 145(1) by applying a flat rate of 10 per cent on the aforesaid gross receipts without excluding the value of the materials supplied by the Government. The AAC, however, directed that for determining the net profit, flat rate was to be applied only on the net receipts. The Tribunal could not ascertain: (i) the actual position regarding the materials obtained from the department and; (ii) whether the same remained under the control of the department or of the assessee. It, accordingly, restored the ITO's order.

On reference:

HELD: 1. No hard and fast rule could be laid down as to whether the value of the materials should or should not be included in a contractor's gross turnover from business for determining his net profits. It depended upon the manner in which the materials were obtained and used in the execution of the contract. The contracts could be generally classified as (i) contract for labour supply; (ii) a lump sum contract; and (iii) where the material supplied by the department was either an outright sale or was specifically meant to be used in the work allotted. In the types of contracts mentioned in (i) and (iii), the profit had to be calculated on the gross receipts, including the value of the material supplied either by the Government or by the assessee. Whereas, in the case of the other items at (ii) and (iii), profit would be determined en the basis of only the net amount without taking into consideration the value of the materials. In the instant case, in the absence of any stock register or issue register, it was not known whether the materials were supplied by the department as an outright sale to the assessee or it remained under the control of the department throughout and that the same was never under the control of the contractor except for using it in the constitution.

2. The Tribunal was, accordingly, correct in holding that the profit was to be calculated on the gross receipts excluding the recoveries for the material supplied by the Government department.

Kashi Nath Jain, Rameshwar Prasad and A.B. Prasad for the Petitioner. B.P. Rajgarhia and S.K. Sharan for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c), read with section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 2003-04 - Whether ad hoc estimation of income by applying flat net profit ratio can be held either as concealment or as filing of inaccurate particulars of income for purpose of levying penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Held, no [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee was a contractor undertaking project of Indian Railways on turnkey basis. A search action under section 132 was carried out at the assessee's premises. As the assessee, at the relevant point of time, was not able to collect information about such contracts or produce relevant personnel, it proposed for fixing net profit rate at 11 per cent. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, applied net profit rate at the rate of 11 per cent on the total contract receipts on estimate basis which however, was reduced to 8 per cent by the Tribunal. A penalty under section 271(1)(c) was also levied upon the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the penalty on the ground that the estimation of income by applying flat net profit ratio did not tantamount to concealment or filing inaccurate particulars of income.

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: The issue of disparity between the assessed income and the returned income is not sustainable as the addition was purely on ad hoc estimation of net profit ratio. The Assessing Officer applied a particular flat rate of 11 per cent against the declared profit rate of 3 per cent by the assessee. The Tribunal has reduced the estimated income by adopting 8 per cent of profit rate which is also based on ad hoc estimation. Ultimately, the addition sustained or survived is ad hoc estimation of income by applying flat rate of 8 per cent of the profit which cannot be held either as concealment or filing inaccurate particulars. The Tribunal, in the quantum appeal, has also observed that suppression of the profit had not been established and the allegations have not been proved. On the basis of the explanation submitted by the assessee, the Tribunal has found no justification in applying and confirming the net profit rate of 11 per cent which has been reduced to 8 per cent on ad hoc basis subject to the allowability of depreciation and interest thereon. For levying penalty under section 271(1)(c), there has to be concealment of particulars of income by the assessee or the assessee must have furnished inaccurate particulars of income. Ultimately, in assessee's case, addition sustained was based on ad hoc estimation of income by applying a flat rate of 8 per cent of profit which can neither be held as concealment of income nor filing of inaccurate particulars of income. Further, the assessee's offering of the profit rate was a conditional proposal as the assessee was not able to collect the whole information about the context and produce the same. Thus, offer made by assessee was to buy peace and not to enter into dispute with revenue authorities. To purchase the peace and avoid any dispute with the revenue authorities in the quantum of income, assessee offered the estimated rate of profit. Considering all these facts and circumstances, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in deleting the penalty levied under section 271(1)(c ). [Para 5]

FACT: The assessee carried on contract business of construction of roads by obtaining contracts from the Government departments. For the assessment year 1992-93, the assessee filed the return of income along with the tax audit report under section 44AB. It was accepted that the books maintained by the assessee were not verifiable. During the course of the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer asked the assessee to furnish the names and addresses of the parties and sundry creditors from whom raw material for construction of the roads had been purchased. The assessee furnished the addresses and the Assessing Officer issued letters of enquiry under section 133(6). However, the letters sent to 17 parties returned unserved to the Assessing Officer. The assessee was directed to prove the genuineness of the transactions made with the parties. The assessee filed copies of the accounts and copies of the confirmation letters stated to have been obtained from the parties before the Assessing Officer. However, the Assessing Officer did not agree with the confirmation letters as the letters sent to the parties had returned unserved. The assessee was asked to prove the genuineness of those parties but could not prove except filing confirmation letters from those parties. The Assessing Officer further pointed out that there might be standard specification but it was difficult to arrive at a definite conclusion in the absence of specific formula for construction of roads of various thickness and it was further observed that in the absence of details, general statement would not support any measurement and it was not possible to arrive at the exact consumption of raw material. He therefore, made certain additions to income of the assessee on that account.

The Bombay Bench of the Tribunal in the case of ITO v. Jaishree Trading Corpn. [1978] Taxation 50(6) 142 had also held that it was not possible for the assessee to churn out a uniform G.P. rate from year to year irrespective of the varying conditions. HEADNOTE: Section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil construction business - Assessment year 2001-02 - Assessee had entered into a contract with a civil contractor ‘U’ Ltd. for supply of sand for construction of roads from specified zones - For said purpose, assessee had to pay royalty to Government, engage labourers for loading and unloading and arrange for transportation of sand up to site for construction of road - Contractor had made payments to assessee in two parts, one for supplying of material, and other for transportation charges - Whether since assessee had executed work of supplying and transporting sand from particular area to a civil contractor, assessee was to be considered as a sub-contractor and in such circumstances, section 44AD would be applicable  - Held, yes - Whether  however, if there was a reasonable basis for bifurcation of payments, for cost of material separately and for transportation charges, then profit should be computed at rate of 8 per cent in respect of payments made for transportation charge and at rate of 5 per cent for supply of material and if there was a composite agreement, then entire receipts would be subject to 8 per cent under section 44AD - Held, yes [Matter remanded to Assessing Officer for purpose of calculating net profits after verification of nature of payments to assessee]

FACT: The assessee had entered into a contract with a civil contractor ‘U’ Ltd. for supply of sand for the construction of roads from specified zones. The assessee had received a payment of Rs. 36,58,267 and out of the said payment ‘U’ Ltd. had deducted tax in respect of Rs. 16,85,044. The assessee filed the return of income for the assessment year 2001-02, disclosing income at the net profit of 8 per cent under section 44AD in respect of the said payment. During the course of assessment proceedings, when assessee was asked about the gross receipts, assessee filed revised return disclosing the gross receipts at Rs. 36,58,267 but computed the income at the rate of 5 per cent under section 44AF instead at the rate of 8 per cent under section 44AD. It was claimed by the assessee that no books of account had been maintained by him and the profits in respect of the payments were required to be assessed under section 44AF, which is applicable in respect of retail trades. The assessee, pleaded before the Assessing Officer that provisions of section 44AD were not applicable in the instant case. The Assessing Officer on consideration of the terms and conditions of the agreement between the assessee and U Ltd. held that the assessee had executed the contract work and, accordingly, income was to be computed in accordance with provisions of section 44AD. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The revenue supported the Commissioner (Appeals) determination of a 30 per cent profit rate, contending that franchise and royalty fees generally yield higher profit margins compared to other revenue streams. It was also contended that no specific bifurcation of amounts relating to Franchise Fees and Royalties, was provided by the assessee. [Para 25.1]

■ The profit percentages from appellate orders and the financial statements of the assessee’s group entities were examined. It was noted that the profit margins varied significantly, ranging from 10 per cent to 50 per cent across different segments. Franchise fees and royalties typically have higher margins compared to income from hospitality operations and Reality business where expenses are relatively higher. The seized records indicated that a considerable portion of the unaccounted receipts pertained to franchise fees and royalties. These revenue streams inherently carry larger profit margins due to minimal operating costs compared to hospitality services or real estate projects. While the assessee’s offer of 25 per cent profit was conservative, the Commissioner (Appeals) adoption of a 30 per cent rate was justified based on the nature of the business activities and available profit data. The chosen rate must reflect the average profit embedded in the unaccounted receipts, especially for high-margin streams such as franchise fees and royalties. Judicial discretion in determining profit rates must be exercised within the bounds of factual evidence and judicial precedents. The 30 per cent rate was consistent with past assessments of the group and reflected the diverse income streams of the business, especially Franchise Fees and Royalty. Revenues such as Franchise Fees and Royalty were not present in case of other group entities. Accordingly, the addition across the relevant assessment years calculated at the rate of 30 per cent of receipts is confirmed. [Para 26]

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 256(1), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income - Assessment year 1985-86 - Assessing Officer by invoking proviso to section 145(1) estimated assessee’s income applying a net profit rate of 10 per cent on total contract receipts and on basis of some unexplained cash credits, made additions - Commissioner (Appeals) upholding application of proviso to section 145 reduced profit rate to 5 per cent and deleted addition in respect of unexplained cash credits, as addition on account of application of rate would cover unexplained cash credits as well - Whether what net profit could be applied to estimate income from contract was essentially a question of fact, which could not give rise to any question of law - Held, yes - Whether Commissioner (Appeals) order of granting set off of cash credits against trading account addition was justified and as such no question of law did arise therefrom - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, an individual, deriving income from contracts, filed his return for the assessment year 1985-86. On finding that the assessee did not maintain regular books of account, the Assessing Officer invoked the proviso to section 145 and estimated income by applying a net profit rate of 10 per cent on the total contract receipts. And further on finding that the assessee had introduced some cash credits in different names which were not satisfactorily explained, the Assessing Officer made further addition and completed the assessment accordingly.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), upheld the application of the proviso to section 145 but reduced the net profit rate from 10 per cent to 5 per cent and held that no separate addition in respect of unexplained cash credits was warranted as the addition on account of application of rate would cover the unexplained cash credits as well.

On the revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal upheld the Commissioner (Appeals) orders.

On reference :

HELD: The question as to what net profit rate could be applied to estimate the income from contract was essentially a question of fact, which could not give rise to any question of law. Granting of set off of cash credits against the trading account addition was fully justified in view of the decision of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in the case of CIT v. Ram Sanehi Gian Chand [1972] 86 ITR 724 , as well as the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Anantharam Veerasinghaiah & Co. v. CIT [1980] 123 ITR 457 . As such no referable question, arose from the order of the Tribunal as the order of the Tribunal was based on the decision of the jurisdictional High Court, as well as of the Supreme Court.

In the result, the reference application was dismissed.

Vinay Karan for the Applicant. Sudhir Sehgal for the Respondent.

Section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Depreciation - Allowance/Rate of (In case of estimated income) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether in view of facts stated under heading 'Method of accounting - Estimation of income', since Assessing Officer had adopted reasonable rate of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts, further deductions towards depreciation could not be allowed as it would result into determination of total income below income returned by assessee - Held, yes [Para 11] [In favour of revenue]

Section 56 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income from other sources - Chargeable as (Interest) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether in view of facts stated under heading 'Method of accounting - Estimation of income', since there was no nexus between interest receipts and works contracts executed by assessee, interest on fixed deposits was separately assessable under head 'Income from other sources' - Held, yes [Para 14] [In favour of revenue]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of execution of civil works contract. He filed his return of income for the relevant assessment years declaring certain taxable income.

During the course of assessment proceedings, on verification of books of account and other details filed by the assessee, the Assessing Officer noticed that most of the expenditure in respect of labour charges, work expenses, mess charges and other indirect expenses were not supported by proper bills and vouchers. The Assessing Officer further observed that the assessee had kept self-made vouchers in support of major expenditure and, accordingly, opined that the books of account maintained by the assessee were not amenable for verification.

He thus rejected books of account under the provisions of section 145(3) and estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts net of all deductions. In addition to estimation of net profit, the Assessing Officer made separate additions towards income from other sources being interest earned on fixed deposits.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal:

On the other hand, the revenue contended, inter alia, that there was no res judicata in income-tax proceedings and the only thing to be examined was whether in an impugned assessment order, the ITO’s action was within the law and that in this case the ITO had not exceeded his jurisdiction by accepting the profit and loss account and computing the income after taking into consideration the expenses that could be allowed under the law. HELD: It is true that there is no res judicata in the income-tax law and that the ITO has authority to take a different view from what has been taken in an earlier year. But neither he can exercise this authority in caprice, nor has he an unrestricted, unlimited, unconditional or absolute right in this matter. It was undisputed that the ITO had completed the assessments of the assessee’s income for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 on a flate rate basis observing, inter alia, that in the absence of maintenance of vouchers and receipts for the expenditure incurred by the assessee, the books of account were not acceptable. Now to examine whether the books of account kept in all the years inclusive of the year under appeal were maintained in the same manner or not, the trading and profit and loss accounts were the best available guide on which one should rely. There was no difference in the manner in which they had been kept in any of the assessment years inclusive of the assessment year under appeal. However, it was strange that though the assessee was a big contractor and executions of many of the contracts were spread in these years, no work-in-progress or closing stock had been recorded in the trading account. In view of the circumstances, it was not possible for the ITO to presume that the true profit could be computed on the basis of the books of account. He had overlooked the orders for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 framed by his predecessors. As a matter of fact, his finding was not very much different. He had also overlooked his own letter dated 16-2-1985 addressed to the assessee. Again, there was no whisper in his order as to what were the defects in the earlier years, which were not present in the relevant assessment year. He failed to prove his finding. Accordingly, the reasoning of the ITO to change the mode of assessment could not be accepted and the estimate of profit at a flat rate method as adopted in earlier years in the same circumstances should also apply in the assessment year under appeal, except that, in view of the finding that a large amount of expenses claimed was unestablished, the profit rate to be applied should be 12½ per cent instead of 10 per cent adopted for the earlier years.

M.J. Swamy for the Appellant. B.P. Ramana Naik for the Respondent.
