Section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Best judgment assessment - Assessment year 1974-75 - Whether while making a best judgment assessment, though there must necessarily be guess work in matter, it must not be arbitrary - Held, yes - Assessee-contractor did not main books of account - He filed his return of income on estimate basis by computing profit at flat rate of 10 per cent on gross receipts - ITO, however, computed net profit at rate of 15 per cent - Revision petition filed by assessee was dismissed by Commissioner - Whether since neither ITO nor Commissioner had referred to any material for applying flat rate of 
15 percent while estimating net profits, impugned orders passed by them deserved to be set aside - Held, yes

Section 145(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment year 1991-92 - Assessee, carrying on construction business, declared net profit of 5 per cent on gross receipts - Assessing Officer applied rate of 7 per cent - Commissioner (Appeals) applied 10 per cent rate relying on a case purported to be comparable and by generalising that normal rate of profit in construction business was 10 per cent - In the preceding years rate of 6 per cent was applied in assessee’s own case - Whether history of assessee’s case itself was a guide in applying rate of profit and, therefore, Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in enhancing rate - Held, yes

Section 254, read with section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Appellate Tribunal - Powers of [Reasoned order] - Assessment year 1997-98 - Assessee was civil contractor and declared gross profit and net profit against contract receipts - Assessing Officer rejected books of account and applied net profit rate of 10 per cent - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) reduced rate of profit to 8 per cent - On second appeal, Tribunal affirmed rate of 8 per cent observing that as regards earlier assessment years application of 8 per cent was held reasonable and even in respect of present assessment year question involved was one and same - Department contended that cogent reason had not been assigned by Tribunal while passing impugned order - Whether since what was being decided by Tribunal under order impugned was a question of fact and there was only an order of affirmance, no detailed reasons were further required - Held, yes [Paras 7  8] [In favour of assessee]IT: No detailed reasons is required in passing an order of affirmance by ITAT, where question involved is one and same as that decided in respect of preceding assessment years

Section 145, read with section 143, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 2003-04 - Assessee-firm, a labour contractor, got a contract of labour from Railways for transporting, loading and unloading of sleepers and for stone-ballast supply - For relevant assessment year, it had shown its gross profit rate at 2.88 per cent as against 7 per cent shown in previous assessment year - Explanation submitted by assessee for such steep fall of gross profit rate was rise in price of diesel and requirement of skilled labour in relevant year - Further, assessee had accepted transportation contract below tender rate but in earlier year position was just opposite - Assessing Officer, having found various faults in books of account, rejected same and adopted gross profit rate of 6.5 per cent - In another case for same assessment year, same Bench of Tribunal under identical facts and circumstances had adopted a gross profit rate of 3 per cent as reasonable - Whether, in view of aforesaid order of Tribunal and further keeping in view facts in totality, adoption of gross profit rate of 3 per cent would be justified - Held, yes

Section 145,  read with section 44AD, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Gross profit rate) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee was engaged in business of execution of civil works contract - He filed his return of income for relevant assessment year declaring certain taxable income - In course of assessment, Assessing Officer noted that assessee had kept self-made vouchers in support of major expenditure and, accordingly, opined that books of account maintained by assessee were not amenable for verification - He thus rejected books of account under provisions of section 145(3) and estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts net of all deductions - Whether since assessee failed to controvert findings of Assessing Officer with any positive evidence to come to conclusion that books of account maintained by him gave a true and correct profit from business, Assessing Officer was right in rejecting books of account - Held, yes - Whether as regards rate of profit, since assessee had disclosed 6.73 per cent to 7.44 per cent net profit in earlier period, impugned estimation made by Assessing Officer was justified - Held, yes - Whether even otherwise, since nature of business carried on by assessee was squarely fit into specified business referred to in provisions of section 44AD, estimation of net profit at rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts specified in said section was rightly adopted - Held, yes [Paras 8, 9 and 10] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee had kept self-made vouchers in support of major expenditure and books of account maintained by him did not give true and correct profit from business, Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting said books of account and estimating net profit of 8 per cent of gross receipts  IT : Where Assessing Officer had adopted reasonable rate of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts, further deduction towards depreciation could not be allowed as it would result into determination of total income below income returned by assessee   IT : Where there was no nexus between interest receipts and works contracts executed by assessee, interest on fixed deposits was separately assessable under head 'Income from other sources'

Section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil Construction business
¦ In case of a civil construction contractor, even prior to introduction of section 44AD with effect from assessment year 1994-95, estimate of profit at 8 per cent of gross receipts, where income returned was less than 8 per cent of gross receipts, would be justified [Assessment year 1993-94]
It is true that section 44AD was inserted in the statute book with effect from 1-4-1994 to apply to assessment for the assessment year 1994-95 onwards, and it was not a mandatory requirement for the assessment year 1993-94 to assess profit of civil construction at such rate (8 per cent), yet the rate which is mandatorily required to be applied in the cases of business which the assessee was carrying on, where income returned was less than 8 per cent of its gross receipts, cannot be said to be an irrelevant consideration while considering the rate to be applied for estimating the income from like businesses for earlier years in its discretion by the authorities under the Act.

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of net profits - Assessment year 1989-90 - Assessee, and individual contractor, received certain payments and declared net profit rate which worked out to 6.54 per cent if claims for interest and depreciation were ignored - Assessing Officer in absence of proper record about labour and Hazri expenses as also on consumption of material, applied net profit rate of 10 per cent on total receipts subject to interest and depreciation - whether engaging of employees to carry out work was not a very special feature which should weigh heavily while determining income on basis adopted by department, and thus, Commissioner (Appeals)’s order reducing it to 9 per cent subject to interest and depreciation was to be upheld - Held, yes

II. Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit (GP rate) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee was fully engaged in labour oriented contract work - Commissioner (Appeals) directed Assessing Officer to estimate net profit of assessee at rate of 8 per cent on gross bills - Assessee submitted that it had taken contracts from a construction company, which in turn had taken main contract from Government - Whether in view of decision of Coordinate Bench of Tribunal rendered in case of C. Eiswara Reddy  Co. v. Asstt. CIT [IT Appeal No. 668 (Hyd.) of 2009, dated 31-1-2011], Assessing Officer was to be directed to apply 5 per cent net profit on gross receipts of assessee - Held, yes [Para 53] [Partly in favour of assessee]

I. Section 44AD, read with section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Presumptive income - Civil Construction business (Disallowance of expenses) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee was a contractor executing contract works under various Government departments - Assessee claimed huge expenses under heads 'freight', 'salaries and wages', 'travelling expenses', etc. - Assessee was asked to produce salary and wages register and other he evidences of expenses but he did not produce any evidence before Assessing Officer - Assessing Officer rejected books and estimated profit at 8 per cent of gross contract receipts - Whether since assessee had not produced any evidence, Assessing Officer was justified in estimating profit on presumptive basis - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where a civil contractor did not produce salary and wage register and other evidences in support of expenses incurred, Assessing Officer was justified in estimating profit at 8 per cent of gross contract receipts  IT : Where assessee paid interest to bank for housing loan and it was duly supported by bank statement, deduction under section 80C was allowable

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income [Gross profit rate] - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee was engaged in business of contract work of military engineering services - Assessing Officer having found that assessee disclosed lower gross profit rate 7.20 per cent in relevant year, in comparison to 10.25 per cent in immediately preceding year despite three fold increase in gross receipt and assessee had not maintained salary register, payment register etc., rejected books of account of assessee and estimated income of assessee by applying net profit rate of 12.5 per cent - Whether since explanations of assessee that gross receipts had substantially increased by three times for which assessee had to reduce margin, and that contract works were executed in military and air force areas where working hours were lesser in comparison to normal civil work and that cost of various expenses and material had also been increased, was not rebutted by revenue, gross profit rate applied by Assessing Officer could not be sustained - Held, yes - Whether on facts, it would be fair and reasonable if net profit rate of 7.50 per cent was applied subject to interest to third parties, depreciation, interest to partners and salary to partners - Held, yes [Para 2.12] [Partly in favour of assessee]IT : Explanations of assessee which were not rebutted by revenue, were to be considered in estimation of his income

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 2001-02 - Whether applying net profit rate on basis of best judgment assessment in a given situation will be a question of fact unless, such an assessment is shown to be arbitrary or perverse - Held, yes - Assessee was a contractor engaged in work of civil construction and filed its return for assessment year in question - Assessing Officer made addition to returned income mainly on account of claim for wages being found to be not verifiable - On appeal, Tribunal while considering issue of addition on account of unverifiable wages, considered it appropriate to apply reasonable rate of profit, which was assessed at rate of 12 per cent on contract receipts, excluding material supplied by department - Whether since assessment of 12% of net profit rate of contract receipt was not shown to be arbitrary or perverse, no question of law arose from Tribunal's order - Held, yes

I. Section 44AD, read with section 69, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil construction business (Computation of income) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee was engaged in business of supply of labour for civil and technical job assigned by company B - During assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer noticed difference in total contract receipts shown by assessee in his books of account and that shown by contractee in Form No. 26AS - In absence of any satisfactory explanation, Assessing Officer made addition of such differential receipts - Whether since differential receipts were not shown by assessee in regular books of account, expenses related thereto might have also not been shown in books of account and in such circumstances, income was to be determined by applying net profit rate of 8 per cent on said receipts - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where there was difference in civil contract receipts shown by assessee in books of account and by contractee in form 26AS, net profit rate at rate of 8 per cent was to be applied to determine income embedded in said receipts  IT : In case of cash payment of meal charges exceeding Rs. 20,000 daily, Assessing Officer should verify whether amount paid was a reimbursement or it was itself towards an expense

Section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil construction business - Assessment year 1992-93 - Assessee-company, engaged 
in construction work, filed return showing 0.48 per cent net 
profit on total contract receipt - Assessing Officer rejected books of account maintained by assessee and applied net profit rate at
 12.5 per cent for computing assessee’s income - Whether provisions of section 44AD, though strictly inserted in Act with effect from 1-4-1994, can be a guideline for purpose of applying a particular net profit in case of civil contractor even in earlier years - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, net profit rate of 12.5 per cent applied by authorities below in case of assessee was excessive and exorbitant and, accordingly, application of net profit rate was modified from 12.5 per cent to 8 per cent on gross receipt shown by assessee - Held, yes

Section 44AD, read with sections 143 and 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Presumptive taxation of - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee, a civil contractor, declared net profit ratio of 5.64 per cent of gross contract receipts - His gross receipts from contract business exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs - Assessing Officer rejected book results by invoking section 145(3) and determined total income by estimating net profit ratio of 15 per cent of gross receipts - Before Tribunal, assessee had canvassed for adoption of net profit ratio of 8 per cent on contract receipts in order to estimate income from business of contracting - Whether presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD reflects a legislative approved rate of net profit, which can be considered as fair and reasonable to estimate income from contract business in cases like that of instant assessee, where books of account were not found reliable by Assessing Officer - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, income from contract business of assessee be estimated at 8 per cent of gross receipts - Held, yes [Para 7][Partly in favour of assessee]IT: Where assessee, a civil contractor, declared net profit ratio of 5.64 per cent of gross contract receipts and Assessing Officer after rejecting book results determined total income by estimating net profit ratio of 15 per cent of gross receipts, income from contracting business be estimated by applying net profit ratio of 8 per cent of gross receipts

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income- Assessment year 2010-11 - Where despite various opportunities given, assessee, civil contractor failed to produce books of account and relevant vouchers and there had been a lot of variation in profit rate of assessee during different years, Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting audited balance-sheet filed by assessee and making assessment by applying net profit rate of 12 per cent [In favour of revenue]

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits (Gross profit rate) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Where assessee-firm derived income from work contracts, net profit of assessee should be estimated at 8 per cent as against 10 per cent adopted by Assessing Officer [Partly in favour of assessee]

Section 145, read with  section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounts - Estimation of income (Rate of profit) - Block period 2008 to 2010-11 - Assessee-company was a sub-contractor - In course of assessment proceedings assessee produced audited books of account, bills relevant vouchers, etc. - Assessing Officer observed that labour register had not been maintained in conventional manner - He rejected books of account and estimated net profit at 8 per cent of gross contract receipt - Whether it was not correct to compare profit of principal contractors with profit margin of sub-contractor - Held, yes - Whether since net profit rate of principal contractors was ranging from 5.19 per cent to 6.15 per cent, there would be lower profit in case of assessee sub-contractor and, therefore, Commissioner (Appeals) rightly estimated net profit rate at 4 per cent - Held, yes [Paras 5 and 6] [In favour of assessee]IT: On rejection of books of account under section 145, profit margin of assessee, a sub-contractor, is to be estimated at rate much less than average profit margin worked out by Assessing Officer of its principal (i.e., contractor)

Section 9  of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with Rule 10 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Income - Deemed to accrue or arise in India - Assessment years 1995-96 and 1997-98 - Assessee-company, a resident of Australia, claimed certain loss arising from a contract entered into with an Indian company - Assessee, however, did not produce books of account, etc., in support of such loss - Assessing Officer applied rule 10 and determined income at rate of 10 per cent of total revenue - Commissioner (Appeals) directed Assessing Officer to apply rate of 8 per cent for arriving at income - Whether since Commissioner (Appeals) had arbitrarily reduced profit rate to 8 per cent without assigning any basis, impugned order was to be set aside and matter was to be remanded to file of Assessing Officer with a direction to compute income from all projects as per books of account which assessee was now claiming to have in its possession - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1999-2000 and 2000-01 - Where in case of assessee civil contractor, Commissioner (Appeals) directed adoption of gross profit rate of 12 per cent and Tribunal upheld it, in absence of challenge by assessee as well as revenue to said rate, order of Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld [In favour of assessee]

Section 2(1)(u1), read with section 5B, of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957 and rule 6 of the Karnataka Sales Tax Rules, 1957 - Taxable turnover - In case of works contract - Deductions - Assessment years 2003-04 and 2004-05 - Assessee-company was engaged in execution of civil works contracts such as construction of buildings and apartments - It was not in a position to show actual amount that it had incurred towards labour and like charges and, therefore, it had adopted standard rate of deduction provided under rule 6(4)(n)(v) and claimed standard deduction of 30 per cent on its contract receipt towards labour and like charges - It had apportioned gross profit earned between value of goods transferred and labour and like charges - Assessing Authority had allowed deduction towards labour charges and other like charges at 30 per cent of actual contract receipts relatable to civil works contracts executed by assessee after deducting amount paid to registered sub-contractors and also allowed deduction of gross profit at 27.44 per cent on labour charges - Subsequently Revisional Authority revised order of assessment holding that when assessee availed deduction of 30 per cent towards labour charges and other like charges under rule 6(4)(n)(v), it was not entitled for deduction of 27.44 per cent of gross profit on labour charges - Whether in view of clear, express and unambiguous provisions of rule 6 and in particular Explanation II thereto assessee was entitled for deduction of 27.44 per cent of gross profit on labour charges in addition to standard deduction at 30 per cent available towards labour and like charges - Held, yes [Paras 13  15] [In favour of assessee]CST  VAT: Where assessee was engaged in execution of civil works contracts and it had adopted standard rate of deduction provided under rule 6(4)(n)(v) and claimed standard deduction of 30 per cent on its contract receipt towards labour and like charges, in view of clear, express and unambiguous provisions of rule 6 of Karnataka Sales Tax Rules, 1957 and in particular Explanation II thereto, Assessing Authority was correct in allowing deduction of 27.44 per cent of gross profit on labour charges in addition to standard deduction at 30 per cent available towards labour and like charges

Section 145, read with section 256, of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13, read with section 66, of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessee’s accounts were so complicated that its not for auditor could not prepare profit and loss statement therefrom - ITO assessed assessee at flat rate of 10 per cent on total turnover instead of 6¼ per cent as adopted for other similarly placed assessees - Whether charging of flat rate was only one mode of arriving at assessment in absence of clearly and properly kept accounts - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, no referable question of law arose from order of ITO - Held, yes

Section 256(1), read with section 143, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Reference to  High Court - Question of law - Assessment year 1988-89 - Assessee was carrying on business of building contractors - Books of various accounts were rejected by  Assessing Officer on ground that expenses like wages to labourers were not verifiable in absence of supporting vouchers -  Assessing Officer applied rate of profit at 10 per cent of gross receipts and disallowed assessee’s claim for depreciation - Whether  Tribunal was right in allowing depreciation after adopting profit at 10  per cent and no referable question of law arose out of said order - Held, yes

Section 145, read with section 36(1)(iia) and section 32, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment year 1992-93 - Assessee carried on contract business of construction of roads by obtaining contracts from Government departments - Books maintained by assessee were not verifiable - Assessee filed his return of income along with tax audit report under section 44AB - During assessment proceedings, assessee was asked to prove genuineness of transactions with various parties from whom raw material had been purchased - Assessee filed confirmation letters from parties but failed to produce them in person before Assessing Officer for verification - Assessing Officer rejected books of assessee and estimated profits - Assessing Officer also made disallowance on account of labour payments holding that payments were excessive and inflated - Further, Assessing Officer disallowed depreciation - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) held that assessee had not maintained verifiable accounts and he applied net profit rate of 10 per cent on receipt - He also granted depreciation after applying net profit rate - Whether in absence of verifiable accounts maintained by assessee, Assessing Officer should have examined past history of assessee and should have adopted net profit rate instead of making additions on account of purchases in raw materials - Held, yes - Whether since department itself had accepted net profit rate in case of same assessee in different years at 8 per cent to 8.25 per cent on receipt after deducting material and sales tax in past, looking to past history and comparable cases, it would be reasonable and appropriate if net profit rate of 8 per cent on receipts after deducting cost of material supplied by Government department was applied in instant case - Held, yes - Whether keeping in view past history of assessee in which depreciation was allowed, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in allowing depreciation after applying net profit rate - Held, yes - Whether assessee was entitled to deduction of interest paid to third parties after applying net profit rate - Held, yes

Section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil Construction Business [Applicability of] - Assessment years 2006-07 and 2007-08 - Assessee was a civil contractor - In absence of proper books of account maintained by assessee, Assessing Officer estimated taxable income at 8 per cent of gross contractual receipts by invoking provisions of section 44AD - Commissioner (Appeals) held that net profit of assessee was to be assessed at 5 per cent of contractual receipts - Tribunal, however, restored order of Assessing Officer - It was apparent from records that assessee's gross receipts were in excess of amount prescribed at relevant time and, thus, section 44AD was not applicable to its case - Moreover, Commissioner (Appeals) had considered assessee's case as regards profit margin in earlier years to refix taxable income at 5 per cent of gross turnover - Whether in aforesaid circumstances, Tribunal was not justified in straightaway restoring assessment at 8 per cent of gross turnover without any discussion on merits of order of Commissioner (Appeals) - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned order of Tribunal was to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 11] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where assessee, a civil contractor, did not maintain proper books of account and, thus, Commissioner (Appeals) having regard to profit margin of earlier years, adopted profit rate of 5 per cent of contractual receipts, in absence of any discussion on merits, Tribunal could not enhance said profit rate to 8 per cent of gross turnover by invoking provisions of section 44AD

Section 144, read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Best judgment assessment - Assessee did not produce appropriate books of account - Tribunal applied best judgment assessment and worked out profits at rate which was generally applied to contracts of nature entered into by assessee - Whether rate applied by Tribunal could not be said to be arbitrary nor any question of law arose in that regard - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - For estimating income of assessee, civil contractor, Assessing Officer applied net profit rate of 12.5 per cent as against 8.10 per cent applied by assessee - Commissioner reduced net profit rate to 10 per cent and Tribunal confirmed same - Whether no substantial question of law arose from Tribunal’s order - Held, yes

I. Section  44AD,  read with sections  144  and  147, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  58,  read with sections  271  and  279  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Presumptive taxation (Best judgment assessment) - Assessment years 2013-14 and 2017-18 - Assessee, a civil contractor executing works for Government departments/PWD, was flagged in NMS for contractual receipts of about Rs. 17.27 crores and interest income of about Rs. 0.24 lakhs during FY 2012-13 relevant to AY 2013-14 but did not file return of income - Assessing Officer completed assessment ex parte under sections 147 read with section 144 treating contractual receipts as business turnover, noting that turnover exceeded audit threshold and no books of account/audit report were produced, and estimated net profit at 15% of gross receipts (about Rs. 2.59 crores), rejecting assessee’s lower profit margin and depreciation-related submissions due to non-filing and absence of supporting records - Whether best judgment assessment must be based on material on record which could be gathered by Assessing Officer on proper investigation - Held, yes - Whether since assessee’s entire contractual receipts were from Government departments/PWD and all proceeds were received through banking channels and assessee’s estimation of net profit at 6.06% of turnover was higher than rate of 6% prescribed under section 44AD, flat estimation of income at 15% of turnover was highly unjustified - Held, yes - Whether net profit rate of 7% in civil contract business, particularly when all contract receipts were received through proper banking channels on which tax had been deducted at source, was reasonable and accordingly Assessing Officer was to be directed to recompute net profit of assessee at 7% of total turnover declared by assessee - Held, yes [Para 10.4] [Partly in favour of assessee]

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Gross profit rate) - Assessment years 2006-07 to 2009-10 - Assessment was passed in case of assessee/revision petitioner for relevant years wherein gross profit claimed by assessee was rejected - Assessing Officer adopted a notional gross profit of 10 per cent and arrived at corresponding deemed sales turnover on civil works contract executed - Tribunal upheld order of Assessing officer - Assessee submitted that Tribunal erred in adopting a thumb rule of 10 per cent gross profit, disregarding actual book profit certified by a Chartered Accountant for calculation of deemed sale value of goods transferred during execution of works contract - However, it was found that Tribunal verified audited Profit  Loss statement and Balance Sheet of assessee/revision petitioner, for relevant years and held that adoption of notional 10 per cent gross profit on purchase value to arrive at deemed sales turnover by Assessing Officer was correct - Whether Tribunal, having considered submissions, perused relevant documents and passed well considered orders, same did not call for any interference - Held, yes [Paras 28, 29 and 36][In favour of revenue]IT: Where Tribunal verified audited Profit  Loss statement and Balance Sheet of assessee/revision petitioner, for relevant years and held that adoption of notional 10 per cent Gross Profit on purchase value to arrive at deemed sales turnover by Assessing Officer was correct, same did not call for any interference

Section 28 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Assessee, carrying contract work under government departments, did not maintain proper account books - Whether net profit could be estimated at a flat rate on gross receipts including value of material supplied by government - Held, on facts, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income - Assessment year 1977-78 - Rate of 12½ per cent is normal rate applied to contractors and mere fact that assessee declared higher net profit in preceding year cannot be ground to make additions

Section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 1950-51 - Assessee was dealing in sales of certain goods both on commission basis as was as on his own account - As assessee failed to produce proper books of account in pursuance of notice under section 23(2) of Act, 1922, ITO applied proviso to section 13 of Act 1922 and estimated sales of assessee at Rs. 2,50,000 on which flat rate of 5 percent was applied to determine profit - In applying said rate ITO took into consideration fact that assessee did some business on his own account - Tribunal reduced turnover determined by ITO, but upheld flat rate of 5 percent as gross profit - Before Tribunal, assessee referred comparable case for consideration but he had made no attempt to split up turnover of business on commission basis and on own account so that different rates might be applied to such turnovers - Whether, in such circumstances, Tribunal was justified in confirming flat rate of 5 per cent as applied by department authorities - Held, yes

Section 143, read with section 44AD, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Additions to income - Assessment year 1988-89 - Assessee constructed flats and shops and as per agreement with Government had to sell flats at Rs. 90 per sq. ft. even though cost of construction came to Rs. 180 per sq. ft. - Assessee made profit from sale of shops and showed net profits worked out as per books of account, after adjusting loss from flats - Assessing Officer, however, made addition after estimating profits from construction and sale of flats and shops at 8 per cent net of sale proceedings - Whether since assessee’s case was not comparable with other builders who could sell at their own determined prices and cost of construction also appeared very reasonable, and Assessing Officer had not pointed out any specific incident of assessee selling flats at higher prices, there was no justification for addition made - Held, yes - Whether Assessing Officer should, therefore, be directed to accept profits shown by assessee in its books of account - Held, yes

III. Section  145  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 /  Section  276   of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Method of accounting  -  Rejection of accounts  (Net profit rate) - Assessment year  2010-11  - Assessee had filed no return of income - Assessing Officer on basis of information in his possession from Form No. 26AS of assessee that assessee had received contractual income of Rs. 4.37 crores from one, IGHPL, but, no return of income was filed by assessee, he rejected books of account of assessee and further estimated profits on said contractual receipts by applying rate of 12 per cent thereon - It was noted that no justification was given by Assessing Officer for rejecting assessee's rate of 8 per cent applied except a general dismissal of same stating that 12 per cent rate was justified - Whether therefore, Assessing Officer was not justified in applying net profit rate of 12 per cent on contractual receipts and same was to be set aside - Held, yes [Para 23] [In favour of assessee]

Section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil construction business - Assessment years 2001-02 and 2002-03 - Assessing Officer rejecting book results of assessees engaged in contract work, estimated income of assessees by applying net profit rate of 8 per cent on contract receipts as per section 44AD - Commisisoner (Appeals) confirmed Assessing Officer's order - Whether since it was not clear from orders of lower authorities as to whether activities undertaken by assessees were contracts of civil work, supply of labour to civil contractors or contracts falling under Explanation to section 44AD, matter was to be remitted back to Commissioner(Appeals) with a direction to modify earlier orders by applying net profit rate of 6 per cent instead of 8 per cent only if it was found that nature of contract work done by assessees was other than supply of labour for civil contracts or cases falling under Explanation to section 44AD - Held, yes

Section 44AD, read with section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil construction business (Applicability of) - Assessee filed his return declaring income at rate of 8 per cent on gross receipts - Assessing Officer allowed expenses to extent of 75 per cent and computed gross profit at rate of 25 per cent - Tribunal, however, assessed income at rate of 8 per cent on gross receipts - Whether since Assessing Officer had computed gross projects at rate of 25 per cent without any justification, Tribunal was justified in adopting gross profit rate of 8 per cent as mentioned in section 44AD even though gross receipts of assessee were in excess of Rs. 40 lakh - Held, yes [Paras 2 and 3] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where Assessing Officer computed gross profit rate of assessee at 25 per cent of gross receipts without any justification, Tribunal was justified in adopting gross profit rate of 8 per cent as mentioned in section 44AD even though turnover of assessee was in excess of Rs. 40 lakh

u Section 145 of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where assessee, a construction company, did not maintain any books of account and it was also an undisputed fact that the assessee did not produce before the Assessing Officer the vouchers or any other documentary evidence to support the correctness of various expenses shown in the profit and loss account submitted long with the returns of income, Assessing Officer was justified in estimating assessee’s profits by applying net profit rate
Eastern Construction Co. v. ITO [1997] 59 TTJ (Delhi) 723
It is true that the assessing Officer, while making the best judgment, has to make a fair, just and reasonable estimate of income. Such estimation of profit in a fair and just manner could be done by the Assessing Officer either by applying a net profit rate on the contract receipts or he could also estimate the profit in any other manner which can be regarded as fair and reasonable. 
Where assessee, a construction company, did not maintain any books of account and it was also an undisputed fact that the assessee did not produce before the Assessing Officer the vouchers or any other documentary evidence to support the correctness of various expenses shown in the profit and loss account submitted long with the returns of income, and the Assessing Officer completed assessment by resorting to section 145 and he estimated profits by applying net profit rate of 12.5 per cent : 
Held that, on the facts of the case, it was incumbent upon by the Assessing Officer to have resorted to estimation of profit from the contract business. It could not, therefore, be said that the method of computing the taxable income adopted by the Assessing Officer while making the best judgment was patently erroneous or invalid. The year under consideration was the first accounting year of the firm. The contention that the income ought to have been assessed on the basis of past assessed history was, therefore, not relevant and justified on the facts of the present case.

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits Assessment year 1964-65 - Assessee was a military contractor - Finding some irregularities in accounts, ITO assessed profits of assessee from military contracts by applying flat rate of 10 per cent on total receipts - Tribunal held that price of stores supplied by Government was to be excluded while applying flat rate to assessee's contract receipts - Whether order passed by Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

Section 29 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Assessee-firm was carrying on contract business, in which materials were supplied by Government at fixed rates - It filed return in which net income was estimated at 12 per cent on net bills received from Contracts - Whether profit rate was to be applied only on net receipts excluding work in progress - Held, yes

Section 143 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Additions to income - Assessment year 1988-89 - Additions were made to returned income by assessing authority on assumption that assessee-contractor made a profit of 10 per cent on gross profits - Commissioner (Appeals) partly allowing assessee’s claim reduced net profit - Tribunal confirmed order of Commissioner (Appeals) - Whether Tribunal’s order that net profit rate of 10 per cent be applied after deducting cost of material supplied by PWD from gross receipts even if PWD itself allowed benefit of 10 per cent net profit on project cost, was merely a factual issue and no referable question of law arose therefrom - Held, yes

facts.text:
The business of the assessee was execution of construction contracts. The assessee commenced its business from 25-1-1958, and the accounts were closed for the first time on 25-1-1959. During the accounting year the assessee undertook three contracts with respect to which it submitted separate profit and loss statements.

The accounts in respect of the first two contracts were accepted by the authorities under the Act in toto but with regard to the accounts relating to the third contract the ITO declined to accept the assessee's reasons for low profits at the rate of 9% in respect of that contract. He, therefore, applied a flat rate of 12Â½% profit and made certain addition to the assessee's income.

On appeal, the AAC had accepted the assessee's reasons for the low profit of 9% but had sustained an addition of Rs. 10,000 on the ground that the assessee's representative had not denied before him that full quantitative details might not be available in respect of the stores of the value of over Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of the contract. When the case came up before the Tribunal the addition of Rs. 10,000 was found to be excessive and was reduced to Rs. 6,000.

On reference :

The assessee was a military contractor. During the relevant accounting period, the assessee took three military engineering service contracts. The ITO found that the expenditure of the assessee was not supported by vouchers and he detected some other mistakes also in the accounts. After applying the provisions of section 145(1), the ITO assessed the profit from these contracts by applying a flat rate of 10 per cent on the total receipts. The AAC allowed the appeal of the assessee and held that no rate of profit could be applied on the value of the stores supplied by the Government and this order was upheld by the Tribunal.

On reference, the Division Bench noticed the divergent views taken by the various High Courts and particularly because of the challenge laid to the correctness of the judgment in Brij Bhushan Lal v. CIT [1971] 81 ITR 497 (Punj.) and, thus, referred the matter for decision of the Full Bench.

The assessee, a contractor, was assessed to income-tax for the relevant assessment year in respect of certain contracts which commenced in 1922 and were finished some time in 1924. The assessee produced his accounts, but the accounts for the relevant accounting year could not be separated. The ITO considered the accounts to be unreliable. He, therefore, assumed profit at the standard rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of his assessment. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner concluded that in any case it was impossible to ascertain from the assessee’s accounts what the income had been for one year and, therefore, the only way of ascertaining it was to apply the usual rate of 10 per cent on the total payments received. On application under section 66(2) of the 1922 Act, the Commissioner declined to make any reference.

On application under section 66 (3) of the 1922 Act.

The assessee-firm which was engaged in the work of civil construction in public works department, filed returns for the assessment years 1993-94 to 1997-98. The Assessing Officer on the analogy of section 44AD, after rejecting the books of account, made best judgment assessment determining 8 per cent profit at flat rate. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reduced the rate of profit from 8 per cent to 5 per cent, mainly on the ground that since the turnover of the assessee exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs, it was bound to incur more expenses and rate of profit would be less. On further appeal, the Tribunal reduced the rate of profit to 4 per cent on the ground that the assessee was doing the work for PWD and normally the net profit rate was much less for the work of PWD, as the contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under the supervision of the PWD authorities.

On appeal :

The assessee was a contractor undertaking project of Indian Railways on turnkey basis. A search action under section 132 was carried out at the assessee's premises. As the assessee, at the relevant point of time, was not able to collect information about such contracts or produce relevant personnel, it proposed for fixing net profit rate at 11 per cent. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, applied net profit rate at the rate of 11 per cent on the total contract receipts on estimate basis which however, was reduced to 8 per cent by the Tribunal. A penalty under section 271(1)(c) was also levied upon the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the penalty on the ground that the estimation of income by applying flat net profit ratio did not tantamount to concealment or filing inaccurate particulars of income.

On revenue's appeal:

The assessee-company was engaged in the execution of civil works contracts such as construction of the buildings and apartments. It was not in a position to show the actual amount that it had incurred towards the labour and like charges and, therefore, it had adopted standard rate of deduction provided under rule 6(4)(n)(v) and claimed standard deduction of 30 per cent on its contract receipt towards the labour and like charges. It had apportioned the gross profit earned between the value of goods transferred and labour and like charges.

The Assessing Authority had allowed deduction towards labour charges and other like charges at 30 per cent of the actual contract receipt relatable to civil works contracts executed by the assessee after deducting the amount paid to the registered sub-contractors and also allowed deduction of gross profit at 27.44 per cent on labour charges.

Subsequently the Revisional Authority took revisional proceedings against the assessee. He held that when the assessee availed deduction of 30 per cent towards labour charges and other like charges under rule 6(4)(n)(v), it was not entitled for deduction of 27.44 per cent of gross profit on labour charges. He, therefore, revised the assessment order and remanded some of the issues to the Assessing Authority for fresh examination.

On appeal to High Court:

The assessee was a contractor deriving income from installation of hand pumps under Government contract. He was not maintaining day to day details of the expenses and, therefore, showed the net profit rate at 1.76 per cent.The Assessing Officer found it too low and estimated the same at the rate of 8 per cent. The assessee had another unit dealing in hire charges. He showed the net profit at the rate of 1.8 per cent on the hire receipts. The Assessing Officer found it too low. So, he estimated the same at 8 per cent and made the addition. The Assessing Officer also charged interest under sections 234B and 234C in demand notice. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) gave some relief in respect of hire charges.

On second appeal :

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on construction business. It declared net profit of 5 per cent on gross receipts. The Assessing Officer applied the rate of 7 per cent subject to allowance of depreciation and interest on the basis of past history of assessee as well as the defective position of accounts. The Commissioner (Appeals) viewed that the normal rate of profit in construction business was 10 per cent and he, accordingly, applied 10 per cent rate relying on a case, purported to be a comparable case.

On second appeal :

During the course of the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer noticed that the assessee, a civil contractor, did not maintain register of day-to-day consumption of raw material and record of labourers in the form of muster-roll and work done by them. He also noticed that some vouchers of the expenses claimed were not on record and that rate of profit at 3.97 per cent returned by the assessee was very low. Therefore, he rejected assessee’s books of account, invoked provisions of section 145 and applied gross profit rate of 12.5 per cent of contract receipts before depreciation against 9.84 per cent and 7.6 per cent returned by the assessee in the assessment years 1988-89 and 1989-90. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the action of the Assessing Officer, but reduced the rate of profit to 11 per cent.

On second appeal :

The assessee-firm, carrying on construction business, showed a net profit of 5.6 per cent on total contract receipts. As most of the payments were unvouched, the Assessing Officer applied the provisions of section 145 and adopted net profit rate of 8 per cent and made additions accordingly. The Commissioner (Appeals) gave some relief by adopting rate of 7.44 per cent. The Tribunal applied 7 per cent and held that it was fair and just and would also cover depreciation and interest.

On reference :

The assessee was a contractor executing contract works under various Government departments.

The Assessing Officer verified the profit and loss account and found that the assessee had claimed huge expenses under heads 'freight', 'salaries and wages', 'travelling expenses' and 'other expenses'. The assessee was asked to produce salary and wage register and evidences of the above expenses. The assessee did not produce the same. The Assessing Officer rejected the book profit and estimated the profit at 8 per cent of the gross contract receipts.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal :

The assessee-company was engaged in construction work taken on contract. The Assessing Officer found that the net profit at the rate of 0.48 per cent shown by the assessee on its gross contract receipts was low in the line of the civil construction business; the labour charges/cartages paid by it were not verifiable from the vouchers/books of account; and that it had not maintained muster roll depicting the name of the person employed for the particular work and the rate paid to them. Consequently, he rejected the books of account maintained by the assessee and by applying the net profit at the rate of 12.5 per cent on the total receipts shown by the assessee, computed its income accordingly. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal :

The assessee carried on business of construing buildings and doing the work of maintenance of buildings, inter alia, for railways. As per the specific terms of the contract entered into with the railway authorities, cement and iron had to be supplied by them for execution of the work and no accounting of the cost of these materials was to be done while making the bill in respect of contract payment. The assessee did not maintain books of account. In the absence of the books of account, the ITO estimated not profit at the rate of 15 per cent on total receipts, in which the ITO included the value of materials supplied by the railway authorities.

On appeal the AAC reduced the rate of net profit to 12.5 per cent of the total receipts and held that the ITO was not justified in including the value of the materials supplied by the railway authorities in the total receipts for the purpose of calculating the net profit by application of the rate.

The Tribunal held that the value of the materials supplied by the railway authorities should be included in the receipts for the purpose of ascertaining the net profits by applying the percentage rate.

The Tribunal however held that the profit should be calculated on the basis of 10 per cent.

On reference :

For the assessment year 1989-90, the assessee, a contractor, had shown net profit before depreciation and financial charges at the net profit rate of 6 per cent as against the net profit rate at 9.6 per cent in the preceding year. The Assessing Officer found that the assessee had not maintained stock register for purchase and consumption nor the details of work-in-progress were verifiable. The stock of material at site had not been taken into account,besides certain unverifiable credit on account of miscellaneous receipts. He, therefore, applied section 145(2) and estimated the net profit at the rate of 9 per cent. On appeal,the commissioner (Appeals) upheld the rejection of book results but applied a reduced net profit rate of 8 per cent.

On second appeal :

The petitioner assessee, who was carrying on business as a contractor filed his return on estimated basis by computing the profit at a flat rate of 10 per cent, on gross receipts, as he did not maintain any books of account. The ITO, however, computed the net profit at 15 per cent, on the contract payments received by the assessee. The revision petition filed under section 263 was dismissed by the Commissioner.

On writ:

The gross profit rate on receipts of a contract as shown by the assessee-contractor in his return was found by Assessing Officer to be on lower side. According to the assessee, that was because of increase of the total contract receipt of the relevant years by 4 and 7 times, respectively, in comparison with last 2 years. Secondly, for the last 10 to 12 years the place of contract had also been changed. The Assessing Officer did not accept the explanation and on further examination of books of account noticed that the assessee had shown acceptance of new credits from 20 persons. The Assessing Officer was of the opinion that out of the 20 cash credits, 17 were not genuine. The Assessing Officer, rejecting the books of account, applied higher net profit rate of 12.5 per cent and thereby made additions.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) granted some relief to the assessee.

On cross-appeals :

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of executing work contracts of civil construction, supply of labour and trading in shares.

In response to a notice under section 153C, the assessee filed its return of income declaring certain income. The assessee also produced books of account, vouchers, invoices, bank statements, bank reconciliation and explained the credit entries.

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee failed to produce all the relevant vouchers, bills, invoices in support of the expenses. He further noted from the Labour Registers that it did not contain signature/thumb impression of all the recipients of the payment. He, therefore, rejected the books of account and estimated the net profit at 8 per cent of gross contract receipt and estimated net profit.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) after considering submissions of assessee, restricted the net profit rate at the rate of 4 per cent of the gross contractual receipts.

On further appeal by the revenue:

The assessee-firm was engaged in business of execution of government contract. It filed return of income which came on scrutiny. During assessment proceeding, while examining books of account, some discrepancies were found that expenditure claimed by assessee was very much on the higher side as the work executed by it. Consequently, the assessee was asked to produce proof of expenditure, incurred on wages and labour, wages register and also to correlate wages paid with the project executed.

Thereupon, the Assessing Officer, thus, applied 12 per cent rate on gross receipt after excluding cost of material supplied by the department and made addition accordingly.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reduced the net profit rate to 8 per cent as against 12 per cent on the contract receipt and allow depreciation and salary paid to partners as claimed.

On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On appeal:

The assessee carried on contract business of construction of roads by obtaining contracts from the Government departments. For the assessment year 1992-93, the assessee filed the return of income along with the tax audit report under section 44AB. It was accepted that the books maintained by the assessee were not verifiable. During the course of the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer asked the assessee to furnish the names and addresses of the parties and sundry creditors from whom raw material for construction of the roads had been purchased. The assessee furnished the addresses and the Assessing Officer issued letters of enquiry under section 133(6). However, the letters sent to 17 parties returned unserved to the Assessing Officer. The assessee was directed to prove the genuineness of the transactions made with the parties. The assessee filed copies of the accounts and copies of the confirmation letters stated to have been obtained from the parties before the Assessing Officer. However, the Assessing Officer did not agree with the confirmation letters as the letters sent to the parties had returned unserved. The assessee was asked to prove the genuineness of those parties but could not prove except filing confirmation letters from those parties. The Assessing Officer further pointed out that there might be standard specification but it was difficult to arrive at a definite conclusion in the absence of specific formula for construction of roads of various thickness and it was further observed that in the absence of details, general statement would not support any measurement and it was not possible to arrive at the exact consumption of raw material. He therefore, made certain additions to income of the assessee on that account.

As regards the payments made to the labourers, the assessee had submitted samples and muster rolls before the Assessing Officer. They were examined by the handwriting expert, which indicated that the thumbs’ impressions were not of different parties and the Assessing Officer observed that it could be easily deduced that the labour payments were excessive and inflated and, accordingly, made certain disallowance. However, the Assessing Officer allowed depreciation to the assessee as per profit and loss account. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee had not maintained verifiable accounts and as such, net profit rate should be applied. The consumption of the raw material claimed was within the parameters laid down by the laboratories for particular type of road construction. He also held that the Assessing Officer had not made out a fool-proof case for addition on account of bogus purchases and the road constructed by the assessee during the year was found up to the specification by the principals while making payment to the contractor and it could not be held that the assessee had not utilized grit and had not paid the wages for construction of roads. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) applied net profit rate of 10 per cent on the receipts as against 8 per cent applied in the immediately preceding year, keeping in view the discrepancy pointed out in the maintenance of the books of account. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) granted the depreciation after applying net profit rate as allowed by the Assessing Officer also.

On further appeal :

The assessee was engaged in the contract work of Government of Haryana.

It had not filed the return of income for the relevant assessment year 2007-08.

The Assessing Officer framed the assessment of the assessee for the above assessment year under section 144 and after rejecting the account books adopted the net profit rate of 8 per cent.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

The Tribunal reduced the net profit rate to 7 per cent.

In the mean time the Assessing Officer also levied the penalty upon the assessee under section 271(1)(c).

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the penalty order.

On second appeal:

The assessee was a contractor and its total receipts received during the relevant period were less than Rs. 40,00,000. It declared the net profit rate at 8.15 per cent against 8 per cent of the immediate preceding year. The Assessing Officer applied the net profit at 12.5 per cent which was reduced to 9 per cent by the Commissioner (Appeals). On instant appeal, the assessee contended that its case was squarely covered under section 44AD as the receipts were less than Rs. 40,00,000 and the profit was more than 8 per cent, as such, the addition, sustained by the Commissioner (Appeals) was unjustified.

The assessee filed his income-tax return on estimate basis by adopting flat rate of 10 per cent on gross contract receipts, while the ITO adopted flat rate of 15 per cent thereon. The assessee's revision petition before the Commissioner was unsuccessful.

On writ petition:

The assessee, firm was carrying on the business of executing contracts and works on behalf of the Government. During the accounting period relevant to the assessment year in question, it derived income from one such contract with the Government department. The ITO computed the assessee's income from the contract on estimate basis after rejecting his account books. He estimated the income at 12½ percent on an aggregate amount of Rs. 13,55,819 including the cost of material supplied by the Government Department and also the amounts of the deposit retained by them, after rejecting the assessee's plea that the income was liable to be computed only on the actual cash receipts amounting to Rs. 9,51,000. The AAC upheld the order of the ITO except as regards the rate of profit which he reduced to 11 percent. The Tribunal held that the rate of profit was liable to be applied to the gross receipts and not to the cash receipts only and also that the rate of profit ought reasonably be fixed at 9 percent and not 11 percent.

On reference:

The assessee-firm, a labour contractor, got a contract of labour from Railways for transporting, loading and unloading of sleepers and for stone-ballast supply. For the relevant assessment year, gross profit rate was shown by it at 2.88 per cent as compared to 7 per cent for the previous assessment year. The reasons submitted by the assessee regarding steep fall in gross profit rate were the rise in the rates of diesel and requirement of skilled labour as compared to last year. The Assessing Officer found various faults in the books of assessee like non-maintenance of stock register, unvouched expenditure having been claimed, inter alia, and, therefore, rejected the books of account and, invoked the provisions of section 145. Thereafter, he added a sum to total income of the assessee by adopting gross profit rate as 6.5 per cent. Such addition was confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On appeal :

The assessee, a firm of contractors, executed certain contracts given by the State Government during the assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74. For the assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74, the total gross receipts under the work contract respectively amounted to Rs. 19,41,472 and Rs. 22,86,353 out of which a sum of Rs. 1,27,215 and Rs. 4,82,527 was deducted, being the value of materials supplied by the Government. Since the assessee did not maintain proper account books or any stock book or material issue register, the ITO determined the net profit under the proviso to section 145(1) by applying a flat rate of 10 per cent on the aforesaid gross receipts without excluding the value of the materials supplied by the Government. The AAC, however, directed that for determining the net profit, flat rate was to be applied only on the net receipts. The Tribunal could not ascertain: (i) the actual position regarding the materials obtained from the department and; (ii) whether the same remained under the control of the department or of the assessee. It, accordingly, restored the ITO's order.

On reference:

During the assessment year 1989-90 the assessee, an individual doing construction work, received payments on which he declared a net profit rate of 0.58 per cent after allowing claim for interest and depreciation. Ignoring these two items, the net profit rate worked out to 6.54 per cent. The Assessing Officer, in the absence of record in support of expenses like labour and hazri carriage as also day to day consumption of material, invoked the provisions of section 145 and applied a net profit rate of 10 per cent on total receipts subject to interest and depreciation which was, on appeal, reduced to 9 per cent by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On second appeal :

The assessee was a firm of labour contractors doing loading and unloading work of gunny bags from mandi to godowns and from the godowns to Railway Station and vice versa. It received payment of Rs. 25,40,127 from the FCI for the assessment year 1987-88 and made payments on account of freight charges to the Truck Operators' Union amounting to Rs. 11,45,650 by cheque and Rs. 8,66,130 in cash. The Assessing Officer after examining the evidence produced by the assessee rejected the books of account and applied the rate of profit at 8 per cent on gross receipts amounting to Rs. 25,40,127 and estimated the total income from contract work at Rs. 2,03,000 as against the declared income of Rs. 24,895. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the payments made towards freight as a deduction. On revenue's appeal, the Tribunal dismissed the same.

On reference, the question that arose for consideration was as to whether freight charges paid by the assessee to the Truck Operators' Union were to be deducted from gross receipts and then net profit rate was to be applied to the gross receipts.

During the previous year relevant to the assessment year in question, the assessee-firm was paid certain amount towards the works executed on contract for one H. The AAC divided the amount paid to the assessee under two categories. First was the value of materials supplied by H to the assessee. In the balance amount, the AAC had taken 12½ per cent as profit of the assessee. In regard to the value of materials supplied by H, the AAC assessed profit at the rate of 5 per cent. The Tribunal upheld the AAC's order.

On reference :

The assessee, a railway contractor, was in the field of conversion of old traditional signaling system to the modern colour light signaling system for various divisions of Indian Railways It was also manufacturing railway signaling equipments. The accounts maintained by the assessee were audited by the firm of Chartered Accountants. The assessee returned income which stood revised within the statutory period.

The Assessing Officer noticed that the assessee did not maintain stock register, site-wise expenses vouchers, payment vouchers and attendance or labour control register. Since true profits could not be deduced from the books of account of the assessee, he after applying provisions of section 145(3), estimated its income by applying gross profit rate at 8 per cent and, thus, made trading addition.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the rejection of books of account but directed the Assessing Officer to apply net profit rate of 7 per cent on gross contract receipts and sustained addition accordingly following earlier decision of Tribunal in assessee's own case.

On second appeal:

The assessee civil contractor doing sub-contractor’s work returned his income for the assessment year 1994-95. The percentage of profit as per the said return worked out to 5 per cent as against 7.1 per cent and 8.7 per cent in the assessment years 1992-93 and 1991-92, respectively. During the assessment proceedings the Assessing Officer from a scrutiny of the books of account noticed six payments received by the assessee during the first quarter itself, payments made to a certain person in cash while payment vouchers indicated less than bills received, and other irregularities in payment of labour charges as well as claim of transportation charges, etc. Considering these defects the Assessing Officer rejected the books of account under section 145(2) and applying the provisions of section 44AD estimated the net profits at 8 per cent of the contract receipts.

The matter was taken in appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) by the assessee contending that the Assessing Officer was not justified in applying the provisions of section 44AD inasmuch as the profits and gains of the business in question were lower and supported by proper evidence. The assessee filed a comparative chart of the gross profits and explained the fall in GP rate by arbitrary reduction of agreed rate by his contractor which resulted in reduction of 18.5 per cent in profits of total turnover. He further contended that the labour payments were made as per the norms of the BSP and the assessee had no choice. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s pleas and the estimation of income under section 44AD was held unjustified and the Assessing Officer was directed to accept the income from business returned by the assessee.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee was engaged in business of construction work as a contractor and claimed deduction on account of payments made to sub-contractors. In the absence of evidence to substantiate the said payments, the Assessing Officer made assessment by applying a net profit rate of 10 per cent of the contract receipts, disallowing deduction of the amount assessee paid by assessee to the sub-contractors. This view was upheld by the Commissioner (Appeals) but the Tribunal allowed the claim of the assessee by observing that he had maintained accounts of the sub-contractors in the books of account and had sought appointment of Commission for examination of the sub-contractors, who were located at different stations

On revenue's appeal:

The assessee, a civil contractor, showed his gross receipts less cost of material at Rs. 25 lakhs and disclosed a net profit of 8.4 per cent. The Assessing Officer estimated net profit at 12 per cent on the ground that in the succeeding year the assessee had disclosed a net profit of 12.8 per cent. While doing so, the Assessing Officer did not allow any separate deduction by way of depreciation. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessment order.

On second appeal :

The assessee was a wholesale dealer in solid spices for the relevant assessment year – Gross profit rate disclosed was 6-7 per cent. The ITO found that although the books of account were maintained, no day-to-day stock analysis was found. He also cited a comparable case of a dealer who, had dealt in powder spices as well as in solid spices and had shown 22.2 per cent gross profit for solid spices. The ITO, basing his judgment on the said case, rejected the book version of the profit of the assessee and applied a flat rate of 10 per cent and added a sum of Rs. 31,056.

On appeal, the Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal held that the ITO, on the basis of the case cited, had come to the conclusion that the profit shown by the assessee was low. Therefore, the Tribunal confirmed the addition.

On reference:

During the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1958-59, the assessee-firm executed MES contract for the construction of a part of an air-field and received total payment of Rs. 26,32,361 comprising Rs. 17,02,824 in cash and Rs. 9,29,437 representing value of material supplied free of cost. It included in its tax returns the profit computed only with reference to cash receipts of Rs. 17,02,824 by showing a gross profit rate of 18 per cent. The ITO, however, included the said value of the material also while computing the total income which was pitched up by applying a gross profit rate of 26 per cent after invoking the proviso to section 13, as the account books were not reliable. The AAC confirmed the ITO's order. The Tribunal, however, reduced the profit rate.

On reference :

The assessee-firm was carrying on business of civil contractors. In the course of assessment, the Assessing Officer was of the view that the net profit rate declared by the assessee was very low in the line of civil contractual business. The Assessing Officer issued various notices to the assessee but there was no response from assessee's side. The Assessing officer thus took note of fact that as per provisions of section 44AD, the rate of 8 per cent was applicable to gross receipts, and there was no requirement of maintaining books of account. The Assessing Officer thus applied the GP rate of 8 per cent to the gross contractual receipts after deducting the value of material supplied by the Government and sales-tax from the gross receipts. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the Assessing Officer had neither rejected the books of account nor passed an order under section 144 but had estimated the income at rate of 8 per cent of the gross receipts while passing the order under section 143(3). The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the Assessing Officer had not given any basis for adopting the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts to work out the net income of the assessee even after accepting the plea of the assessee that its business was adversely affected on the death of the working partner. In the circumstances, the Commissioner (Appeals) estimated the income at the rate of 5 per cent of the gross receipts.

On revenue's appeal :

The assessee was a labour contractor. For the assessment year 1986-87, the assessee agreed to the application of GP rate of 10 per cent. The Assessing Officer, however, noticed certain credits in the cash book which he filed to bank with bank withdrawals. The Assessing Officer ultimately concluded that Rs. 1,98,298 represented unexplained cash credits which he treated as income from undisclosed sources. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) holding that the books of account were not of any relevance, deleted the addition made by the Assessing Officer but applied the G.P. rate of 12.5 per cent. The revenue appealed against the deletion of addition of Rs. 1,98,298 and the assessee objected to the application of the rate of 12.5 per cent for calculating profits as against 10 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer.

On appeal:

The assessee, an interior decorator, had declared an income of Rs. 8,80,300 against gross contractual receipts amounting to Rs. 1,97,58,476. He debited job work charges amounting to Rs. 92,55,404 to the profit and loss account. The Assessing Officer required the assessee to produce the five parties to whom job work payments had been made in cash, along with relevant account books and bank pass books for examination. Only one party appeared before the Assessing Officer. After examination the Assessing Officer accepted the job work given to him as genuine. The other four parties were neither produced nor confirmations were filed. Therefore, the Assessing Officer added to the income of the assessee entire job work payments amounting to Rs. 44,14,495 allegedly paid to the parties. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), accepting the alternative plea of the assessee that he would agree to the application of net profit rate of 8 per cent on gross contractual receipts as has been prescribed under section 44AD for computing profits and gains of business of civil construction, applied the provisions of section 44AD and net profit of 8 per cent was applied on gross receipts.

On appeal by the revenue :

The assessee had income from sale of goods and also from money lending business. For the assessment year 1934-35, the assessee produced his books which showed only that he had sold a certain quantity of goods but they did not show as to what profits were obtained by the assessee. Under these circumstances the ITO assessed the profits at a flat rate of 12½ per cent on sale proceeds making allowances for legitimate expenses. The Assistant Commissioner and the commissioner were of the opinion that no further allowance in the shape of expenses could be allowed under the circumstances of the case, because the flat rate adopted by the ITO took into consideration all admissible expenses.

On reference:

The assessee was carrying on business of executing contracts. The assessee was a civil contractor. In the absence of details and there being no proper books of account maintained, the Assessing Officer estimated the assessee's income from contract business at 8 per cent of the gross contract receipts by invoking the provisions of section 44AD.

The assessee-firm was engaged in business as contractors. It filed returns of income in which net income was estimated at 12 per cent of the net bills received from contracts. For the assessment year 1989-90. the ITO completed the assessment under section 143(1) in the assessee’s case, but the assessment order was never served on the assessee. The assessee was engaged in business of civil construction. He filed his return for the assessment year 1998-99 along with audited books of account. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the rejection of books of account and estimation of profit at the rate of 8 per cent.

The assessee constituted 217 flats for weaker sections of society and 22 shops. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal:

The assessee was a building contractor. The Assessing Officer examined the books of account and found various defects. He invoked the provisions of section 145(1) and applied the net profit rate of 10 per cent and had thereafter, allowed deduction for the depreciation. In further appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) applied the net profit rate of 7 per cent. However, no depreciation was allowed by him.

On second appeal :

The assessee, a contractor, was engaged in construction work. For the assessment year 1992-93, the Assessing Officer rejected the book result and applied net profit rate of 10 per cent on gross payment. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the action of the Assessing Officer invoking the provisions of section 145, but reduced the net profit rate to 8 per cent. On cross appeals, the Tribunal held that in the absence of proper books of account, vouchers and registers, the provisions of section 145 could not be applied when their absence itself constituted a defence in the books of account.

For the assessment year 1962-63, the assessee's gross receipts included the cost of materials supplied by the Government for construction of a building. As no books of account were maintained by the assessee, the ITO proceeded with the computation invoking section 145 and applied a flat rate on the gross receipts. In appeal before the AAC, a certificate from the executive engineer, Public Works Department, was produced in support that no profit was allowed to the assessee on the cost of materials supplied by the Government. On reference :

The assessee was a co-operative society engaged in the business of civil construction work. For the relevant assessment year, it had shown the total gross receipt at Rs. 1,63,53,985 which was accepted by the Assessing Officer and had further shown the profit rate at 3.7 per cent. However, during course of assessment proceedings the assessee was asked to furnish books of account, bills/vouchers to verify expenses claimed on certain purchases and as it failed to do so, the Assessing Officer subjected purchases for verification. As purchases were not found completely verifiable the Assessing Officer applied gross profit rate at 7 per cent on total gross receipts of Rs. 1,63,53,985 and, thus, he completed assessment at Rs. 11,44,780. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reduced profit rate to 6 per cent. In the meantime, the Assessing Officer also imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c) upon the assessee holding that its conscious effort not to furnish books of account for verification amounted to concealment of income.
