On second appeal :

held.text:
In the instant case the assessee did not allege that he derived no income at all from any contracts, nor did the assessment proceed definitely on the ground that the accounts were unreliable. The Assistant Commissioner adopted a standard rate for the assessment merely because no separate accounts were available for the accounting year. This was apparently due to the manner in which the accounting were kept. As the assessee failed to produce correct and complete accounts for the accounting year, it was open to the Income-tax Officer to make an assessment to the best of his judgment: vide section 23, read with section 11, of the 1922 Act. The Assistant Commissioner, however, gave no reasons for adopting what he called the usual rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of the assessment, and it was not known how that rate was arrived at. In the circumstances of the case, the point of law emerged for decision was whether in the case of a contract spread over a number of years when accounts for the year under assessment could not be separated, the ITO was legally justified in assessing profits at a flat rate without informing the assessee of the information or evidence on which the rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal.

Accordingly, the petition was accepted and the Commissioner was directed to state the case and refer the point of law to the High Court for decision.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Sardha Ram for the Assessee .

Jagan Nath Aggarwal for the Crown.

In the instant case, the assessee contractor had not been able to satisfy the lower authorities as to what were the terms of the contract with the contractee and in what terms and consideration the materials were supplied by the contractee to the contractor. Furthermore, in the instant case the total amount of profit had to be computed by applying the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act. The rate of profit had also to be determined by applying the proviso to section 13 of the 1922, Act. As the Tribunal had pointed out that if the normal experience and expectation of a contractor as to how the profit would vary, were taken into consideration and in the circumstances where the contractor had not been actually able to satisfy the terms of the contract and where the estimates were to be based by applying the provisions to section 13 of the 1922 Act, it could not be said that the Tribunal was not justified in upholding the decision of the AAC in the manner as it did. In cases where there was clear and unambiguous evidence that there was contract which provided sufficient limit, beyond which the tender could not be quoted and there was a stipulation that the contract was to be quoted at a particular rate, excluding the cost of materials, to be supplied by the contractee, other considerations might apply.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

Undisputably, the assessee placed before the taxation authorities its own account books and they were not found reliable and, therefore, the ITO, the AAC and the Tribunal had acted under the provisions of section 145(1) and the proviso thereto. The flat rate when it was calculated on the basic of available data, could not be called arbitrary or perverse. It had been said by the Tribunal that the firm, from whom the assessee bought manufactured confectionery and sold it made a profit of 19 per cent and the assessee made a profit of 10 per cent which had been charged by the Tribunal and against which there was no grievance. Therefore, at least up to 19 per cent there was clear evidence about the flat rate being just. If the Tribunal made it 20 per cent one could not say it capricious, conjectural or based on irrelevant or no evidence. A question relating to the flat rate was a pure question of fact. Although from the language of the questions which were asked to be referred to the High Court the grievance of enhancement was there yet it was not pressed. Therefore, it was not necessary to enter into the question whether the tax was enhanced because it was factually incorrect to say that the total liability of the assessee was increased. It was not necessary to enter into the argument whether the question arose from the order of the Tribunal or not because clearly no question of law arose in the instant case.

Note: The case was decided against the assessee.

There was no reason for the Commissioner (Appeals) to enhance the rate of profit to 10 per cent. The books of assessee, though defective, were not such which could not enable the assessing authorities to determine a fair rate of profit. Moreover, the assessee-firm itself also had its own history which could be a guide. Therefore, there was no reason for the Commissioner (Appeals) to rely on any other case and also to determine the rate by generalising that the normal rate of profit in construction business was 10 per cent.

Keeping the past history of assessee in view, it would be fair and meet the ends of justice if a net profit rate of 6 per cent, subject to depreciation and interest, was applied.

N.M. Ranka and J.K. Ranka for the Appellant. G.C. Bansal for the Respondent.

to be rational and is to be based on an honest guesswork for which, some valid basis is available to the ITO. The order involves exercise of 'judgment' by the Officer. A fair estimate of the income has to be made. Further, the Jurisdictional High Court held that Guesswork is inevitable; but, it cannot be wild guess; the guesswork should have a reasonable nexus to the available material and the circumstances of each case. [Para 10.3]

■ Now coming to the present facts of the case, it is found that the assessee is a civil contractor and the entire contract receipts were from government departments/PWD as can be verified from form 26AS and all the proceeds were received through proper banking channels on which the tax had been deducted at source. On perusal of the assessment order, we also noticed that in absence of any details/evidences filed by the assessee, the AO estimated the income @ 15% by holding that once the profit is determined on estimated basis, the assessee is not entitled to any further deduction as per provisions of section 30 to 43D and by holding that when the net profit rate to gross receipts is determined on estimation basis, no further deduction is to be allowed. The AO while applying the net profit @15% was guided by the provisions of section 44AD only & held that once the profit is determined on estimated basis, the assessee is not entitled to any further deduction as per provisions of section 30 to 43D as contained in section 44AD. It is the considered opinion that the AO estimated the profit of the assessee @15% without reference to any material gathered. The AO should not make his best judgment assessment on mere suspicion, impulsively or arbitrarily. The best judgment assessment must be based on the material on record which could be gathered by the AO on proper investigation. In the present case, the assessee's entire contractual receipts were from Government department & all proceeds were received through banking channel & thus the assessee's estimation of the net profit @ 6.06% of the turnover is higher than the rate of 6% prescribed u/s 44AD. It is viewed that flat 15% income on turnover is highly unjustified. However, it is the considered opinion that net profit rate of 7% in civil contract business especially when all the contract receipts were received through proper banking channel on which the tax has been deducted at source is a reasonable one and accordingly the AO is directed to recompute the net profit of the assessee @7% of the total turnover declared by the assessee i.e. Rs.17.40 crores. Accordingly, this ground of Appeal of the assessee is partly allowed. [Para 10.4]

■

Since the grounds raised as well as issues involved in this appeal is exactly similar to that appeal in ITA No. 161/Bang/2026 except change in figures, the findings & result of ITA No. 161/Bang/2026 for the AY 2013-14 will mutatis-mutandis apply to this appeal also. [Para 15]

the observations, it was to be held that when the Assessing Officer offered to apply a net profit rate of more than 11 per cent, the assessee had only alternatively given a counter-proposal which, in fact, was not acted upon by the Department and as such, such an offer made thereof by the appellant was of no consequence and the same did not bind the assessee in any manner and, accordingly, it could not be validly held that the instant assessment was an agreed assessment. Having come to the conclusion that the proposal made by the assessee was not a binding proposal and as such not an agreed assessment, the next question for consideration was as to what could be the reasonable profit that could have been applied on the basis of material on record and the submissions of the parties. On that issue, the observations of the Accountant Member as well as the findings for arriving at the conclusion for application of profit rate of 8 per cent were contained in his order. The Bench fully agreed with the findings as well as the observations contained in the orders of the Accountant Member. As pointed out by the Accountant Member, the Assessing Officer himself had analysed each and every transaction with reference to the reply furnished by the assessee and he was of the firm opinion that the assessee could justify only a few transactions and the Assessing Officer, however, did not bring any material with respect to any remaining transactions with which he was not satisfied though admittedly the reply thereto was duly furnished by the assessee; that merely because some of the sub-contractors could not be produced at the relevant time could not lead to the conclusion of application of exorbitant rate of 11 per cent, that too without giving a finding that the expenditure so claimed was not for business necessity or that it did not relate wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business or the carrying on of business as required under section 37; and that, in fact, the Assessing Officer did ask the assessee through various queries to give explanation but he had not stated basis of its estimate nor given chance to the assessee to rebut basis for or the application of arriving at the precision rate of 11 per cent.

As observed by the Accountant Member, assessment is a quasi-judicial proceeding in which the personal will or rough estimation does not have any place, that the Assessing Officer is bound to disclose the mental process through which he arrived at a particular figure of income as his orders are being subjected to appeal and, therefore, should be speaking one. The Accountant Member observed that it was evident from the past history of the appellant that never a profit rate of more than 7 per cent was applied in the case of the appellant, more particularly when two of the past assessments had already been completed as a consequence of the search and incriminating documents as alleged in the year under appeal were also available with the Assessing Officer in those assessments; that keeping in view the peculiar circumstances like nature of business, expenses on public issue, etc., in the year under appeal, the assessee’s own history for the earlier years, over all facts, findings and circumstances of the case, suppression of profits having not been established, allegations having not been proved, explanation rendered by the appellant and the legislative history, that there was no justification in applying or confirming net profit rate of 11 per cent and that the ad-hoc application of 8 per cent net profit rate subject to allowability of depreciation and interest thereon in the case of the assessee was justified.

The department referred to the statement of ‘S’, in reply to a query as to what was the income of the company from the contract work usually. He replied that it was 10 per cent to 15 per cent to the total receipts. That statement was taken at the time of search without confronting ‘S’ with the books of account or any contract work specifically. The question posed to him was not in respect of the specific income of the year under consideration nor do the income from total contract work of the assessee. There was no clarification sought by the authorized officer or by the Assessing Officer as to the fact whether the said ‘S’ was stating so in respect of any of a single venture forming part of the one and individual business of the appellant comprised of several contract works secured by it, for which the assessee had maintained a combined profit and loss account or it was only a hypothetical calculation. The affidavit filed before the Assessing Officer of the same person was also not found false. The statement so given before the authorized officer was, thus, not a conclusive statement as the same was not based on any material on record but was only on approximation basis and not relevant to the facts of the case. The statement also did not quantify any correct rate as to whether it should be 10 per cent or 11 per cent or any higher rate. Thus, the statement so given by ‘S’ was of no credence and the same could not be used against the assessee for applying a profit rate of 11 per cent, which was not supported by any material or basis and was contrary to the facts of the case.

There is no reason to interfere with the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals), affirmed by the Tribunal, scaling down the net profit to 8 per cent against 12 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer. The reasons assigned by the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal are clear and cogent and even otherwise no two contractors can have a similar rate of profit. The profit of a contractor would necessarily depend upon various factors like place of execution of the contract, the accessibility of labour, raw material etc. and would, therefore, vary from contractor to contractor. The assessee in the instant case, was admittedly laying optical fiber cables etc. in a remote border area of Jammu and Kashmir. [Para 3]

The issue before this Court in CIT v. Chopra Bros. India (P.) Ltd. [2001] 252 ITR 412/119 Taxman 866 and Girdhari Lal v. CIT [2002] 256 ITR 318/[2001] 119 Taxman 863 was with regard to deduction to be made on account of depreciation from the gross receipts while applying net profit rate. It was held on the basis of a circular issued by the Board, which was binding on the revenue that the gross receipts to which net profit rate is to be applied shall be determined after giving allowance on account of depreciation. [Para 7]

In view of the above, no substantial question of law arises in the instant appeal. Accordingly, dismissed. [Para 9]

As far the ground taken by the assessee in his cross objection regarding the application of the rate of 12.5 per cent by the Commissioner (Appeals) against the rate of 10 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer was concerned, looking to the fact that the assessee was a labour contractor, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not fair and reasonable to apply the GP rate of 12.5 per cent against the rate of 10 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer which was also agreed to by the assessee. Hence, it was fair and reasonable to apply a net rate of 10 per cent in the case of the assessee while calculating the profits.

As regards the addition of Rs. 1,98,295 made by the Assessing Officer by invoking the provisions of section 68, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) did not suffer from any illegality or infirmity regarding his conclusion that the deposits as well as withdrawals of contract receipts had not been properly reflected in the books of account and as such, no reliance could be placed on the bank account. Hence, the Commissioner (Appeals) was fully justified in deleting the addition of Rs. 1,98,298 made by the Assessing Officer.

Sudhir Sehgal for the Appellant. S.C. Pahwa for the Respondent.

Even in respect of the main contract, in respect of civil contracts 8 per cent is taken normally as the income earned out of such contracts. When such a contractor gives the work to a sub-contractor normally about 5 per cent is taken as the income of the contractor. In the instant case, it works out to 6.4 per cent. The tenor of the order of the Commissioner under section 263 discloses that because the net profit shown in the profit and loss account was only Rs. 4.63 lakhs which works out to 0.12 per cent, the proceedings are initiated. Factually it is incorrect. In this circumstances, in the absence of any other material which was before the Commissioner, he was not justified in recording a finding that the assessing authority has not applied its mind, not verified the expenses, not verified the receipts and looked into the book and, therefore, a case for interference under section 263 is made out, cannot be accepted. The Tribunal by a considered order rightly set aside the order passed by the Commissioner relying on several judgments on the question after appreciating the entire evidence on record. Under these circumstances, the instant Court do not finds no justification to interfere with the said order. [Para 8]

In the instant case the assessee as sub-contractor to execute the civil construction works awarded by the principals, which was a small part of the projects executed by the principals. On the contract receipts, the principals had also deducted the tax under section 194C. Besides, the assessee was also engaged in the business of trading of sarees. It was also a fact that the assessee filed duly audited profit and loss account and balance sheet along with its annexure. It also produced the audited books of account, bills/vouchers and bank statements before the Assessing Officer as admitted by him in the assessment order. Besides, it further produced all the details and explanations called for by the Assessing Officer from time to time. It also produced labour registers before the Assessing Officer. However, he was of the opinion that the said registers had not been maintained in a conventional manner and according to him, there were no signatures or thumb impressions of all the recipients. Because of the aforesaid observations, the Assessing Officer rejected the audited books of account of the assessee and estimated the net profit. The Assessing Officer gave the examples of net profit earned by three companies and, thereafter, he relied on the provisions of section 11AD and estimated the net profit at the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts. Now the assessee argued that the estimation of net profit at the rate of 8 per cent by relying on provisions of section 44AD was totally incorrect and without any basis for the reason that the assessee was sub-contractor and its profit margin was low in comparison to the contractors. Further, the Assessing officer had compared the profit of the assessee with the companies whose turnover and business paraphernalia was huge in comparison to the assessee. Further, the assessee had executed the part of work of civil construction for these companies and, therefore, it was not correct to compare the profit of those companies with the profit margin of the assessee. In fact the profit margin of those companies was also less than the margin which had been estimated by the Assessing Officer in the case of assessee. In the case of assessee as per audited books of account, the net profit margin for assessment years 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10 and 2010-11 was 1.94 per cent, 0.67 per cent, 0.20 per cent and 0.09 per cent respectively. Now, the assessee argued that the Assessing Officer had failed to appreciate that the profit margins of contractors and sub-contractors could not be same. In the assessment order he had worked out the average profit margins in the case of those three companies at 5.93 per cent, 6.15 per cent and 5.19 per cent respectively and in the case of assessee he had estimated the profit at the rate of 8 per cent, whereas, in the case of assessee the profit margin would be much less than in these companies being a sub-contractor of these companies. [Para 5]

In view of the above factual position and comparative figures given by assessee of its principal, wherein the net profit was ranging from 5.19 per cent to 6.15 per cent, it was held that definitely there would be lower profit in the case of sub-contractor, i.e., the assessee and, hence, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly estimated the net profit rate at 4 per cent. Accordingly, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) and this issue of revenue's appeal was dismissed. [Para 6]

The assessee did not satisfy the Assessing Officer with regard to correctness of the vouchers for the purpose of claiming deduction on account of labour charges as well as cartage expenses. The onus was upon the assessee to prove the genuineness of the payments made on account of labour charges and cartage expenses, because the assessee claimed deduction of the same amount. However, the assessee did not discharge the onus of proving genuineness of the claim of the expenses. The Assessing Officer also held that the assessee had not maintained proper muster roll as to where the labourers were employed and for which particular work they were engaged. Considering the finding of the authorities below, there was no merit in the case of the assessee with regard to the rejection of the books of account with the aid of section 145(2). The orders of the authorities below, to that extent, were to be confirmed. [Para 29]

As regards the question as to whether net profit rate of 12.5 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer was justified in the matter, the assessee had shown the gross receipts of Rs. 26,74,885 and the net profit declared was at the rate of 0.48 per cent. Though it was case of the assessment year 1992-93, and the provisions of section 44AD were strictly inserted in the Act with effect from 1-4-1994, yet the same could be a guideline for the purpose of applying a particular net profit rate in the case of civil contractor even in earlier years. The assessee was also civil contractor engaged in construction work taken on contract and the gross receipts of the assessee were below Rs. 40 lakhs. Therefore, the net profit rate of 12.5 per cent applied by the authorities below in the case of the assessee was excessive and exorbitant. Accordingly, the application of net profit rate was to be modified from 12.5 per cent to 8 per cent on the gross receipt shown by the assessee. The Assessing Officer should work out the profit accordingly. [Para 30]

As a result, the appeal of the assessee was partly to be allowed. [Para 31]

A bare perusal of the findings recorded by the Assessing Officer would indicate that he had applied the principles determining the profit vide section 44AD, whereas the aforesaid provision was not at all applicable in the case of assessee in the relevant assessment years. This factual position was not being disputed by either of the parties. That being so, the question arose as to what should be the profit rate for the purpose of determining the profit accrued or gained by the parties. Since the Assessing Officer, had not dealt with this question independent of section 44AD, the rate of profit could not be upheld. [Para 3]

So far as the determination of profit of 5 per cent by the Commissioner (Appeals) was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) had also not given any reason nor any material was placed before the Commissioner (Appeals), or for that matter before the Assessing Officer for arriving at a conclusion about the rate of profit. Merely on assumption that since the assessee was performing the work for the PWD and as the contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under supervision of the PWD authorities, the rate of profit would be low or merely because the turnover exceeded Rs. 10 lakhs, it would incur more expenses, the aforesaid rate of profits could not have been arrived at. Neither the Commissioner (Appeals) nor the Tribunal had taken into consideration the relevant material or facts which might be necessary for arriving at such a conclusion. [Para 4]

The rate of profit cannot be assumed merely on assumptions or surmises and conjectures. It is the first liability of the assessee to produce such records, evidence and material so as to substantiate his plea about the rate of profit that he claims and in case the books of account have been rejected , the onus shifts on to the Assessing Officer to determine the rate of profit on consideration of the material which may be brought before him or even on making such inquiry, which may be necessary and which may include the requirement of having any information from the assessee also during the course of determination of such rate of profit, namely, during the assessment proceedings. In no case, simply because the turnover was more than Rs. 40 lakhs or the assessee was performing civil construction work for Public Works Department, neither the rate of profits could be determined nor it could be taken to be less nor it could be reduced nor could be arrived at any presumptions. [Para 5]

Since the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) as also the Tribunal had not recorded any finding based on any material, and the findings recorded were merely based on surmises and conjectures or on purely guess work and imagination of the authorities, as it had not been brought to the notice of the High Court that any such rate of profit could be assessed under the rules or any law in that manner, the findings of rate of profit could not be sustained and were liable to be set aside and the matter deserved to be remanded to the assessing authority for re-determination thereof. [Para 6]

EDITOR’S NOTE

As regards the assessee’s claim as in its case best judgment assessment was made after rejection of books of account, it was entitled to the benefit of section 40(b)(iv ) and (v), namely, on the salary and interest paid to the partners, the revenue’s case was that whether the assessee had put forward the case before the Assessing Officer that the assessee was a registered partnership firm, which was working under the registered partnership deed; that in the partnership deed there was any clause for payment of salary; and that the partners were the working partners. It was held that the specific case of the assessee before the assessing authority that it was registered partnership firm and was having registered partnership deed, the partners were working partners and they were entitled to salary and interest, as per terms of the deed in accordance with section 40(b). In the absence of any material having brought by the revenue in rebuttal and more so when no such plea was ever taken or raised in the appeal, as also no substantial question of law had been framed in that regard, the aforesaid revenue's plea was bound to fail.

D.D. Chopra for the Appellant. Rajan Roy for the Respondent.

The main case of the revenue was that the assessee should have disclosed profits on the receipts of contract on the basis of percentage completion method of accounting. As against that it was the case of the assessee that the initial price for which the contract was awarded was later on found to be unreliable as it was increased to 29 per cent, therefore, the percentage completion method was not applicable even according to the accounting standard AS-7.The assessee had never shown any profit out of the contract and the loss shown by the assessee was accepted by the lower authorities in the immediately preceding year and succeeding year. Thus, according to the accounts, the assessee had never earned profit from this contract. The accounts of the assessee were audited and it was not the case of the revenue that the assessee did not furnish details regarding accounts maintained by it. No defects whatsoever had been found in the account books maintained by the assessee. What can be assessed as income under the Act, is income. If there is an existence of income, then only it can be estimated. Therefore, not going into the controversy whether the accounting standard AS-7 was properly employed by the assessee or not, it would be considered that whether Assessing Officer was justified in assessing the net profit of the assessee from such contract at the rate of 10 per cent. There was no substance in the argument of the revenue that the assessee was under an obligation to maintain its account on the basis of the accounting standard AS-7, as the said accounting standard was not mandatory for the assessee for the year under consideration. Even if the percentage of completion method was held to be applicable to the case of the assessee, then the question would arise that what would be the basis for estimate. It is well-established law that the estimate made must be honest and fair. There must exist reasonable nexus between the available material and the estimate. Thus, the only question for determination arose whether there existed some material on the basis of which it could be said that application of net profit rate of 10 per cent was appropriate. It was the contention of the assessee that it had incurred losses while performing the contract. No material had been brought on record by the Assessing Officer that such contention of the assessee was contrary to the facts. Addition had been made without indicating any material or basis on which it could be decided that application of net profit rate of 10 per cent was appropriate. On the contrary, material was on the record to show that the assessee had incurred loss in performing such a contract. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was not justified in rejecting the books of account by invoking the provisions of section 145(3) without bringing on record any cogent reasons and infirmities in the maintenance of books of account of the assessee and further estimating the net profit. [Para 13]

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had decided the issue correctly.

■

The Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee had earned net profit at the rate of 1.25 per cent during the year as against the net profit of 1.23 per cent in earlier years. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) has determined to resort to estimation of profit at the rate of 8 per cent of contract receipt of ₹ 33.75 lakhs and an addition of ₹ 2.70 lakhs (₹ 33.75 lakhs × 8 per cent) was made. In respect of trading business, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee has shown gross profit of 4.09 per cent last year and same rate of 4.09 per cent applied on the turnover of trading business during the year and addition of ₹ 1.55 crores was determined in trading business. The Commissioner (Appeals) had taken cognizance of actual business predominantly carried during the year i.e. trading in electrical goods and it compared the gross profit derived in earlier years from the very same trading activity. He has also taken cognizance of the fact that the assessee had started sub-contract work related to civil work only during the year earning a meagre turnover of ₹ 33.75 lakhs and the same was not prevalent in earlier years. There was no infirmity in the said adoption of profit by the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 34]

It appeared that the figure of sales was worked out by taking a rough average of the business of the assessee for the last ten years. Past assessments therefore provided the material for the fixing of the sales. The word 'evidence' as used in sub-section (2) of section 23 of the 1922 Act obviously cannot be confined to direct evidence. This word is comprehensive enough to cover circumstantial evidence. The circumstances alluded to above, provided material for fixing the sales during the year under review.

In the year 1933-34, the assessee himself showed that he had made a profit of 15 per cent on the sales. There was, therefore, material for the ITO to come to the conclusion that a flat rate of 15 per cent was a reasonable rate of profit in instant case. The rate of profit so far as retail trade in caps was concerned, according to the ITO, was 25 per cent.

Having regard to aforesaid circumstances, it could be concluded that there was evidence justifying the rejection of the accounts and justifying the fixing of the sales and applying a flat rate of 15 per cent profits under section 23(3) of 1922 Act.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

In the instant case there was material before the Tribunal on which its finding could be based: the assessee's representative had admitted before the AAC that full quantitative details in respect of the stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of that contract might not be available. In the circumstances, recourse to estimating the profits on the contract was inevitable. He, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 10,000 as against Rs. 26,434 added by the ITO. If the assessee wished to displace the AAC's estimate it was open to him to adduce evidence in support of its claim that the consumption of stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 was fully justified. This the assessee apparently did not do. For the subsequent year 1960-61 the assessee itself declared a net profit rate of 9.9% as against 9% declared in the assessment year in question. It could not be disputed that this was additional material which the Tribunal could take into consideration as it did. There was thus material before the Tribunal on which its estimate was based. The Tribunal's decision was, therefore, in conformity with the decision in the case of CIT v. Maharajadhiraj of Darbhanga [1933] 1 ITR 94 (P.C.).

The Tribunal was therefore justified in holding that the proviso to section 13 was applicable and there was material before it to sustain the aforesaid addition.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of revenue.

After coming to the conclusion that the trading results were not prone to verification, the Assessing Officer was left with only one alternative to estimate the income of the assessee in the most appropriate and reasonable manner. In such type of cases, the net profit rate or gross profit rate could be applied or the Assessing Officer could adopt any method of estimation and work out the income from profession or business. But the method adopted must be reasonable and logical. In all civil contract cases, if accounts are not maintained or defective accounts are maintained, a net rate of 10 per cent is applied which was admitted by the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order. In those cases neither depreciation nor interest nor any other expenditure debitable to profit and loss account are separately allowed. By allowing depreciation and interest, net profit rate of approximately 3.5 per cent had been applied consequent to the order of the Commissioner (Appeals). The rate itself was absolutely abnormal. There was no evidence on record whatsoever that there were abnormal conditions prevailing with the assessee to earn such a low net profit by executing the contract. Once net rate was applied it was not open to the Assessing Officer to allow any other claim debited to profit and loss account. Depreciation and interest were definitely items which were debited in profit and loss account before the net profit was arrived at. It could have been the case of the appellant to justify the net profit rate shown as .27 per cent or to justify the net profit rate applied by the Commissioner (Appeals) at 3.5 per cent approximately. But no such discussion was available on record. The logical conclusion of the circular of the CBDT regarding claim of depreciation that in case profits were estimated, the same should be made subject to the allowance of depreciation and the assessee should file complete details of the claim of depreciation. One has again to look into the power given by the statute to the Assessing Officer when he invoked proviso to section 145(1). The first proviso to section 145(1) gives power to the Assessing Officer to decide whether or not income can properly be deduced from the accounts maintained by the assessee, even if the accounts are correct and complete.

Keeping in view the law laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. British Paints India Ltd. [1991] 188 ITR 44/ 54 Taxman 499 the Assessing Officer has to adopt rationale and reasonable method in arriving at the estimate of income, after he gives finding that the accounts maintained by the appellant are neither prone to verification nor reliable. He can use his own method but his method should be rationale and reasonable. In the case of the assessee he had used rationale and reasonable method. The application of net rate is directly dependent on the net rate shown by other cases in the line of the business. Other cases of contractors are being applied net rate of profit without giving them advantage of depreciation some contractors debit various items which relate to profit & loss or trading account expenditure and claimed 100% of depreciation. This method creates an abnormal situation in the net profit. The Assessing Officer had, therefore, taken a proper course by ignoring depreciation and the interest and applied net rate of 10%. The second positive feature in the assessment of the ITO related to the observation that the net profit rate of the person who used heavy machinery was going to be more than the net profit of a person who was not using the mechanical aid for execution of civil work.

Hence, there was no infirmity in the method adopted by the Assessing Officer. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was reversed and the order of the Assessing Officer maintained.

It is noted that the audited financial statements were available before the Assessing Officer but without disputing the sales turnover during the year he disallowed the total expenses including the purchase of material towards contract work undertaken by the assessee during the year. When the matter travelled before the Commissioner (Appeals) he observed in the impugned order that the net profit rate for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 disclosed by the assessee in its regular audited books of account is 0.22 per cent, 0.17 per cent and 0.25 per cent. Even during the course of scrutiny proceeding for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 net profit rate applied by the Assessing Officer was 0.16 per cent, 0.93 per cent and 0.18 per cent. Though the Commissioner (Appeals) appreciated the fact that undisputed revenue just could not have come without incurring an expenditure, but based on his observation that the purchase made by the assessee in the past were in dispute and genuineness of the same had not been proved, the Commissioner (Appeals) computed the net profit applying the rate of 8 per cent on the total revenue for the year of Rs. 87.46 crores.[Para 9]

The revenue has challenged the relief given by the Commissioner (Appeals) and the assessee is agitating for the higher net profit rate applied by the Commissioner (Appeals) and ignoring past net profit track of the assessee.[Para 9.1]

It is found that the net profit rate of 0.4 per cent has been accepted by this Tribunal in one of the sister concern of the assessee. It is also found that the net profit declared by the assessee for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 was within the range of 0.2 per cent to 0.29 per cent and even in the scrutiny proceedings the revenue authorities in assessee's own case have estimated net profit below the rate of 1 per cent so by no means estimating the net profit at the rate of 8 per cent could be justified, looking to the fact that there is no change of business during all these years, books of account are duly audited, no specific error has been pointed out by both lower authorities.[Para 9.3]

One more important fact which is relevant in the instant appeal is that subsequent to the assessment proceeding search and seizure operation was carried out at 'B' Group on 27-4-2017 and subsequent to search notice under section 153C were issued to the assessee company also and the assessments were framed under section 143(3) for assessment years 2012-13 to 2014-15 on 27-12-2019 assessing the income only to the extent of additions confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals). In other words the grounds raised by the revenue will have no merit in these cases because revenue authorities have themselves accepted the income determined by the Commissioner (Appeals) giving part relief given in the grounds raised by the assessee. Certainly another fact which cannot be ignored is that there was a complete non-compliance on the part of the assessee, thereby, not allowing the Assessing Officer to examine the documents of sales, purchase and expenditure thoroughly.[Para 9.4]

Therefore, under the given facts and circumstances of the case, respectfully following the decision of this Tribunal in the case of ITO v. B.B.C. Project Services (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No.1669 (Kol.) of 2016, dated 30-11-2018] consistent business of contract work carried out by the assessee and the net profit rate offered in the financial statements and being fair to both the parties, it is viewed that application of net profit rate of 0.6 per cent on the turnover of contract business during the year i.e. Rs. 87.46 crores will meet the end to justice. It is accordingly ordered and the revenue is directed to compute the net profit for the year at the rate of 0.6 per cent. Further, it is made clear that this net profit rate of 0.6 per cent will take care of all the business expenses including interest and depreciation incurred for the purpose of running contract business and related to the turnover of Rs. 87.46 crores. Accordingly assessee will get part relief on this common issue and revenue fails to succeed.[Para 9.5]

The firm is the proprietary concern of one of the managing trustees. As per the stand of the revenue, the payments made to the said firm is hit by the provisions of section 13(2)(c) read with section 13(3). The assessee has placed on record a copy of the order of the co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in Dy. DIT(Exemptions) v. Sri Vekkaliamman Educational & Charitable Trust [2013] 40 taxmann.com 478 (Chennai) in the assessee's own case for the assessment year 2009-10, wherein similar issue has been decided in favour of the assessee in which it was held that the construction contract has been awarded to the firm on the basis of open bid. Since, the firm quoted lowest rates, the contract was awarded to the firm. The Commissioner (Appeals) has given a categoric finding that in cases of civil construction contracts, especially were not proper books are maintained the Act recognizes normal profit margins at 8 per cent. Whereas, the firm has earned a profit of 5.8 per cent which is very reasonable. Therefore since, the contract was awarded on competitive basis and the profit earned is reasonable, the provisions of section 13(2)(c) are not violated. [Para 7]

In the assessment year under consideration, the assessee has paid Rs. 5.02 Crores and the firm has allegedly earned net profit of Rs. 21.51 Lakhs. The profit earned by the firm is 4.28 per cent which is quite reasonable. For the reasons stated in the order of Tribunal re-produced herein above, the present issue in appeal of the revenue is dismissed. [Para 8]

the head under which the amount is entered in the account books of the assessee concerned.

It is thus, substance of the contract which matters and if, the agreement between the parties right from the beginning is that certain materials are to be supplied by the other party to the contract, that is, the Government department, or the authority concerned, then it is obvious that the contract was entered into on the footing that no profit would be made by the building contractor in respect of the supply of those materials. In the instant case, the contract between the parties, namely, the assessee and the railway authorities, was that cement and iron had to be supplied by the railway authorities for the execution of the work and no accounting of the cost of these materials was to be done while making out a bill in respect of the contract payment. Under these circumstances it must be held that since this particular contract falls in the first category where at the time of entering into the contract the quotation did not take into account the materials like iron and cement which were to be supplied by the railway authorities, all calculations at the time of entering into the contract were made on the footing that iron and cement were to be supplied by the railway authorities and it was obvious that these items could not be included in the total receipts of the assessee for the purpose of arriving at the figure of net profits by working out the percentages of that total figure.

The Tribunal fixed the figure of 10 per cent of the total receipts only in view of the fact that the cost of the materials supplied by the railway authorities was to be taken into consideration at the time of fixing the receipts. Since it was held in the instant case that the cost of these materials supplied by the railway authorities was not to be taken into consideration at the time of determining the receipts in the light of the facts and circumstances of this particular case, it was but fair that the matter should be left to the Tribunal to decide as to which particular percentage it would apply to the total receipts in order to arrive at the net profits earned by the assessee

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The assessee is not right in his contention that whenever an assessment is made by applying a flat rate of profit to the declared turnover or receipts, which is higher than the rate adopted by the assessee in the return of income, there can be no inference that the assessee concealed his profits. [Para 9]

The number of discrepancies and irregularities listed by the special auditor in his report which are reproduced in the assessment order bear testimony to the fact that the books of account maintained by the assessee were wholly unreliable. If they were so, there can be no sanctity attached to the figure of gross contract receipts on which the assessee estimated 3 per cent as its income. It is true that the Assessing Officer did not enhance the figure of gross receipts but that is not because he gave a clean chit to the books of account allegedly maintained by the assessee; he could not have given a clean chit in the face of the defects, discrepancies and irregularities reported by the special auditor. In order to take care of those discrepancies he resorted to a much higher estimate of the profits by adopting 11 per cent on the gross contract receipts. He gave due opportunity to the assessee to explain the discrepancies and also to show why the profit rate of 11 per cent cannot be adopted but these opportunities were not availed of by the assessee. He also has recorded in the assessment order that the assessee was permitted to inspect the seized documents and was given photocopies of the desired documents. This is not denied by the assessee. In these circumstances, the mere fact that the estimate was reduced by the Tribunal to 8 per cent would in no way take away the guilt of the assessee or explain its failure to prove that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on its part. It appears that the assessee was taking a chance - sitting on the fence - despite the fact that there was a search towards the close of the relevant accounting year in the course of which incriminating documents were found. It appears that the intention of the assessee was to take a risk and disclose a lesser income than what it actually earned and rely upon the minor variations in the rate of profits adopted by the taxing authorities and the Tribunal as a defence in the penalty proceedings. The plea - accepted by the Tribunal - that the assessee agreed to be assessed at 11 per cent of the gross receipts only "to buy peace" and "avoid litigation" cannot be accepted in view of the judgment of the Supreme Court in MAK Data (P.) Ltd. [2013] 358 ITR 593/38 taxmann.com 448. The Tribunal, was in error in upholding the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelling the penalty. Accordingly, the substantial questions of law is answered against the assessee and in favour of the Revenue. [Para 12]

As per provisions of section 158BB, the block assessment is to be made based on evidence before the Assessing Officer. The word 'Evidence' has to be construed in a comprehensive manner and it includes all circumstantial evidence also. The material or evidence with the Assessing Officer on which assessment may be based is not confined to direct testimony by witnesses. Such evidence need not only be evidence found during the course of search but also material gathered by him. The Assessing Officer was not fettered by the Technical rules of evidence and the like and he may act on material which may not strictly speaking, be accepted as an evidence in the Court of law. It may be circumstantial evidence or assessment based on the preponderance of probabilities judged by human conduct. For this purpose, the past history of the case, and general market conditions will constitute relevant material for the purpose of assessment. For the purpose of block assessment under Chapter XIV-B, in view of amendment by Finance Act, 2002 to section 158BC(b) of the Income-tax Act which is effective retrospectively from 1-7-1995 wherein there is insertion of section 145 for the purpose of determining the undisclosed income. As per amendment to section 158BC(b ), the section 145 could also be invoked by Assessing officer for determining the undisclosed income. [Para 37]

However, it is to be made clear that if no material was found during the search which could show suppression of income, no estimation of undisclosed income of block period by resorting to section 145 could be made. In other words, where there is a material, such an estimation of income can be made. It is not necessary that addition should be limited to what is found during the search. [Para 38]

Adverting to the facts of the instant case, assessment was made by applying the flat rate of net profit at the rate of 10 per cent for the Assessment years 1998-99 and 1999-2000 for which no reasons has been given except stating that considering the nature of contract works executed by the assessee-company and the percentage of income admitted for the assessment years 1996-97, 1997-98 and 2000-01 and also for the percentage of income admitted by other contractors viz., M/s Prasad & Co. (PW) and M/s SEW Construction Ltd., income was estimated before depreciation at the rate of 10 per cent for the assessment years 1998-99, 1999-2000, 2001-02 and for the period 1-4-2001 to 20-12-2001 and treated the difference of income estimated and the income admitted as undisclosed income of the assessee-company for such assessment year. The Commissioner (Appeals) though held that for the assessment year 1998-99, income declared at the rate of 9.08 per cent before depreciation and 8.5 per cent for the assessment year 1999-2000 as reasonable. However, he has given different finding for the assessment year 2001-02 and for the period from 1-4-2001 to 20-12-2001. The assessee explained the reasons for low profit as to that the company has been in the construction industry for more than two decades. The company for quite some years focused its core activity in civil works consisting of mostly industrial/housing structures. Besides such civil contracts, the company diversified its activities into cement industry, wind power, manufacture of cylinders and other incidental jobs. Heavy losses resulted in closure of its cement division during financial year 1999-2000. The company also started focusing on infrastructure projects because of its line of business in construction and contracts. Hence, in the initial years, the company had undertaken some of the smaller projects especially the road works outside the State of Andhra Pradesh. To intrude into the competitive section like this, and to withstand the obvious competition from the established giants and multinationals, obviously the company had to quote the price in tenders either without a profit or with nominal profit. During the financial years 2000-01 and 2001-02 (up to 31-12-2001) the company has incurred losses in certain major projects. [Para 39]

In so far as the action of the income-tax authorities in rejecting the book results by invoking section 145(3) is concerned, the same is not adjudicated on account of the submission of the assessee. The assessee has canvassed for adoption of the net profit ratio of 8 per cent on contract receipts in order to estimate the income from the business of contracting. Ostensibly there is no hard and fast rule for estimating income from the business of civil Construction. However, section 44AD prescribes estimation from contract business in cases specified there at the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts. Section 44AD covers cases of civil construction, where the gross receipts from contract business do not exceed Rs. 40 lakhs. Of course, the assessee does not fall within the prescription of section 44AD, as its contract receipts exceed Rs. 40 lakhs. However, the presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD reflects a legislative approved rate of net profit, which can be considered as fair and reasonable to estimate income from contract business in cases like that of the instant assessee, where the books of account are not found reliable by the Assessing Officer. Moreover in the assessee's own case in the assessment year 2010-11 the determination of income from contracting business is also proximate to the rate of net profit of 8 per cent contained in section 44AD. Therefore, considering the overall facts and circumstances of the case, it would be just and proper that the income from contract business of the assessee be estimated at 8 per cent of the gross receipts and the addition be worked out accordingly. [Para 7]

from facts or even as a guess work it has not been arrived at by an honest exercise of judgment, it may be disturbed by the appellate authority or Tribunal. In the instant case, the ITO arrived at the figure on the basis of the receipts extending over three accounting year. He took the sum total of these receipts to be the base for the net income that had accrued to the assessee during the accounting year 1943-44 as the entire contract work had been completed during that year. Mere execution of the contract work will not necessarily entitle the contractor to make a demand for payment until it is ascertained that the works are up to the standard agreed upon between the parties. Some parts of such work may be wholly rejected and like bad debts in every earning may be ignored in computing the gains or profits. It might have been open to the ITO, in exercise of his discretion, to make an enquiry into whether and when the bills for payment became due to the assessee. Much depended upon the terms in the contract, and the manner of its performance. Even as a basis of guess work, which the Income-tax Officer was entitled to do, the basis could not be said to be in consonance with honest guess work. The ITO did not seem to have taken into consideration why the payments which, according to him, were due to the assessee in the accounting year were not fully paid till three years after. Sometimes the payments to the contractors are withheld on account of unsatisfactory execution and they are held entitled to payments only if and when they replace the rejected work by acceptable and accepted ones. The bare possibility of such contingency could not be wholly eliminated in the instant case. If the ITO, in arriving at the figure for assessment, left out these considerations, he certainly could not be said to have exercised his judgment which he was none the less called upon to do in making the assessment in cases of assessee's default under sections 23(4) and 13 proviso of the 1922 Act. Any method of accounting adopted by the ITO acting under the proviso of section 13 of 1922 Act can be rejected if the method in fact does not show the true income, profits and gains. In this view of the matter, the Appellate Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipt basis with regard to contracts carried out and completed during the year of accounting, there being every presumption that the incomes were paid as soon as they became due. At any rate, the Tribunal's decision might be upheld on the ground that when two methods of guess work are available for the purpose of assessment, the one which is more just to the assessee and which involves a much less margin of chance of uncertainty should be taken as the basis.

In the result, the Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipts basis with regard to contracts carried on and completed during the year of account.

As regards the reduction of flat rate, the Appellate Tribunal had arrived at the lesser flat rate on the basis of their decisions in similar cases in the district. Their opinions were not receivable evidence in the instant case. The decisions in different cases must have been based upon different facts and different inferences deducible from such facts. In this connection, it might be observed that the ITO had been very fair to the assessee bearing in mind the difference between the gross value and net value of the bills. The Appellate Tribunal, therefore, did commit a mistake of law in arriving at a finding for which there was no relevant evidence to support.

Therefore, the reduction of the estimated profit rate from 40 per cent adopted by the ITO to 30 per cent by the Tribunal on the ground that 30 per cent was the general rate adopted by it in the cases of other assessees doing the same kind of contract works during the same assessment year was not legal.

Note : The case was partially decided in favour of the assessee.

■

Coming to the aspect of the applicability of net profit rate for determining the profit earned from the contract receipts, while the assessee has applied rate of 8 per cent, the Assessing Officer has held a rate of 12 per cent to be justified. No justification has been given by the Assessing Officer for rejecting assessee’s rate of 8 per cent applied except a general dismissal of the same stating that 12 per cent rate is justified. In the light of the same, there is no reason to agree with the Assessing Officer that the net profit rate of 12 per cent on the contractual receipts was justified. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals), therefore, confirming the addition made to the income of the assessee on account of application of net profit made of 12 per cent to the contractual receipts is set aside and the application to 8 per cent rate to the contractual receipts, as claimed by the assessee, is held to be justified. The addition, therefore, made to the income of the assessee on account of application of net profit rate of 12 per cent to the extent of Rs. 17.51 lakhs is directed to be deleted. [Para 23]

The award was confirmed by the High Court only upon a concession being made by the State. The concession was that the loss of profit must be deemed to cover the basis of claims in respect of other items. Therefore, the sum of Rs. 16 lakhs could be treated only as part of the total contract receipts. In case of contractors, the total contract is not treated as income straightaway. Only a certain percentage thereof is estimated as the profit since the contractor will have to make out lays on men, material and machines in order to earn such receipts.

The ITO had himself estimated the income at 10 per cent of Rs. 83 lakhs awarded by the arbitrator against other claims though those parts of the award were not sustained by the High Court. The Commissioner (Appeals) had applied the same yardstick of 10 per cent adopted by the ITO to the receipt of Rs. 16 lakhs, and the same was to be upheld. As regards interest at 15 per cent awarded by the arbitrator, the High Court had set aside the award of Rs. 83 lakhs. Therefore, as on date there was no basis for bringing to tax the interest at 15 per cent on that sum. Only interest at 15 per cent on Rs. 16 lakhs was, therefore, sustainable.

It is no doubt true that in the case of a contractor, work-in-progress has to be brought into accounts in order to show the profits earned in respect of the work turned out and the profit embedded in the receipts received during the year. The concept of bringing to accounts the work-in-progress is no different from the concept of bringing into accounts the closing in the case of a trader or a manufacturer. But unlike the case of a trader or a manufacturer, in the case of a contractor the workin-progress cannot be exactly arrived at with reference to any particular books because there are so many components which go to make up the work-in-progress and which have to be estimated. Therefore, estimate in arriving at the work-in progress was necessary and there was bound to be certain amount of approximation and guess work. Merely on the ground that the work-in-progress is estimated, it cannot be said that the book results were not to be accepted and that proviso to section 145 is applicable unless it is shown that the work-in-progress was arrived in such a way as to be too far from reality. In the instant case, the ITO attempted to prove the unreliability of the amount of work-in-progress arrived at by pointing out that the closing stock ought to have been Rs. 3,82,000 as against Rs. 1 lakh shown by the assessee. The basis for this was the assumption that normally the advance was given at 75 per cent of the material lying at site. There was no basis for this assumption nor any figure were given to show that this hypothesis could be accepted as correct. It was mere ipsi dixit of the ITO, without any basis to support it. The advance could be given at 75 per cent. It could be more, it could be less. This was, therefore, a surmise and conjecture.

As regards the receipts, following the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524 , in the instant case, the value of the material supplied by the Government must be excluded. So the balance of receipts should come to only Rs. 14.63 lakhs shown by the assessee. The estimate of the income at Rs. 1,50,000 on those receipts of Rs. 14.63 lakhs would work out to about 10.4 per cent. In none of the previous years, the assessee had shown such a high rate of profit nor had the department estimated the profit at such a rate nor the books of account were ever rejected. The previous results are only the points of reference, in relation to which the results of subsequent years are to be judged and reasons for variations are investigated. The range of profit would be discernible from the previous records. The lowest rate of net profit rate shown and accepted by the department was 2.8 per cent. In the immediately preceding assessment year rate of net profit shown and accepted was 2.75 per cent and the gross profit was 11.75 per cent. The estimate made by the ITO in the year in question of the profit at 10.5 per cent was very excessive and unreasonable. The ITO had not shown the basis for determining the income of Rs. 1,50,000. It is now the settled law that whenever estimates of income are resorted to in order that they are not arbitrary, unreasonable and unjustified, the ITO must show the basis on which and the method by which and the manner in which the estimate was made. These are the safeguards provided to act as an insurance against arbitrary estimates. None of these guidelines settled by the law of the land was disclosed by the ITO except leaving one to infer that because of the variations in the closing stock, he determined to fix the income at Rs. 1,50,000. Therefore, the estimate made by the ITO was not justified.

In the case of ‘U’, the contract receipts for the assessment year 2001-02 exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs i.e., Rs. 41,20,790. Therefore, the provisions of section 44AD were not applicable to case of ‘U’ for the assessment year 2001-02. Following the decision of the Tribunal Amritsar (SMC) Bench, in the case of the Nangal Khurad Co-operative L & C Society Ltd. v. AO, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was set aside and the Assessing Officer was directed to compute the income for the assessment year 2001-02 by applying net profit rate of 6 per cent instead of 8 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer. The appeal for the assessment year 2001-02 was partly allowed.

In the case of ‘D’ for the assessment year 2002-03, the contract receipts were Rs. 10,21,919 and in the case of ‘U’, the contract receipts for the assessment year 2002-03 were Rs. 14,25,627. Thus, in both the cases, receipts were less than Rs. 40 lakhs. The provisions of section 44AD are applicable to the contracts of civil construction or supply of labour for civil construction for contract receipts below 40 lakhs. Explanation to section 44AD further provides that the expression ‘civil construction’ includes the construction or repair of any building, bridge, dam or other structure or of any canal or road. It was not clear from the orders of the lower authorities whether, the activities undertaken by the assessees were contracts of civil work, supply of labour to civil contractors or the contracts falling under Explanation to section 44AD. If the activities of the assessees fell in the above categories, the provisions of section 44AD would be applicable and the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) for upholding the net profit rate of 8 per cent would not warrant any interference. However, if the activities of the assessees did not fall in those categories, the income would require to be computed by applying net profit rate of 6 per cent. In the light of those facts and circumstances of the cases, it was appropriate to set aside the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) and same were restored to his file with a direction to modify the earlier orders only if it was found that nature of contract work done by the assessees was other than supply of labour for civil contracts or the cases falling under Explanation to section 44AD. Otherwise, the earlier orders would stand confirmed.

In the result, the appeal was partly allowed.

The books of account regularly maintained in the course of business which are duly audited under the provisions of the Act and are free from any qualification by the auditors should be taken as correct unless there are strong and sufficient reasons to indicate that they are unreliable. For rejecting the books of account, it is the revenue's onus to prove that either the books of account maintained by the assessee are not correct and complete or the method of accounting adopted by the assessee is such that true profits cannot be deduced therefrom. In the instant case, while rejecting the books of account, the adverse observation of the Assessing Officer was with respect to delay in payment of labour charges for the month of January, 1998. That was not sufficient cause for rejecting the audited accounts wherein no adverse comment had been made by the auditor, nor any specific defect had been pointed out by the Assessing Officer. It was not the case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee had recorded excess payment of labour charges, nor there was any allegation that labour charges were disproportionate to the nature of contract work executed. On the other hand, even as per the Government manuals, the percentage of labour expenses as a percentage of total value of contract, in respect of civil contract, is 25 per cent whereas in the instant case, the expenses claimed under labour charges worked out to 20.67 per cent (total contract receipts Rs. 364.54 lakhs, labour charges Rs. 75.37 lakhs.) Income-tax provisions nowhere either authorize the Assessing Officer or cast an obligation on the assessee to prove the negative result, i.e., to prove as to why he had failed to make a profit at a particular rate.

The accounts may be rejected as unreliable if important entries and transactions are omitted therefrom or if proper particulars and vouchers, bills, etc., are not forthcoming or if they do not include entries relating to particular class of business transaction. While examining the books of the assessee, the Assessing Officer has to consider the following aspects : (i) whether the assessee has regularly employed a method of accounting; (ii) even if regular adoption of a method of accounting is there, whether the annual profits can properly be deduced from the method employed; (iii ) whether the accounts have been correctly maintained; (iv) whether the accounts maintained are complete in the sense that there is no significant omission therein. If the answers to above four questions would be in the affirmative, then the assessee's profits would be computed on the basis of his accounts. In such cases, proviso to section 145(1) or section 145(2) cannot be invoked. On the perusal of the materials placed on record in the instant case, it was found that the answers to all the above four questions were in the affirmative. No finding had been recorded by either of the lower authorities as to the unacceptability of the method and to the irregularity of the accounts kept by the assessee. It is well-settled that in the absence of such a finding recorded by the authorities, the book results cannot be ignored or brushed aside.

In the instant case, the assessee had been regularly maintaining the percentage of profit between 1 per cent to 2 per cent. It was also not the case of the Assessing Officer that any part of the contract receipt had not been entered in the books of account or that the assessee had accounted for expenses more than what had actually been incurred.

In the instant case the assessee had not maintained any books of account and the revenue applied a rate of profit of 12.6 per cent on the gross amounts of bills received by the assessee. The assessee had tendered for the contract as a whole including the cost of materials which were subsequently supplied by the Government. There was no evidence on record to show that the assessee did not know about the supply of materials by the Government to be made or at what price. Furthermore, the gross profit had been computed on the total gross bill of the assessee. In the aforesaid background the Tribunal had come to the conclusion that the assessee, though tendered the contract as a whole, it must have included the cost of materials which were supplied by the Government as an element of profit in respect of cost of materials also. In the aforesaid background, it could not be said that the Tribunal was indulging in any surmise or acting without any proper evidence. It was evident from the terms and conditions of the contract that the assessee had not simply sold the sand to the civil contractor. The sand was available at the site on payment of royalty to the State Government. The assessee had to engage labourers for loading and unloading of the same. The assessee had to engage vehicle for carriage of sand up to the site. The sand was to be unloaded from the vehicle. The assessee was also required to pay octroi in respect of the said supply of sand. It was evident from these facts that the assessee was not engaged in the retail business of trading of goods. The price fixed by ‘U’ Ltd. was inclusive of all the above charges. Section 44AF is applicable in respect of retail traders. The assessee was not engaged in any retail trading - buying or selling of goods to customers. The assessee was neither a retailer nor a wholesale trader. The only business conducted by the assessee was the work executed by the assessee on account of contract for supply and transportation of sand, etc., to U Ltd. for construction of road. No other income had been disclosed. Therefore, the assessee could not be said to be engaged in the retail business of trading of goods. The assessee had engaged himself in the execution of contract with U Ltd. only. Hence, provisions of section 44AF were not attracted in the instant case. In the instant case, the assessee had executed the work of supplying and transportation of sand from a particular area to a civil contractor. In other words, the assessee was a sub-contractor to the civil contractor for execution of part of the work involved in the construction of the road. In view of Explanation 3 to section 194C, execution of work includes the carriage of goods by any mode of transport of goods other than by railways. Therefore, for the purpose of section 44AD, the execution of any works contract would include carriage of goods by any mode of transport other than by railways. In the instant case, the assessee had engaged himself in the supply and transportation of sand from a particular area to the civil contractor. If one were to go by the composite contract, then the entire payments made to the assessee would fall within the ambit of section 44AD being the payment received for the execution of works contract in the construction of a road. In this view of the matter, the entire payment would fall within the ambit of section 44AD. However, the contractor had made payments to the assessee in two parts - one for supplying of material, i.e., the sand at specified rates and the other for transportation charges including loading and unloading, octroi, etc. In case the contract was divisible in two parts - one for the supply of material and another for transport of the same, then section 44AD would be applicable only in respect of transportation charges and for the supply of material it would be reasonable to apply a net rate of profit of 5 per cent as applicable in the case of retail transfers, notwithstanding the fact that the assessee’s case might not strictly fall within the ambit of section 44AF in respect of the supply of the material. In the absence of relevant material, it would be just and reasonable to restore the issue to the file of Assessing Officer for the purpose of determination of the net profits after verification of the nature of payments to the assessee. In case there was a composite contract and there was no basis for bifurcation of transportation charges and cost of material, then the profit of the assessee should be computed at the rate of 8 per cent as provided under section 44AD. However, if there was a reasonable basis for bifurcation of payments, for the cost of material separately and for transportation charges, then the profit should be computed at the rate of 8 per cent in respect of payments made for transportation charge and at the rate of 5 per cent for the supply of the material. The Assessing Officer should decide the issue accordingly.

Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c ) which was amended with effect from 1-4-1976, goes to show that to discharge ‘the revenue of its initial burden it has to be established that there was concealment of particulars of income, when additions are made in the income or any disallowance of expenses claimed by the assessee’ has been made. It was to be noticed, in the instant case, that the result of the business as disclosed in the books of account having not been accepted, instead the assessing authority accepted and adopted gross receipts by the assessee as basis for applying flat profit rate, for making the assessment. That resulted in addition of Rs. 28,520 in the income of the assessee and the ITO was justified initially for holding satisfaction that the assessee had concealed particulars of his income in respect of said additions made in the income and initiated penalty proceedings for that purpose.

However, it is settled that Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c ) only provides a rule of evidence for raising a rebuttable presumption in favour of the revenue and does no more. It can be rebutted by leading new material as well as from existing material on record. The presumption is not carried to height of a conclusive proof. Once jurisdiction has been assumed, matter has to be decided in terms of evidence that has come before the assessing authority and it must depend upon dealing with such matters by the Assessing Officer thereof.

In the instant case, while presumption had been raised in respect of additions made in the returned income of the assessee by applying flat profit rate on gross receipts by the assessee, the assessment order revealed that the enquiry had proceeded on the basis of finding whether the claim of deductions against the income had rightly been disclosed in the books of account and the same had been rightly rejected.

The Tribunal had misdirected itself in considering the ambit and scope of the said Explanation and also in dealing with the case where additions had been made not on any specific count but by applying a gross profit rate while rejecting the result shown in the books of account, that is to say, not on the basis of entries made in the books of account. Once books of account are rejected and income is assessed by applying gross profit rate which results in addition of income, though the provisions of Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) may be attracted for the purpose of initiating penalty proceedings by raising presumption under the Explanation 1, the same by itself cannot take place of conclusive proof so as to discard the evidence and attending circumstances on that basis alone.

In view of the Supreme Court decision in Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978 ] 115 ITR 524 , even where an assessment had been made on estimate by applying the provisions of section 145 and a flat rate of profit is applied on the turnover such turnover cannot include the cost of materials supplied by the Government as it does not involve any element of profit.

Accordingly, in the instant case, the Tribunal was right in holding that the cost of materials supplied by the Government could not be included before applying a flat rate to the assessee's receipts.

The assessee had given specific facts peculiar to the assessee’s business, viz., Compulsion of selling of 217 flats at price not exceeding Rs. 90 per sq. ft. except for charging some extra amount for additional amenities that might be provided at the request of the buyer. When all those facts were viewed together, it did not appear to be surprising that the assessee’s profits would be considerably lower than the profits of other builders who may be free to sell the properties they constructed at their own determined prices. In those circumstances, the profits shown by the assessee in its books of account may be accepted. Therefore, the addition made by the Assessing Officer any sustained by the Commissioner (Appeals) was directed to be deleted.
