[1996] 85 TAXMAN 214 (ART) TAXATION OF PROFITS FROM CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS EXTENDING OVER SEVERAL YEARS

R. Balasubramanian B. Sridhar

In certain types of contracts relating to construction of multi-storeyed buildings, dams, bridges, etc., the work is spread over a number of years and the question of determining profits therefrom on an annual basis bristles with difficulties. There are two basic recognised methods of accounting, viz., (i ) the 'percentage of completion' method and (ii ) the 'completed contract' method, available to an assessee-contractor to choose from, but once he has made his choice, he must stick to it for the duration of the contract. In this article, the author discusses some of the issues involved in detail and, on the basis of copious case-law cited by him, comes to the conclusion that the ITO need not wait for the completion of the contract to determine the taxable profits arising from the project and that he can determine such profits for any given assessment year on the basis of the regular method of accounting followed by the assessee - EDITOR

Introduction

1. Under section 145(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act'), income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession", is computed in accordance with the method of accounting regularly employed by the assessee. Even if the accounts are correct and complete, but the method employed is such that in the Assessing Officer's view the income cannot be properly be deduced therefrom, he may compute the income as he thinks best in the given circumstances. In contracts relating to construction of multi-storeyed building, bridges, dams, ships, etc., which entail operations for a number of years, a problem arises as to the allocation of revenues and related costs to various accounting periods over the duration of the contract. The determination of annual income in such cases for purposes of levy of tax under the tax statute bristles with difficulties.

Two basic types of contracts

2. According to the International Accounting Standard-(IAS-11) effective from January 1, 1980 and the Accounting Standard-7 (AS-7) of the Institute of Chartered Accountants made mandatory from April 1, 1991 in the case of companies and from April 1, 1993 in the case of non-companies, construction contracts, formulated in a variety of ways, generally fall into two basic types:

(i)fixed price contracts - the contractor agrees to a fixed contract price or rate, in some cases subject to cost escalation clauses;

(ii)cost plus contracts - the contractor is reimbursed for allowable or otherwise defined costs, and is also allowed a percentage of these costs or a fixed fee.

Two methods of accounting

3. Two methods of accounting for contracts generally followed by contractors are (i) the percentage of completion method and (ii) the completed contract method.

Under the percentage of completion method, revenue is recognised as the contract activity progresses based on the stage of completion reached. The costs incurred in reaching the stage of completion are matched with this revenue, resulting in reporting of results which can be attributed to the proportion of work completed.

Under the completed contract method, revenue is recognised only when the contract is completed or substantially completed; that is, when only minor work is expected other than warranty obligation. Costs and progress payments received are accumulated during the course of contract but revenue is not recognised until the contract activity is substantially completed.

Under both these methods, provision is made for losses for the stage of completion reached on the contract. In addition, provision is usually made for losses on the remainder of the contract. When a contractor uses a particular method of accounting for a contract, then, in respect of all other contracts that meet similar criteria, the same method is used.

Flow of attribution of profits in Judicial Context : The Observed Transition

Evolution of attribution of profits in judicial context

Anglo French Textile Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1953] 23 ITR 101 (SC) is one of the early rulings in Indian Judiciary on attribution dating to the year 1952. The Supreme Court ('SC') considered figure of 10% on British Indian sales as reasonable for attribution, basis the extent of operations carried out in British India. Similarly, in Hukum Chand Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1967] 63 ITR 232 (SC), based facts of the case, 15% allocation was considered reasonable for operations relating to contracts undertaken in British India (in the pre-independence era the territory of British India was demarcated from Indore, where the company had operational mills for manufacturing textiles.) In arriving at this figure, emphasis was laid on the then Rule 33 of the Income Tax Rules, 1922. Rule 33 has now been replicated as Rule 10 explained above.

In recent past, rulings pertaining to profit attribution were pronounced considering Rule 10 together with specific provisions in the Act. In Dy. DIT (International Taxation) v. Nipro Asia Pte Ltd. [2017] 79 taxmann.com 154 (Delhi - Trib.)6, the AO, in absence of any correct TP study, adopted provisions of Rule 10 using 'selective financial figures' from public websites. ITAT rejected AO's computation (negating use of publicly available data) and assessed income based on Section 44BB and 44BBB of the Act which provides for presumptive profit rate of 10%. Similar view was upheld in Nortel Networks India International Inc. v. Dy. CIT (International Taxation) [2014] 65 SOT 158 (URO)/49 taxmann.com 147 (Delhi - Trib.) and GE Energy Parts Inc. v. ADIT (International Taxation) [2017] 78 taxmann.com 2 (Delhi - Trib.)

Going further, in Motorola Inc., ITAT allocated 20% profits to PE contending that PE played role in negotiation and conclusion of contracts and supply of equipment in India. Similarly, in Galileo International Inc., 15% profit attribution was considered sufficient owing to the role played by PE in negotiating contracts.

Formulary Apportionment in attribution of profits

In 2013, in Convergys Customer Management Group Inc. v Asstt. DIT [2013] 58 SOT 69/34 taxmann.com 24 (Delhi - Trib.), formulary apportionment was adopted as the basis of allocation. The Tribunal used end customer revenue as the base to which a global operating income percentage was applied to arrive at profits attributable to the Indian operations.

In India, current provisions on attribution as defined under Rule 10 are akin to the formulary approach. However, globally, there has been no agreement on the use of formulary apportionment owing to practical difficulties.

Importance of FAR analysis in Arms-Length attribution of profits

Landmark decision by SC in DIT (International Taxation) v. Morgan Stanley and Co. [2007] 292 ITR 416/162 Taxman 165 (SC) Inc. throws light on the importance of transfer pricing analysis in attribution of profits to PE. It lays, "The impugned ruling is correct in principle insofar as the associated enterprise, that also constitutes a PE, has been remunerated on an arm's length basis taking into account all the risk-taking functions of the enterprise. In such cases, nothing further would be left to be attributed to the PE."

Similarly, in Rolls Royce Singapore (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. DIT [2012] 347 ITR 192/202 Taxman 45/13 taxmann.com 81 (Delhi), it was emphasized that profits attributable to PE in India is made having regard to FAR Analysis. The AO held that 25% of the profits on sale of spare parts to customers in India was chargeable to tax which was reduced to 10% by CIT (A)7 and upheld by ITAT. To substantiate this reduction, it explained, "The risk assumed by PE in India is very limited. It is only performing the functions of soliciting contracts for sale of assessee's products or promoting the sales. All other main or core activities regarding the arrangements or acquisition of products supplied by the assessee company to the Indian customers are performed in Singapore."Hence, a detailed transfer pricing analysis is imperative.

In a recent decision in Arrow Electronics India Limited, a Singapore Company, opened Liaison Office ('LO') in Bangalore which was established to be the Indian PE. Placing considerable reliance on FAR analysis for profit attribution, it was held, "there is no mathematical formula for working out profits of Indian operations and that of Singapore operations. Functions, Assets and Risk analysis is the best way to arrive at profits". Allocation of weights in terms of functions performed, risk borne and assets owned (FAR) by the LO formed basis of profit allocation. The final quantification computed by AO, based on detailed FAR analysis, upheld by the Tribunal, was attributable as 40:60 to the LO and the Head Office.

Concluding remarks

CIT [1980] 124 ITR 31, the Supreme Court has observed that the provisions of the Act relating to the charge on income apply in relation to a specific assessment year and the provisions of the Act providing for the computation of the chargeable income apply, in the absence of anything to the contrary, in relation to the relevant previous year. Therefore, the profits and gains have to be computed for each accounting year separately.

Completed contract method - Its acceptability 4. In the case of completed contract method, the profits of a contract are determined on the completion of the contract and not every year. It may happen that a particular contract may take several years for its completion. Therefore, if an assessee has adopted the completed contract method of accounting, he will not be in a position to compute the profits of his contract business every year. In such a situation the Assessing Officer may invoke the provisions of the proviso to section 145(1) and hold that the method of accounting employed by the assessee is such that true profits of the business cannot be deduced therefrom.

It is, no doubt, true that the completed contract method is a recognized method of accounting as per the Accounting Standard issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. However, the main defect of this method is that it does not enable an assessee to compute his income from the contract business every year. In para 10.2 of the aforesaid Accounting Standard this defect has been highlighted in the following words:

"The principal disadvantage of the completed contract method is that periodic reported income does not reflect the level of activity on contracts during the period. For example, when a few large contracts are completed in one accounting period but no contracts have been completed in the previous period or are to be completed in the subsequent period, the level of reported income can be erratic although the level of activity on contracts may have been relatively constant throughout. Even when numerous contracts are regularly completed in each accounting period, and reported income may appear to reflect the level of activity on contracts, there is a continuous lag between the time when work is performed and the related revenue is recognized."

Since under the Act, each year is a separate self-contained year and profits and gains have to be computed each year separately, the Assessing Officer may not accept the completed contract method, even if regularly employed by the assessee, on the ground that income cannot be properly deduced therefrom. He may invoke the provisions of section 145 and compute the income either by applying a flat rate on the contract receipts or by some other method.

Relevant case law

5. Here it will be relevant to refer to a few decided cases on the subject. In the case of Tirath Ram Ahuja (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 15 , the Delhi High Court has held that in the case of contracts, in order to ascertain the income, one need not wait till the contract is completed, and that it is open to the revenue to estimate the profits on the basis of the receipts in each year of construction, although the contract is not complete. The same view has been taken by the Patna High Court in the case of Sri Sukhdeodas Jalan v. CIT [1954] 26 ITR 617. In this case a military contract extended beyond the accounting period and the accounts were closed only after the completion of the contract. The question for determination was whether the profits should be assessed only after the completion of the contract or whether the profits accruing during the accounting period could be assessed. The Patna High Court held that it is fallacious to argue that merely because the military contract was completed after the accounting period, no profits arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year and that in the case of an incomplete contract there is a well-established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year. In the case of P.M. Mohammed Meerakhan v. CIT [1969] 73 ITR 735 , the Supreme Court also has held that the profits of an adventure can be determined even if the adventure is not completed.

Conclusion

6. Although the completed contract method is a recognized method of accounting as per the Accounting Standard issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, it is not a suitable method of accounting from income-tax point of view, as it does not enable determination of the profits of the contract business every year. Since under the Act each year is a separate self-contained year, it is necessary to determine the profit of the contract business each year separately. For this purpose, it will be advisable to adopt the percentage of completion method, which is the other method recognized by the aforesaid Accounting Standard.

The authors are of the view that the herald of safe harbour as a tool for reducing TP disputes in India is far flung from reality. Much of the disputes around contract service providers in the fields of IT, ITeS, KPO and R&D, arise due to the uniqueness of the Indian TP regulations in its use of arithmetic mean and a band around the mean, as against the use of median and inter-quartile range adopted by most other TP regimes.

The authors had earlier analysed8 comparable sets widely used for determination of arm's length prices for IT and ITeS companies in the TP assessments for fiscal year (FY) 2006-07, i.e. relevant to the assessment year 2007-08. The IT set comprised of 26 companies with current year operating profitability in the form of operating profit/total cost, ranging from 1.38% to 60.23%, with an arithmetic mean of 25.04%. Similarly, the ITeS set comprised of 27 companies with current year operating profitability in the form of operating profit/total cost, ranging from 13.55% to 113.49%, with an arithmetic mean of 30.24%.

Thus, any captive IT or ITeS company with an operating margin of less than 19% and 24% respectively, namely after considering the band of 5% around the arithmetic mean, as prevalent during the material time, would have failed to satisfy the arm's length test for FY 2006-07, as per the country-wide comparable benchmarking sets adopted by the Indian Revenue.

It may be pertinent to highlight that the lower quartiles of the same IT and ITeS sets were at about 14% and 12% respectively. Therefore, the use of inter-quartile range on the same comparables would have enabled captive taxpayers with an operating profitability of 15%, being the intuitive mark-up for most captive IT and ITeS companies, to comply with the arm's length standard. The analysis was re-run on the ITeS comparables used in the TP assessment cycle relating to FY 2007-08, i.e., relevant to the assessment year 2008-09. The lower limit of arm's length price, computed with reference to the 5% tolerable limit around the arithmetic mean, was again observed to be at 19%, while the lower quartile was at 9%.

These analyses vindicate that, but for the ingenuity of the Indian TP regulations, a large fraction of taxpayers falling within the bracket of 15% of operating profitability or even lower, would have remained unscathed, even if one were to otherwise accept the selection of comparables by the Indian Revenue for the IT and ITeS sets, which itself left enough room for debate. Therefore, the introduction of inter-quartile range and median would have better addressed the TP disputes in India and obviated the need for safe harbours, as the pre-dominant objective of introducing safe harbours is to reduce TP litigations in India.

Some may attribute the adoption of arithmetic mean by the Indian Revenue, for the purposes of computing the arm's length price, to the brevity of comparable data available in public databases in the formative years of transfer pricing in India, which inhibited the usage of quartiles. It is observed that ProwessTM, a public database widely used for the purposes of comparable benchmarking analyses in India, reported only 8,067 companies in the year 2002, as compared to 25,949 companies in 2011. Presently another database used for benchmarking analyses, namely Capita line PlusTM, provides data of around 1,000 additional companies over and above the companies provided in ProwessTM. Thus, brevity of data can no longer be the reason or cause for not adopting the more sophisticated approach of the inter-quartile range by the Indian Revenue, as several of the other developing economies, let alone the developed ones, have advocated the usage of inter-quartile range and median for the purposes of computing the arm's length range.

The safe harbour rates proclaimed by India are still not reasonable enough to entice large captive service providers, since opting for safe harbour rates in India might result in such taxpayers facing economic double taxation, as Revenue authorities of the headquarter countries are unlikely to accept the high mark-ups under the unilateral safe harbour rules of India. Furthermore, as the taxpayers adopting safe harbours would be precluded from seeking refuge of MAP, as expressly provided in the safe harbour regulations, the risk of double taxation at headquarter countries is aggravated.

Accounting for changes in foreign currency rates - AS 11

7. With regard to changes in foreign currency liabilities relating to fixed assets on account of difference in exchange rates, there is not much variance between the standard (AS 11) and the provisions of the Act. However, in the case of assets acquired in India utilized borrowings made in foreign currency, provisions of section 43 A of the Act do not provide for adjustment, as in the case of liabilities incurred for acquiring assets abroad, while under AS 11, such difference has to be adjusted even in case of money borrowed directly or indirectly in foreign currency specifically for the purpose of acquiring such assets. This distinction between the standard and provisions of the Act on the one hand and between the liability incurred in foreign currency for acquisition of assets abroad and the borrowings made in foreign currency utilized for acquiring assets in India on the other, is not warranted and there is a need for amending the provisions of section 43A for bringing about uniformity. The omission might have been unintended, as when the provisions of section 43A were introduced way back in 1967 primarily to compensate for devaluation of the Indian rupee on June 6, 1966, it might not have been estimated that there would be occasion for Indian business community to borrow in foreign currency for acquisition of fixed assets within India, as is presently being resorted to in the liberalised economy. In relation to liabilities on account of revenue expenditure, there is a distinction. As per AS 11, increase in such liability on the balance sheet date has to be accounted for, ignoring the decrease, if any, while under the Act such increase in liability is not considered ascertained and is, therefore, allowable as a deduction only in the year of actual settlement.

Goods which are purchased under cenvatable invoices and undergoing further process not amounting to manufacture lose their cenvatable advantage when they are sold again in the processed stage; the processor is not a manufacturer of any new goods and the CENVAT chain is broken at his level and cannot be continued further into the hands of the next consumer. Another issue is the clearance of goods under Central Excise. In respect of notified goods, the MRP rate applies under section 4A and at the first point the goods are taxed at the MRP rate less the deduction mentioned in the notification issued by CBEC. This point of clearance provides the cenvatable invoice as the further sales are to dealers in the market. But the first buyer is invariably a dealer or distributor who is not a registered one under the Central Excise as he is not the first stage dealer. The State Sales tax element plays a very important role here. Another important fact is the cost of sales promotion including dealer margin which determine how many hands the goods will pass through after excise clearance. The input tax credit for such goods is not available unless the manufacturer directly sells the goods to the service provider for consumption in services. The volume of consumption, the credit facility and other terms of supply make it easy for the goods to be procured from the dealer and not from the manufacturer for the service provider.

The other issue is production of goods in certain specified areas like North East where the goods do not suffer Central Excise. When such goods are consumed in providing services, they suffer service tax on their value. Often a standard deduction from the billed amount is given under the Service Tax Rules to determine the taxable value of services, but this may not cover the cost of goods used in service contracts resulting in levy of service tax on goods consumed - an unintended effect and cost-push factor.

Tax evasion

7. Clinging to one recommendation out of the many in the Tax Reforms Committee Report and enhancing the service tax rate under one pretext or other is bound to result in a distorted taxation of certain services leading to tax evasion. In the present context which is far away from the envisaged situation for convergence of goods and services tax rate, 12 per cent service tax is certainly high without real input tax credit and this was voiced by many service sectors soon after the presentation of the Budget.

For example, the building construction activity is presumed under section 44AD of the Income-tax Act to yield a net profit of 8 per cent on gross turnover. If it is subject to 12 per cent service tax and 2 per cent surcharge, the service tax levy comes to 4.04 per cent under the summary assessment to service tax. Added to that the sales tax levy on works contract which comes to 2 per cent or more under the State Sales-Tax law. (Tamilnadu General Sales Tax Act provides for 2 per cent under summary assessment of civil works contract value). Thus as against the net profit of 8 per cent which the contractor gets, the indirect tax levy on him is 6.04 per cent which is more than 75 per cent of his net profit. It is a tall order to expect compliance with the all the tax laws when more than 75 per cent of the net profit he earns is to be shelled out as indirect tax, no matter the same can be recovered from the client. Similar situations arise in the case of catering contractors, cleaning service providers, dry cleaners, and other persons operating with low profit margins.

Conclusion

8. What is to be noted is that the tax levy at each point cannot be disproportionate to the income earned out of the activity at that point. Every businessman looks at the tax content of a transaction in comparison with his profit arising out of it. The temptation to evade arises when profit with evasion is much more than the profit with compliance; and this leads to corruption in administration and generation of unaccounted money. The convergence concept advocated by the Tax Reforms Committee, it is reiterated, rests on the basic principle of moderate taxes which will not breed resistance to taxation and result in black money generation. It is essential that tax rates induce and promote voluntary compliance on the part of the taxpayer.

Mere speeches that ‘the net effect will be very small’ do not inspire such voluntary compliance in the face of hard realities in the business world. It is wiser to continue with lower rates of service tax with more services roped in than to skew the rate on existing services year after year in short spells. Increase from 5 per cent to 12 per cent rate, a 140 per cent increase at that with partial palliatives, in such a short time points to avarice and haste in taxation of the services sector.

Why this change has brought into the Act: The Central Government has notified ten disclosure standards effective from 1st April 2017 relating to AY 2017-18. Judicial decisions and decisions of Appellate Tribunal

6. The question of exigibility to tax of income from long-term contracts has been considered by the juridiciary as well as the Tribunal in a number of cases. To highlight their views on the issue, the gist of some of the decisions is set out below:

(i)( a)Sukhdeodas Jalan v. CIT [1954] 26 ITR 617 (Pat.)

(b) Tirath Ram Ahuja (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 15 (Delhi)

A military contract entered into by the assessee Sukhdeodas Jalan extended beyond the accounting period and the accounts were closed only after the completion of the contract. The question arose for determination whether the profits should be assessed only after the completion of the contract or whether the profits accruing during the accounting period could be assessed. A Division Bench of the Patna High Court held that it was fallacious to argue that merely because the contract was completed after the accounting period, no profits arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year and that in the case of an incomplete contract there was a well established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year (vide page 971 of Batliboi's Advanced Accounting) . To quote from the High Court's decision:

"In the case of contracts, if accounts are maintained and completed on contract basis the profits or gains of the previous year cannot properly be extracted from the accounts, for a contract may take several years for being completed and payments in regard to it may also be received by the assessee in several years. It may be convenient from the point of view of the assessee that profit should be ascertained on the completion of the contract and assessment of the profit should take place after the completion of the contract. But section 3 imposes a charge of income-tax upon the profits and gains of the assessee for the accounting year and it is the duty of the income-tax authorities to ascertain the profits and gains accruing to the assessee in respect of the payment received during the accounting year.

It cannot be said that merely because a contract was completed after the accounting year, no profits arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year...." (p. 618)

The ratio of the decision supra was followed by the Delhi High Court in the case of Tirath Ram Ahuja (P.) Ltd. ( supra). It was held that in the case of contracts, one need not wait till the contract was completed in order to ascertain the income, and that it was open to the revenue to estimate the profit on the basis of the receipts in each year of construction, although the contract was not complete.

Tax credit illusory

6. It appears that cross settlement of input tax credit between the services and the goods is more on paper than real. Often the input tax credit for goods consumed in the service sector is obtained from dealers who cannot provide cenvatable invoices. The supply of goods is widespread among various dealers not all of whom provide cenvatable bills or cater to the requirements of the end-user who is a taxable service provider.

Similarly goods used in service contracts are not necessarily purchased from the first stage or second stage dealer or from the manufacturer directly. The input credit for goods consumed in service contracts is largely illusory as the output service provider purchases inputs from available sources of supply and on such terms as to credit and quantity which suit his business needs. The input credit for goods is thus not available as the cenvatable invoice essential for claiming the input credit is not there but only an ordinary purchase invoice to support the purchase of goods. Goods which are purchased under cenvatable invoices and undergoing further process not amounting to manufacture lose their cenvatable advantage when they are sold again in the processed stage; the processor is not a manufacturer of any new goods and the CENVAT chain is broken at his level and cannot be continued further into the hands of the next consumer.

Ascertainment of profit in the abovementioned manner puts the real estate developer on par with other businessmen who treat profit as a function of sale, not as a function of the scale of production. If a manufacturer only manufactures without selling a single unit, he will not recognise revenue on the basis of scale of production. Likewise, a real estate developer should not be required to recognise revenue on the basis of progress of work, in complete disregard of the fact of sale.

Modification of AS-7

6. As would be apparent from the foregoing, AS-7 recommends revenue recognition without taking into consideration whether any sale has been made or not. The percentage of completion method no doubt serves one purpose, viz., that of attributing the expected profit to different accounting periods based on the scale of progress achieved in the accounting periods. However, it also gives a very artificial figure of profit which is totally divorced from the resultant cash flow for the reason that cash flow emanates from sale, not from the scale of progress, and no profit is good profit unless there is reasonable certainty of its realisation. AS-7 does take into account the element of such uncertainty and recommends appropriate provision. However, AS-7 should be applicable to that part of project pre-sold only where such pre-sale is achieved by real estate developers. Making it applicable to the entire project does not achieve the ideal of revenue recognition. It is proper of make it applicable to a contractor because in his case pre-sale of the project is achieved; but it is inappropriate to apply it in the case of a real estate developer. Secondly, the taxation authorities are very reluctant to allow provisions for contingencies recommended by AS-7 for uncertainties not yet arisen. Therefore, application of AS-7 to real estate developers can create problems in income-tax assessment.

It may not be out of place here to state that the International Accounting Standard-11 (IAS-11) is applicable only to contractors. Its application to contractors poses no problems as they are not functioning in an atmosphere of uncertainty about sale in the way the real estate developers are functioning.

The CBDT has started laying down accounting standards under section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. It is very likely that they may lay down a standard for construction industry on the lines of AS-7. Therefore, if the Institute does not recognise the crucial difference between the nature of the business of real estate developers and that of the business contractors, the new standard by the CBDT may also overlook the difference, and may prescribe a standard which gives profits that are anything but profits as understood in the world of commerce.

Conclusion

7. It is, therefore, imperative to suitably modify AS-7, and leave real estate developers to follow the normal accounting principles, or to make AS-7 applicable only to the area in respect of which sale is achieved.

K.R. Gupta

In the case of long-term contracts, the determination of profits from the contract business annually is not an easy task. For this reason, a contractor executing a long-term contract may like to determine the profit of the contract only after the contract has been completed and to file his income-tax return on that basis. Difficulty in determining profits annually

1. In the case of long-term contracts, the determination of profits from the contract business annually is not an easy task. For this reason, a contractor executing a long-term contract may like to determine the profit of the contract only after the contract has been completed and to file his income-tax return on that basis. In this connection, a question that arises for consideration is whether under the Income-tax Act. 1961 ('the Act') it is permissible to adopt such a method of accounting in respect of the contract business.

Position from accountancy point of view

2. Before examining the matter from the income-tax angle, it will be appropriate to discuss the position in this regard from the accountancy point of view. The Accounting Standard of 'Accounting for construction contracts' issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India has recognized the following two methods of accounting for contracts :

(i)the percentage of completion method;

(ii)the completed contract method.

In para 7 of the Accounting Standard (AS-7) these methods have been described as under :

"7.2 Under the percentage of completion method, revenue is recognized as the contract activity progresses based on the stage of completion reached. The costs incurred in reaching the stage of completion are matched with this revenue, resulting in the reporting of results which can be attributed to the proportion of work completed. Although (as per the principle of 'prudence') revenue is recognized only when realised, under this method, the revenue is recognized as the activity progresses even though in certain circumstances it may not be realised.

7.3 Under the completed contract method, revenue is recognized only when the contract is completed or substantially completed; that is, when only minor work is expected other than warranty obligation.

Costs and progress payments received are accumulated during the course of the contract but revenue is not recognized until the contract activity is substantially completed."

It will be seen that from the accountancy point of view, the completed contract method is a recognized method of accountancy.

Under the Act the assessee has the choice of adopting whatever method of accounting he wants to adopt, provided he follows the method regularly for his own purposes. Section 145 of the Act clearly makes the method of accounting, if regularly employed by the assessee, a compulsory basis of computation unless, as provided in the first proviso to section 145(1), in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, the income, profits and gains cannot be properly deduced therefrom. If the true income, profits and gains cannot be ascertained on the basis of the assessee's method of accounting, the Assessing Officer has the power to compute the income on such basis and in such manner as he may determine.

Each year as a self-contained unit

3. Under the Act, for the purpose of computing the profits and gains, each year is a separate self-contained period of time. In the case of Mahamudabad Properties ( P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 31, the Supreme Court has observed that the provisions of the Act relating to the charge on income apply in relation to a specific assessment year and the provisions of the Act providing for the computation of the chargeable income apply, in the absence of anything to the contrary, in relation to the relevant previous year. Therefore, the profits and gains have to be computed for each accounting year separately.

[1994] 75 TAXMAN 450 (ART) DISTINCTION BETWEEN CAPITAL AND REVENUE RECEIPTS

Dr. T.P. Ghosh *

The author's view is that in deciding the issue whether a particular receipt is a revenue receipt or a capital receipt, useful assistance can be derived from the Accounting Standards devised in India and abroad by the authoritative accounting bodies. The author also stresses the point that the term 'profits and gains' has to be understood in a practical commercial sense and pleads that this interpretation of the term should be given a statutory base - EDITOR

Capital versus revenue receipts

1. Very often the income-tax law fails to give a ready solution to the problem of distinguishing between capital and revenue receipts. Also, quite often, the confusion whether a receipt forms part of business income or income from other sources wastes the time and energy of the tax administration. Section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 which, inter alia, provides that profits and gains of any business or profession which is carried on by the assessee at any time during the previous year would be charged to income-tax under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession', is not self-explanatory. The term 'profits and gains' is not defined in the Act. Rather, the Courts have attempted to find out an appropriate answer whenever disputes arose. However, 'profits and gains' are accounting concepts and the distinction between capital and revenue is purely an accounting issue which can be solved better by paying attention to accounting principles, excepting the cases wherein, by specific provisions in the Act itself the distinction between capital and revenue receipts has been removed.

A recent decision of the Supreme Court

2. The Supreme Court has recently decided a case involving this issue – CIT v. Govinda Choudhury & Sons [1994] 74 Taxman 331 which rolled over 22 years. A partnership firm engaged in contract business got an arbitration award for interest of Rs. 4,30,549 out of which Rs. 2,77,612 related to the assessment year 1972-73. Two fundamental issues arose in the process of tax assessment: (i) whether the interest is a revenue receipt, and (ii) if yes, whether such interest is profits and gains of business or income from other sources ?

The ITO charged the interest income as a revenue receipt. The Tribunal ruled that such interest was not a natural trading receipt and decided to treat the same as income from other sources. The High Court opined that such interest was not revenue receipt. Finally, the Supreme Court arrived at the conclusion that such interest was a revenue receipt as well as a trading receipt. The reasoning given by the Supreme Court is that since the assessee was a contractor and his business was to enter into contracts, he had also to face disputes with customers and he had also to reckon with delays in the payment of his dues. If the amount was for such delay, such interest was only accretion to the assessee's receipts from the contracts. Accordingly, such interest was a trading and revenue receipt.

Commercial sense of the term 'profits and gains'

3. It is a well-established proposition that profits and gains which are liable to be taxed under section 28 are what are understood to be such, following ordinary commercial principles - Badridas Daga v. CIT [1958] 34 ITR 10 (SC). The expression 'profits and gains' has to be understood in the commercial sense - Calcutta Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 37 ITR 1 (SC).

To understand the meaning of the term 'profits and gains', it is necessary to look into the accounting standards and the conceptual framework of accounting. When the concept of 'commercial sense' was floated during the fifties, no accounting standard was formulated in India. Although certain basic accounting principles of profit measurement were propagated by the accountancy bodies in the developed countries, there was no international forum like the International Accounting Standards Committee for popularising and harmonising the accounting standards globally.

The situation today is altogether different. During the last two decades accounting standards have gained global acceptance. In India, thirteen accounting standards have been formulated and some such accounting standards have already got a mandatory status within the chartered accountancy profession. The Companies Bill, 1993 (presently being reconsidered) has also recognised such accounting standards.

So, while deciding any tax case that raises the basic identification issues like the distinction between capital and revenue receipt or between business income or other income a reference to the accounting standards and the conceptual framework of accounting can be usefully made.

The principle that is firmly entrenched not only in our country but also the world over is that the levy of tax is on 'income' which, so far as a business enterprise is concerned, denotes the commercial profits, determined with' the aid of applicable principles of commercial accounting subject to the extent they are varied or modified to subserve the socioeconomic objectives of the welfare state. Precision in Accounting : International and national Accounting Standards 9. The accounting profession has clearly recognised this managerial compulsion and has been making efforts to bring a modicum of standardisation in the area of accounting. The formation of International Standards Accounting Committee (IASC) in 1973 was a right step in this direction. The major objective of the IASC is to improve and harmonise the regulations, accounting standards and procedures relating to the presentation of financial information. The members of the IASC have to ensure that financial statements comply with the International Accounting Standards in all material respects and disclose the fact of such compliance.

Prior to the formation of the IASC there were wide variations in the form and content among the published accounting standards of most countries. Hence, one of the objects of the IASC is to harmonise, as far as possible, the diverse accounting standards and accounting policies of different countries. International accounting standards, however, cannot override the local regulations.

Thus, it is clear that the major objective of the IASC in the initial years or even for a considerable time will be to bring about a desirable degree of harmony between widely differing accounting standards. An International Accounting Standard (IAS) cannot, by its very nature, be precise. It cannot rule out options completely. This is an inherent limitation of an IAS which will continue to be there in the foreseeable future. Accounting being a language of business, its growth and maturity will certainly depend upon the degree of economic development, the spread of commerce education and the inclination of business to adopt fair accounting practices. Computerisation and sophisticated information systems will go a long way in improving the presentation of financial information.

India is committed to the adoption and spread of International Accounting Standards. Our own standards are very similar to them. The important question is: are they precise? Do they give a large number of options and, thereby, flexibility to the management? To answer these questions, let us take a very brief look at some of the standards.

The preface to the accounting standards observes that in the task of formulation of Accounting Standards the intention is to concentrate on basic matters. The endeavour would be to confine Accounting Standards to essentials and not to make them so complex that they cannot be applied effectively on a nationwide basis. In future, a greater degree of sophistication may be attempted. Accounting Standard-1, clearly perceives the limitations of accounting policies. There is no single list of accounting policies which are applicable to all circumstances. The differing circumstances in which enterprises operate in a situation of diverse and complex economic activity make alternative accounting principles and method of applying those principles acceptable. The choice of appropriate accounting principles and the methods of applying those principles in the specific circumstances of each enterprise call for considered judgment by the management of the enterprise. No accounting standard can provide for all these circumstances. There are several areas in which differing accounting policies are encountered. Depreciation methods, treatment of expenditure during construction, recognition of profit on long-term contracts and, valuation of inventories are some of the instances where this is possible. Accounting Standard-2, dealing with valuation of inventories, recognises 8 methods of valuation in use in various types of businesses. Further, the fundamental accounting assumptions, namely, going concern and consistency, are themselves very vague. Of course some barometers have, of late, been identified to check whether a concern is really a going concern. Even then much is left to the professional judgment of the auditor. A lot of probability is involved in determining a contingent loss or contingent interest. Correct estimation of depreciation bristles with judgmental factors. In determining the useful life of a depreciable asset, important factors like expected physical wear and tear, obsolescence, etc., are involved. These factors are highly subjective and are not amenable to precise calculation and, hence, depreciation will continue to be an estimate. Coming to construction contracts, each contract is a species in itself and, hence, to prescribe a standard which will achieve the object of attributing the correct costs to all types of construction contracts is an impossibility. As regards recognition of revenue, a multiplicity of problems will be encountered if a precise standard is attempted. For example, as per the standard, in a transaction involving the rendering of services, performance should be measured either under the completed service contract method or under the proportionate completion method which relates the revenue to the work accomplished. How can we prescribe a precise standard to determine the exact proportion of the contract completed in each case? The fact that much sophistication or precision has not been achieved is a pointer to the difficulties involved in the matter. Further, managements will certainly resist restrictions on their discretion to adopt accounting policies to suit their needs. The stiff opposition to the introduction of the standard on leasing is a case in point.

[1997] 90 TAXMAN 1 (ART) ACCOUNTING FOR REAL ESTATE DEVELOPERS

Kirit S. Sanghvi*

In case of long-duration projects spread over more than one accounting period of an assessee, it is difficult to estimate profits attributable to any one of the accounting periods involved The two methods generally followed for calculation of profits in such cases are the 'percentage of completion' method and the 'completed project' method Both these methods are recommended in Accounting Standard- 7 laid down by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India for contractors and reale- state developers who generally take up long-duration projects. In this article, the author, pointing out the difference between the nature of the business of a contractor and that of a realestate developer, and pinpointing the limitations of the two methods in estimation of profits in such cases, goes on to suggest certain modifications which will achieve better revenue recognition in the case of real estate developers. In this context, the author also highlights the necessity of modifying AS-7 - EDITOR

Introduction

1. The implications of the accounting period concept, or of the cut-off date concept, are nowhere more pronounced than in accounting for long-lasting projects. Such projects are spread over more than one accounting period. When the projects are completed, it is easy to find out the income or loss of the project. However, it is difficult to find out the income or loss of the intervening accounting periods when the projects are in progress.

To overcome this basic difficulty, Accounting Standards have been developed to guide one as to how to account for long-duration projects. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India has prescribed an Accounting Standard (AS-7) dealing with the subject. The standard applies to real estate developers as well as contractors.

It is proposed to deal with the accounting for real estate developers, more particularly in the light of AS-7, and to make out a case for making AS-7 applicable to the real estate developers, and others placed in similar circumstances, with suitable modifications. However, the discussion that follows is in the context of real estate developers.

The term 'real estate developers' here means entrepreneurs developing on their own account saleable real estate units and undertaking such activity as a business venture.

A contractor, on the other hand, is a person who undertakes work for others.

Nature of real estate development

2. A real estate developer develops property initially on his own account. The nature of his undertaking is distinguishable from that of a contractor who undertakes a contractual job for another person. A real estate developer operates under uncertainty of sale; a contractor on the other hand faces no such uncertainty. The cash flow of a real estate developer is first linked with the sale that he is able to make, and then it is linked with the progress of work. In other words, if there is no sale, there is no cash flow, whatever the progress of work. The cash flow of a contractor, on the other hand, is usually linked with the progress of his work only. He does not have to worry about sale. These features distinguish a real estate developer from a contractor. And these distinguishing features should have a bearing on the methods of accounting followed by the real estate developer and the contractor. They should not be asked to follow identical methods when the nature of their businesses differs vastly.

Methods of accounting

3. Generally, two methods are recommended to be followed by organisations undertaking long-duration projects. The methods are: The percentage of completion method and the completed project method.

The first method is an attempt to estimate profit of the entire project, and attribute it to an accounting period based on the progress of work achieved during the accounting period.

The second method accumulates all project-related expenses to be set off against revenue on completion of the project. No revenue is recognised in the intervening accounting periods.

AS-7 also recommends the two methods for contractors as well as real estate developers.

Why AS-7 requires reconsideration ?

4. As stated earlier, the real estate developer operates under uncertainty of sale its quantity as well as value. His is a business venture where profits spring from sales, not only from the progress of work. One can see that the first method recommended in AS-7 suggests that revenue be recognised with the progress of work. It disregards the fact whether sale is achieved or not. The second method also disregards sale made in the intervening periods, as it suggests that revenue be recognised only on completion of the project.

It is not surprising that the validity of reference was upheld in the light of the binding decisions in Sony India (P.) THERE SHOULD BE PROFIT BEFORE APPLICATION OF THE RULES 4. The ultimate object is to find out whether there was any profit for the non-resident in respect of the transactions with the associate enterprise in India. The Delhi Bench of the Tribunal in Galileo International Inc. v. Dy. CIT [2008] 19 SOT 257 (Delhi) and Rolls Royce PLC v. Dy. DIT [2008] 19 SOT 42 (Delhi) had decided that the non-resident did not have profit from the transaction. In coming to the conclusion after finding against the assessee on the question of permanent establishment by way of a dependent agency and upholding the need for adoption of arbitration principle to estimate the income attributable to such permanent establishment, they inferred that the income may well be taken at 15 per cent of the gross receipts before remuneration payable to the agents. Since such remuneration exceeded the amount of profit, there was no income that was found to be assessable. Though these two decisions appear to be fair in their result, the reasoning leaves much to be desired. The issue whether location of the equipment in India by itself would lead to the inference of ‘permanent establishment or dependent agency or fixed base’ is unresolved. The further inference of income at 15 per cent in this case is on an ad hoc basis. The estimate of net income may well have been, say, 10 per cent of the gross receipts after payment of dependent agency. The reasonableness of estimate at 15 per cent subject to dependent agents’ commission, so as to absolve the entire profits from liability, is best supported with reference to the non-resident’s accounts, whether there is any surplus from Indian operations. At any rate, on the matters of discussion of the method of choice for determination of arm’s length price, these two decisions offer no guidance, though the principle that there could be no liability for non-resident, if there is no profit at all is undisputable.

Where no profit is inferable, U.S. Courts would hold that there is no option except to accept declared price. In Exxon Corpn. & Affiliated Companies et al v. Commissioner TC Memo 1993-616, sale of Saudi crude oil by the subsidiary below international price did not attract transfer pricing rules, because of restrictive covenant with Saudi Arabian Government, which did not permit charging of price higher than the stipulated rate. Where there was prohibition on royalty payment by Spanish Government, it held that there can be no inference of shifting in Procter & Gamble Co. 961 F.2d 1255 (CA-6,1992). Same view was taken in similar circumstances by the U.S. Supreme Court in Texaco Inc. & Subsidiaries v. CIR No.95-60696 and Commissioner v. First Security Bank of Utah 405 U.S. 394 (1972).

In this context, one may also refer to the principle that there can be no income for the permanent establishment in respect of intra-organisation transaction as held in Dresdner Bank A.G. v. Addl. CIT [2007] 108 ITD 375 (Mum.). It is on this reasoning that it was held in ABN Amro Bank v. ADI [2006] 280 ITR (AT) 117 (Kol.) (SB), that interest paid by Indian branch to the head office is not allowable as it is payment to self. However, the situation may be different if the head office has actually raised loans for the benefit of the branch.

CHOICE OF METHOD

5. The statute has prescribed the following five methods, viz., Comparable Uncontrolled Price Method (CUPM), Resale Price Method (RPM), Cost Plus Method (CPM), Profit Split Method (PSM) and Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM) (sixth method yet to be prescribed). The method chosen by the assessee to justify his declared price to be arm’s length price should be ‘the Most Appropriate Method (MAP) under section 92C(2)’, since proviso to section 92C recognises that there may be circumstances, where there can be more than one appropriate method in which case arithmetical means of the arm’s length price so arrived at can be taken, subject to variation of 5 per cent at the option of the assessee.

It is seen that there is flexibility in the standards issued by the ICAI which makes it possible for an assessee to avoid payment of correct taxes by following a particular system. Therefore, there is an urgent need to standardise two or more of the alternatives in various standards so that the income for tax purposes can be computed precisely and objectively".

Notification of Accounting Standards by the Central Government 4. The Bill proposes to amend the Income-tax Act to empower the Central Government to prescribe by a Notification in the Official Gazette the accounting standard which an assessee will have to follow in computing the income under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession' or 'Income from other sources'. The new section 145(2) provides for notification of accounting standards from time to time. Section 145(3) as brought in by the Finance Act, 1995 lays down that if the Assessing Officer is not satisfied about the correctness or completeness of the accounts of the assessee or where the method of accounting provided or the accounting standards notified have not been regularly followed by the assessee, the Assessing Officer may make an assessment in the manner provided in section 144 of the Act. This is the law applicable to the current assessment year 1997-98 and subsequent years. The amendment re moved the proviso to section 145 which enabled the Assessing Officer to compute the income on such basis and in such manner as he may determine wherever the method of accounting is such that income cannot be properly deduced therefrom. The removal of the proviso is no doubt a handicap to the Assessing Officers. As long as the accounting standards are followed, the Assessing Officer is bound to accept the results shown in the books of account.

Accounting Standards notified by the CBDT

5. The CBDT followed up the amendment in the law and notified certain accounting standards under section 145(2) to be followed by all assessees following the mercantile system of accounting - [1996] 218 ITR (St.) 1. These standards related to disclosure of accounting policies, prudential norms, presentation of accounts showing how substance prevailed over form, the materiality of the financial statement, etc. Expressions like 'Accounting Policies', 'accrual', 'consistency', etc., were all defined. Standard-II related to the disclosure of prior period and external items and changes in accounting policies. The notification came into effect from April 1, 1996 and applied to the assessment year 1997-98 and subsequent years.

Schedule IV to the Companies Act, 1956 also refers to disclosure practices. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India issued accounting standards making them mandatory. In its notification issued in July 1990, the ICAI required that wherever the disclosure norms set by the accounting standards were not followed, the Chartered Accountants should qualify such audited reports with regard to non-disclosure. Fifteen Standards running from AS-1 to AS-15 were issued by the ICAI.

Old law proposed to be revived

6. Now comes the rub. With such great fanfare, section 145 was amended and the new law is in place in the current assessment year. At this stage of the development of the law, the Working Draft proposes a complete somersault. Section 106 of the Draft Bill brings back the legal position as it was before the amendment of the present section 145 by the Finance Act of 1995 and even the proviso is back in the Bill. This reversion to the old law is explained by the Expert Group in the following words : "Section 145 of the Act is sought to be brought under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession'. Apart from this change, an important departure from the present law is to allow assessees to compute the profits in accordance with the method of accounting regularly employed. Even if an assessee is employing the hybrid method of accounting in respect of business or profession, he would be permitted to employ such method and the requirement that only mercantile or cash system should be followed is proposed to be done away with".

Section 106(4) of the Bill proposes that the Central Government may, in consultation with the ICAI, prescribe the basis of accounting to be followed by any class of assessees or in respect of any class of income or any category of transactions.

Criticism of new proposal

5. There would be many other challenges, to be faced. The two important, amongst these, are (i) fixation of tax rate; and (ii) constitution of GST Council and its efficient and orderly functioning. In the discussion to follow, the problem of rate fixation is being considered.

Fixation of GST rate

6. The issue regarding rate fixation could be considered under two broad heads namely –

[a]

Principles, to be kept in view while fixing the rate;

[b] Fixation of actual rate, to be adopted.

These aspects are considered in later discussion.

[a]

Principles, to be kept in view

The rate, to be fixed for GST, need to be 'Revenue Neutral Rate' (RNR) – a rate, which will not result in loss of revenue to Centre and states. This will need consideration of the following aspects:-

*

The tax should not be a burden on the consumers;

*

It should not undermine the simplicity of GST regime;

*

Compliance required should be easy; and;

*

The impact on tax revenue should be minimal.

[b]

Fixation of the actual rate

The issues, that need consideration in this context, are:-

[i]

Whether there should be slabs or merely a single rate

There seems to be a favourable inclination towards slab system on the following lines:-

*

Essential commodities should be taxed at lower rate;

*

Luxury goods, to be taxed at (sin) higher rate;

*

In between, there could be a standard rate for most of the goods.

Arvind Subramanian's recommendation concerning GST rate

7. The Arvind Subramanian committee has raised different scenario and given a range of 16.9%-18.9%. Its final recommendations are: "Meanwhile, we recommend a three-rate structure. In order to ensure that the standard rate is kept close to the RNR, the maximum possible tax base should be taxed at the standard rate. The committee would recommend that lower rates be kept around 12% (Centre plus states) with standard rates varying between 17% and 18%". This 18% has got stuck with the chief economic adviser, the FM said in a lighter vein. There is one reason for that. Most of the analysis, for instance, on inflation rate, is based on the 18% standard rate. He has recommended 40% tax on luxury goods and zero percent for essentials.

Examination of the issue regarding rate fixation

8. FM's view regarding GST rate

Rate has to be finally fixed by the GST Council. The FM's observations on rate, as appearing in the media, read as under:-

"Currently, what the taxpayers are paying is phenomenally much higher. For almost 60-70% of the commodities, on a weighted average are paying 27% plus a large number of other small taxes. Some of the states have even called it 30-32% or more. Now, the guiding principle laid by the empowered committee is that this rate has to come down. It will gradually slide down but even in the first instance, it will come down. This will have to be married with their second intent that the states need enough money for their own developmental activities….. So, a balance between the two will always have to be maintained by the GST Council."

8.1 Suggestions regarding rate(s) have to be examined from a neutral angle. While State FMs had initially said that there should be a significant reduction in the rate, the standard rate could finally be fixed at higher than 18% i.e. as high as 20-22%. Newspaper reports indicate that some states levy 27-28% tax, including VAT, and other levies like entry tax. In this scenario, there could be pressure for fixing the standard rate at 22-23%. The Kerala FM, it is reported, advocated a rate of 22-24% during the meeting of the empowered committee of State FMs on 25th July at Kolkata, which could be repressive for final consumer. The Congress seems to be insisting on 18% rate.

Concluding comments

9. The fixing of rate could be a ticklish point in the exercise relating to GST. It can neither be too high nor too low. High rates could lead to inflation. Too low rate may affect schemes relating to poverty alleviation and development schemes. Thus, by lower rates, public interest could be impacted. Hence, a way will have to be worked out to arrive at a rate, which should be fair and lead to optimum revenue without hurting any interest. This can be well said than done. Already differences seem to have surfaced. Kerala has already pitched up for higher rate. The Tamil Nadu MP walked out of the Parliament at the time of voting. This state may like to have its own rate(s). Thus, the vision of "one country one market one tax rate" may not fortify.

9.1 Slab rates will, obviously, be equitable. One (standard) rate will ensure simplicity. The GSTC will have to take a decision balancing the two aspects.

9.2 In working out the rate(s), regard will have to be taken of the exemptions from the GST in respective legislations. This too may be challenging work.

Revenue recognition according to the Expert Committee of the Institute of Chartered Accountants

5. Some illustrative cases dealt with by the Expert Advisory Committee of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India not only throw more light on the two methods of accounting, namely, (i) the percentage of completion method and (ii) the completed contract method of accounting, recommended for adoption in executing contracts running for a number of years, but also clarify the various issues involved in accounting for and taxation of profits. Three cases are discussed below in brief.

(i) First illustrative case. - A heavy engineering equipment manufacturing company sold equipment on turnkey basis. In almost all turnkey projects, the payments for supply and erection were received separately in instalments dependent on the stage of development. According to the terms agreed to, the final balance of 5 per cent of each, i.e., 10 per cent of the total cost, was receivable on successful commissioning and acceptance by the customer or on submission of bank guarantee covering the guarantee period.

The company was recognising sales at 100 per cent contract value on despatch of equipments to the site. Due to this, sales was taken at 100 per cent though the final 10 per cent became due only after 36 months, i.e., after commissioning. This accounting procedure had necessitated payment of income-tax on the portion of 10 per cent also taken as income in the year of despatch of equipment.

Considering the disadvantages from the taxation angle, the company sought the opinion of the Expert Advisory Committee as to whether the said 10 per cent of the contract price which was not due could be recognised as revenue in the year in which it fell due, i.e., after completion of the project, thereby deferring the tax liability.

The Expert Committee observed (April 1987) that according to AS-7,

"under the percentage of completion method, the amount of revenue recognised is determined by reference to stage of completion of the contract activity at the end of each accounting period (para 9.1)... The stage of completion used to determine revenue to be recognised in the financial statements, is measured in an appropriate manner. For this purpose no special weightage should be given to a single factor; instead, all relevant factors should be taken into consideration, for example, the proportion that costs incurred to date bear to the estimated total costs of the contract, by surveys which measure work performed and completion of physical proportion of the contract work (para 9.2) . . . progress payments and advances received from customers may not necessarily reflect the stage of completion ... (para 9.3)."

Further according to AS-9, "In a transaction involving the rendering of services, performance should be measured either under the completed service contract method or under the proportionate completion method, whichever relates the revenue to the work accomplished. Such performance should be regarded as being achieved when no significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of the consideration that will be derived from rendering the service."

As the company was following the percentage of completion method for revenue recognition, the Committee opined that the company should recognise 100 per cent contract price as revenue in the year in which the entire equipment was despatched and the contract was performed to a substantial extent. However, the estimated liability of 10 per cent must be provided in the accounts for fulfilling possible claims. According to the Committee, the question of admissibility of the provision for possible claims as a deduction in computation of taxable income, was a separate question which had to be resolved keeping in view the facts and circumstances of each case, [vide page 12 of Vol. VII of Compendium of Opinions].

(ii) Second illustrative case. - A public limited company, wholly owned by a State Government, undertook construction works exclusively for Government departments/undertakings, both on turnkey and non-turnkey basis and followed the mercantile system of accounting.

So long as a recognised standard followed consistently from year to year, the results are to be accepted and even this does not prevent the Assessing Officer from questioning the correctness or completeness of the accounts. Deviations from the standards prescribed by the ICAI warrant qualificatory remarks from the auditor and the Assessing Officer will be well within his rights to probe into such issues and quantify the proper income while framing the assessment even under the existing provisions. By its very nature income from business or profession defies precision in computation. A mathematically correct income from a running business is not generally feasible to arrive at due to various factors affecting the business and such factors are not amenable to precise computation. Risks in business both in relation to completed transactions and those lying in the womb of future compel the businessman to estimate his income and not measure it mathematically. Conservatism is built into business computations and lurking fear of the unknown future influences business sentiment.

Any system of accounting will have to come to terms with the business realities and be acceptable from the business point of view for wide acceptance and implementation. A pedantic approach, however, scholarly it may seem, is unlikely to be widely followed unless it is realistic from the point of view of the businessman.

Certainly the ICAI has not come in for praise in the memorandum accompanying the Finance Bill for setting Accounting Standards after much research and debate. The standards are described as lacking requisite rigidity with too many alternatives, butter-fingered and so resulting in tax avoidance.

But the standards are mandatory and disclosed in published accounts compulsorily and when contravened, reported upon by the auditor. The user of such accounts now knows the effects of non-compliance with the standards of accounting prescribed by the ICAI, though such reporting may be in fine print. But the Assessing Officer is posted with this information and equipped with the Tax Audit Report under section 44AB of the Act, he can unravel the mystery in the accounts to assess the proper income.

In prescribing accounting standards for the entire field of business and industry and profession, a certain amplitude necessarily comes in. This is because of the different requirements of accounting for various types of business, but the underlying requirement in any business accounting is the true and fair view of the final results.

The accounting standards prescribed by the ICAI after due deliberation cannot, thus, be termed as ‘flexible’ with a connotation that they help avoid payment of tax. Nor can they be truncated in the name of standardisation as that would result in inadequate coverage.

Instead of venturing to set fresh standards under section 145, the Government would do well to adopt the standards set by the ICAI under the Income-tax Act as it has done for the companies under the recently promulgated Companies (Amendment) Ordinance, 1998. It would be wiser to align the measurement of income under section 145 with the scope of total income under section 5 to avoid potential litigation.

Conclusion

7. An attempt has been made above to look at the amended section 145 from the standpoint of section 5 and the inherent nature of income as it comes in for measurement is also seen. Income is often found to present itself rather than accrue continuously on a time-bound linear scale and any system of measurement has to face this fact.

And income is such a concept that it is not confined to the two domains of accounting methods exclusively. The observation of Lord Tankerton in CIT v. Sarangpur Cotton Mfg. Co. Ltd. [1938] 6 ITR 36, 40 (PC) on section 145 that "their Lordships are clearly of the opinion that the section relates to a method of accounting regularly employed by the assessee for his own purposes - in this case for the purpose of the company’s business - and does not relate to a method of making up a statutory return for assessment of income-tax" appears to be valid even after the amendment of section 145 by the Finance Act, 1995 [Emphasis supplied].

This article examines the two issues which have been decided by the Bombay High Court.

Applicability of cost plus method

3. Circular dated 26 September, 2012 addresses the queries regarding liability to be worked out on cost plus basis, i.e., cost of material and profit as per balance sheet. The Circular, clarified that no method apart from the one statutorily prescribed and mentioned above in the rules will be admissible. Circular specifically precludes adoption of any other method apart from the statutorily prescribed methods. However, MCHI argued that Rule 58(1) stipulates the value of the goods at the time of transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of a works contract may be determined by effecting certain specified deductions from the value of the entire contract. The use of the expression 'may be' is symptomatic of the legislative objective that the method prescribed by Rule 58(1) is not the only eligible method for computation of the Value Added Tax. Consequently, it would be in the hands of the assessee to adopt the computation of the assessable value on the basis of the actual cost of the material/goods supplied coupled with a mark up element. In the light of the above, MCHI argued that cost plus method is a recognized method of assessment. Rule 58(1) does not preclude an assessee while filing returns from taking recourse to the cost plus method.

Department, however, argued that the provisions of Rule 58(1) including deduction's are in conformity with the judgment of the constitution bench of the Supreme Court in Gannon Dunkerly & Co v. State of Rajasthan [1993] 1 SCC 364. So long as the method which has been adopted is not an arbitrary one and bears a reasonable nexus with the object of the legislation, the Court would not interfere in a statutory choice made by the Legislature or by its delegates. In the present case, Rule 58 mandates how the value of goods involved in the execution of a construction contract at the time of the transfer of property in the goods is to be determined in those cases where contract also involves a transfer of land or interest in land. Therefore, Court pronounced that circulars dated 6 August, 2012 and 26 September, 2012 not ultra vires were and only statutorily prescribed method will be admissible for computation of the Value Added Tax.

Controversy on effective date of 1% Composition Scheme

4. MCHI lead high level discussions on applicability of 1% Composition Scheme to be retrospectively applicable from 20 June, 2006. MCHI submitted that there could be no legitimate distinction between agreements which were executed from 20 June, 2006 until 30 March, 2010 and those registered after 1 April, 2010. Both sets of agreements formed, the same class. Evaluation under the Composition Scheme of the value of the goods transferred in the execution of a works contract is determined at 1% of the contract value and there is no justification why this should not apply to the period commencing from 20 June, 2006 for which such transactions have come into the crease of value added taxation. Moreover, since the amendment which was brought out with effect from 20 June, 2006, proceedings were pending before the Court and there was ambiguity on the issue until the judgment of the Division Bench dated 10 April, 2012. In these circumstances, the Composition Scheme applicable to agreements which have been registered after 1 April, 2010 should uniformly apply to agreements registered prior to April, 2010.

Department, however, argued that "the State Government is empowered by notification to provide a scheme of composition for registered dealers who undertake the construction of flats, dwelling buildings or premises and transfer them in pursuance of the agreement along with land or interest underlying the land. Now as a matter of first principle, in framing a scheme of composition the revenue has to balance several competing considerations, many of which are of a policy with nature. One of the objects of a scheme of composition is to encourage compliance. In framing a scheme for composition, the State, as a delegate of the Legislature, has to balance numerous considerations including the interest of the revenue, the need to encourage compliance and the burden on the tax administration which is obviated by the introduction of a composition option. A scheme for composition is, therefore, in the nature of a concession which is granted by the State to a certain class or category of assessee's who fulfil the conditions which are spelt out in the scheme. In the present case, the date of 1 April, 2010 which has been prescribed for composition is not an act of inadvertence on the part of the delegate of the Legislature. In framing a scheme of composition, it is open to the Legislature and its delegates to determine a cut off date with effect from which an option of composition is available. Reliance was placed by the department on judicial precedence in this regard.

The Valuation Rules cannot override provisions of the Act. For example, if actual expenses incurred are Rs. 10,000 and the service provider charges Rs. 11,000, at the most, he will be liable to pay service tax on Rs. 1,000 and not on Rs. 11,000.

The department may ask CHA to produce copy of agreement with each customer. Otherwise, the entire reimbursable expenses may be held as liable to service tax.

Really the Contract Act does not require any agreement to be in writing. It is not necessary that contract need not be in writing, unless there is specific provision in law that the contract should be in writing - Tarsem Singh v. Sukhinder Singh AIR 1998 SC 1400 (see section 10 of the Contract Act).

As per section 7(2) of the Contract Act, acceptance of a proposal can be expressed in some ‘usual and reasonable mode’. Acceptance can be by conduct.

Sitting in a bus is acceptance of proposal (offer) by conduct - Bhagwandas Govardhandas Kedia v. Girdharilal Parshottamdas & Co. AIR 1966 SC 543. Section 8 of the Contract Act states that acceptance of proposal can be by performing condition or receiving consideration for a reciprocal promise. This is also acceptance by conduct.

Thus, accepting bills of CHA by customer and making payments is ‘acceptance by conduct’. An oral agreement is equally valid and binding, if evidence of such agreement is available. Such evidence can be even gathered by conduct of parties or general trade and business practices.
