Additions in 'no account' cases

Assessee, earning income from contract business and plying trucks, did not maintain any books of account and had been assessed on estimated profit basis. In assessment year in question he purchased two vehicles allegedly out of sale proceeds of old vehicles and taking some loan. Assessing Officer, however, found that source of Rs. 13,000 invested in purchase was unexplained and further several deposits in Canara Bank was found. Assessee explained that Rs. 13,000 had come from his contract business and deposits in Canara Bank were out of withdrawals from UCO Banks. Since it was a 'no account' case Assessing Officer disbelieving oral statement of assessee made an addition of Rs. 1,50,000 as income from unexplained sources. Held - Availability of funds in hands of assessee from sale proceeds as well as from contract work, being obvious no adverse inference could be drawn simply because assessee did not maintain books of account when income from contract business had been assessed on the basis of profit rate, and as such, there was no sufficient reason to require assessee to explain entries in the bank account. Though it was a 'no account' case but keeping in view that assessment had been made in respect of contract business, treating rate of profit at 12.5 per cent on total receipts, it could not be assumed that whatever deposits were made in bank account flowed from unexplained income. Therefore, addition was unjustified. - Mohinder Pal Singh v. ITO [1995] 83 Taxman 116 (Chd.) (Mag.)

1.3 Section 44AC (as existed prior to assessment year 1993-94), which deemed a certain amount of profits related to purchase price, as assessable profits from the business of trading in certain goods, was challenged, inter alia, on a ground that the provisions raised a conclusive presumption of law that the assessee will make a net taxable income of the specified amount and this presumption was not allowed to be rebutted. The Kerala High Court upheld the vires of the provisions in T.K Aboobacker v. Union of India [1989] 177 ITR 358. The Andhra Pradesh High Court in A. Sanyasi Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh [1989] 178 ITR 31 held the provisions to be constitutional by reading it down and observing that it would be upon assessee to prove in the assessment proceedings his real assessable income.

The new provisions incorporate a provision permitting a rebuttal of the presumption. Accordingly, it is felt that the new provisions may stand the test, in case of a challenge of its vires.

Applicability of the new provisions

■ The execution of any 'works contract'.

The expression 'civil construction', as such, is not defined or explained but, apparently, has been used as nomenclature for grouping certain activities as part of the Civil Construction business.

(a) Construction; and

(b) Structure:

It has earned a profit of Rs. 3.5 lakhs from specified business, its net profit is Rs. 5 lakhs. It has been advised that in respect of specified business, it can return Rs. 2.4 lakhs (8% of Rs. 30 lakhs) as its income. For computing its income in respect of other business income, which amount should be adjusted? The specified amount of Rs. 2.4 lakhs or actual profits of Rs, 3.5 lakhs? As said above, the real issue is in what manner business income from unspecified business should be computed? The business income of the unspecified business have to be computed in the manner laid down in sections 28 to 43C read with section 44AD. As income from specified business has to be computed as per section 44AD, the actual profits of the specified business will have to be reduced. Accordingly, its business income would be as follows:

Business income of specified business as per section 44AD: Rs. 2.4 lakhs (8% of Rs. 30 lakhs).

Business income of unspecified business:

JCIT [2007] 158 Taxman 71 (SC)].

Estimation of profits - Where the assessee has given a comparative instance of gross profit rate, it is necessary for the department to come to a finding as to the norm of the gross profit on the basis of comparative cases. Therefore, it is the duty of the AO to counter the comparative statement cited by the assessee before he can have the option to estimate the gross profit [CIT v. Eastern Commercial Enterprises [1994] 210 ITR 103 (Cal.)].

Even if the ITO considered the material placed before him by the assessee to be unreliable keeping in view the comparative statement of accounts of the previous years, he cannot proceed to make an arbitrary addition and base his conclusion purely on guesswork. He ought to have related his estimate to some evidence or material on the record as it is now well-settled that if the profits shown by the assessee in his return are not accepted, it is for the taxing authorities to prove that the assessee has made more profits than returned [International Forest Co. v. CIT [1975] 101 ITR 721 (J&K)].

The law says that the ITO shall make the assessment to the best of his judgment; it means that he must make it according to the rules of reason and justice, not according to private opinion, but according to law and not humour, and the assessment is to be not arbitrary, vague and fanciful, but legal and regular [Mysore Fertiliser Co. v. CIT [1966] 59 ITR 268 (Mad.)].

Estimation by the ITO of the assessee's gross profit on the basis of the fact that the other dealers doing the same business as that of assessee had made profits by selling goods in black market would not be justified unless the ITO proves that the assessee has also sold goods in black market [A. S. Sivan Pillai v. CIT [1958] 34 ITR 328 (Mad.)].

An assessment made by estimating the profits of the assessee on flat rate basis on the basis of comparable cases, without furnishing details of such cases to the assessee, is illegal [Joseph Thomas & Bros. v. CIT [1968] 68 ITR 796 (Ker.)].

Assessee to be given opportunity to rebut the estimated profits - Where, after rejecting the accounts of the assessee, an estimate of the turnover and gross profits is fixed to the detriment of the assessee, the assessee is entitled to know the basis and also to an opportunity to rebut the same [Yaggina Veeraraghavulu & Mavuleti Somaraju & Co. v. CIT [1966] 62 ITR 528 (AP)].

No best judgment assessment - Mere fact that there was a less rate of gross profit declared by an assessee as compared to the previous year would not by itself be sufficient to justify the addition [Aluminium Industries (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1995] 80 Taxman 184 (Gau.)].

and circumstantial evidence which establishes a claim for assessment at a lower amount.

ILLUSTRATIONS

1. An assessee engaged in Transport Business acquires a truck on 1st September for, say, Rs. 5 lakhs and the purchase is financed by borrowing about Rs. 3 lacs @ 18% p.a. The truck is leased to a public sector undertaking for a rent of Rs. 18,000 per month. The income computation may work out as follows: The assessee can claim loss (and thus, declare a lower amount than the specified amount) by filing appropriate return, complying with other requirements (like, maintenance of books, audit, adduce evidence, etc.). He may have to produce evidence relating to:

■ Date of acquisition and when it was put to use.

■ Cost of acquisition of truck.

■ Proof of borrowing for acquisition of truck.

■ Amount borrowed was actually used for acquiring truck.

■ Agreement for lease.

■ Amount of rent and that no other consideration was received; and the truck was used by lessee only and was not given to any one else and that no other income arose from the truck.

■ Confirmation from the lessee.

2. An assessee engaged in civil construction business has agreed to carry out certain work relating to fixing tiles of particular brand. The cost of tiles is, say Rs. 18 per sq. ft. Total area is, say 20,000 sq.ft. It has got a fixed price contract of say Rs. 5,00,000, including cost of tiles, without escalation. Labour contract given is say @ Rs. 3 per sq. ft. His estimated profit was Rs. 80,000. The deemed profits were Rs. 40,000. After completing l/4th work, the tile manufacturer increases the rate of tiles by Rs. 4 per sq.ft. Thus, his profits went down to Rs. 20,000. He can return Rs. 20,000 as his income, and submit the following as evidence:

■ Fixed price contract.

■ Fact that no escalation was allowed to him.

■ Purchase costs.

■ Fact that he did purchase the 75% requirement after price increase.

■ Labour contract and its costs.

The evidence requirement stated above is only illustrative. However, it may be pointed out that it will have to be proved that profits earned were lower than the specified profits.

1.11-4 At what stage evidence should be produced? - Section 44AD(5)/44AE(6) reads:

"Nothing contained in... this section shall apply, where the assessee claims and proves that the profits ... are lower... and thereupon..." [Emphasis supplied]

Considering the language of the provisions, it is felt that evidence should be produced or filed along with the return/claim.

In practical life this may be difficult inasmuch as the degree of proof and satisfaction required are difficult to determine. Accordingly, an assessee will have to take an utmost care while making such claim.

If an assessee does not substantiate his claim and/or does not file evidence to prove the claim, it could be contended by the tax department that requirement of the above provisions are not complied with and, accordingly, it may apply the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 44AD and/or sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 44AE, as the case may be.

However, considering the practical difficulties, it is felt that the CBDT may lay down instructions in this behalf and may direct at least that an opportunity may be provided to an assessee to lead the evidence.

If no evidence is produced by the assessee, it is evident that the requirements cannot be considered to have been met and accordingly, AO may then be free to make an assessment based on prescribed amount(s) as per the New Provisions.

l.11-5 Effects of 'Claim for a lower amount' - Following effects of a 'claim for the lower amount' will ensue:

■ Once a claim for assessment at a lower amount of profits is made, the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 44AD/44AE would not apply, as a result of which, if the claim is accepted, the taxable profits may be the lower amount, subject to any addition or disallowance.

■ The profits computation will have to be made in accordance with the provisions of sections 28 to 43C.

■ Exemption from maintenance of books of account or audit would not be available. Accordingly, the provisions of section 44AA and/or section 44AB will have to be complied with.

■ As discussed in details above, the necessary evidence in support of lower profits will have to be produced.

■ The Assessing Officer will have to proceed to make assessment under section 143(3) which implies:

(a) Notices under section 142 and/or under section 143(2) of the Act.

(b) Formal hearing(s) at which the evidence may be produced by the assessee as also further evidence as may be required will have to be produced.

(c) Consideration of all evidences and material.

(d) On that basis, a written order of assessment of the income and determination of sum payable by the assessee.

In other words, the assessment would still be governed by normal provisions and by virtue of return under section 44AD(5)/44AE(6), the assessment cannot be reverted back to sub-section (1). It seems that having regard to the intent and purpose of the law to give an option to an assessee of rebuttal, the necesssary consequences have to follow and having exercised the option, the assessee cannot claim that the fiction should be applied.

This can also be supported on the ground that once an assessee makes the claim which is not found to be acceptable on the facts and in law the assessee cannot be given benefit of the provisions of sub-section (1).

Revision of return, whether possible, in the above circumstances ? - A further question, which may arise is that in the course of assessment, can an assessee revise the return of income and claim that he may be assessed at the specified amount, by declaring income in the revised return at the specified amount. A retrun, subject to the other provisions of section 139, can be revised under sub-section (5), if the assessee has discovered any omission or any wrong statement therein. While filing the return under section 139, read with section 44AD or section 44AE, the assessee in substance exercises the option to be assessed at an amount out of three options available to him. While considering the options, assessee may have overlooked certain aspects relating to computation of income under sections 28 to 43C. Would this amount to any omission or a wrong statement ? It is felt that in the situations contained in Illustrations 1 to 3 it may be possible to contend that there was an omission or wrong statement. However, in the situation considered in Illustration 4, the option exercised, it may be noticed that that was not based on correct facts and, accordingly, assessee may not be able to revise the return.

Effect of new provisions on a firm

1.12 In case of a firm:

■ In case of a firm, where interest and remuneration are paid to partners:

(a) insofar as the firm is concerned, such remuneration and interest, if an assessment under sub-section (1) of the new provisions is made, would be presumed to have been allowed; and

(b) insofar as the partner(s) are concerned, the remuneration/ interest would be taxable in their hands.

Rate of tax for firms

9.7 The Finance Act, 1997 has amended section 167A of the Income-tax Act. The said section provided that in the case of a partnership firm which is assessable as a firm, tax shall be charged on its total income at the maximum marginal rate (MMR). The MMR, in turn, is defined in section 2(29) to mean the rate of tax applicable to the highest slab of income in the case of individuals. Such highest slab, hereinto, was 40%. Tax rate for firms as provided in the Finance Act also used to be 40%. However the Finance Act, 1997 now provides for highest slab rate for individuals at 30% and the tax rate for firms at 35%. Thus, in order to bring about a harmony between section 167A of the Income-tax Act and the tax rate provided in the Finance Act for firms, the said section 167A has been amended to provide that the firms will be charged to tax at the rates as specified in the Finance Act.

Employers' contribution to provident fund

9.8 At present, under clause (a) of rule 6 of Schedule TV to the Income-tax Act, employers' contribution to a recognised provident fund in excess of 10% of the employee's salary is liable to tax in the hands of the employee. This limit of 10% is now increased to 12% with effect from assessment year 1998-99. In other words, employer's contribution to recognised provident fund will now be exempt in the hands of the employees to the extent of 12% of the salary.

Standard deduction

9.1 With a view to increase the limit of standard deduction for employees having income chargeable under the head 'Salaries', amendments are made in section 16(i) from year to year.

The last of the amendments was made by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1996 and as a result the position as regards the standard deduction for the assessment year 1997-98 is as follows :

■ General provisions - Standard deduction is equal to one-third of the salary or Rs. 15,000, whichever is less.

■ Exceptions - The aforesaid rule will be subject to the following two exceptions :—

1. In the case of an employee having salary income before standard deduction not exceeding Rs. 60,000, standard deduction will be equal to one-third of salary or Rs. 18,000, whichever is lower.

2. In the case of an assessee (being a woman) whose total income (from all sources including salary income) before standard deduction does not exceed Rs. 75,000, standard deduction will be one-third of salary or Rs. 18,000, whichever is lower.

The Finance Act, 1997, once again amends the above provision so as to equalise standard deduction for all.

Thus, with the amendment, all the above categorization and distinctions have been done away with. From the assessment year 1998-99 and thereafter any employee having salary income, chargeable under the head 'Salaries', would be entitled to a deduction of an amount equal to l/3rd of the salary or Rs. 20,000, whichever is lower.

Thus, all the employees whether male or female have been put on par. Further, the extra deduction available in case of a woman employee having salary of less than Rs. 75,000 has also been deleted.

Receipts multiplied by the rate of profit prescribed, would be the amount of profits from Profession which would be chargeable to tax, as a part of total income.

To illustrate, suppose, Receipts of Profession are Rs. 20 lakhs, 50 per cent thereof would be Rs. 10,00,000. 1.3-5 Satisfaction of the condition of receipts below Rs. 50 lakhs

In the application of the condition or otherwise, it would be necessary to establish that Receipts do not exceed the specified amount. In case of an assessee carrying on Profession, there is no requirement under the new provision as to maintenance of books of account. Determination and proving of Receipts beyond the limit may not be difficult if an assessee maintains books of account. However, otherwise, if the books of account are not maintained, it could cause some difficulties and for the purpose of proving Receipts the following records or documents or evidence may be relevant:

Cash memos and other bills issued by the assessee.

Rough cash book/cash records.

Purchase bills.

Bank statements.

Returns, if any, filed under service tax laws.

If an assessee returns profits from Profession by applying the new provision, he may have to establish, with evidence, Receipts as declared by him in the return and that it does not exceed the limit laid down.

For the purpose, an Assessing Officer may, in a given case, issue notices under section 142 or 143(2) as the case may be. The new provision does not exclude applicability of the provisions of sections 142, 143, etc., unlike erstwhile Chapter XII-C under which a retailer could not have been assessed.

Supreme Court in case of Sutlej Cotton Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 116 ITR 1] held that exchange rate difference pertaining to capital account transaction could be considered as capital receipt and accordingly, not liable to tax and the relevant observations are as follows:

"The law may, therefore, now be taken to be well settled that where profit or loss arises to an assessee on account of appreciation or depreciation in the value of foreign currency held by it, on conversion into another currency, such profit or loss would ordinarily be trading profit or loss if the foreign currency is held by the assessee on revenue account or as a trading asset or as part of circulating capital embarked in the business. But, if on the other hand, the foreign currency is held as a capital asset or as fixed capital, such profit or loss would be of capital nature."

The section mandates, subject to section 43A, any gain or loss arising on account of any change in foreign exchange rates shall be treated as income or loss.

It appears, the section overrides the decision of Supreme Court (supra). Although Finance Act, 2018 does not make any amendment in definition of income, which includes profits and gains. Applicable Accounting Standards, as such, regard gain or loss on account of an exchange rate difference as part of Statement of profit and loss and require recognition as income or profit or loss.

Accordingly, any gain or loss due to exchange rate difference pertaining to any capital account transaction of business or profession should be chargeable to tax as business income.

However, the amendment does not affect computation of income under other heads of income implying that the exchange rate difference gain or loss pertaining to capital account transaction not chargeable as business income may not be liable to tax having regard to above Supreme Court decision.

6.11 Computation of income from construction and service contracts [Section 43CB]

ICDS III relates to Construction Contracts and ICDS IV relates to Revenue Recognition recommended percentage of completion method ("POCM") in respect of construction contracts and certain service contracts, respectively.

Finance Act, 2018 inserts section 43CB, with effect from April 1, 2017, that is, assessment year 2017-18 to provide authority to the said recommendation and lays down that:

In case of construction contracts and service contracts (for a period exceeding 90 days or which does not involve indeterminate number of acts over a specific period of time) profits and gains arising therefrom should be computed on the basis of POCM, as per ICDS III/IV.

It is further provided that in case of service contracts:

for a duration not exceeding 90 days, profits and gains should be determined on project completion method basis; and

involving indeterminate number of acts over a specified period profits and gains should be determined on the basis of straight-line method (that is spread over duration of the contract).

It is also provided that the profits and gains as per any of the methods (POCM or project completion or straight-line) should be computed by:

including retention money in contract revenue; and

not reducing any incidental income, like, interest or dividends or capital gains from the contract costs (in other words, it should be treated as income and accordingly considered for computation of total income).

The High Court had two options before it. One was to strike down section 44AC and the other, to read it down to make it consistent with the guarantees in articles 14 and 19(1)(g) and came to the conclusion in favour of the latter. In doing so, the High Court kept in view the overall object underlying the provisions and language of the section, of serving the public interest and the intendment of the Parliament. The High Court read section 44AC as an adjunct to, and as an explanatory to section 206. Literally read section 44AC brings about a legislative assessment of the profits and gains of persons trading in specified goods. The normally applicable provisions, sections 28 to 43C are dispensed with altogether. It is declared that for assessment of every person, irrespective of his circumstances, volume of business, finance, expenditure or other attendant matters, his profits and gains from the said business shall be deemed to be the specified percentage of the purchase price. What all remains to be done thereafter is to find out whether any of the deductions provided by Chapter VI-A of the Income-tax Act are to be allowed and then to make an assessment. However, the High Court read section 44AC an adjunct to, and as an explanatory to section 206C, and not as independent section, and held it a valid section. 1.3-3 Illustration of receipts forming/not forming part of total gross receipts

The following receipts may or may not form part of Receipts: Advance or deposits received should not form part of Receipts.

Consideration received on sale of fixed assets employed in Profession should not form part of turnover or receipts.

Any security or other deposit obtained from employees should not form part of Receipts.

Service tax or any other levy (to be charged, collected and paid to the Government), as such, should not form part of Receipts, inter alia, for the following reasons: CBDT by its Circular No. 4 of 2008, dated 28-4-2008 clarified that while deducting tax at source from rent, tax should not be deducted from the service tax charged on the rent, as service tax paid by the tenant does not partake of the nature of 'income' of the landlord and the landlord only acts as a collecting agency for the Government for collection of service tax; Rajasthan High Court in CIT (TDS) v. Rajasthan Urban Infrastructure [2013] 37 taxmann.com 154/359 ITR 385 held that where service tax is separately charged, tax need not be deducted from the same; following that decision, once again, CBDT clarified by its Circular No. 1 of 2014, dated 13-1-2014 that while deducting tax at source, service tax shall not be included; and based on Receipts, income is computed at specified percentage and, accordingly, Receipts must be of such nature that income is comprised therein or Receipts must be in the nature of income.

Reimbursement of expenditure (incurred by a person rendering services and reimbursed by a person for whom the expenditure is incurred) should also not form part of Receipts based on the same reasoning as above that it is not in the nature of income or it does not comprise of income; apart from that, a reference may also be made to the following observations by Tribunal in WNS North America Inc v. Asstt. DIT [2012] 28 taxmann.com 173 (Mum. - Trib.) : 'reimbursement of expenses means that the expenses earlier incurred by a person on behalf of another are recovered as such. Ordinarily there is no element of profit in such a reimbursement'; further, in a number of cases courts have taken a view that reimbursement of expenditure does not constitute income.

Receipts arising on account of sale of unusables, empties and packages may constitute part of Receipts.

Interest (on surplus funds) and other receipts of similar nature cannot form part of Receipts.

Incentive received from the suppliers should actually go to reduce the cost of purchase and should not form part of Receipts. Similarly, cash or other discount received on purchase should not form part of Receipts.

Value of work-in-progress should not form part of Receipts.

Service charges charged for delivery may form part of Receipts, having regard to terms of contract.

1.3-4 Computation of profit chargeable

Receipts multiplied by the rate of profit prescribed, would be the amount of profits from Profession which would be chargeable to tax, as a part of total income.

To illustrate, suppose, Receipts of Profession are Rs. 20 lakhs, 50 per cent thereof would be Rs. 10,00,000. Accordingly, Rs. 10,00,000 would be includible as profit chargeable under the head 'Profits & gains of Business or Profession' in total income of the person carrying on Profession and he would be liable to pay tax accordingly.

Cash memos and other bills issued by the assessee.

Purchase bills.

Bank statements.

Returns, if any, filed under service tax laws.

It would appear that there are certainly going to be admirable mammoths as well as the one-person wonders of companies side-by-side doing business in goods and services, the latter more of the business process outsourcing model, both thriving and kicking up the economy now and in the years to come.

Job reservations

Job reservations in private sector companies in favour of the weaker sections of the society has been mooted by the Government but not yet enforced.

Professionalism - Era of non-traditional professionals/brokers

1.39-5 Professionals : Companies professionally managed claim to be a cut above the others which in the traditional mould are family-managed in our country, and this development is regarded as a facet of modernism which undoubtedly it is whether at working or controlling level. However, professionalism in corporate management, whether it is founded on formal degrees/diplomas awarded by the academies or universities or those conferred by the guild-type professional bodies like ICAI, ICSI or ICWA being moulded as functionally closer to the business world expectations as may be from time to time, it forms just one side of professionalism a priori.

1.39-5a Do-how masters - The other side is filled with the do-how masters of various character: the commission agents in commercial purchases and sales tied to the dealers and distributors, the clearing and forwarding agents involved with shipping inwards and outwards and movement of goods by surface, air or multi-modal containerized/palletized transport, servicing agents to attend to after-sales services, insurance and small-savings investment agents, travel and passport agents, authorised customs-clearing agents, mere graduates recognized as Income Tax Practitioners, agents to procure the pre-authenticated way-bill-books, C-Form books and E-1 Form books from the State Commercial Taxes Officers needed for every-day operations, RBI-related banking transactions clearance agents, or the share and stock brokers and sub-brokers, or for that matter the handling agents to facilitate the landing of chartered air-crafts with cargo tied to the Director General of Civil Aviation to the audit-clerks employed by practicing CAs or the Advocates’ clerks to licensed scribes tied to the Registries of transfer of property or the touts guiding the mere filing of FIRs or the Labour Law compliance or filing petitions and appeals before the Courts and the Tribunals and all that liaisoning with the Government agencies and Regulators or settlement of family disputes of succession in reputed business-houses etc.

Accounting Standard (AS) 7 : Construction Contracts*

(This Accounting Standard includes paragraphs set in bold italic type and plain type, which have equal authority. Paragraphs in bold italic type indicate the main principles. This Accounting Standard should be read in the context of its objective and the General Instructions contained in Part A of the Annexure to the Notification.)

Objective

The objective of this Standard is to prescribe the accounting treatment of revenue and costs associated with construction contracts. Because of the nature of the activity undertaken in construction contracts, the date at which the contract activity is entered into and the date when the activity is completed usually fall into different accounting periods. Therefore, the primary issue in accounting for construction contracts is the allocation of contract revenue and contract costs to the accounting periods in which construction work is performed. This Standard uses the recognition criteria established in the Framework for the Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements to determine when contract revenue and contract costs should be recognised as revenue and expenses in the statement of profit and loss. It also provides practical guidance on the application of these criteria.

Scope

1. This Standard should be applied in accounting for construction contracts in the financial statements of contractors.

Definitions

2. The following terms are used in this Standard with the meanings specified:

2.1 A construction contract is a contract specifically negotiated for the construction of an asset or a combination of assets that are closely interrelated or interdependent in terms of their design, technology and function or their ultimate purpose or use.

2.2 A fixed price contract is a construction contract in which the contractor agrees to a fixed contract price, or a fixed rate per unit of output, which in some cases is subject to cost escalation clauses.

2.3 A cost plus contract is a construction contract in which the contractor is reimbursed for allowable or otherwise defined costs, plus percentage of these costs or a fixed fee.

3. A construction contract may be negotiated for the construction of a single asset such as a bridge, building, dam, pipeline, road, ship or tunnel. A construction contract may also deal with the construction of a number of assets which are closely interrelated or interdependent in terms of their design, technology and function or their ultimate purpose or use; examples of such contracts include those for the construction of refineries and other complex pieces of plant or equipment.

4. For the purposes of this Standard, construction contracts include:

(a)

contracts for the rendering of services which are directly related to the construction of the asset, for example, those for the services of project managers and architects; and

(b)

contracts for destruction or restoration of assets, and the restoration of the environment following the demolition of assets.

5. Construction contracts are formulated in a number of ways which, for the purposes of this Standard, are classified as fixed price contracts and cost plus contracts. Some construction contracts may contain characteristics of both a fixed price contract and a cost plus contract, for example, in the case of a cost plus contract with an agreed maximum price. In such circumstances, a contractor needs to consider all the conditions in paragraphs 22 and 23 in order to determine when to recognise contract revenue and expenses.

Combining and Segmenting Construction Contracts

6. The requirements of this Standard are usually applied separately to each construction contract. However, in certain circumstances, it is necessary to apply the Standard to the separately identifiable components of a single contract or to a group of contracts together in order to reflect the substance of a contract or a group of contracts.

7. When a contract covers a number of assets, the construction of each asset should be treated as a separate construction contract when:

(a)

separate proposals have been submitted for each asset;

(b)

each asset has been subject to separate negotiation and the contractor and customer have been able to accept or reject that part of the contract relating to each asset; and

(c)

the costs and revenues of each asset can be identified.

8. A group of contracts, whether with a single customer or with several customers, should be treated as a single construction contract when:

(a)

the group of contracts is negotiated as a single package;

(b)

the contracts are so closely interrelated that they are, in effect, part of a single project with an overall profit margin; and

(c)

the contracts are performed concurrently or in a continuous sequence.

9. A contract may provide for the construction of an additional asset at the option of the customer or may be amended to include the construction of an additional asset. The construction of the additional asset should be treated as a separate construction contract when:

(a)

the asset differs significantly in design, technology or function from the asset or assets covered by the original contract; or

(b)

the price of the asset is negotiated without regard to the original contract price.

HEADNOTE: Section 143, read with section 256, of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 33, read with section 66, of Indian Income tax Act, 1922] - Assessment - General - Assessment year 1924-25 - In respect of contracts spread over a number of years, assessee produced accounts but accounts for relevant accounting year could not be separated - ITO assessed profit at a standard rate without informing assessee of information or evidence on which rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal - Whether question of law arose out of order of ITO - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a contractor, was assessed to income-tax for the relevant assessment year in respect of certain contracts which commenced in 1922 and were finished some time in 1924. The assessee produced his accounts, but the accounts for the relevant accounting year could not be separated. The ITO considered the accounts to be unreliable. He, therefore, assumed profit at the standard rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of his assessment. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner concluded that in any case it was impossible to ascertain from the assessee’s accounts what the income had been for one year and, therefore, the only way of ascertaining it was to apply the usual rate of 10 per cent on the total payments received. On application under section 66(2) of the 1922 Act, the Commissioner declined to make any reference.

On application under section 66 (3) of the 1922 Act.

HELD: In the instant case the assessee did not allege that he derived no income at all from any contracts, nor did the assessment proceed definitely on the ground that the accounts were unreliable. The Assistant Commissioner adopted a standard rate for the assessment merely because no separate accounts were available for the accounting year. This was apparently due to the manner in which the accounting were kept. As the assessee failed to produce correct and complete accounts for the accounting year, it was open to the Income-tax Officer to make an assessment to the best of his judgment: vide section 23, read with section 11, of the 1922 Act. The Assistant Commissioner, however, gave no reasons for adopting what he called the usual rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of the assessment, and it was not known how that rate was arrived at. In the circumstances of the case, the point of law emerged for decision was whether in the case of a contract spread over a number of years when accounts for the year under assessment could not be separated, the ITO was legally justified in assessing profits at a flat rate without informing the assessee of the information or evidence on which the rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal.

Accordingly, the petition was accepted and the Commissioner was directed to state the case and refer the point of law to the High Court for decision.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Sardha Ram for the Assessee .

Jagan Nath Aggarwal for the Crown.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Valuation of stock - Assessment year 1959-60 - While completing assessment ITO did not accept assessee's reasons for low profits at rate of 9% in respect of a contract undertaken by him and applied flat rate of 12Â½% profit - On appeal assessee had not derived before AAC that full quantitative details were not available in respect of stores of value of Rs. 1,30,000 - For subsequent assessment year assessee declared a profit of 9.9% - Whether on facts provisions of section 13 were applicable to assessee's case and therefore, Tribunal was justified in upholding addition in assessee's income - Held, yes

FACT: The business of the assessee was execution of construction contracts. The assessee commenced its business from 25-1-1958, and the accounts were closed for the first time on 25-1-1959. During the accounting year the assessee undertook three contracts with respect to which it submitted separate profit and loss statements.

The accounts in respect of the first two contracts were accepted by the authorities under the Act in toto but with regard to the accounts relating to the third contract the ITO declined to accept the assessee's reasons for low profits at the rate of 9% in respect of that contract. He, therefore, applied a flat rate of 12Â½% profit and made certain addition to the assessee's income.

On appeal, the AAC had accepted the assessee's reasons for the low profit of 9% but had sustained an addition of Rs. 10,000 on the ground that the assessee's representative had not denied before him that full quantitative details might not be available in respect of the stores of the value of over Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of the contract. When the case came up before the Tribunal the addition of Rs. 10,000 was found to be excessive and was reduced to Rs. 6,000.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case there was material before the Tribunal on which its finding could be based: the assessee's representative had admitted before the AAC that full quantitative details in respect of the stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of that contract might not be available. In the circumstances, recourse to estimating the profits on the contract was inevitable. He, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 10,000 as against Rs. 26,434 added by the ITO. If the assessee wished to displace the AAC's estimate it was open to him to adduce evidence in support of its claim that the consumption of stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 was fully justified. This the assessee apparently did not do. For the subsequent year 1960-61 the assessee itself declared a net profit rate of 9.9% as against 9% declared in the assessment year in question. It could not be disputed that this was additional material which the Tribunal could take into consideration as it did. There was thus material before the Tribunal on which its estimate was based. The Tribunal's decision was, therefore, in conformity with the decision in the case of CIT v. Maharajadhiraj of Darbhanga [1933] 1 ITR 94 (P.C.).

The Tribunal was therefore justified in holding that the proviso to section 13 was applicable and there was material before it to sustain the aforesaid addition.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of revenue.

On further appeal by the revenue: HELD: In the instant case the assessee as sub-contractor to execute the civil construction works awarded by the principals, which was a small part of the projects executed by the principals. On the contract receipts, the principals had also deducted the tax under section 194C. Besides, the assessee was also engaged in the business of trading of sarees. It was also a fact that the assessee filed duly audited profit and loss account and balance sheet along with its annexure. It also produced the audited books of account, bills/vouchers and bank statements before the Assessing Officer as admitted by him in the assessment order. Besides, it further produced all the details and explanations called for by the Assessing Officer from time to time. It also produced labour registers before the Assessing Officer. However, he was of the opinion that the said registers had not been maintained in a conventional manner and according to him, there were no signatures or thumb impressions of all the recipients. Because of the aforesaid observations, the Assessing Officer rejected the audited books of account of the assessee and estimated the net profit. The Assessing Officer gave the examples of net profit earned by three companies and, thereafter, he relied on the provisions of section 11AD and estimated the net profit at the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts. Now the assessee argued that the estimation of net profit at the rate of 8 per cent by relying on provisions of section 44AD was totally incorrect and without any basis for the reason that the assessee was sub-contractor and its profit margin was low in comparison to the contractors. Further, the Assessing officer had compared the profit of the assessee with the companies whose turnover and business paraphernalia was huge in comparison to the assessee. Further, the assessee had executed the part of work of civil construction for these companies and, therefore, it was not correct to compare the profit of those companies with the profit margin of the assessee. In fact the profit margin of those companies was also less than the margin which had been estimated by the Assessing Officer in the case of assessee. In the case of assessee as per audited books of account, the net profit margin for assessment years 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10 and 2010-11 was 1.94 per cent, 0.67 per cent, 0.20 per cent and 0.09 per cent respectively. Now, the assessee argued that the Assessing Officer had failed to appreciate that the profit margins of contractors and sub-contractors could not be same. In the assessment order he had worked out the average profit margins in the case of those three companies at 5.93 per cent, 6.15 per cent and 5.19 per cent respectively and in the case of assessee he had estimated the profit at the rate of 8 per cent, whereas, in the case of assessee the profit margin would be much less than in these companies being a sub-contractor of these companies. [Para 5]

In view of the above factual position and comparative figures given by assessee of its principal, wherein the net profit was ranging from 5.19 per cent to 6.15 per cent, it was held that definitely there would be lower profit in the case of sub-contractor, i.e., the assessee and, hence, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly estimated the net profit rate at 4 per cent. Accordingly, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) and this issue of revenue's appeal was dismissed. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with Sections 29 and 32, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Profit rate) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether profit of a contractor would necessarily depend upon various factors like place of execution of contract, accessibility of labour, raw material, etc. and would, therefore, vary from contractor to contractor - Held, yes - Whether gross receipts to which net profit rate is to be applied shall be determined after giving allowance on account of depreciation - Held, yes - Assessee-firm, engaged in business of execution of government contract, executed works of laying optical fibre cables in a remote border area of Jammu and Kashmir - Assessing Officer made addition to income applying net profit rate of 12 per cent on gross receipt - However, both Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal scaled down net profit to 8 per cent and also reduced depreciation out of gross receipt - Whether no question of law arose from order of Tribunal - Held, yes [Paras 3 and 7] [In favour of assessee]IT: Profit of contractor depend upon various factors like place of execution of contract, accessibility of labour, raw material, etc. and would, therefore, vary from contractor to contractor

FACT: The assessee-firm was engaged in business of execution of government contract. It filed return of income which came on scrutiny. During assessment proceeding, while examining books of account, some discrepancies were found that expenditure claimed by assessee was very much on the higher side as the work executed by it. Consequently, the assessee was asked to produce proof of expenditure, incurred on wages and labour, wages register and also to correlate wages paid with the project executed.

Thereupon, the Assessing Officer, thus, applied 12 per cent rate on gross receipt after excluding cost of material supplied by the department and made addition accordingly.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reduced the net profit rate to 8 per cent as against 12 per cent on the contract receipt and allow depreciation and salary paid to partners as claimed.

On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On appeal:

HELD: There is no reason to interfere with the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals), affirmed by the Tribunal, scaling down the net profit to 8 per cent against 12 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer. The reasons assigned by the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal are clear and cogent and even otherwise no two contractors can have a similar rate of profit. The profit of a contractor would necessarily depend upon various factors like place of execution of the contract, the accessibility of labour, raw material etc. and would, therefore, vary from contractor to contractor. The assessee in the instant case, was admittedly laying optical fiber cables etc. in a remote border area of Jammu and Kashmir. [Para 3]

In the present case, the assessee's entire contractual receipts were from Government department & all proceeds were received through banking channel & thus the assessee's estimation of the net profit @ 6.06% of the turnover is higher than the rate of 6% prescribed u/s 44AD. It is viewed that flat 15% income on turnover is highly unjustified. However, it is the considered opinion that net profit rate of 7% in civil contract business especially when all the contract receipts were received through proper banking channel on which the tax has been deducted at source is a reasonable one and accordingly the AO is directed to recompute the net profit of the assessee @7% of the total turnover declared by the assessee i.e. Rs.17.40 crores. Accordingly, this ground of Appeal of the assessee is partly allowed. [Para 10.4]

FACT: The assessee, a contractor undertaking projects of Indian Railways on turnkey basis, filed its return of income.

On the basis of the materials gathered by the income-tax authorities in the course of a search carried out in the assessee's premises as well as in the premises of the directors and trusted persons, the Assessing Officer referred the matter to a special audit in terms of section 142(2A). The special audit report, inter alia, reported that there were large number of transactions in which several discrepancies were noticed.

In response to the queries raised by the Assessing Officer on the basis of the special audit report the assessee could not give any proper explanation and wherever an explanation was sought to be given, it was found to be evasive. The assessee was also allowed inspection of the seized documents and was supplied photocopies of the seized records. Despite such opportunity, no convincing reason was given by the assessee.

The Assessing Officer proceeded to estimate the net profit of the assessee at 11 per cent of the gross receipts from the contracts. The Assessing Officer also found that some income from business activities was not included in the aforesaid receipts and the profit from such activity was taken at Rs.13.34 lakhs. Demands were accordingly raised.

Penalty proceedings were initiated by the Assessing Officer for concealment of income and after rejecting the assessee's explanation, a penalty was imposed for concealment of income under section 271(1)(c).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelled the penalty order on the ground that the Assessing Officer has not stated the basis of this estimate nor did he give an opportunity to the assessee to rebut the proposal to estimate the profits at 11 per cent of the gross receipts. He held that the assessee made a counter proposal which was a conditional offer as to the taxability of the profits and even if it is assumed that there was an agreement on the part of the assessee for being taxed at the rate of 11 per cent of the gross receipts, it does not follow automatically that the assessee concealed its income.

On second appeal by Revenue, the Tribunal dismissed it.

Reasons for rejecting wages record as commented by the Assessing Officer related to full address of the labour, which was not given on the muster roll register. The wages record had been kept by the assessee as per regulation known as 'Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970. The Assessing Officer had also alleged that the actual date of payment was not mentioned by the payee receiving the wages. The date on which the entry had been made in the wages register was the actual date of payment. As per the nature of the contract work executed by the assessee, he had got a contract to carry out a particular job or a contract for which the material was supplied by the CPWD/DOT and the labour was provided by the assessee-contractor. The assessee used to make payments to the labourers on the basis of mandays put in by the labourers and not on the basis of work performed by them on each day. Therefore, there was no merit in the allegations of the Assessing Officer that work performed by the labour was not mentioned on the payment vouchers and in making them as basis for rejection of books of account. The payment to the assessee-contractor was also made on the basis of work completed which was measured by the department itself and not on the basis of what the labourer had done. The bills for such a contract were prepared, which were not verified by the engineers of contractee before making payments. On the basis of those bills which were finally approved by the Government engineers/contractee, the payment was given to the assessee-contractor after deducting TDS. Thus, it was humanly not possible to provide the details as to what work a particular labourer had done at the site. Further, the Assessing Officer had also not indicated any defect in the system of accounting regularly followed by the assessee, or its correctness, nor was there any change in the method of accounting during the year under consideration as compared to the earlier years to indicate any intention of the assessee to show low profit.

While examining the books of the assessee, the Assessing Officer has to consider the following aspects : (i) whether the assessee has regularly employed a method of accounting; (ii) even if regular adoption of a method of accounting is there, whether the annual profits can properly be deduced from the method employed; (iii ) whether the accounts have been correctly maintained; (iv) whether the accounts maintained are complete in the sense that there is no significant omission therein. If the answers to above four questions would be in the affirmative, then the assessee's profits would be computed on the basis of his accounts. In such cases, proviso to section 145(1) or section 145(2) cannot be invoked. On the perusal of the materials placed on record in the instant case, it was found that the answers to all the above four questions were in the affirmative. No finding had been recorded by either of the lower authorities as to the unacceptability of the method and to the irregularity of the accounts kept by the assessee. It is well-settled that in the absence of such a finding recorded by the authorities, the book results cannot be ignored or brushed aside.

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts - Assessment years 1993-94 to 1997-98 - Assessee-firm was engaged in work of civil construction in Public Works Department (PWD) - Assessing Officer, after rejecting books of account, made assessment determining 8 per cent profit at flat rate - Commissioner (Appeals) reduced rate of profit from 8 per cent to 5 per cent on ground that since turnover of assessee exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs, it was bound to incur more expenses and rate of profit would be less - Further, Tribunal reduced profit rate to 4 per cent on ground that assessee was doing work for PWD and normally, profit rate was much less for work of PWD, as contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under supervision of PWD authorities - Whether rate of profit cannot be assumed, merely on assumptions or surmises and conjectures - Held, yes - Whether since Assessing Officer as well as Commissioner (Appeals) as also Tribunal had not recorded any finding based on any material and findings recorded were merely based on surmises and conjectures, findings of rate of profit could not be sustained and 
 matter deserved to be remanded to assessing authority for re-determination thereof - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm which was engaged in the work of civil construction in public works department, filed returns for the assessment years 1993-94 to 1997-98. The Assessing Officer on the analogy of section 44AD, after rejecting the books of account, made best judgment assessment determining 8 per cent profit at flat rate. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reduced the rate of profit from 8 per cent to 5 per cent, mainly on the ground that since the turnover of the assessee exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs, it was bound to incur more expenses and rate of profit would be less. On further appeal, the Tribunal reduced the rate of profit to 4 per cent on the ground that the assessee was doing the work for PWD and normally the net profit rate was much less for the work of PWD, as the contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under the supervision of the PWD authorities.

On appeal :

HELD: A bare perusal of the findings recorded by the Assessing Officer would indicate that he had applied the principles determining the profit vide section 44AD, whereas the aforesaid provision was not at all applicable in the case of assessee in the relevant assessment years. This factual position was not being disputed by either of the parties. That being so, the question arose as to what should be the profit rate for the purpose of determining the profit accrued or gained by the parties. Since the Assessing Officer, had not dealt with this question independent of section 44AD, the rate of profit could not be upheld. [Para 3]

So far as the determination of profit of 5 per cent by the Commissioner (Appeals) was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) had also not given any reason nor any material was placed before the Commissioner (Appeals), or for that matter before the Assessing Officer for arriving at a conclusion about the rate of profit. Merely on assumption that since the assessee was performing the work for the PWD and as the contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under supervision of the PWD authorities, the rate of profit would be low or merely because the turnover exceeded Rs. 10 lakhs, it would incur more expenses, the aforesaid rate of profits could not have been arrived at. Neither the Commissioner (Appeals) nor the Tribunal had taken into consideration the relevant material or facts which might be necessary for arriving at such a conclusion. [Para 4]

The rate of profit cannot be assumed merely on assumptions or surmises and conjectures. It is the first liability of the assessee to produce such records, evidence and material so as to substantiate his plea about the rate of profit that he claims and in case the books of account have been rejected , the onus shifts on to the Assessing Officer to determine the rate of profit on consideration of the material which may be brought before him or even on making such inquiry, which may be necessary and which may include the requirement of having any information from the assessee also during the course of determination of such rate of profit, namely, during the assessment proceedings. In no case, simply because the turnover was more than Rs. 40 lakhs or the assessee was performing civil construction work for Public Works Department, neither the rate of profits could be determined nor it could be taken to be less nor it could be reduced nor could be arrived at any presumptions. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Best judgment assessment - Assessment year 1974-75 - Whether while making a best judgment assessment, though there must necessarily be guess work in matter, it must not be arbitrary - Held, yes - Assessee-contractor did not main books of account - He filed his return of income on estimate basis by computing profit at flat rate of 10 per cent on gross receipts - ITO, however, computed net profit at rate of 15 per cent - Revision petition filed by assessee was dismissed by Commissioner - Whether since neither ITO nor Commissioner had referred to any material for applying flat rate of 
15 percent while estimating net profits, impugned orders passed by them deserved to be set aside - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner assessee, who was carrying on business as a contractor filed his return on estimated basis by computing the profit at a flat rate of 10 per cent, on gross receipts, as he did not maintain any books of account. The ITO, however, computed the net profit at 15 per cent, on the contract payments received by the assessee. The revision petition filed under section 263 was dismissed by the Commissioner.

On writ:

HELD: It is now well settled that while making a best judgment assessment, though there must necessarily be guess-work in the matter, it must not be arbitrary. In the instant case, the basis on which the computation was made was not disclosed in the order.

Neither the ITO nor the Commissioner had referred to any material for applying the flat rate of 15 per cent while estimating the net profits.

In such circumstances, the assessment order could not but be held to be arbitrary. The order passed by the ITO and that passed by the Commissioner, therefore, deserved to be set aside. The petition was allowed accordingly.

Note: The case has been decided in favour of the petitioner-assessee.

In the instant case, the ITO arrived at the figure on the basis of the receipts extending over three accounting year. He took the sum total of these receipts to be the base for the net income that had accrued to the assessee during the accounting year 1943-44 as the entire contract work had been completed during that year. Mere execution of the contract work will not necessarily entitle the contractor to make a demand for payment until it is ascertained that the works are up to the standard agreed upon between the parties. Some parts of such work may be wholly rejected and like bad debts in every earning may be ignored in computing the gains or profits. It might have been open to the ITO, in exercise of his discretion, to make an enquiry into whether and when the bills for payment became due to the assessee. Much depended upon the terms in the contract, and the manner of its performance. Even as a basis of guess work, which the Income-tax Officer was entitled to do, the basis could not be said to be in consonance with honest guess work. The ITO did not seem to have taken into consideration why the payments which, according to him, were due to the assessee in the accounting year were not fully paid till three years after. Sometimes the payments to the contractors are withheld on account of unsatisfactory execution and they are held entitled to payments only if and when they replace the rejected work by acceptable and accepted ones. The bare possibility of such contingency could not be wholly eliminated in the instant case. If the ITO, in arriving at the figure for assessment, left out these considerations, he certainly could not be said to have exercised his judgment which he was none the less called upon to do in making the assessment in cases of assessee's default under sections 23(4) and 13 proviso of the 1922 Act. Any method of accounting adopted by the ITO acting under the proviso of section 13 of 1922 Act can be rejected if the method in fact does not show the true income, profits and gains. In this view of the matter, the Appellate Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipt basis with regard to contracts carried out and completed during the year of accounting, there being every presumption that the incomes were paid as soon as they became due. At any rate, the Tribunal's decision might be upheld on the ground that when two methods of guess work are available for the purpose of assessment, the one which is more just to the assessee and which involves a much less margin of chance of uncertainty should be taken as the basis.

In the result, the Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipts basis with regard to contracts carried on and completed during the year of account.

As regards the reduction of flat rate, the Appellate Tribunal had arrived at the lesser flat rate on the basis of their decisions in similar cases in the district. Their opinions were not receivable evidence in the instant case. The decisions in different cases must have been based upon different facts and different inferences deducible from such facts. In this connection, it might be observed that the ITO had been very fair to the assessee bearing in mind the difference between the gross value and net value of the bills. The Appellate Tribunal, therefore, did commit a mistake of law in arriving at a finding for which there was no relevant evidence to support.

Therefore, the reduction of the estimated profit rate from 40 per cent adopted by the ITO to 30 per cent by the Tribunal on the ground that 30 per cent was the general rate adopted by it in the cases of other assessees doing the same kind of contract works during the same assessment year was not legal.

The revenue further referred to the decision of the Supreme Court in P.M. Mohammed Meerakhan v. CIT [1969] 73 ITR 735 to contend that income-tax authorities have power to estimate profits by treating unsold stock in trade and value it according to normal accountancy practice. HELD: The main case of the revenue was that the assessee should have disclosed profits on the receipts of contract on the basis of percentage completion method of accounting. As against that it was the case of the assessee that the initial price for which the contract was awarded was later on found to be unreliable as it was increased to 29 per cent, therefore, the percentage completion method was not applicable even according to the accounting standard AS-7.The assessee had never shown any profit out of the contract and the loss shown by the assessee was accepted by the lower authorities in the immediately preceding year and succeeding year. Thus, according to the accounts, the assessee had never earned profit from this contract. The accounts of the assessee were audited and it was not the case of the revenue that the assessee did not furnish details regarding accounts maintained by it. No defects whatsoever had been found in the account books maintained by the assessee. What can be assessed as income under the Act, is income. If there is an existence of income, then only it can be estimated. Therefore, not going into the controversy whether the accounting standard AS-7 was properly employed by the assessee or not, it would be considered that whether Assessing Officer was justified in assessing the net profit of the assessee from such contract at the rate of 10 per cent. There was no substance in the argument of the revenue that the assessee was under an obligation to maintain its account on the basis of the accounting standard AS-7, as the said accounting standard was not mandatory for the assessee for the year under consideration. Even if the percentage of completion method was held to be applicable to the case of the assessee, then the question would arise that what would be the basis for estimate. It is well-established law that the estimate made must be honest and fair. There must exist reasonable nexus between the available material and the estimate. Thus, the only question for determination arose whether there existed some material on the basis of which it could be said that application of net profit rate of 10 per cent was appropriate. It was the contention of the assessee that it had incurred losses while performing the contract. No material had been brought on record by the Assessing Officer that such contention of the assessee was contrary to the facts. Addition had been made without indicating any material or basis on which it could be decided that application of net profit rate of 10 per cent was appropriate. On the contrary, material was on the record to show that the assessee had incurred loss in performing such a contract. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was not justified in rejecting the books of account by invoking the provisions of section 145(3) without bringing on record any cogent reasons and infirmities in the maintenance of books of account of the assessee and further estimating the net profit. [Para 13]

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had decided the issue correctly.

On reference : HELD: Contracts for building construction or of similar type can be divided into two broad categories. Category No. (1) will cover contracts where, at the time of entering into the contract, the contractor is told that some of the materials required for construction work will be supplied by the person or authority who entrusts the construction work to him and it is on that footing of such construction materials being supplied by the authorities or the other party to the contract, that the contractor enters into the contract for the construction quoting a particular figure for the entire contract. A sub-category of this first category of contract is the type of contract where, for notional purposes, a total figure is mentioned for the construction contract inclusive of materials and on the footing that the contractor is to supply all the materials for the construction work. However, at the time when the contract is entered into, it is clearly agreed between the contracting parties that some of the building materials will be supplied by the other party to the contract, that is, the person or authority entrusting the construction work to the contractor, and that credit will have to be given by the contractor for the materials, thus, received and the rates at which the credit is to be given is also agreed upon between the contractor and the other party to the contract. It was designated as a sub-category of category No. (1) because though notionally and on the face of it the contract has been entered into for a much larger amount and on the footing that the contractor is to supply all the materials, because of the clear agreement between the parties about the materials to be supplied by the other party to the contract and also about rates at which those materials are to be supplied, it is clear that in fact and in substance the parties have entered into the contract where certain specified materials are to be supplied not by the contractor but by the other party to the contract and the contractor right from the beginning enters into the contract on this footing and puts forward his quotation and ultimately gets the contract for the amount where he does not take into consideration supply of those particular materials or rates for those materials. Category No. (2) of contracts is the type where, right from the beginning, the contractor enters into the construction contract on the footing that he has to supply all the materials but while the contract is being executed, the other party to the contract supplies some of the materials and when the bill is finally paid, the other party to the contract claims credit for the price of the materials supplied to the building contractor. In that eventuality, it is really the total figure of the original contract or figure worked out in accordance with the terms of the original contract which will constitute the original receipts of the building contractor and the fact that, instead of going into the market and purchasing the materials for himself, the contractor gets these materials for himself, the party to the contract, does not enter into the picture so far as this aspect of the case is concerned. The question as to under which particular category, category No. (1) or category No. (2) set out above, a particular contract falls, will have to be decided looking to the substance of the transaction between the parties in each individual case. If the case falls under the first category, then it is obvious that the cost of the materials supplied by the other party to the contract cannot be taken into consideration in arriving at the figure of the total receipts of the contractor in respect of the particular contract for building construction. On the other hand, if the case falls, on the facts and circumstances of the particular case, in the second category, then the total receipts of the building contractor in respect of that particular contract will be the total amount of the contract notwithstanding the fact that the other party to the contract has supplied some of the materials required for building construction work.

It is, therefore, clear that in matters of this kind, when deciding whether a particular amount should or should not be considered to be trading receipt, it is the true nature and quality of the receipt, either actual or deemed, which has to be considered and not the outward form or the head under which the amount is entered in the account books of the assessee concerned.

It is thus, substance of the contract which matters and if, the agreement between the parties right from the beginning is that certain materials are to be supplied by the other party to the contract, that is, the Government department, or the authority concerned, then it is obvious that the contract was entered into on the footing that no profit would be made by the building contractor in respect of the supply of those materials.

On appeal to the High Court:

HELD: The assessee is not right in his contention that whenever an assessment is made by applying a flat rate of profit to the declared turnover or receipts, which is higher than the rate adopted by the assessee in the return of income, there can be no inference that the assessee concealed his profits. [Para 9] The number of discrepancies and irregularities listed by the special auditor in his report which are reproduced in the assessment order bear testimony to the fact that the books of account maintained by the assessee were wholly unreliable. If they were so, there can be no sanctity attached to the figure of gross contract receipts on which the assessee estimated 3 per cent as its income. It is true that the Assessing Officer did not enhance the figure of gross receipts but that is not because he gave a clean chit to the books of account allegedly maintained by the assessee; he could not have given a clean chit in the face of the defects, discrepancies and irregularities reported by the special auditor. In order to take care of those discrepancies he resorted to a much higher estimate of the profits by adopting 11 per cent on the gross contract receipts. He gave due opportunity to the assessee to explain the discrepancies and also to show why the profit rate of 11 per cent cannot be adopted but these opportunities were not availed of by the assessee. He also has recorded in the assessment order that the assessee was permitted to inspect the seized documents and was given photocopies of the desired documents. This is not denied by the assessee. In these circumstances, the mere fact that the estimate was reduced by the Tribunal to 8 per cent would in no way take away the guilt of the assessee or explain its failure to prove that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on its part. It appears that the assessee was taking a chance - sitting on the fence - despite the fact that there was a search towards the close of the relevant accounting year in the course of which incriminating documents were found. It appears that the intention of the assessee was to take a risk and disclose a lesser income than what it actually earned and rely upon the minor variations in the rate of profits adopted by the taxing authorities and the Tribunal as a defence in the penalty proceedings. The plea - accepted by the Tribunal - that the assessee agreed to be assessed at 11 per cent of the gross receipts only "to buy peace" and "avoid litigation" cannot be accepted in view of the judgment of the Supreme Court in MAK Data (P.) Ltd. [2013] 358 ITR 593/38 taxmann.com 448. The Tribunal, was in error in upholding the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelling the penalty. Accordingly, the substantial questions of law is answered against the assessee and in favour of the Revenue. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c), read with section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 2003-04 - Whether ad hoc estimation of income by applying flat net profit ratio can be held either as concealment or as filing of inaccurate particulars of income for purpose of levying penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Held, no [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee was a contractor undertaking project of Indian Railways on turnkey basis. A search action under section 132 was carried out at the assessee's premises. On revenue's appeal:

HELD: The issue of disparity between the assessed income and the returned income is not sustainable as the addition was purely on ad hoc estimation of net profit ratio. The Assessing Officer applied a particular flat rate of 11 per cent against the declared profit rate of 3 per cent by the assessee. The Tribunal has reduced the estimated income by adopting 8 per cent of profit rate which is also based on ad hoc estimation. Ultimately, the addition sustained or survived is ad hoc estimation of income by applying flat rate of 8 per cent of the profit which cannot be held either as concealment or filing inaccurate particulars. The Tribunal, in the quantum appeal, has also observed that suppression of the profit had not been established and the allegations have not been proved. On the basis of the explanation submitted by the assessee, the Tribunal has found no justification in applying and confirming the net profit rate of 11 per cent which has been reduced to 8 per cent on ad hoc basis subject to the allowability of depreciation and interest thereon. For levying penalty under section 271(1)(c), there has to be concealment of particulars of income by the assessee or the assessee must have furnished inaccurate particulars of income. Ultimately, in assessee's case, addition sustained was based on ad hoc estimation of income by applying a flat rate of 8 per cent of profit which can neither be held as concealment of income nor filing of inaccurate particulars of income. Further, the assessee's offering of the profit rate was a conditional proposal as the assessee was not able to collect the whole information about the context and produce the same. Thus, offer made by assessee was to buy peace and not to enter into dispute with revenue authorities. To purchase the peace and avoid any dispute with the revenue authorities in the quantum of income, assessee offered the estimated rate of profit. Considering all these facts and circumstances, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in deleting the penalty levied under section 271(1)(c ). [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits - Assessment year 1986-87 - Assessee was a labour contractor - Assessing Officer made certain additions as unexplained cash credits based on entries in cash book which were deleted on appeal - Whether since deposits as well as withdrawals of contract receipts were not properly reflected in books of account and as such, no reliance could be placed on bank accounts, order of Commissioner (Appeals) was valid in order - Held, yes - Whether considering that assessee was labour contractor, Commissioner (Appeals) was, however, not fair and reasonable to apply GP rate of 12.5 per cent against 10 per cent applied by Assessing Officer which was also agreed to by assessee - Held, yes

HELD: As far the ground taken by the assessee in his cross objection regarding the application of the rate of 12.5 per cent by the Commissioner (Appeals) against the rate of 10 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer was concerned, looking to the fact that the assessee was a labour contractor, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not fair and reasonable to apply the GP rate of 12.5 per cent against the rate of 10 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer which was also agreed to by the assessee.
