FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of supply of labour for civil and technical job works assigned by 'B'.

During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer noticed difference between the receipts that the assessee had shown and the receipts as per form no. 26AS submitted by the contractee company. The assessee did not produce any evidence in support of his contention that the difference was on account of adjustment entry made by company 'B'.

Accordingly, the Assessing Officer made addition of amount of difference to the income of the assessee.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition.

On second appeal:

HELD: It is an admitted fact that there was a difference between the total receipts shown by the assessee in his books of account and by the contractee in Form No. 26AS. The assessee could not produce any evidence in support of his contention that the difference was on account of adjustment entry. The Assessing Officer made the addition on account of difference in those receipts.

When the receipts were not shown by the assessee in the regular books of account, it cannot be presumed without bringing cogent material on record that the expenses related to the said receipts were shown in the books of account. In other words, when the receipts were out of the books of account, the payment on account of expenses may also be out of the books of account. In such circumstances, the only way to determine the income is application of net profit rate. In the instant case, the assessee in the earlier years was showing the income under section 44AD, which provides that the net profit rate must be applied at 8 per cent. Since certain contract receipts were not shown by the assessee, the net profit rate was to be applied on those receipts. HELD: There was no reason for the Commissioner (Appeals) to enhance the rate of profit to 10 per cent. HEADNOTE: Section 28 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Assessee, carrying contract work under government departments, did not maintain proper account books - Whether net profit could be estimated at a flat rate on gross receipts including value of material supplied by government - Held, on facts, yes

FACT: The assessee, a firm of contractors, executed certain contracts given by the State Government during the assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74. For the assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74, the total gross receipts under the work contract respectively amounted to Rs. 19,41,472 and Rs. 22,86,353 out of which a sum of Rs. 1,27,215 and Rs. 4,82,527 was deducted, being the value of materials supplied by the Government. Since the assessee did not maintain proper account books or any stock book or material issue register, the ITO determined the net profit under the proviso to section 145(1) by applying a flat rate of 10 per cent on the aforesaid gross receipts without excluding the value of the materials supplied by the Government. The AAC, however, directed that for determining the net profit, flat rate was to be applied only on the net receipts. The Tribunal could not ascertain: (i) the actual position regarding the materials obtained from the department and; (ii) whether the same remained under the control of the department or of the assessee. It, accordingly, restored the ITO's order.

On reference:

HELD: 1. No hard and fast rule could be laid down as to whether the value of the materials should or should not be included in a contractor's gross turnover from business for determining his net profits. It depended upon the manner in which the materials were obtained and used in the execution of the contract. The contracts could be generally classified as (i) contract for labour supply; (ii) a lump sum contract; and (iii) where the material supplied by the department was either an outright sale or was specifically meant to be used in the work allotted. In the types of contracts mentioned in (i) and (iii), the profit had to be calculated on the gross receipts, including the value of the material supplied either by the Government or by the assessee. Whereas, in the case of the other items at (ii) and (iii), profit would be determined en the basis of only the net amount without taking into consideration the value of the materials. In the instant case, in the absence of any stock register or issue register, it was not known whether the materials were supplied by the department as an outright sale to the assessee or it remained under the control of the department throughout and that the same was never under the control of the contractor except for using it in the constitution.

2. The Tribunal was, accordingly, correct in holding that the profit was to be calculated on the gross receipts excluding the recoveries for the material supplied by the Government department.

Kashi Nath Jain, Rameshwar Prasad and A.B. Prasad for the Petitioner. B.P. Rajgarhia and S.K. Sharan for the Respondent.

HELD: Section 44AD clarifies that if the assessee's gross receipts are more than Rs. 1 crore and if the assessee did not maintain the books of account, then his profit has to be estimated at the rate of 8 per cent and depreciation should not be allowed. In the instant case, the assessee did not produce the books of account and also did not appear before the Assessing Officer, therefore the Assessing Officer was not able to verify the claim made in profit and loss account. HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1964-65 and 1965-66 - Assessee manufactured sweets and other eatables and also sold confectionery articles which he purchased on wholesale from another merchant-Tribunal rejecting assessee’s books of account acting under section 145 and, on basis of data available, adopted flat rate for calculating profit - Whether, question relating to flat rate was pure question of fact and thus, no question of law arose from Tribunal’s order - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was carrying on business of manufacturing sweets and another eastables and selling confectionery articles which he purchased on wholesale from another merchant. He submitted his return for the year 1965-66, showing gross turnover in the sum of Rs. 2,34,576. According to the assessee the gross profit rate of the confectionery manufactured by him was 17.5 per cent and for the one that was purchased by him it was 8.5 per cent, yielding an average profit of 11.2 per cent. The ITO, not finding the books of account entirely, reliable estimated the turnover at Rs. 2,50,000 and calculated the average rate of profit at 17.5 per cent and taxed the assessee accordingly. The AAC reduced the gross turnover to Rs. 2,44,000 and reduced the average rate to 15 per cent profit. The Tribunal for the purposes of calculation firstly, reduced the total gross turnover to Rs. 2,40,000 and treating the portion relating to the confectionery manufactured by the assessee at Rs. 75,000, the profit rate assessed by the Tribunal was 20 per cent. Regarding the sale of the confectionery which was purchased by the assessee and sold by him, the turnover was taken at Rs. 1,65,000 and the rate applied to it was 10 per cent resulting in an average at 13.1 per cent. Similar rates of profit were applied by the Tribunal for the assessment year 1964-65. The Tribunal declined to make reference under section 256(1).

On application under section 256(2) :

HELD: Undisputably, the assessee placed before the taxation authorities its own account books and they were not found reliable and, therefore, the ITO, the AAC and the Tribunal had acted under the provisions of section 145(1) and the proviso thereto. The flat rate when it was calculated on the basic of available data, could not be called arbitrary or perverse. It had been said by the Tribunal that the firm, from whom the assessee bought manufactured confectionery and sold it made a profit of 19 per cent and the assessee made a profit of 10 per cent which had been charged by the Tribunal and against which there was no grievance. Therefore, at least up to 19 per cent there was clear evidence about the flat rate being just. If the Tribunal made it 20 per cent one could not say it capricious, conjectural or based on irrelevant or no evidence. A question relating to the flat rate was a pure question of fact. Although from the language of the questions which were asked to be referred to the High Court the grievance of enhancement was there yet it was not pressed. Therefore, it was not necessary to enter into the question whether the tax was enhanced because it was factually incorrect to say that the total liability of the assessee was increased. It was not necessary to enter into the argument whether the question arose from the order of the Tribunal or not because clearly no question of law arose in the instant case.

Note: The case was decided against the assessee.

, opined that the books of account maintained by the assessee were not amenable for verification.

He thus rejected books of account under the provisions of section 145(3) and estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts net of all deductions. In addition to estimation of net profit, the Assessing Officer made separate additions towards income from other sources being interest earned on fixed deposits.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal: HELD: The Assessing Officer has rejected books of account for the reason that the assessee has failed to produce necessary bills and vouchers in respect of expenditure. The Assessing Officer has observed that most of the expenditure are supported by self-made vouchers. Although, the assessee claims that it has produced bills and vouchers in respect of major expenditure, fails to substantiate the claim with necessary evidences. The assessee failed to controvert the findings of the Assessing Officer with any positive evidence to come to the conclusion that the books of account maintained by him gave a true and correct profit from the business. The Assessing Officer was therefore right in rejecting books of account under the provisions of section 145(3) of the Act. [Para 8]

Having said, one has to examine, on facts and circumstances of the case whether the Assessing Officer was right in adopting net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts. There is no dispute with regard to the facts that the assessee is in the business of execution of works contracts. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee had disclosed 6.73 per cent to 7.44 per cent net profit, in the earlier period. For the assessment year 2007-08 in the scrutiny assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer has estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts for which the assessee has not preferred any appeal. Estimation of net profit from the business is one of the accepted method of determination of income from business. But, there is no hard and fast rule for estimation of income.

The department is following estimation of net profit on various rates depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. But, while estimating net profit from the business, there should be a basis for adopting a particular rate of net profit, either based on comparable cases of similar nature of business or assessee's own book results for earlier years. When there is no possibility of getting a comparable cases, and there is no possibility of reference to assessee's own book results for earlier periods, a reference to the provisions of section 44AD can be made, wherein the Act provides for estimation of net profit from the specified businesses subject to certain conditions. [Para 9]

The provisions of section 44AD provide for estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on gross receipts, in case where the assessees are involved in specified businesses and turnover from the business does not exceed specified limit. Although, the assessee's case does not fall within the ambit of the provisions of section 44AD of the Act, as its contract receipts exceed the specified limit, the analogy provided in the provisions of section 44AD can be adopted for estimation of net profit because of nature of business carried out by the assessee. The nature of business carried on by the assessee was squarely fit into the specified businesses referred to in the provisions of section 44AD of the Act. The presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD, reflects the legislative approved rate of net profit, which can be considered as fair and reasonable to estimate income from civil contract business, where the books of account are not found reliable by the Assessing Officer.

In this case, admittedly, the Assessing Officer had rejected books of account for the reason that the assessee has failed to produce supporting bills and vouchers in respect of expenditure. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee himself has admitted about 8 per cent net profit in the earlier period net of all deductions including depreciation. Therefore, considering the overall facts and circumstances of the case, the rate of net profit adopted by the Assessing Officer appears to be fair and reasonable. Hence, estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on total receipts net of all deductions including depreciation is upheld. [Para 10]

In so far as separate deductions towards depreciation is concerned, the assessee submitted that when estimation of net profit is made, separate deductions towards depreciation should be allowed, as depreciation is a notional deduction for normal wear and tear of the assets.

In this case, the assessee is involved in the business of execution of main works which carries more profit than sub-contract works and hence, the Assessing Officer has rightly adopted reasonable net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts and accordingly, further deductions towards depreciation is not allowed. Whether separate deductions can be allowed towards depreciation or not is a fact which is to be decided based on the facts and circumstances of each case and also based on the rate of net profit adopted for estimation of profit.

HEADNOTE: Section 254, read with section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 33(4), read with section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Appellate Tribunal - Order of - Assessment years 1943-44 to 1945-46 - Assessee-firm carried on business of aerodrome work, katcha building constructions etc. - On firm's failure to produce books of account for relevant assessment years, ITO took sum total of receipts of assessee for three accounting years and, thereupon adopted profit rate of 40 per cent in exercise of his power under section 13, read with section 23(4) of 1922 Act - Tribunal, however, opined that ITO should have applied rate of profit to annual receipts instead of total receipts and that by amalgamating receipts under one assessment ITO raised tax liability of assessee which was not fair - Besides, Tribunal also reduced profit rate from 40 per cent to 30 per cent - Whether Tribunal was right in asking ITO to assess assessee on receipt basis with regard to contracts carried out and completed during year of accounting, there being every presumption that incomes were paid as soon as they became due - Held, yes - Whether, however, as regards reduction of flat rate of profit, Tribunal did commit a mistake of law in arriving at said finding for which there was no relevant evidence to support - Held, yes

FACT: Two persons 'S' and B constituted an unregistered firm sharing the profits and losses in the proportion of 9-as and 7-as respectively. The business, of which the profits and gains were the subject of assessment, consisted of aerodrome work under the Central Public Works Department, certain katcha building constructions under the Military Engineering Service and small supply of potatoes to Garrison Engineer. During the accounting year 1942-43, the assessee received a sum of Rs. 2,92,256. During the next year, that is 1-4-1943 to 31-3-1944, they received a sum of Rs. 86,434 and during the following accounting year of 1-4-1944 to 31-3-1945, they received a sum of Rs. 25,703. Besides it appeared, there were certain estimated outstanding bills to the credit of the assessee which had been excluded from assessment. On firm's failure to produce, books of account, the ITO took the sum total of the above sums received in course of three years, that is Rs. 4,54,948, as the basis of his assessment. He deducted the income at Rs. 1,18,975, on the ratio of 40 per cent, a flat rate on the gross receipts. Deducting the excess profits tax of Rs. 1,13,317 the assessable income was set at Rs. 65,659 which was reduced by the AAC by a sum of Rs. 28,270 by way of rectification of an error in calculation of Rs. 24,270 and deducting the profits of Rs. 4,000 representing 40 per cent of the estimated outstanding bills. The AAC, on appeal, came to the conclusion that since it was a question of determination of that year's income, in the absence of account books and since this was the first assessment in the case, the proviso to section 13 came into operation and no question of cash basis could arise.

The Tribunal, however, thought that in the circumstances of the case, the ITO should have applied the rate of profit to the annual receipts instead of to the total receipts and that by amalgamating the receipts under one assessment the ITO raised the tax liability of the assessee which was not fair. The Tribunal, therefore, set aside the basis of the said assessment and remanded the case back to the ITO to assess the income on the basis of the receipts during each year.

On the question of the flat rate, the Tribunal reduced the estimate of 40 per cent to 30 per cent.

On reference :

HELD: The Tribunal's power of dealing with an order passed by an AAC is plenary and has been expressed as widely as can be conceived. According to the section, every order of assessment passed by an AAC either under section 28 or section 31 of 1922 Act, is appealable to the Tribunal. The latter can substitute its own order of assessment for the one passed by the appellate income-tax authority. This very widely expressed power, however, shall not be immune from such limitation to which ordinarily an appellate authority or tribunal is subject in the disposal of its duty.

sar (SMC) Bench, in the case of the Nangal Khurad Co-operative L & C Society Ltd. v. AO, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was set aside and the Assessing Officer was directed to compute the income for the assessment year 2001-02 by applying net profit rate of 6 per cent instead of 8 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer. The appeal for the assessment year 2001-02 was partly allowed. In the case of ‘D’ for the assessment year 2002-03, the contract receipts were Rs. 10,21,919 and in the case of ‘U’, the contract receipts for the assessment year 2002-03 were Rs. 14,25,627. Thus, in both the cases, receipts were less than Rs. 40 lakhs. The provisions of section 44AD are applicable to the contracts of civil construction or supply of labour for civil construction for contract receipts below 40 lakhs. Explanation to section 44AD further provides that the expression ‘civil construction’ includes the construction or repair of any building, bridge, dam or other structure or of any canal or road. It was not clear from the orders of the lower authorities whether, the activities undertaken by the assessees were contracts of civil work, supply of labour to civil contractors or the contracts falling under Explanation to section 44AD. If the activities of the assessees fell in the above categories, the provisions of section 44AD would be applicable and the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) for upholding the net profit rate of 8 per cent would not warrant any interference. However, if the activities of the assessees did not fall in those categories, the income would require to be computed by applying net profit rate of 6 per cent. In the light of those facts and circumstances of the cases, it was appropriate to set aside the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) and same were restored to his file with a direction to modify the earlier orders only if it was found that nature of contract work done by the assessees was other than supply of labour for civil contracts or the cases falling under Explanation to section 44AD. Otherwise, the earlier orders would stand confirmed.

In the result, the appeal was partly allowed.

On the other hand, the revenue contended, inter alia, that there was no res judicata in income-tax proceedings and the only thing to be examined was whether in an impugned assessment order, the ITO’s action was within the law and that in this case the ITO had not exceeded his jurisdiction by accepting the profit and loss account and computing the income after taking into consideration the expenses that could be allowed under the law. HELD: It is true that there is no res judicata in the income-tax law and that the ITO has authority to take a different view from what has been taken in an earlier year. But neither he can exercise this authority in caprice, nor has he an unrestricted, unlimited, unconditional or absolute right in this matter. It was undisputed that the ITO had completed the assessments of the assessee’s income for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 on a flate rate basis observing, inter alia, that in the absence of maintenance of vouchers and receipts for the expenditure incurred by the assessee, the books of account were not acceptable. Now to examine whether the books of account kept in all the years inclusive of the year under appeal were maintained in the same manner or not, the trading and profit and loss accounts were the best available guide on which one should rely. There was no difference in the manner in which they had been kept in any of the assessment years inclusive of the assessment year under appeal. However, it was strange that though the assessee was a big contractor and executions of many of the contracts were spread in these years, no work-in-progress or closing stock had been recorded in the trading account. In view of the circumstances, it was not possible for the ITO to presume that the true profit could be computed on the basis of the books of account. He had overlooked the orders for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 framed by his predecessors. As a matter of fact, his finding was not very much different. He had also overlooked his own letter dated 16-2-1985 addressed to the assessee. Again, there was no whisper in his order as to what were the defects in the earlier years, which were not present in the relevant assessment year. He failed to prove his finding. Accordingly, the reasoning of the ITO to change the mode of assessment could not be accepted and the estimate of profit at a flat rate method as adopted in earlier years in the same circumstances should also apply in the assessment year under appeal, except that, in view of the finding that a large amount of expenses claimed was unestablished, the profit rate to be applied should be 12½ per cent instead of 10 per cent adopted for the earlier years.

HEADNOTE: Section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil construction business - Assessment year 2001-02 - Assessee had entered into a contract with a civil contractor ‘U’ Ltd. for supply of sand for construction of roads from specified zones - For said purpose, assessee had to pay royalty to Government, engage labourers for loading and unloading and arrange for transportation of sand up to site for construction of road - Contractor had made payments to assessee in two parts, one for supplying of material, and other for transportation charges - Whether since assessee had executed work of supplying and transporting sand from particular area to a civil contractor, assessee was to be considered as a sub-contractor and in such circumstances, section 44AD would be applicable  - Held, yes - Whether  however, if there was a reasonable basis for bifurcation of payments, for cost of material separately and for transportation charges, then profit should be computed at rate of 8 per cent in respect of payments made for transportation charge and at rate of 5 per cent for supply of material and if there was a composite agreement, then entire receipts would be subject to 8 per cent under section 44AD - Held, yes [Matter remanded to Assessing Officer for purpose of calculating net profits after verification of nature of payments to assessee]

FACT: The assessee had entered into a contract with a civil contractor ‘U’ Ltd. for supply of sand for the construction of roads from specified zones. The assessee had received a payment of Rs. 36,58,267 and out of the said payment ‘U’ Ltd. had deducted tax in respect of Rs. 16,85,044. The assessee filed the return of income for the assessment year 2001-02, disclosing income at the net profit of 8 per cent under section 44AD in respect of the said payment. During the course of assessment proceedings, when assessee was asked about the gross receipts, assessee filed revised return disclosing the gross receipts at Rs. 36,58,267 but computed the income at the rate of 5 per cent under section 44AF instead at the rate of 8 per cent under section 44AD. It was claimed by the assessee that no books of account had been maintained by him and the profits in respect of the payments were required to be assessed under section 44AF, which is applicable in respect of retail trades. The assessee, pleaded before the Assessing Officer that provisions of section 44AD were not applicable in the instant case. The Assessing Officer on consideration of the terms and conditions of the agreement between the assessee and U Ltd. held that the assessee had executed the contract work and, accordingly, income was to be computed in accordance with provisions of section 44AD. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

FACT: ■

The assessee, a contractor executing works for Government departments/PWD, was flagged in NMS for contractual receipts of about Rs. 17.27 crores and interest income of about Rs. 0.24 lakhs during FY 2012-13 relevant to AY 2013-14 but did not file a return of income. Notice under section 148 was issued on 31-03-2021 after obtaining sanction under section 151(1) from PCIT since four years had elapsed from end of relevant assessment year. Despite notices under sections 148 and 142(1), assessee neither filed return nor furnished any details. In response to show-cause notice/draft assessment order, assessee filed a statement of income declaring turnover of about Rs. 17.40 crores and net profit of about Rs. 1.05 crores (NP 6.06%), stating that depreciation of about Rs. 70 lakhs had been debited and cash profit before depreciation was about Rs. 1.75 crores (about 10.08%), and further submitted that after adding back bank interest cost, cash profit margin would exceed 12%.

The AO completed assessment ex parte under sections 147 read with section 144 treating contractual receipts of about Rs. 17.27 crores as business turnover, noting that turnover exceeded audit threshold and no books of account/audit report were produced, and estimated net profit at 15% of gross contractual receipts at about Rs. 2.59 crores, rejecting assessee’s lower profit margin and depreciation-related submissions.

■

On appeal, CIT(A)/NFAC dismissed appeal in limine on account of delay of 957 days and, on merits, upheld AO’s estimation of net profit at 15%.

The appeals for AYs 2013-14 (lead case) and 2017-18 were clubbed and heard together.

HELD: ■

But in the instant case, the Commissioner (Appeals) had not followed any precedents. He had only appreciated the factual position by referring to some other cases of builders with a view to ascertain the normal rate of net profit of such case. In this context, the Commissioner (Appeals) had observed that in similar cases net profit rate of around 10 to 15 per cent was being considered reasonable. Therefore, there was no merit in the contention of the revenue. [Para 17] The Commissioner (Appeals) had properly taken into account all the facts and circumstances for arriving at his conclusion. The total incomes estimated by the Assessing Officer for the assessment years under appeal appeared to be arbitrary. This was established from the fact that for the assessment year 1999-2000, while application of net profit rate of 15 per cent resulted into total income of Rs. 10,46,778, the Assessing Officer had actually under assessed at Rs. 6,15,397. This was a case, where regular books of account were not maintained. The Assessing Officer proceeded on the basis of papers found during the course of survey. Such papers apparently were not complete record of the income or expenditure of the assessee. Therefore, the total income could not be properly calculated on the basis of such papers. The Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly directed the Assessing Officer that the profits of the assessee’s business as a builder should be estimated by applying net profit rate of 15 per cent of the total consideration as per the sale agreements and also on the on money received by the assessee. Thus, the net profit rate of 15 per cent could not be said to be on the lower side. Even section 44AD prescribes net profit rate of 8 per cent only in the case of an assessee engaged in the civil construction. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had decided the issue correctly. HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with  section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee- firm was carrying on business of Civil contractors - In course of assessment, Assessing Officer took a view that net profit rate declared by assessee was very low in civil contractual business - In absence of compliance by assessee to various notices issued, Assessing Officer by taking recourse to provisions of section 44AD, applied rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts to calculate assessee's taxable income - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) found that Assessing Officer had not given any basis for adopting the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts to work out the net income of the assessee even after accepting the plea of the assessee that its business was adversely affected on the death of the working partner - He thus estimated income at rate of 5 per cent of gross receipts - Whether since assessee had failed to file evidence in respect of material purchased and other expenses, impugned order of Commissioner (Appeals) adopting net rate of 5 per cent of gross receipts for working out assessee's income was to be upheld - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was carrying on business of civil contractors. In the course of assessment, the Assessing Officer was of the view that the net profit rate declared by the assessee was very low in the line of civil contractual business. The Assessing Officer issued various notices to the assessee but there was no response from assessee's side. The Assessing officer thus took note of fact that as per provisions of section 44AD, the rate of 8 per cent was applicable to gross receipts, and there was no requirement of maintaining books of account. The Assessing Officer thus applied the GP rate of 8 per cent to the gross contractual receipts after deducting the value of material supplied by the Government and sales-tax from the gross receipts. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the Assessing Officer had neither rejected the books of account nor passed an order under section 144 but had estimated the income at rate of 8 per cent of the gross receipts while passing the order under section 143(3). The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the Assessing Officer had not given any basis for adopting the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts to work out the net income of the assessee even after accepting the plea of the assessee that its business was adversely affected on the death of the working partner. In the circumstances, the Commissioner (Appeals) estimated the income at the rate of 5 per cent of the gross receipts.

On revenue's appeal :

HELD: On the facts of the case, there was no merit in adoption of rate of 8 per cent to the book results for working out the income for the relevant assessment year. However, as the assessee had failed to file evidence in respect of the material purchased and certain expenses and in the absence of the assessee filing the same on record, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) adopting rate of 5 per cent to the gross receipts for working out the income of the assessee was to be upheld.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 1959-60 - Assessee was a contractor who had undertaken construction of houses under a project for relevant assessment year - Assessee showed expenditure incurred on jobs during year at 
Rs 4,45,904 which was treated by assessee as work-in-progress and showed a sum of Rs 3,21,358 as received against contracts from executive engineer - Assessee did not show any profit or loss from jobs and claiming overhead expenses at Rs 12,764 a net loss was returned - ITO considered that a profit had to be calculated on basis of receipts from authorities and he accordingly computed gross profit of Rs. 40,169 at 12½ per cent of receipts - Before AAC, assessee claimed that since accounts were maintained on completed job basis which was recognised system of accounting, proviso to section 13 of 1922 Act could not be invoked - AAC did not accept assessee’s contention and upheld order of ITO in invoking provisions of section 13 of 1922 Act for computing assessee’s income - However, he computed gross profit by applying rate of 12½ per cent on gross value of work done and not on net payments received by assessee - Tribunal upheld order of AAC - Whether order of Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a contractor. In the year in question, the assessee had undertaken the construction of houses under a project. The expenditure incurred on the jobs during the year was shown at Rs. 4,45,904 and that was treated by the assessee as work-in-progress and a sum of Rs. 3,21,358 was shown as received against the contracts from the Executive Engineer. The assessee did not show any profit or loss from the jobs and, claiming overhead expenses at Rs. 12,764, a net loss was returned. The ITO considered that a profit had to be calculated on the basis of the receipts from the authorities and he had, accordingly, computed the gross profit of Rs. 40,169 at 12½ per cent of the receipts. The assessee appealed before the AAC. The assessee claimed that the accounts were maintained on what was known as the completed job basis which was the recognised system of accounting and that the accounts having been maintained in a proper manner, the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act could not be invoked. The AAC did not accept the assessee's contention. According to the AAC, the tax had to be levied on the total income of the previous year and not on the total income of a period of 2, 3, 4 or more years, the period that would be required for completing any contracted work. Accordingly, he upheld action of the ITO in invoking the provisions of section 13 of the 1922 Act, for computing the assessee’s income, however, the AAC, held that the rate was to be applied on the gross value of the work done and not on the net payments received by the assessee and accordingly computed the gross profits at Rs. 1,04,926 by applying the rate of 12½ per cent on Rs. 8,29,412 as the gross value of the work done during the previous year. On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the AAC.

On reference:

HELD: In the instant case, the assessee contractor had not been able to satisfy the lower authorities as to what were the terms of the contract with the contractee and in what terms and consideration the materials were supplied by the contractee to the contractor. Furthermore, in the instant case the total amount of profit had to be computed by applying the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act. The rate of profit had also to be determined by applying the proviso to section 13 of the 1922, Act. As the Tribunal had pointed out that if the normal experience and expectation of a contractor as to how the profit would vary, were taken into consideration and in the circumstances where the contractor had not been actually able to satisfy the terms of the contract and where the estimates were to be based by applying the provisions to section 13 of the 1922 Act, it could not be said that the Tribunal was not justified in upholding the decision of the AAC in the manner as it did. In cases where there was clear and unambiguous evidence that there was contract which provided sufficient limit, beyond which the tender could not be quoted and there was a stipulation that the contract was to be quoted at a particular rate, excluding the cost of materials, to be supplied by the contractee, other considerations might apply.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

The next point taken by the Commissioner for revision was based on the CBDT instruction whereby scrutinizing of the case in which the net profit rate disclosed is less than 5 per cent has been made compulsory. But it does not mean that every civil contractor should at least earn net profit rate of 5 per cent on its turnover. This instruction enables the authorities to scrutinize the return and nothing more. Therefore, that objection of the Commissioner was also baseless. The third point taken by the Commissioner to carry out proposed revision was that the Assessing Officer had not conducted any enquiry to verify the genuineness of purchases, particularly when the assessee could not produce the complete bills and vouchers relating to purchases and sales. That objection of the Commissioner could not be agreed with. The Assessing Officer had definitely made proper enquiries from the assessee which was evident from the assessment order itself. The assessee had filed its return of income alongwith audited trading and profit and loss account and balance sheet. A detailed questionnaire was served on the assessee. The notices under sections 143(2) and 142(1) were also issued and served on it. The books of account, bills and vouchers produced were test-checked by the Assessing Officer. The assessee had filed various replies and details and the same were examined by the Assessing Officer. The only discrepancy having worth was with regard to the bills and vouchers issued for supplies, etc., which were stolen and against which FIR had been lodged by the assessee. The documents appended in the paper book of the assessee contained a copy of the detailed reply of notice under section 263, in which entire enquiries made by the Assessing Officer after the assessee filed reply of the notice under section 142(1), copy of reply sent to the Assessing Officer, etc., which were on record were also examined. In fact, it was not the case, where the Assessing Officer had not made proper enquiries and had simply passed the assessment in haste. The Assessing Officer had made ample enquiries, which were evident from the assessment order itself. The Assessing Officer, after considering all the replies of the assessee and in the interest of the revenue, proposed to the assessee an addition of Rs. 7 lakhs which was accepted by the assessee to avoid further litigation. Insofar as, the application of 8 per cent net profit rate in view of the provisions of section 44AD was concerned, the same was against the intention and purport of the Act. Insofar as, the CBDT circular was concerned, which said that the net profit rate being below 5 per cent in civil contractor's case, scrutiny could be ensued, was entirely on different footing. The Assessing Officer had made the scrutiny in the instant case and it did not mean by any stretch of imagination that the said circular meant that 5 per cent net profit rate had to be adopted in all such cases. The Assessing Officer had definitely made enquiry regarding purchases but obviously entire bills could not be produced and that was why the Assessing Officer made the proposal which was accepted by the assessee. It was not correct to say that the assessment had been made and completed in a hurry without making proper enquiry, to ascertain the actual income and verify the expenses claimed in the trading and profit and loss account. The Allahabad High Court, which was jurisdictional High Court in the instant case, while deciding another case, had given a clear verdict by holding that merely because the ITO had not written a lengthy order, it would not establish without bringing on record specific instance that the assessment order passed under section 143(3)/148 was erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. In the instant case, the Assessing Officer had made all the enquiries by issuing questionnaire and asking for entire details. The Assessing Officer had even mentioned all the details examined by him. The books of account of the assessee were audited and it had filed audited trading and profit and loss account and balance sheet. The assessee replied to different notices and questionnaire issued to him. The case was discussed with the advocate and the accountant of the assessee from time-to-time. Various replies and details were produced and examined. The books of account, bills and vouchers were produced and test-checked. The assessee was required to produce complete bills and vouchers for purchases and supplies made during the year under consideration. It was also required to produce the vouchers for expenses debited under various heads. It had produced various papers and vouchers, but complete vouchers for entire expenses could not be produced. Some of the vouchers could not be made available, but entries in their accounts were found to be made. From the above, it was clearly established that the Assessing Officer had made complete enquiry. It was clearly perceived by the Assessing Officer that the assessee had done contract work and had also made supplies of sand, morag, mitti, gover, plants, tractor, trolley, JCB machines and labours, etc. Thus, total receipt was not only from civil construction. It was brought to the notice of the Bench that in the immediately preceding year, i.e., 2004-05 in similar nature of business, the assessment was made at Rs. 6,10,070 by making ad hoc addition of Rs. 4,50,000 on the turnover of Rs

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of net profits - Assessment year 1989-90 - Assessee, and individual contractor, received certain payments and declared net profit rate which worked out to 6.54 per cent if claims for interest and depreciation were ignored - Assessing Officer in absence of proper record about labour and Hazri expenses as also on consumption of material, applied net profit rate of 10 per cent on total receipts subject to interest and depreciation - whether engaging of employees to carry out work was not a very special feature which should weigh heavily while determining income on basis adopted by department, and thus, Commissioner (Appeals)’s order reducing it to 9 per cent subject to interest and depreciation was to be upheld - Held, yes

Sections 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Depreciation - Allowance/Rate of - Assessment year 1989-90 - Whether amount incurred by assessee on temporary structures in form of hutments for its labour force at work sites should be treated as capital expenditure subject to 100 per cent depreciation allowance - Held, yes

FACT: During the assessment year 1989-90 the assessee, an individual doing construction work, received payments on which he declared a net profit rate of 0.58 per cent after allowing claim for interest and depreciation. Ignoring these two items, the net profit rate worked out to 6.54 per cent. The Assessing Officer, in the absence of record in support of expenses like labour and hazri carriage as also day to day consumption of material, invoked the provisions of section 145 and applied a net profit rate of 10 per cent on total receipts subject to interest and depreciation which was, on appeal, reduced to 9 per cent by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On second appeal :

HELD: Engaging of employees to carry out the work was not a very special feature which should weigh heavily while determining the income on the basis adopted by the department. A person would undertake only so much of quantum of work which he could shoulder without affecting the profitability. Also, in a particular line of business when certain basis has been accepted to determine the income, the constitution of business entity cannot be distinguished and varying rates cannot be either prescribed or accepted as a practice.

Hence, the Commissioner (Appeals)’s order was to be confirmed.

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits-Assessment year 1990-91 - Whether, when Assessing Officer found that accounts maintained by assessee were neither prone to verification nor reliable, he could estimate and adopt net profit rate which should 
 be rationale and reasonable - Held, yes - Whether based on all civil contract cases where net profit rate of 10 per cent was applied but neither depreciation nor interest debitable to profit and loss account were separately allowed, a net profit rate of 10 per cent estimated by Assessing Officer in instant case was rationale and reasonable - Held, yes

Section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil construction business - Assessment year 1992-93 - Whether Assessing Officer was justified in applying net profit rate of 10 per cent of contract receipts where assessee was himself ready to accept that rate and he had already accepted 9.52 per cent of net profit rate for immediately preceding year - Held, yes - Whether when net rate is applied, there is no question of depreciation - Held, yes

Section 145(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment year 1991-92 - Assessee, carrying on construction business, declared net profit of 5 per cent on gross receipts - Assessing Officer applied rate of 7 per cent - Commissioner (Appeals) applied 10 per cent rate relying on a case purported to be comparable and by generalising that normal rate of profit in construction business was 10 per cent - In the preceding years rate of 6 per cent was applied in assessee’s own case - Whether history of assessee’s case itself was a guide in applying rate of profit and, therefore, Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in enhancing rate - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of net profits - Assessment year 1989-90 - Assessee, and individual contractor, received certain payments and declared net profit rate which worked out to 6.54 per cent if claims for interest and depreciation were ignored - Assessing Officer in absence of proper record about labour and Hazri expenses as also on consumption of material, applied net profit rate of 10 per cent on total receipts subject to interest and depreciation - whether engaging of employees to carry out work was not a very special feature which should weigh heavily while determining income on basis adopted by department, and thus, Commissioner (Appeals)’s order reducing it to 9 per cent subject to interest and depreciation was to be upheld - Held, yes

u Section 44AD of Income-tax Act, 1961
Presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD represents a just, fair and equitable rate of net profit, which can be taken into consideration for determining income from contract business in a case where no books of account were maintained and no voucher or documentary evidence was produced before the Assessing Officer to support correctness of various expenses claimed in profit and loss account
Eastern Construction Co. v. ITO [1997] 59 TTJ (Delhi) 723
The presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD represents a just, fair and equitable rate of net profit, which can be taken into consideration for determining the income from contract business in a case where no books of account were maintained and no voucher or documentary evidence was produced before the Assessing Officer to support the correctness of various expenses claimed in the profit and loss account.

Section 254, read with section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Appellate Tribunal - Powers of [Reasoned order] - Assessment year 1997-98 - Assessee was civil contractor and declared gross profit and net profit against contract receipts - Assessing Officer rejected books of account and applied net profit rate of 10 per cent - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) reduced rate of profit to 8 per cent - On second appeal, Tribunal affirmed rate of 8 per cent observing that as regards earlier assessment years application of 8 per cent was held reasonable and even in respect of present assessment year question involved was one and same - Department contended that cogent reason had not been assigned by Tribunal while passing impugned order - Whether since what was being decided by Tribunal under order impugned was a question of fact and there was only an order of affirmance, no detailed reasons were further required - Held, yes [Paras 7  8] [In favour of assessee]IT: No detailed reasons is required in passing an order of affirmance by ITAT, where question involved is one and same as that decided in respect of preceding assessment years

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 2001-02 - Whether applying net profit rate on basis of best judgment assessment in a given situation will be a question of fact unless, such an assessment is shown to be arbitrary or perverse - Held, yes - Assessee was a contractor engaged in work of civil construction and filed its return for assessment year in question - Assessing Officer made addition to returned income mainly on account of claim for wages being found to be not verifiable - On appeal, Tribunal while considering issue of addition on account of unverifiable wages, considered it appropriate to apply reasonable rate of profit, which was assessed at rate of 12 per cent on contract receipts, excluding material supplied by department - Whether since assessment of 12% of net profit rate of contract receipt was not shown to be arbitrary or perverse, no question of law arose from Tribunal's order - Held, yes

Section 145,  read with section 44AD, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Gross profit rate) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee was engaged in business of execution of civil works contract - He filed his return of income for relevant assessment year declaring certain taxable income - In course of assessment, Assessing Officer noted that assessee had kept self-made vouchers in support of major expenditure and, accordingly, opined that books of account maintained by assessee were not amenable for verification - He thus rejected books of account under provisions of section 145(3) and estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts net of all deductions - Whether since assessee failed to controvert findings of Assessing Officer with any positive evidence to come to conclusion that books of account maintained by him gave a true and correct profit from business, Assessing Officer was right in rejecting books of account - Held, yes - Whether as regards rate of profit, since assessee had disclosed 6.73 per cent to 7.44 per cent net profit in earlier period, impugned estimation made by Assessing Officer was justified - Held, yes - Whether even otherwise, since nature of business carried on by assessee was squarely fit into specified business referred to in provisions of section 44AD, estimation of net profit at rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts specified in said section was rightly adopted - Held, yes [Paras 8, 9 and 10] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee had kept self-made vouchers in support of major expenditure and books of account maintained by him did not give true and correct profit from business, Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting said books of account and estimating net profit of 8 per cent of gross receipts  IT : Where Assessing Officer had adopted reasonable rate of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts, further deduction towards depreciation could not be allowed as it would result into determination of total income below income returned by assessee   IT : Where there was no nexus between interest receipts and works contracts executed by assessee, interest on fixed deposits was separately assessable under head 'Income from other sources'

Section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil Construction business
¦ In case of a civil construction contractor, even prior to introduction of section 44AD with effect from assessment year 1994-95, estimate of profit at 8 per cent of gross receipts, where income returned was less than 8 per cent of gross receipts, would be justified [Assessment year 1993-94]
It is true that section 44AD was inserted in the statute book with effect from 1-4-1994 to apply to assessment for the assessment year 1994-95 onwards, and it was not a mandatory requirement for the assessment year 1993-94 to assess profit of civil construction at such rate (8 per cent), yet the rate which is mandatorily required to be applied in the cases of business which the assessee was carrying on, where income returned was less than 8 per cent of its gross receipts, cannot be said to be an irrelevant consideration while considering the rate to be applied for estimating the income from like businesses for earlier years in its discretion by the authorities under the Act.

Section 145, read with section 143, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 2003-04 - Assessee-firm, a labour contractor, got a contract of labour from Railways for transporting, loading and unloading of sleepers and for stone-ballast supply - For relevant assessment year, it had shown its gross profit rate at 2.88 per cent as against 7 per cent shown in previous assessment year - Explanation submitted by assessee for such steep fall of gross profit rate was rise in price of diesel and requirement of skilled labour in relevant year - Further, assessee had accepted transportation contract below tender rate but in earlier year position was just opposite - Assessing Officer, having found various faults in books of account, rejected same and adopted gross profit rate of 6.5 per cent - In another case for same assessment year, same Bench of Tribunal under identical facts and circumstances had adopted a gross profit rate of 3 per cent as reasonable - Whether, in view of aforesaid order of Tribunal and further keeping in view facts in totality, adoption of gross profit rate of 3 per cent would be justified - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income- Assessment year 2010-11 - Where despite various opportunities given, assessee, civil contractor failed to produce books of account and relevant vouchers and there had been a lot of variation in profit rate of assessee during different years, Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting audited balance-sheet filed by assessee and making assessment by applying net profit rate of 12 per cent [In favour of revenue]

Section 143 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Additions to income - Assessment year 1988-89 - Additions were made to returned income by assessing authority on assumption that assessee-contractor made a profit of 10 per cent on gross profits - Commissioner (Appeals) partly allowing assessee’s claim reduced net profit - Tribunal confirmed order of Commissioner (Appeals) - Whether Tribunal’s order that net profit rate of 10 per cent be applied after deducting cost of material supplied by PWD from gross receipts even if PWD itself allowed benefit of 10 per cent net profit on project cost, was merely a factual issue and no referable question of law arose therefrom - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1999-2000 and 2000-01 - Where in case of assessee civil contractor, Commissioner (Appeals) directed adoption of gross profit rate of 12 per cent and Tribunal upheld it, in absence of challenge by assessee as well as revenue to said rate, order of Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld [In favour of assessee]

Section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil construction business - Assessment year 1992-93 - Assessee-company, engaged 
in construction work, filed return showing 0.48 per cent net 
profit on total contract receipt - Assessing Officer rejected books of account maintained by assessee and applied net profit rate at
 12.5 per cent for computing assessee’s income - Whether provisions of section 44AD, though strictly inserted in Act with effect from 1-4-1994, can be a guideline for purpose of applying a particular net profit in case of civil contractor even in earlier years - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, net profit rate of 12.5 per cent applied by authorities below in case of assessee was excessive and exorbitant and, accordingly, application of net profit rate was modified from 12.5 per cent to 8 per cent on gross receipt shown by assessee - Held, yes

Section 145, read with  section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounts - Estimation of income (Rate of profit) - Block period 2008 to 2010-11 - Assessee-company was a sub-contractor - In course of assessment proceedings assessee produced audited books of account, bills relevant vouchers, etc. - Assessing Officer observed that labour register had not been maintained in conventional manner - He rejected books of account and estimated net profit at 8 per cent of gross contract receipt - Whether it was not correct to compare profit of principal contractors with profit margin of sub-contractor - Held, yes - Whether since net profit rate of principal contractors was ranging from 5.19 per cent to 6.15 per cent, there would be lower profit in case of assessee sub-contractor and, therefore, Commissioner (Appeals) rightly estimated net profit rate at 4 per cent - Held, yes [Paras 5 and 6] [In favour of assessee]IT: On rejection of books of account under section 145, profit margin of assessee, a sub-contractor, is to be estimated at rate much less than average profit margin worked out by Assessing Officer of its principal (i.e., contractor)

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - For estimating income of assessee, civil contractor, Assessing Officer applied net profit rate of 12.5 per cent as against 8.10 per cent applied by assessee - Commissioner reduced net profit rate to 10 per cent and Tribunal confirmed same - Whether no substantial question of law arose from Tribunal’s order - Held, yes

I. Section 44AD, read with section 69, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil construction business (Computation of income) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee was engaged in business of supply of labour for civil and technical job assigned by company B - During assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer noticed difference in total contract receipts shown by assessee in his books of account and that shown by contractee in Form No. 26AS - In absence of any satisfactory explanation, Assessing Officer made addition of such differential receipts - Whether since differential receipts were not shown by assessee in regular books of account, expenses related thereto might have also not been shown in books of account and in such circumstances, income was to be determined by applying net profit rate of 8 per cent on said receipts - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where there was difference in civil contract receipts shown by assessee in books of account and by contractee in form 26AS, net profit rate at rate of 8 per cent was to be applied to determine income embedded in said receipts  IT : In case of cash payment of meal charges exceeding Rs. 20,000 daily, Assessing Officer should verify whether amount paid was a reimbursement or it was itself towards an expense

Section 256(1), read with section 143, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Reference to  High Court - Question of law - Assessment year 1988-89 - Assessee was carrying on business of building contractors - Books of various accounts were rejected by  Assessing Officer on ground that expenses like wages to labourers were not verifiable in absence of supporting vouchers -  Assessing Officer applied rate of profit at 10 per cent of gross receipts and disallowed assessee’s claim for depreciation - Whether  Tribunal was right in allowing depreciation after adopting profit at 10  per cent and no referable question of law arose out of said order - Held, yes

Section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil Construction Business [Applicability of] - Assessment years 2006-07 and 2007-08 - Assessee was a civil contractor - In absence of proper books of account maintained by assessee, Assessing Officer estimated taxable income at 8 per cent of gross contractual receipts by invoking provisions of section 44AD - Commissioner (Appeals) held that net profit of assessee was to be assessed at 5 per cent of contractual receipts - Tribunal, however, restored order of Assessing Officer - It was apparent from records that assessee's gross receipts were in excess of amount prescribed at relevant time and, thus, section 44AD was not applicable to its case - Moreover, Commissioner (Appeals) had considered assessee's case as regards profit margin in earlier years to refix taxable income at 5 per cent of gross turnover - Whether in aforesaid circumstances, Tribunal was not justified in straightaway restoring assessment at 8 per cent of gross turnover without any discussion on merits of order of Commissioner (Appeals) - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned order of Tribunal was to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 11] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where assessee, a civil contractor, did not maintain proper books of account and, thus, Commissioner (Appeals) having regard to profit margin of earlier years, adopted profit rate of 5 per cent of contractual receipts, in absence of any discussion on merits, Tribunal could not enhance said profit rate to 8 per cent of gross turnover by invoking provisions of section 44AD

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Rate of income) - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee was a contractor and undertook works for municipal corporation - Assessee declared a net taxable income which represented his share of profit from a firm, in addition to his own income from proprietary concern - During course of assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer made enquiries into loans taken, purchases made, genuineness of some sub-contracts awarded by assessee and penalty paid by him - Assessing Officer treated said sums as income of assessee - Commissioner (Appeals) took cognizance of several irregularities in accounts of assessee and estimated income of assessee at 8 per cent of turnover - On cross-appeals, assessee contended that rate of estimated income was to be 6.5 per cent whereas revenue contended that estimated rate of income by Commissioner (Appeals) was on lower side - Tribunal concluded that in comparable cases net profit rate had varied from 2.93 per cent to 9.96 per cent; but these were big concerns, which maintained proper accounts and also maintained quality standards and in instant case accounts were not reliable and, hence, estimation of net profit at 8 per cent was justified - Whether since estimation of net profit by Assessing Officer was on higher side, Tribunal's order was to be upheld - Held, yes [Paras 7 and 8] [Partly in favour of assessee]IT : Where Tribunal after referring to comparable cases applied net profit at 8 per cent, since estimation of net profit by Assessing Officer was on higher side, order passed by Tribunal was justified

Section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 1950-51 - Assessee was dealing in sales of certain goods both on commission basis as was as on his own account - As assessee failed to produce proper books of account in pursuance of notice under section 23(2) of Act, 1922, ITO applied proviso to section 13 of Act 1922 and estimated sales of assessee at Rs. 2,50,000 on which flat rate of 5 percent was applied to determine profit - In applying said rate ITO took into consideration fact that assessee did some business on his own account - Tribunal reduced turnover determined by ITO, but upheld flat rate of 5 percent as gross profit - Before Tribunal, assessee referred comparable case for consideration but he had made no attempt to split up turnover of business on commission basis and on own account so that different rates might be applied to such turnovers - Whether, in such circumstances, Tribunal was justified in confirming flat rate of 5 per cent as applied by department authorities - Held, yes

II. Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit (GP rate) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee was fully engaged in labour oriented contract work - Commissioner (Appeals) directed Assessing Officer to estimate net profit of assessee at rate of 8 per cent on gross bills - Assessee submitted that it had taken contracts from a construction company, which in turn had taken main contract from Government - Whether in view of decision of Coordinate Bench of Tribunal rendered in case of C. Eiswara Reddy  Co. v. Asstt. CIT [IT Appeal No. 668 (Hyd.) of 2009, dated 31-1-2011], Assessing Officer was to be directed to apply 5 per cent net profit on gross receipts of assessee - Held, yes [Para 53] [Partly in favour of assessee]

Section 44AD, read with sections 143 and 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Presumptive taxation of - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee, a civil contractor, declared net profit ratio of 5.64 per cent of gross contract receipts - His gross receipts from contract business exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs - Assessing Officer rejected book results by invoking section 145(3) and determined total income by estimating net profit ratio of 15 per cent of gross receipts - Before Tribunal, assessee had canvassed for adoption of net profit ratio of 8 per cent on contract receipts in order to estimate income from business of contracting - Whether presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD reflects a legislative approved rate of net profit, which can be considered as fair and reasonable to estimate income from contract business in cases like that of instant assessee, where books of account were not found reliable by Assessing Officer - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, income from contract business of assessee be estimated at 8 per cent of gross receipts - Held, yes [Para 7][Partly in favour of assessee]IT: Where assessee, a civil contractor, declared net profit ratio of 5.64 per cent of gross contract receipts and Assessing Officer after rejecting book results determined total income by estimating net profit ratio of 15 per cent of gross receipts, income from contracting business be estimated by applying net profit ratio of 8 per cent of gross receipts

I. Section 44AD, read with section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Presumptive income - Civil Construction business (Disallowance of expenses) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee was a contractor executing contract works under various Government departments - Assessee claimed huge expenses under heads 'freight', 'salaries and wages', 'travelling expenses', etc. - Assessee was asked to produce salary and wages register and other he evidences of expenses but he did not produce any evidence before Assessing Officer - Assessing Officer rejected books and estimated profit at 8 per cent of gross contract receipts - Whether since assessee had not produced any evidence, Assessing Officer was justified in estimating profit on presumptive basis - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where a civil contractor did not produce salary and wage register and other evidences in support of expenses incurred, Assessing Officer was justified in estimating profit at 8 per cent of gross contract receipts  IT : Where assessee paid interest to bank for housing loan and it was duly supported by bank statement, deduction under section 80C was allowable

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income - Assessment year 1977-78 - Rate of 12½ per cent is normal rate applied to contractors and mere fact that assessee declared higher net profit in preceding year cannot be ground to make additions

Section 143, read with section 44AD, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Additions to income - Assessment year 1988-89 - Assessee constructed flats and shops and as per agreement with Government had to sell flats at Rs. 90 per sq. ft. even though cost of construction came to Rs. 180 per sq. ft. - Assessee made profit from sale of shops and showed net profits worked out as per books of account, after adjusting loss from flats - Assessing Officer, however, made addition after estimating profits from construction and sale of flats and shops at 8 per cent net of sale proceedings - Whether since assessee’s case was not comparable with other builders who could sell at their own determined prices and cost of construction also appeared very reasonable, and Assessing Officer had not pointed out any specific incident of assessee selling flats at higher prices, there was no justification for addition made - Held, yes - Whether Assessing Officer should, therefore, be directed to accept profits shown by assessee in its books of account - Held, yes

Section 2(1)(u1), read with section 5B, of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957 and rule 6 of the Karnataka Sales Tax Rules, 1957 - Taxable turnover - In case of works contract - Deductions - Assessment years 2003-04 and 2004-05 - Assessee-company was engaged in execution of civil works contracts such as construction of buildings and apartments - It was not in a position to show actual amount that it had incurred towards labour and like charges and, therefore, it had adopted standard rate of deduction provided under rule 6(4)(n)(v) and claimed standard deduction of 30 per cent on its contract receipt towards labour and like charges - It had apportioned gross profit earned between value of goods transferred and labour and like charges - Assessing Authority had allowed deduction towards labour charges and other like charges at 30 per cent of actual contract receipts relatable to civil works contracts executed by assessee after deducting amount paid to registered sub-contractors and also allowed deduction of gross profit at 27.44 per cent on labour charges - Subsequently Revisional Authority revised order of assessment holding that when assessee availed deduction of 30 per cent towards labour charges and other like charges under rule 6(4)(n)(v), it was not entitled for deduction of 27.44 per cent of gross profit on labour charges - Whether in view of clear, express and unambiguous provisions of rule 6 and in particular Explanation II thereto assessee was entitled for deduction of 27.44 per cent of gross profit on labour charges in addition to standard deduction at 30 per cent available towards labour and like charges - Held, yes [Paras 13  15] [In favour of assessee]CST  VAT: Where assessee was engaged in execution of civil works contracts and it had adopted standard rate of deduction provided under rule 6(4)(n)(v) and claimed standard deduction of 30 per cent on its contract receipt towards labour and like charges, in view of clear, express and unambiguous provisions of rule 6 of Karnataka Sales Tax Rules, 1957 and in particular Explanation II thereto, Assessing Authority was correct in allowing deduction of 27.44 per cent of gross profit on labour charges in addition to standard deduction at 30 per cent available towards labour and like charges

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Gross profit rate) - Assessment years 2006-07 to 2009-10 - Assessment was passed in case of assessee/revision petitioner for relevant years wherein gross profit claimed by assessee was rejected - Assessing Officer adopted a notional gross profit of 10 per cent and arrived at corresponding deemed sales turnover on civil works contract executed - Tribunal upheld order of Assessing officer - Assessee submitted that Tribunal erred in adopting a thumb rule of 10 per cent gross profit, disregarding actual book profit certified by a Chartered Accountant for calculation of deemed sale value of goods transferred during execution of works contract - However, it was found that Tribunal verified audited Profit  Loss statement and Balance Sheet of assessee/revision petitioner, for relevant years and held that adoption of notional 10 per cent gross profit on purchase value to arrive at deemed sales turnover by Assessing Officer was correct - Whether Tribunal, having considered submissions, perused relevant documents and passed well considered orders, same did not call for any interference - Held, yes [Paras 28, 29 and 36][In favour of revenue]IT: Where Tribunal verified audited Profit  Loss statement and Balance Sheet of assessee/revision petitioner, for relevant years and held that adoption of notional 10 per cent Gross Profit on purchase value to arrive at deemed sales turnover by Assessing Officer was correct, same did not call for any interference

Section 145, read with section 256, of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13, read with section 66, of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessee’s accounts were so complicated that its not for auditor could not prepare profit and loss statement therefrom - ITO assessed assessee at flat rate of 10 per cent on total turnover instead of 6¼ per cent as adopted for other similarly placed assessees - Whether charging of flat rate was only one mode of arriving at assessment in absence of clearly and properly kept accounts - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, no referable question of law arose from order of ITO - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits Assessment year 1964-65 - Assessee was a military contractor - Finding some irregularities in accounts, ITO assessed profits of assessee from military contracts by applying flat rate of 10 per cent on total receipts - Tribunal held that price of stores supplied by Government was to be excluded while applying flat rate to assessee's contract receipts - Whether order passed by Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income [Gross profit rate] - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee was engaged in business of contract work of military engineering services - Assessing Officer having found that assessee disclosed lower gross profit rate 7.20 per cent in relevant year, in comparison to 10.25 per cent in immediately preceding year despite three fold increase in gross receipt and assessee had not maintained salary register, payment register etc., rejected books of account of assessee and estimated income of assessee by applying net profit rate of 12.5 per cent - Whether since explanations of assessee that gross receipts had substantially increased by three times for which assessee had to reduce margin, and that contract works were executed in military and air force areas where working hours were lesser in comparison to normal civil work and that cost of various expenses and material had also been increased, was not rebutted by revenue, gross profit rate applied by Assessing Officer could not be sustained - Held, yes - Whether on facts, it would be fair and reasonable if net profit rate of 7.50 per cent was applied subject to interest to third parties, depreciation, interest to partners and salary to partners - Held, yes [Para 2.12] [Partly in favour of assessee]IT : Explanations of assessee which were not rebutted by revenue, were to be considered in estimation of his income

I. Section  44AD,  read with sections  144  and  147, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  58,  read with sections  271  and  279  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Presumptive taxation (Best judgment assessment) - Assessment years 2013-14 and 2017-18 - Assessee, a civil contractor executing works for Government departments/PWD, was flagged in NMS for contractual receipts of about Rs. 17.27 crores and interest income of about Rs. 0.24 lakhs during FY 2012-13 relevant to AY 2013-14 but did not file return of income - Assessing Officer completed assessment ex parte under sections 147 read with section 144 treating contractual receipts as business turnover, noting that turnover exceeded audit threshold and no books of account/audit report were produced, and estimated net profit at 15% of gross receipts (about Rs. 2.59 crores), rejecting assessee’s lower profit margin and depreciation-related submissions due to non-filing and absence of supporting records - Whether best judgment assessment must be based on material on record which could be gathered by Assessing Officer on proper investigation - Held, yes - Whether since assessee’s entire contractual receipts were from Government departments/PWD and all proceeds were received through banking channels and assessee’s estimation of net profit at 6.06% of turnover was higher than rate of 6% prescribed under section 44AD, flat estimation of income at 15% of turnover was highly unjustified - Held, yes - Whether net profit rate of 7% in civil contract business, particularly when all contract receipts were received through proper banking channels on which tax had been deducted at source, was reasonable and accordingly Assessing Officer was to be directed to recompute net profit of assessee at 7% of total turnover declared by assessee - Held, yes [Para 10.4] [Partly in favour of assessee]

Section 44AD, read with section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil construction business (Applicability of) - Assessee filed his return declaring income at rate of 8 per cent on gross receipts - Assessing Officer allowed expenses to extent of 75 per cent and computed gross profit at rate of 25 per cent - Tribunal, however, assessed income at rate of 8 per cent on gross receipts - Whether since Assessing Officer had computed gross projects at rate of 25 per cent without any justification, Tribunal was justified in adopting gross profit rate of 8 per cent as mentioned in section 44AD even though gross receipts of assessee were in excess of Rs. 40 lakh - Held, yes [Paras 2 and 3] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where Assessing Officer computed gross profit rate of assessee at 25 per cent of gross receipts without any justification, Tribunal was justified in adopting gross profit rate of 8 per cent as mentioned in section 44AD even though turnover of assessee was in excess of Rs. 40 lakh
