Income-tax provisions nowhere either authorize the Assessing Officer or cast an obligation on the assessee to prove the negative result, i.e., to prove as to why he had failed to make a profit at a particular rate. The accounts may be rejected as unreliable if important entries and transactions are omitted therefrom or if proper particulars and vouchers, bills, etc., are not forthcoming or if they do not include entries relating to particular class of business transaction. Reasons for rejecting wages record as commented by the Assessing Officer related to full address of the labour, which was not given on the muster roll register. The wages record had been kept by the assessee as per regulation known as 'Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970. The addresses of the labourers to whom wages had been paid were not mentioned, since the labourers stayed in the Jhugi Jhoperies at a work site itself and to that effect the assessee had already replied to the Assessing Officer vide its letter dated 23-3-2001, through which site of construction where labourers resided was given which was, however, not taken notice of by the Assessing Officer and the same was sent to him by courier and was found to be duly received by the Assessing Officer. The Assessing Officer had also alleged that the actual date of payment was not mentioned by the payee receiving the wages. The date on which the entry had been made in the wages register was the actual date of payment. As per the nature of the contract work executed by the assessee, he had got a contract to carry out a particular job or a contract for which the material was supplied by the CPWD/DOT and the labour was provided by the assessee-contractor. The assessee used to make payments to the labourers on the basis of mandays put in by the labourers and not on the basis of work performed by them on each day. Therefore, there was no merit in the allegations of the Assessing Officer that work performed by the labour was not mentioned on the payment vouchers and in making them as basis for rejection of books of account. The payment to the assessee-contractor was also made on the basis of work completed which was measured by the department itself and not on the basis of what the labourer had done. The bills for such a contract were prepared, which were not verified by the engineers of contractee before making payments. On the basis of those bills which were finally approved by the Government engineers/contractee, the payment was given to the assessee-contractor after deducting TDS. Thus, it was humanly not possible to provide the details as to what work a particular labourer had done at the site. Further, the Assessing Officer had also not indicated any defect in the system of accounting regularly followed by the assessee, or its correctness, nor was there any change in the method of accounting during the year under consideration as compared to the earlier years to indicate any intention of the assessee to show low profit.

While examining the books of the assessee, the Assessing Officer has to consider the following aspects : (i) whether the assessee has regularly employed a method of accounting; (ii) even if regular adoption of a method of accounting is there, whether the annual profits can properly be deduced from the method employed; (iii ) whether the accounts have been correctly maintained; (iv) whether the accounts maintained are complete in the sense that there is no significant omission therein. If the answers to above four questions would be in the affirmative, then the assessee's profits would be computed on the basis of his accounts. In such cases, proviso to section 145(1) or section 145(2) cannot be invoked. On the perusal of the materials placed on record in the instant case, it was found that the answers to all the above four questions were in the affirmative. No finding had been recorded by either of the lower authorities as to the unacceptability of the method and to the irregularity of the accounts kept by the assessee. It is well-settled that in the absence of such a finding recorded by the authorities, the book results cannot be ignored or brushed aside.

7. We have heard both the parties and perused the material on record. In the present case, the Assessing Officer rejected the books of account on the reason that, the assessee has not maintained proper books of account and also failed to produced vouchers for verification and the expenditure claimed by the assessee arc not substantiated. The assessee in earlier years also has not maintained the proper books of account. The assessee’s past track records show that the assessed has neglected the presenting of the books of account in accordance with law. When the assessee claimed any expenditure, it is mandatory on the part of the assessee to produce the books of account supported by proper bills and vouchers. Since the assessee has not produced the proper books of account, true profits or loss cannot be deduced from the books of account of the assessee. The Assessing Officer having no other option rejected the books of account and estimated the income at 10 per cent of gross receipts. But the position is that, the assessee is carrying on three kinds of contracts, as in earlier years, i.e., (i ) own contracts, (ii) contracts taken from the sub-contractors, (iii) contracts given to other parties on sub-contracts. The assessee had a higher rate of profit on the contracts executed by the assessee itself. In these contracts, the assessee agreed that his income is at 9 per cent of the gross receipts. Thus, accordingly the Assessing Officer is directed to estimate the income on the contracts executed by the assessed own at 9 per cent. In case of contracts taken by assessee on sub-contract, the income to be estimated at 8 per cent of the gross receipts. In case of contracts given by the assessee to the 3rd party on sub-contract, income to be estimated at 4 per cent. This is, because, when the assessee gives contract to the other parties on sub-contract, the assessee cannot keep the same percentage of profit at 9 per cent, it has to forgo certain portion of profit i.e., around 5 per cent to the sub-contractors. Similar position in the case of contracts taken by assessee on sub-contract from other parties. Further, the assessee is entitled for depreciation and remuneration, and interests to partners on the profit estimated by Assessing Officer at applicable rates, because the income estimated as above of the assessee is before the depreciation and interest and remuneration of the partners. Accordingly, we direct the Assessing Officer to compute the income of the assessee afresh. Accordingly, this ground of the assessee appeal is partly allowed.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reduced the rate of profit from 8 per cent to 5 per cent, mainly on the ground that since the turnover of the assessee exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs, it was bound to incur more expenses and rate of profit would be less. On further appeal, the Tribunal reduced the rate of profit to 4 per cent on the ground that the assessee was doing the work for PWD and normally the net profit rate was much less for the work of PWD, as the contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under the supervision of the PWD authorities.

On appeal :

HELD: A bare perusal of the findings recorded by the Assessing Officer would indicate that he had applied the principles determining the profit vide section 44AD, whereas the aforesaid provision was not at all applicable in the case of assessee in the relevant assessment years. This factual position was not being disputed by either of the parties. That being so, the question arose as to what should be the profit rate for the purpose of determining the profit accrued or gained by the parties. Since the Assessing Officer, had not dealt with this question independent of section 44AD, the rate of profit could not be upheld. [Para 3]

So far as the determination of profit of 5 per cent by the Commissioner (Appeals) was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) had also not given any reason nor any material was placed before the Commissioner (Appeals), or for that matter before the Assessing Officer for arriving at a conclusion about the rate of profit. Merely on assumption that since the assessee was performing the work for the PWD and as the contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under supervision of the PWD authorities, the rate of profit would be low or merely because the turnover exceeded Rs. 10 lakhs, it would incur more expenses, the aforesaid rate of profits could not have been arrived at. Neither the Commissioner (Appeals) nor the Tribunal had taken into consideration the relevant material or facts which might be necessary for arriving at such a conclusion. [Para 4]

The rate of profit cannot be assumed merely on assumptions or surmises and conjectures. It is the first liability of the assessee to produce such records, evidence and material so as to substantiate his plea about the rate of profit that he claims and in case the books of account have been rejected , the onus shifts on to the Assessing Officer to determine the rate of profit on consideration of the material which may be brought before him or even on making such inquiry, which may be necessary and which may include the requirement of having any information from the assessee also during the course of determination of such rate of profit, namely, during the assessment proceedings. In no case, simply because the turnover was more than Rs. 40 lakhs or the assessee was performing civil construction work for Public Works Department, neither the rate of profits could be determined nor it could be taken to be less nor it could be reduced nor could be arrived at any presumptions. [Para 5]

HEADNOTE: Section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Best judgment assessment - Assessment year 1974-75 - Whether while making a best judgment assessment, though there must necessarily be guess work in matter, it must not be arbitrary - Held, yes - Assessee-contractor did not main books of account - He filed his return of income on estimate basis by computing profit at flat rate of 10 per cent on gross receipts - ITO, however, computed net profit at rate of 15 per cent - Revision petition filed by assessee was dismissed by Commissioner - Whether since neither ITO nor Commissioner had referred to any material for applying flat rate of

FACT: The petitioner assessee, who was carrying on business as a contractor filed his return on estimated basis by computing the profit at a flat rate of 10 per cent, on gross receipts, as he did not maintain any books of account. The ITO, however, computed the net profit at 15 per cent, on the contract payments received by the assessee. The revision petition filed under section 263 was dismissed by the Commissioner.

On writ:

HELD: It is now well settled that while making a best judgment assessment, though there must necessarily be guess-work in the matter, it must not be arbitrary. In the instant case, the basis on which the computation was made was not disclosed in the order.

Neither the ITO nor the Commissioner had referred to any material for applying the flat rate of 15 per cent while estimating the net profits.

In such circumstances, the assessment order could not but be held to be arbitrary. The order passed by the ITO and that passed by the Commissioner, therefore, deserved to be set aside. The petition was allowed accordingly.

Note: The case has been decided in favour of the petitioner-assessee.

Because of the aforesaid observations, the AO rejected the audited books of account of the assessee and estimated the net profit. The AO gave the examples of net profit earned by three companies viz. Now before us, Ld. counsel for the assessee argued that the estimation of net profit @ 8% by relying on provisions of section 44AD of the Act is totally incorrect and without any basis for the reason that the assessee company is subcontractor and its profit margin is low in comparison to the contractors. Further, the AO has compared the profit of the assessee with the companies whose turnover and business paraphernalia is huge in comparison to the assessee company. Further, the assessee company had executed the part of work of civil construction for these companies and, therefore, it is not correct to compare the profit of those companies with the profit margin of the assessee. In fact the profit margin of those companies is also less than the margin which has been estimated by the AO in the case of assessee. In the case of assessee as per audited books of account, the net profit margin for A.Ys. 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10 and 2010-11 was 1.94%, 0.67%, 0.20% and 0.09% respectively. Now, before us, Ld. counsel for the assessee argued that the AO has failed to appreciate that the profit margins of contractors and sub-contractors cannot be same. In the assessment order he has worked out the average profit margins in the case of Tantia Constructions Ltd, GPT Infraprojects Ltd. and Allied Infrastructure & Projects Pvt. Ltd at 5.93%, 6.15% and 5.19% respectively and in the case of assessee he has estimated the profit @ 8%, whereas, in the case of assessee the profit margin would be much less than in these companies being a sub-contractor of these companies.

6. In view of the above factual position and comparative figures given by assessee company of its principal, wherein the net profit is ranging from 5.19% to 6.15%, we are of the view that definitely there will be lower profit in the case of sub contractor i.e. the assessee and hence, the CIT(A) has rightly estimated the net profit rate at 4%. Accordingly, we confirm the order of CIT(A) and this issue of revenue's appeal is dismissed.

7. Similar is the position in all the above appeals, hence, taking a consistent view, we uphold the orders of CIT(A) and dismiss the appeals of revenue.

8. In the result, appeals of revenue are dismissed.

The concentrated attack of the learned counsel for the assessee before us is that there was no evidence to sustain the rate of 20% on the confectionery which was manufactured by the assessee. It is not disputed that the assessee placed before the taxation authorities its own account books and they were not found reliable and, therefore, the Income-tax Officer, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal have acted under the provisions of section 145(1) and the proviso thereto and this part of the decision has not been challenged. The only question is whether adopting such basis for the determination of the rate of tax of the assessee could be called as a determination without any evidence? Could it be characterised as based on mere conjecture, suspicion or based on surmises? Could it be called capricious? The answer, in our opinion, is firmly in the negative. The flat rate when it is calculated on the basis of the available data cannot be called arbitrary or perverse. It has been said by the Tribunal that Chhotu Motu, the firm, from whom the assessee before us bought manufactured confectionery and sold it made a profit of 19% and the assessee made a profit of 10% which has been charged by the Tribunal and against which there is no grievance. Therefore, at least up to 19% there is clear evidence about the flat rate being just. If the Tribunal made it 20% we are unable to call it capricious, conjectural or based on irrelevant or no evidence. A question relating to the flat rate as held by the Privy Council in Feroz Shah [1933] 1 ITR 219 (PC) is a pure question of fact. Although from the language of the questions which are asked to be referred to this court the grievance of enhancement is there yet it was not pressed before us. Therefore, it is not necessary to enter into the question whether the tax was enhanced because it is factually incorrect to say that the total liability of the assessee was increased. The case in point is Commissioner of Income-tax v. McMillan & Co. [1958] 33 ITR 182 (SC). In our opinion, it is not necessary to enter into the argument whether the question arises from the order of the Tribunal or not because we are clearly of the opinion that no question of law arises in this case.

10. Section 144 of the Act prescribes the procedure for best judgment assessment, whereas section 145 is the method of accounting and reads as under :

"145(1) Income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" or "Income from other sources" shall, subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), be computed in accordance with either cash or mercantile system of accounting regularly employed by the assessee.

(2) The Central Government may notify in the Official Gazette from time to time accounting standards to be followed by any class of assessees or in respect of any class of income.

(3) Where the Assessing Officer is not satisfied about the correctness or completeness of the accounts of the assessee, or where the method of accounting provided in sub-section (1) or accounting standards as notified under sub-section (2), have not been regularly followed by the assessee, the Assessing Officer may make an assessment in the manner provided in section 144."

11. The aforesaid provision gives power to the Assessing Officer, if he is not satisfied about the correctness or the completeness of the accounts of the assessee, or where no method of accounting has been regularly employed by the assessee to make an assessment in the manner provided in section 144. The provision in sub-section (1) with regard to the income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" or "Income from other sources" has been made subject to the provisions of sub-section (2). This has to be computed with either cash or mercantile system of accounting regularly.

On the question of the principle to be followed in making such an estimate, Mr. Sengupta relied upon two unreported judgments of this court in Income-tax Ref. No. 184 of 1969 and Income-tax Ref. 198 of 1971, respectively intituled Sri Gopendra Krishna Saha v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1978] 113 ITR 421 (Cal) (Appendix No. 2) and Shri Rakhal Chandra Banerjee v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1978] 113 ITR 419 (Cal) (Appendix No. 1).

In the Income-tax Reference No. 184 of 1969 [Gopendra Krishna Saha v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1978] 113 ITR 421 (Cal) (Appendix No. 2)], Sabyasachi Mukharji J. decided a similar question and held that the rate of gross profits was to be applied on the gross value of the bill. In that case, the contractor was not able to satisfy the authorities below as to the terms of the contract and estimate had to be made under section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. Mukharji J. held that where there was a contract which provided sufficient limit beyond which the tender could not be quoted and there was a stipulation that the contract was to be quoted at a particular rate excluding the cost of materials to be supplied by the con-tractee then in such a case the principles laid down in Commissioner of Income-tax v. K.S. Guruswami Gounder [1973] 92 ITR 90 (Mad) might be applied.

In the Income-tax Reference No. 198 of 1971 [Rakhal Chandra Banerjee v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1978] 113 ITR 419 (Cal) (Appendix No. 1)] Mukharji J. again held that where the assessee had tendered for the contract as a whole including the cost of materials which were subsequently supplied by the Government and there was no evidence on record to show that the assessee did not know of such supply of materials to be made by the Government and the price thereof, then the gross profits of the assessee could be computed on his total gross bills and there was no question of excluding the cost of the materials supplied. Commissioner of Income-tax v. K.S. Guruswami Gounder [1973] 92 ITR 90 (Mad) and M.P. Alexander & Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1973] 92 ITR 92 (Ker) (Appendix) were distinguished on facts.

In the facts and circumstances of the instant case, it appears that it is not possible to answer the questions referred without further findings on fact. It is not clear whether the authorities below had seen or considered the terms and conditions of the contracts under which the assessee had carried on the work of construction. The terms and conditions as to supply of materials by the contractee are also not known. Such terms are of some importance. It will be necessary to determine whether the materials to be supplied would be free of cost or price on the basis of market value or otherwise would be charged. On such facts it may be found that an element of profit was there on such apply. Whether the assessee submitted its tenders for the said contracts anticipating on being assured of supply of such materials are also not known. These material facts have to be found before the questions referred can be answered.

In this view, we remand the matter back to the Tribunal. The Tribunal is directed to ascertain the terms and conditions of the contracts in question, if any, in respect of supply of materials and determine whether the assessee bid for such contracts taking into account such materials which were in fact supplied. If it is found on such facts that there was an element of profit involved in the materials supplied then the profits of the assessee will be estimated on the gross receipts of the assessee computed by including the value of the materials supplied to the net receipts. The Tribunal will be at liberty to take further evidence in the matter and will afford opportunity to the parties to adduce further evidence and to make further representations in the matter.

In the instant case, the ITO arrived at the figure on the basis of the receipts extending over three accounting year. He took the sum total of these receipts to be the base for the net income that had accrued to the assessee during the accounting year 1943-44 as the entire contract work had been completed during that year. Mere execution of the contract work will not necessarily entitle the contractor to make a demand for payment until it is ascertained that the works are up to the standard agreed upon between the parties. Some parts of such work may be wholly rejected and like bad debts in every earning may be ignored in computing the gains or profits. It might have been open to the ITO, in exercise of his discretion, to make an enquiry into whether and when the bills for payment became due to the assessee. Much depended upon the terms in the contract, and the manner of its performance. Even as a basis of guess work, which the Income-tax Officer was entitled to do, the basis could not be said to be in consonance with honest guess work. The ITO did not seem to have taken into consideration why the payments which, according to him, were due to the assessee in the accounting year were not fully paid till three years after. Sometimes the payments to the contractors are withheld on account of unsatisfactory execution and they are held entitled to payments only if and when they replace the rejected work by acceptable and accepted ones. The bare possibility of such contingency could not be wholly eliminated in the instant case. If the ITO, in arriving at the figure for assessment, left out these considerations, he certainly could not be said to have exercised his judgment which he was none the less called upon to do in making the assessment in cases of assessee's default under sections 23(4) and 13 proviso of the 1922 Act. Any method of accounting adopted by the ITO acting under the proviso of section 13 of 1922 Act can be rejected if the method in fact does not show the true income, profits and gains. In this view of the matter, the Appellate Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipt basis with regard to contracts carried out and completed during the year of accounting, there being every presumption that the incomes were paid as soon as they became due. At any rate, the Tribunal's decision might be upheld on the ground that when two methods of guess work are available for the purpose of assessment, the one which is more just to the assessee and which involves a much less margin of chance of uncertainty should be taken as the basis.

In the result, the Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipts basis with regard to contracts carried on and completed during the year of account.

As regards the reduction of flat rate, the Appellate Tribunal had arrived at the lesser flat rate on the basis of their decisions in similar cases in the district. Their opinions were not receivable evidence in the instant case. The decisions in different cases must have been based upon different facts and different inferences deducible from such facts. In this connection, it might be observed that the ITO had been very fair to the assessee bearing in mind the difference between the gross value and net value of the bills. The Appellate Tribunal, therefore, did commit a mistake of law in arriving at a finding for which there was no relevant evidence to support.

Therefore, the reduction of the estimated profit rate from 40 per cent adopted by the ITO to 30 per cent by the Tribunal on the ground that 30 per cent was the general rate adopted by it in the cases of other assessees doing the same kind of contract works during the same assessment year was not legal.

Ltd. [2007] 294 ITR 451/ 162 Taxman 60 contended that the accounting standards prescribed by ICAI were required to be followed by the assessee. The revenue further referred to the decision of the Supreme Court in P.M. Mohammed Meerakhan v. CIT [1969] 73 ITR 735 to contend that income-tax authorities have power to estimate profits by treating unsold stock in trade and value it according to normal accountancy practice. HELD: The main case of the revenue was that the assessee should have disclosed profits on the receipts of contract on the basis of percentage completion method of accounting. As against that it was the case of the assessee that the initial price for which the contract was awarded was later on found to be unreliable as it was increased to 29 per cent, therefore, the percentage completion method was not applicable even according to the accounting standard AS-7.The assessee had never shown any profit out of the contract and the loss shown by the assessee was accepted by the lower authorities in the immediately preceding year and succeeding year. Thus, according to the accounts, the assessee had never earned profit from this contract. The accounts of the assessee were audited and it was not the case of the revenue that the assessee did not furnish details regarding accounts maintained by it. No defects whatsoever had been found in the account books maintained by the assessee. What can be assessed as income under the Act, is income. If there is an existence of income, then only it can be estimated. Therefore, not going into the controversy whether the accounting standard AS-7 was properly employed by the assessee or not, it would be considered that whether Assessing Officer was justified in assessing the net profit of the assessee from such contract at the rate of 10 per cent. There was no substance in the argument of the revenue that the assessee was under an obligation to maintain its account on the basis of the accounting standard AS-7, as the said accounting standard was not mandatory for the assessee for the year under consideration. Even if the percentage of completion method was held to be applicable to the case of the assessee, then the question would arise that what would be the basis for estimate. It is well-established law that the estimate made must be honest and fair. There must exist reasonable nexus between the available material and the estimate. Thus, the only question for determination arose whether there existed some material on the basis of which it could be said that application of net profit rate of 10 per cent was appropriate. It was the contention of the assessee that it had incurred losses while performing the contract. No material had been brought on record by the Assessing Officer that such contention of the assessee was contrary to the facts. Addition had been made without indicating any material or basis on which it could be decided that application of net profit rate of 10 per cent was appropriate. On the contrary, material was on the record to show that the assessee had incurred loss in performing such a contract. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was not justified in rejecting the books of account by invoking the provisions of section 145(3) without bringing on record any cogent reasons and infirmities in the maintenance of books of account of the assessee and further estimating the net profit. [Para 13]

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had decided the issue correctly.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits Assessment year 1964-65 - Assessee was a military contractor - Finding some irregularities in accounts, ITO assessed profits of assessee from military contracts by applying flat rate of 10 per cent on total receipts - Tribunal held that price of stores supplied by Government was to be excluded while applying flat rate to assessee's contract receipts - Whether order passed by Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a military contractor. During the relevant accounting period, the assessee took three military engineering service contracts. The ITO found that the expenditure of the assessee was not supported by vouchers and he detected some other mistakes also in the accounts. After applying the provisions of section 145(1), the ITO assessed the profit from these contracts by applying a flat rate of 10 per cent on the total receipts. The AAC allowed the appeal of the assessee and held that no rate of profit could be applied on the value of the stores supplied by the Government and this order was upheld by the Tribunal.

On reference, the Division Bench noticed the divergent views taken by the various High Courts and particularly because of the challenge laid to the correctness of the judgment in Brij Bhushan Lal v. CIT [1971] 81 ITR 497 (Punj.) and, thus, referred the matter for decision of the Full Bench.

HELD: The Supreme Court in Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524 (SC) reversed the said judgment of the High Court (supra) and held that the assessment was to be made excluding the cost of material and stores received for being used in the works undertaken by the contractor. Following, the aforesaid decision, it was to be held in the instant case that the Tribunal was justified in holding that price of stores supplied by Government was not to be included while applying the flat rate to the assessee's contract receipts.

Note : The decision was in favour of assessee.

After coming to the conclusion that the trading results were not prone to verification, the Assessing Officer was left with only one alternative to estimate the income of the assessee in the most appropriate and reasonable manner. In such type of cases, the net profit rate or gross profit rate could be applied or the Assessing Officer could adopt any method of estimation and work out the income from profession or business. But the method adopted must be reasonable and logical. In all civil contract cases, if accounts are not maintained or defective accounts are maintained, a net rate of 10 per cent is applied which was admitted by the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order. In those cases neither depreciation nor interest nor any other expenditure debitable to profit and loss account are separately allowed. By allowing depreciation and interest, net profit rate of approximately 3.5 per cent had been applied consequent to the order of the Commissioner (Appeals). The rate itself was absolutely abnormal. There was no evidence on record whatsoever that there were abnormal conditions prevailing with the assessee to earn such a low net profit by executing the contract. Once net rate was applied it was not open to the Assessing Officer to allow any other claim debited to profit and loss account. Depreciation and interest were definitely items which were debited in profit and loss account before the net profit was arrived at. It could have been the case of the appellant to justify the net profit rate shown as .27 per cent or to justify the net profit rate applied by the Commissioner (Appeals) at 3.5 per cent approximately. But no such discussion was available on record. The logical conclusion of the circular of the CBDT regarding claim of depreciation that in case profits were estimated, the same should be made subject to the allowance of depreciation and the assessee should file complete details of the claim of depreciation. One has again to look into the power given by the statute to the Assessing Officer when he invoked proviso to section 145(1). The first proviso to section 145(1) gives power to the Assessing Officer to decide whether or not income can properly be deduced from the accounts maintained by the assessee, even if the accounts are correct and complete.

Keeping in view the law laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. British Paints India Ltd. [1991] 188 ITR 44/ 54 Taxman 499 the Assessing Officer has to adopt rationale and reasonable method in arriving at the estimate of income, after he gives finding that the accounts maintained by the appellant are neither prone to verification nor reliable. He can use his own method but his method should be rationale and reasonable. In the case of the assessee he had used rationale and reasonable method. The application of net rate is directly dependent on the net rate shown by other cases in the line of the business. Other cases of contractors are being applied net rate of profit without giving them advantage of depreciation some contractors debit various items which relate to profit & loss or trading account expenditure and claimed 100% of depreciation. This method creates an abnormal situation in the net profit. The Assessing Officer had, therefore, taken a proper course by ignoring depreciation and the interest and applied net rate of 10%. The second positive feature in the assessment of the ITO related to the observation that the net profit rate of the person who used heavy machinery was going to be more than the net profit of a person who was not using the mechanical aid for execution of civil work.

Hence, there was no infirmity in the method adopted by the Assessing Officer. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was reversed and the order of the Assessing Officer maintained.

In the instant case there was material before the Tribunal on which its finding could be based: the assessee's representative had admitted before the AAC that full quantitative details in respect of the stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of that contract might not be available. In the circumstances, recourse to estimating the profits on the contract was inevitable. He, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 10,000 as against Rs. 26,434 added by the ITO. If the assessee wished to displace the AAC's estimate it was open to him to adduce evidence in support of its claim that the consumption of stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 was fully justified. This the assessee apparently did not do. For the subsequent year 1960-61 the assessee itself declared a net profit rate of 9.9% as against 9% declared in the assessment year in question. It could not be disputed that this was additional material which the Tribunal could take into consideration as it did. There was thus material before the Tribunal on which its estimate was based. The Tribunal's decision was, therefore, in conformity with the decision in the case of CIT v. Maharajadhiraj of Darbhanga [1933] 1 ITR 94 (P.C.).

The Tribunal was therefore justified in holding that the proviso to section 13 was applicable and there was material before it to sustain the aforesaid addition.

The assessee is not right in his contention that whenever an assessment is made by applying a flat rate of profit to the declared turnover or receipts, which is higher than the rate adopted by the assessee in the return of income, there can be no inference that the assessee concealed his profits. [Para 9]

The number of discrepancies and irregularities listed by the special auditor in his report which are reproduced in the assessment order bear testimony to the fact that the books of account maintained by the assessee were wholly unreliable. If they were so, there can be no sanctity attached to the figure of gross contract receipts on which the assessee estimated 3 per cent as its income. It is true that the Assessing Officer did not enhance the figure of gross receipts but that is not because he gave a clean chit to the books of account allegedly maintained by the assessee; he could not have given a clean chit in the face of the defects, discrepancies and irregularities reported by the special auditor. In order to take care of those discrepancies he resorted to a much higher estimate of the profits by adopting 11 per cent on the gross contract receipts. He gave due opportunity to the assessee to explain the discrepancies and also to show why the profit rate of 11 per cent cannot be adopted but these opportunities were not availed of by the assessee. He also has recorded in the assessment order that the assessee was permitted to inspect the seized documents and was given photocopies of the desired documents. This is not denied by the assessee. In these circumstances, the mere fact that the estimate was reduced by the Tribunal to 8 per cent would in no way take away the guilt of the assessee or explain its failure to prove that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on its part. It appears that the assessee was taking a chance - sitting on the fence - despite the fact that there was a search towards the close of the relevant accounting year in the course of which incriminating documents were found. It appears that the intention of the assessee was to take a risk and disclose a lesser income than what it actually earned and rely upon the minor variations in the rate of profits adopted by the taxing authorities and the Tribunal as a defence in the penalty proceedings. The plea - accepted by the Tribunal - that the assessee agreed to be assessed at 11 per cent of the gross receipts only "to buy peace" and "avoid litigation" cannot be accepted in view of the judgment of the Supreme Court in MAK Data (P.) Ltd. [2013] 358 ITR 593/38 taxmann.com 448. The Tribunal, was in error in upholding the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelling the penalty. Accordingly, the substantial questions of law is answered against the assessee and in favour of the Revenue. [Para 12]

As per provisions of section 158BB, the block assessment is to be made based on evidence before the Assessing Officer. The word 'Evidence' has to be construed in a comprehensive manner and it includes all circumstantial evidence also. The material or evidence with the Assessing Officer on which assessment may be based is not confined to direct testimony by witnesses. Such evidence need not only be evidence found during the course of search but also material gathered by him. The Assessing Officer was not fettered by the Technical rules of evidence and the like and he may act on material which may not strictly speaking, be accepted as an evidence in the Court of law. It may be circumstantial evidence or assessment based on the preponderance of probabilities judged by human conduct. For this purpose, the past history of the case, and general market conditions will constitute relevant material for the purpose of assessment. On reference : HELD: Contracts for building construction or of similar type can be divided into two broad categories. Category No. (1) will cover contracts where, at the time of entering into the contract, the contractor is told that some of the materials required for construction work will be supplied by the person or authority who entrusts the construction work to him and it is on that footing of such construction materials being supplied by the authorities or the other party to the contract, that the contractor enters into the contract for the construction quoting a particular figure for the entire contract. A sub-category of this first category of contract is the type of contract where, for notional purposes, a total figure is mentioned for the construction contract inclusive of materials and on the footing that the contractor is to supply all the materials for the construction work. However, at the time when the contract is entered into, it is clearly agreed between the contracting parties that some of the building materials will be supplied by the other party to the contract, that is, the person or authority entrusting the construction work to the contractor, and that credit will have to be given by the contractor for the materials, thus, received and the rates at which the credit is to be given is also agreed upon between the contractor and the other party to the contract. It was designated as a sub-category of category No. (1) because though notionally and on the face of it the contract has been entered into for a much larger amount and on the footing that the contractor is to supply all the materials, because of the clear agreement between the parties about the materials to be supplied by the other party to the contract and also about rates at which those materials are to be supplied, it is clear that in fact and in substance the parties have entered into the contract where certain specified materials are to be supplied not by the contractor but by the other party to the contract and the contractor right from the beginning enters into the contract on this footing and puts forward his quotation and ultimately gets the contract for the amount where he does not take into consideration supply of those particular materials or rates for those materials. Category No. (2) of contracts is the type where, right from the beginning, the contractor enters into the construction contract on the footing that he has to supply all the materials but while the contract is being executed, the other party to the contract supplies some of the materials and when the bill is finally paid, the other party to the contract claims credit for the price of the materials supplied to the building contractor. In that eventuality, it is really the total figure of the original contract or figure worked out in accordance with the terms of the original contract which will constitute the original receipts of the building contractor and the fact that, instead of going into the market and purchasing the materials for himself, the contractor gets these materials for himself, the party to the contract, does not enter into the picture so far as this aspect of the case is concerned. The question as to under which particular category, category No. (1) or category No. (2) set out above, a particular contract falls, will have to be decided looking to the substance of the transaction between the parties in each individual case. If the case falls under the first category, then it is obvious that the cost of the materials supplied by the other party to the contract cannot be taken into consideration in arriving at the figure of the total receipts of the contractor in respect of the particular contract for building construction. On the other hand, if the case falls, on the facts and circumstances of the particular case, in the second category, then the total receipts of the building contractor in respect of that particular contract will be the total amount of the contract notwithstanding the fact that the other party to the contract has supplied some of the materials required for building construction work.

It is, therefore, clear that in matters of this kind, when deciding whether a particular amount should or should not be considered to be trading receipt, it is the true nature and quality of the receipt, either actual or deemed, which has to be considered and not the outward form or the head under which the amount is entered in the account books of the assessee concerned.

It is thus, substance of the contract which matters and if, the agreement between the parties right from the beginning is that certain materials are to be supplied by the other party to the contract, that is, the Government department, or the authority concerned, then it is obvious that the contract was entered into on the footing that no profit would be made by the building contractor in respect of the supply of those materials.

On revenue’s appeal :

It is no doubt true that in the case of a contractor, work-in-progress has to be brought into accounts in order to show the profits earned in respect of the work turned out and the profit embedded in the receipts received during the year. The concept of bringing to accounts the work-in-progress is no different from the concept of bringing into accounts the closing in the case of a trader or a manufacturer. But unlike the case of a trader or a manufacturer, in the case of a contractor the workin-progress cannot be exactly arrived at with reference to any particular books because there are so many components which go to make up the work-in-progress and which have to be estimated. Therefore, estimate in arriving at the work-in progress was necessary and there was bound to be certain amount of approximation and guess work. Merely on the ground that the work-in-progress is estimated, it cannot be said that the book results were not to be accepted and that proviso to section 145 is applicable unless it is shown that the work-in-progress was arrived in such a way as to be too far from reality. In the instant case, the ITO attempted to prove the unreliability of the amount of work-in-progress arrived at by pointing out that the closing stock ought to have been Rs. 3,82,000 as against Rs. 1 lakh shown by the assessee. The basis for this was the assumption that normally the advance was given at 75 per cent of the material lying at site. There was no basis for this assumption nor any figure were given to show that this hypothesis could be accepted as correct. It was mere ipsi dixit of the ITO, without any basis to support it. The advance could be given at 75 per cent. It could be more, it could be less. This was, therefore, a surmise and conjecture.

As regards the receipts, following the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524 , in the instant case, the value of the material supplied by the Government must be excluded. So the balance of receipts should come to only Rs. 14.63 lakhs shown by the assessee. The estimate of the income at Rs. 1,50,000 on those receipts of Rs. 14.63 lakhs would work out to about 10.4 per cent. In none of the previous years, the assessee had shown such a high rate of profit nor had the department estimated the profit at such a rate nor the books of account were ever rejected. The previous results are only the points of reference, in relation to which the results of subsequent years are to be judged and reasons for variations are investigated. The range of profit would be discernible from the previous records. The lowest rate of net profit rate shown and accepted by the department was 2.8 per cent. In the immediately preceding assessment year rate of net profit shown and accepted was 2.75 per cent and the gross profit was 11.75 per cent. The estimate made by the ITO in the year in question of the profit at 10.5 per cent was very excessive and unreasonable. The ITO had not shown the basis for determining the income of Rs. 1,50,000. It is now the settled law that whenever estimates of income are resorted to in order that they are not arbitrary, unreasonable and unjustified, the ITO must show the basis on which and the method by which and the manner in which the estimate was made. These are the safeguards provided to act as an insurance against arbitrary estimates. None of these guidelines settled by the law of the land was disclosed by the ITO except leaving one to infer that because of the variations in the closing stock, he determined to fix the income at Rs. 1,50,000. Therefore, the estimate made by the ITO was not justified.

On appeal to the High Court:

HELD: The assessee is not right in his contention that whenever an assessment is made by applying a flat rate of profit to the declared turnover or receipts, which is higher than the rate adopted by the assessee in the return of income, there can be no inference that the assessee concealed his profits. [Para 9] The number of discrepancies and irregularities listed by the special auditor in his report which are reproduced in the assessment order bear testimony to the fact that the books of account maintained by the assessee were wholly unreliable. If they were so, there can be no sanctity attached to the figure of gross contract receipts on which the assessee estimated 3 per cent as its income. It is true that the Assessing Officer did not enhance the figure of gross receipts but that is not because he gave a clean chit to the books of account allegedly maintained by the assessee; he could not have given a clean chit in the face of the defects, discrepancies and irregularities reported by the special auditor. In order to take care of those discrepancies he resorted to a much higher estimate of the profits by adopting 11 per cent on the gross contract receipts. He gave due opportunity to the assessee to explain the discrepancies and also to show why the profit rate of 11 per cent cannot be adopted but these opportunities were not availed of by the assessee. He also has recorded in the assessment order that the assessee was permitted to inspect the seized documents and was given photocopies of the desired documents. This is not denied by the assessee. In these circumstances, the mere fact that the estimate was reduced by the Tribunal to 8 per cent would in no way take away the guilt of the assessee or explain its failure to prove that the failure to return the correct income did not arise from any fraud or any gross or wilful neglect on its part. It appears that the assessee was taking a chance - sitting on the fence - despite the fact that there was a search towards the close of the relevant accounting year in the course of which incriminating documents were found. It appears that the intention of the assessee was to take a risk and disclose a lesser income than what it actually earned and rely upon the minor variations in the rate of profits adopted by the taxing authorities and the Tribunal as a defence in the penalty proceedings. The plea - accepted by the Tribunal - that the assessee agreed to be assessed at 11 per cent of the gross receipts only "to buy peace" and "avoid litigation" cannot be accepted in view of the judgment of the Supreme Court in MAK Data (P.) Ltd. [2013] 358 ITR 593/38 taxmann.com 448. The Tribunal, was in error in upholding the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelling the penalty. In the instant case, the contract between the parties, namely, the assessee and the railway authorities, was that cement and iron had to be supplied by the railway authorities for the execution of the work and no accounting of the cost of these materials was to be done while making out a bill in respect of the contract payment. Under these circumstances it must be held that since this particular contract falls in the first category where at the time of entering into the contract the quotation did not take into account the materials like iron and cement which were to be supplied by the railway authorities, all calculations at the time of entering into the contract were made on the footing that iron and cement were to be supplied by the railway authorities and it was obvious that these items could not be included in the total receipts of the assessee for the purpose of arriving at the figure of net profits by working out the percentages of that total figure.

The Tribunal fixed the figure of 10 per cent of the total receipts only in view of the fact that the cost of the materials supplied by the railway authorities was to be taken into consideration at the time of fixing the receipts. Since it was held in the instant case that the cost of these materials supplied by the railway authorities was not to be taken into consideration at the time of determining the receipts in the light of the facts and circumstances of this particular case, it was but fair that the matter should be left to the Tribunal to decide as to which particular percentage it would apply to the total receipts in order to arrive at the net profits earned by the assessee

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The assessee was a contractor. The Assessing Officer determined income by applying a net profit rate of 12.5 per cent on the total contract receipts. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the net profit rate of 12.5 per cent but allowed deductions on account of depreciation and interest as claimed by the assessee. On further appeal, by both the parties, the Tribunal held that the net profit rate of 10 per cent was reasonable on facts and circumstances of the case and that this rate had taken into account the claim for depreciation. In appeal under section 260A, the assessee claimed that in view of the CBDT Circular dated 31-8-1965, the claim for depreciation and interest had been wrongly disallowed.

The main case of the revenue was that the assessee should have disclosed profits on the receipts of contract on the basis of percentage completion method of accounting. As against that it was the case of the assessee that the initial price for which the contract was awarded was later on found to be unreliable as it was increased to 29 per cent, therefore, the percentage completion method was not applicable even according to the accounting standard AS-7.The assessee had never shown any profit out of the contract and the loss shown by the assessee was accepted by the lower authorities in the immediately preceding year and succeeding year. Thus, according to the accounts, the assessee had never earned profit from this contract. The accounts of the assessee were audited and it was not the case of the revenue that the assessee did not furnish details regarding accounts maintained by it. No defects whatsoever had been found in the account books maintained by the assessee. What can be assessed as income under the Act, is income. If there is an existence of income, then only it can be estimated. Therefore, not going into the controversy whether the accounting standard AS-7 was properly employed by the assessee or not, it would be considered that whether Assessing Officer was justified in assessing the net profit of the assessee from such contract at the rate of 10 per cent. There was no substance in the argument of the revenue that the assessee was under an obligation to maintain its account on the basis of the accounting standard AS-7, as the said accounting standard was not mandatory for the assessee for the year under consideration. Even if the percentage of completion method was held to be applicable to the case of the assessee, then the question would arise that what would be the basis for estimate. It is well-established law that the estimate made must be honest and fair. There must exist reasonable nexus between the available material and the estimate. Thus, the only question for determination arose whether there existed some material on the basis of which it could be said that application of net profit rate of 10 per cent was appropriate. It was the contention of the assessee that it had incurred losses while performing the contract. No material had been brought on record by the Assessing Officer that such contention of the assessee was contrary to the facts. Addition had been made without indicating any material or basis on which it could be decided that application of net profit rate of 10 per cent was appropriate. On the contrary, material was on the record to show that the assessee had incurred loss in performing such a contract. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was not justified in rejecting the books of account by invoking the provisions of section 145(3) without bringing on record any cogent reasons and infirmities in the maintenance of books of account of the assessee and further estimating the net profit. [Para 13]

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had decided the issue correctly.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c), read with section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income - Assessment year 2003-04 - Whether ad hoc estimation of income by applying flat net profit ratio can be held either as concealment or as filing of inaccurate particulars of income for purpose of levying penalty under section 271(1)(c) - Held, no [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee was a contractor undertaking project of Indian Railways on turnkey basis. A search action under section 132 was carried out at the assessee's premises. As the assessee, at the relevant point of time, was not able to collect information about such contracts or produce relevant personnel, it proposed for fixing net profit rate at 11 per cent. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, applied net profit rate at the rate of 11 per cent on the total contract receipts on estimate basis which however, was reduced to 8 per cent by the Tribunal. A penalty under section 271(1)(c) was also levied upon the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the penalty on the ground that the estimation of income by applying flat net profit ratio did not tantamount to concealment or filing inaccurate particulars of income.

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: The issue of disparity between the assessed income and the returned income is not sustainable as the addition was purely on ad hoc estimation of net profit ratio. The Assessing Officer applied a particular flat rate of 11 per cent against the declared profit rate of 3 per cent by the assessee. The Tribunal has reduced the estimated income by adopting 8 per cent of profit rate which is also based on ad hoc estimation. Ultimately, the addition sustained or survived is ad hoc estimation of income by applying flat rate of 8 per cent of the profit which cannot be held either as concealment or filing inaccurate particulars. The Tribunal, in the quantum appeal, has also observed that suppression of the profit had not been established and the allegations have not been proved. On the basis of the explanation submitted by the assessee, the Tribunal has found no justification in applying and confirming the net profit rate of 11 per cent which has been reduced to 8 per cent on ad hoc basis subject to the allowability of depreciation and interest thereon. For levying penalty under section 271(1)(c), there has to be concealment of particulars of income by the assessee or the assessee must have furnished inaccurate particulars of income. Ultimately, in assessee's case, addition sustained was based on ad hoc estimation of income by applying a flat rate of 8 per cent of profit which can neither be held as concealment of income nor filing of inaccurate particulars of income. Further, the assessee's offering of the profit rate was a conditional proposal as the assessee was not able to collect the whole information about the context and produce the same. Thus, offer made by assessee was to buy peace and not to enter into dispute with revenue authorities. To purchase the peace and avoid any dispute with the revenue authorities in the quantum of income, assessee offered the estimated rate of profit. Considering all these facts and circumstances, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in deleting the penalty levied under section 271(1)(c ). [Para 5]

It is noted that the audited financial statements were available before the Assessing Officer but without disputing the sales turnover during the year he disallowed the total expenses including the purchase of material towards contract work undertaken by the assessee during the year. When the matter travelled before the Commissioner (Appeals) he observed in the impugned order that the net profit rate for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 disclosed by the assessee in its regular audited books of account is 0.22 per cent, 0.17 per cent and 0.25 per cent. Even during the course of scrutiny proceeding for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 net profit rate applied by the Assessing Officer was 0.16 per cent, 0.93 per cent and 0.18 per cent. Though the Commissioner (Appeals) appreciated the fact that undisputed revenue just could not have come without incurring an expenditure, but based on his observation that the purchase made by the assessee in the past were in dispute and genuineness of the same had not been proved, the Commissioner (Appeals) computed the net profit applying the rate of 8 per cent on the total revenue for the year of Rs. 87.46 crores.[Para 9]

The revenue has challenged the relief given by the Commissioner (Appeals) and the assessee is agitating for the higher net profit rate applied by the Commissioner (Appeals) and ignoring past net profit track of the assessee.[Para 9.1]

It is found that the net profit rate of 0.4 per cent has been accepted by this Tribunal in one of the sister concern of the assessee. It is also found that the net profit declared by the assessee for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 was within the range of 0.2 per cent to 0.29 per cent and even in the scrutiny proceedings the revenue authorities in assessee's own case have estimated net profit below the rate of 1 per cent so by no means estimating the net profit at the rate of 8 per cent could be justified, looking to the fact that there is no change of business during all these years, books of account are duly audited, no specific error has been pointed out by both lower authorities.[Para 9.3]

One more important fact which is relevant in the instant appeal is that subsequent to the assessment proceeding search and seizure operation was carried out at 'B' Group on 27-4-2017 and subsequent to search notice under section 153C were issued to the assessee company also and the assessments were framed under section 143(3) for assessment years 2012-13 to 2014-15 on 27-12-2019 assessing the income only to the extent of additions confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals). In other words the grounds raised by the revenue will have no merit in these cases because revenue authorities have themselves accepted the income determined by the Commissioner (Appeals) giving part relief given in the grounds raised by the assessee. Certainly another fact which cannot be ignored is that there was a complete non-compliance on the part of the assessee, thereby, not allowing the Assessing Officer to examine the documents of sales, purchase and expenditure thoroughly.[Para 9.4]

Therefore, under the given facts and circumstances of the case, respectfully following the decision of this Tribunal in the case of ITO v. B.B.C. Project Services (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No.1669 (Kol.) of 2016, dated 30-11-2018] consistent business of contract work carried out by the assessee and the net profit rate offered in the financial statements and being fair to both the parties, it is viewed that application of net profit rate of 0.6 per cent on the turnover of contract business during the year i.e. Rs. 87.46 crores will meet the end to justice. It is accordingly ordered and the revenue is directed to compute the net profit for the year at the rate of 0.6 per cent. Further, it is made clear that this net profit rate of 0.6 per cent will take care of all the business expenses including interest and depreciation incurred for the purpose of running contract business and related to the turnover of Rs. 87.46 crores. Accordingly assessee will get part relief on this common issue and revenue fails to succeed.[Para 9.5]

in construction work, filed return showing 0.48 per cent net 
profit on total contract receipt - Assessing Officer rejected books of account maintained by assessee and applied net profit rate at
 12.5 per cent for computing assessee’s income - Whether provisions of section 44AD, though strictly inserted in Act with effect from 1-4-1994, can be a guideline for purpose of applying a particular net profit in case of civil contractor even in earlier years - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, net profit rate of 12.5 per cent applied by authorities below in case of assessee was excessive and exorbitant and, accordingly, application of net profit rate was modified from 12.5 per cent to 8 per cent on gross receipt shown by assessee - Held, yes

It is true that there is no res judicata in the income-tax law and that the ITO has authority to take a different view from what has been taken in an earlier year. But neither he can exercise this authority in caprice, nor has he an unrestricted, unlimited, unconditional or absolute right in this matter. It was undisputed that the ITO had completed the assessments of the assessee’s income for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 on a flate rate basis observing, inter alia, that in the absence of maintenance of vouchers and receipts for the expenditure incurred by the assessee, the books of account were not acceptable. Now to examine whether the books of account kept in all the years inclusive of the year under appeal were maintained in the same manner or not, the trading and profit and loss accounts were the best available guide on which one should rely. There was no difference in the manner in which they had been kept in any of the assessment years inclusive of the assessment year under appeal. However, it was strange that though the assessee was a big contractor and executions of many of the contracts were spread in these years, no work-in-progress or closing stock had been recorded in the trading account. In view of the circumstances, it was not possible for the ITO to presume that the true profit could be computed on the basis of the books of account. He had overlooked the orders for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 framed by his predecessors. As a matter of fact, his finding was not very much different. He had also overlooked his own letter dated 16-2-1985 addressed to the assessee. Again, there was no whisper in his order as to what were the defects in the earlier years, which were not present in the relevant assessment year. He failed to prove his finding. Accordingly, the reasoning of the ITO to change the mode of assessment could not be accepted and the estimate of profit at a flat rate method as adopted in earlier years in the same circumstances should also apply in the assessment year under appeal, except that, in view of the finding that a large amount of expenses claimed was unestablished, the profit rate to be applied should be 12½ per cent instead of 10 per cent adopted for the earlier years.

In the instant case, it appeared that the Government had supplied some material for incorporation in the works at a fixed price, which was adjustable against the contract. In such a case, the tender price would not include any profit on the material supplied by the Government itself as it was incorporated in the works. This case was fully covered by the judgment of the Supreme Court in Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978]115 ITR 524 . Hence, the Tribunal was not justified in confirming the inclusion of the cost of materials supplied by the M.E.S. authorities to the assessee-firm in the assessee's total receipts and applying a net rate of profit at 10% on the total receipts for the purposes of computing the assessee's income for the assessment year in question.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 28 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Assessee, carrying contract work under government departments, did not maintain proper account books - Whether net profit could be estimated at a flat rate on gross receipts including value of material supplied by government - Held, on facts, yes

FACT: The assessee, a firm of contractors, executed certain contracts given by the State Government during the assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74. For the assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74, the total gross receipts under the work contract respectively amounted to Rs. 19,41,472 and Rs. 22,86,353 out of which a sum of Rs. 1,27,215 and Rs. 4,82,527 was deducted, being the value of materials supplied by the Government. Since the assessee did not maintain proper account books or any stock book or material issue register, the ITO determined the net profit under the proviso to section 145(1) by applying a flat rate of 10 per cent on the aforesaid gross receipts without excluding the value of the materials supplied by the Government. The AAC, however, directed that for determining the net profit, flat rate was to be applied only on the net receipts. The Tribunal could not ascertain: (i) the actual position regarding the materials obtained from the department and; (ii) whether the same remained under the control of the department or of the assessee. It, accordingly, restored the ITO's order.

On reference:

HELD: 1. No hard and fast rule could be laid down as to whether the value of the materials should or should not be included in a contractor's gross turnover from business for determining his net profits. It depended upon the manner in which the materials were obtained and used in the execution of the contract. The contracts could be generally classified as (i) contract for labour supply; (ii) a lump sum contract; and (iii) where the material supplied by the department was either an outright sale or was specifically meant to be used in the work allotted. In the types of contracts mentioned in (i) and (iii), the profit had to be calculated on the gross receipts, including the value of the material supplied either by the Government or by the assessee. Whereas, in the case of the other items at (ii) and (iii), profit would be determined en the basis of only the net amount without taking into consideration the value of the materials. In the instant case, in the absence of any stock register or issue register, it was not known whether the materials were supplied by the department as an outright sale to the assessee or it remained under the control of the department throughout and that the same was never under the control of the contractor except for using it in the constitution.

2. The Tribunal was, accordingly, correct in holding that the profit was to be calculated on the gross receipts excluding the recoveries for the material supplied by the Government department.

FACT: The assessee was a contractor executing contract works under various Government departments.

The Assessing Officer verified the profit and loss account and found that the assessee had claimed huge expenses under heads 'freight', 'salaries and wages', 'travelling expenses' and 'other expenses'. The assessee was asked to produce salary and wage register and evidences of the above expenses. The assessee did not produce the same. The Assessing Officer rejected the book profit and estimated the profit at 8 per cent of the gross contract receipts.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal :

HELD: Section 44AD clarifies that if the assessee's gross receipts are more than Rs. 1 crore and if the assessee did not maintain the books of account, then his profit has to be estimated at the rate of 8 per cent and depreciation should not be allowed. In the instant case, the assessee did not produce the books of account and also did not appear before the Assessing Officer, therefore the Assessing Officer was not able to verify the claim made in profit and loss account. The assessee did not care to produce the books of account before the Assessing Officer nor before the Commissioner (Appeals). In such circumstances, the Assessing Officer has no alternative except to reject the books and estimated the profit at the rate of 8 per cent on the total turnover. As per section 144, if the assessee fails to comply with the terms of a notice issued under sub-section (1) of section 142 and if the assessee fails to provide the necessary information, the Assessing Officer had liberty to pass the order on the best judgment assessment. Secondly, if the assessee produced the books of account where the Assessing Officer is not satisfied about the correctness or completeness of the accounts of the assessee, or where the method of accounting provide standards as notified under sub-section (2), have not been regularly followed by the assessee, the Assessing Officer may make the assessment in the manner provide in section 145. The best assessment can be made under sections 142 and 144 after rejecting the book results under section 145(3). The assessee has not produced any evidence before the Assessing Officer, therefore the Assessing Officer is justified in estimating the profit at 8 per cent. This ground of appeal is dismissed [Para 8]

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1964-65 and 1965-66 - Assessee manufactured sweets and other eatables and also sold confectionery articles which he purchased on wholesale from another merchant-Tribunal rejecting assessee’s books of account acting under section 145 and, on basis of data available, adopted flat rate for calculating profit - Whether, question relating to flat rate was pure question of fact and thus, no question of law arose from Tribunal’s order - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was carrying on business of manufacturing sweets and another eastables and selling confectionery articles which he purchased on wholesale from another merchant. He submitted his return for the year 1965-66, showing gross turnover in the sum of Rs. 2,34,576. According to the assessee the gross profit rate of the confectionery manufactured by him was 17.5 per cent and for the one that was purchased by him it was 8.5 per cent, yielding an average profit of 11.2 per cent. The ITO, not finding the books of account entirely, reliable estimated the turnover at Rs. 2,50,000 and calculated the average rate of profit at 17.5 per cent and taxed the assessee accordingly. The AAC reduced the gross turnover to Rs. 2,44,000 and reduced the average rate to 15 per cent profit. The Tribunal for the purposes of calculation firstly, reduced the total gross turnover to Rs. 2,40,000 and treating the portion relating to the confectionery manufactured by the assessee at Rs. 75,000, the profit rate assessed by the Tribunal was 20 per cent. Regarding the sale of the confectionery which was purchased by the assessee and sold by him, the turnover was taken at Rs. 1,65,000 and the rate applied to it was 10 per cent resulting in an average at 13.1 per cent. Similar rates of profit were applied by the Tribunal for the assessment year 1964-65. The Tribunal declined to make reference under section 256(1).

On application under section 256(2) :

HELD: Undisputably, the assessee placed before the taxation authorities its own account books and they were not found reliable and, therefore, the ITO, the AAC and the Tribunal had acted under the provisions of section 145(1) and the proviso thereto. The flat rate when it was calculated on the basic of available data, could not be called arbitrary or perverse. It had been said by the Tribunal that the firm, from whom the assessee bought manufactured confectionery and sold it made a profit of 19 per cent and the assessee made a profit of 10 per cent which had been charged by the Tribunal and against which there was no grievance. Therefore, at least up to 19 per cent there was clear evidence about the flat rate being just. If the Tribunal made it 20 per cent one could not say it capricious, conjectural or based on irrelevant or no evidence. A question relating to the flat rate was a pure question of fact. Although from the language of the questions which were asked to be referred to the High Court the grievance of enhancement was there yet it was not pressed. Therefore, it was not necessary to enter into the question whether the tax was enhanced because it was factually incorrect to say that the total liability of the assessee was increased. It was not necessary to enter into the argument whether the question arose from the order of the Tribunal or not because clearly no question of law arose in the instant case.

Note: The case was decided against the assessee.

The assessee has canvassed for adoption of the net profit ratio of 8 per cent on contract receipts in order to estimate the income from the business of contracting. Ostensibly there is no hard and fast rule for estimating income from the business of civil Construction. However, section 44AD prescribes estimation from contract business in cases specified there at the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts. Section 44AD covers cases of civil construction, where the gross receipts from contract business do not exceed Rs. 40 lakhs. Of course, the assessee does not fall within the prescription of section 44AD, as its contract receipts exceed Rs. 40 lakhs. However, the presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD reflects a legislative approved rate of net profit, which can be considered as fair and reasonable to estimate income from contract business in cases like that of the instant assessee, where the books of account are not found reliable by the Assessing Officer. Moreover in the assessee's own case in the assessment year 2010-11 the determination of income from contracting business is also proximate to the rate of net profit of 8 per cent contained in section 44AD. Therefore, considering the overall facts and circumstances of the case, it would be just and proper that the income from contract business of the assessee be estimated at 8 per cent of the gross receipts and the addition be worked out accordingly.
