On second appeal: HELD: The Assessing Officer has rejected books of account for the reason that the assessee has failed to produce necessary bills and vouchers in respect of expenditure. The Assessing Officer has observed that most of the expenditure are supported by self-made vouchers. Although, the assessee claims that it has produced bills and vouchers in respect of major expenditure, fails to substantiate the claim with necessary evidences. The assessee failed to controvert the findings of the Assessing Officer with any positive evidence to come to the conclusion that the books of account maintained by him gave a true and correct profit from the business. The Assessing Officer was therefore right in rejecting books of account under the provisions of section 145(3) of the Act. [Para 8]

Having said, one has to examine, on facts and circumstances of the case whether the Assessing Officer was right in adopting net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts. There is no dispute with regard to the facts that the assessee is in the business of execution of works contracts. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee had disclosed 6.73 per cent to 7.44 per cent net profit, in the earlier period. For the assessment year 2007-08 in the scrutiny assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer has estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts for which the assessee has not preferred any appeal. Estimation of net profit from the business is one of the accepted method of determination of income from business. But, there is no hard and fast rule for estimation of income.

The department is following estimation of net profit on various rates depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. But, while estimating net profit from the business, there should be a basis for adopting a particular rate of net profit, either based on comparable cases of similar nature of business or assessee's own book results for earlier years. When there is no possibility of getting a comparable cases, and there is no possibility of reference to assessee's own book results for earlier periods, a reference to the provisions of section 44AD can be made, wherein the Act provides for estimation of net profit from the specified businesses subject to certain conditions. [Para 9]

The provisions of section 44AD provide for estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on gross receipts, in case where the assessees are involved in specified businesses and turnover from the business does not exceed specified limit. Although, the assessee's case does not fall within the ambit of the provisions of section 44AD of the Act, as its contract receipts exceed the specified limit, the analogy provided in the provisions of section 44AD can be adopted for estimation of net profit because of nature of business carried out by the assessee. The nature of business carried on by the assessee was squarely fit into the specified businesses referred to in the provisions of section 44AD of the Act. The presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD, reflects the legislative approved rate of net profit, which can be considered as fair and reasonable to estimate income from civil contract business, where the books of account are not found reliable by the Assessing Officer.

In this case, admittedly, the Assessing Officer had rejected books of account for the reason that the assessee has failed to produce supporting bills and vouchers in respect of expenditure. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee himself has admitted about 8 per cent net profit in the earlier period net of all deductions including depreciation. Therefore, considering the overall facts and circumstances of the case, the rate of net profit adopted by the Assessing Officer appears to be fair and reasonable. Hence, estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on total receipts net of all deductions including depreciation is upheld. [Para 10]

In so far as separate deductions towards depreciation is concerned, the assessee submitted that when estimation of net profit is made, separate deductions towards depreciation should be allowed, as depreciation is a notional deduction for normal wear and tear of the assets.

In this case, the assessee is involved in the business of execution of main works which carries more profit than sub-contract works and hence, the Assessing Officer has rightly adopted reasonable net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts and accordingly, further deductions towards depreciation is not allowed. Whether separate deductions can be allowed towards depreciation or not is a fact which is to be decided based on the facts and circumstances of each case and also based on the rate of net profit adopted for estimation of profit.

The business, of which the profits and gains were the subject of assessment, consisted of aerodrome work under the Central Public Works Department, certain katcha building constructions under the Military Engineering Service and small supply of potatoes to Garrison Engineer. During the accounting year 1942-43, the assessee received a sum of Rs. 2,92,256. During the next year, that is 1-4-1943 to 31-3-1944, they received a sum of Rs. 86,434 and during the following accounting year of 1-4-1944 to 31-3-1945, they received a sum of Rs. 25,703. Besides it appeared, there were certain estimated outstanding bills to the credit of the assessee which had been excluded from assessment. On firm's failure to produce, books of account, the ITO took the sum total of the above sums received in course of three years, that is Rs. 4,54,948, as the basis of his assessment. He deducted the income at Rs. 1,18,975, on the ratio of 40 per cent, a flat rate on the gross receipts. Deducting the excess profits tax of Rs. 1,13,317 the assessable income was set at Rs. 65,659 which was reduced by the AAC by a sum of Rs. 28,270 by way of rectification of an error in calculation of Rs. 24,270 and deducting the profits of Rs. 4,000 representing 40 per cent of the estimated outstanding bills. The AAC, on appeal, came to the conclusion that since it was a question of determination of that year's income, in the absence of account books and since this was the first assessment in the case, the proviso to section 13 came into operation and no question of cash basis could arise.

The Tribunal, however, thought that in the circumstances of the case, the ITO should have applied the rate of profit to the annual receipts instead of to the total receipts and that by amalgamating the receipts under one assessment the ITO raised the tax liability of the assessee which was not fair. The Tribunal, therefore, set aside the basis of the said assessment and remanded the case back to the ITO to assess the income on the basis of the receipts during each year.

On the question of the flat rate, the Tribunal reduced the estimate of 40 per cent to 30 per cent.

On reference :

HELD: The Tribunal's power of dealing with an order passed by an AAC is plenary and has been expressed as widely as can be conceived. According to the section, every order of assessment passed by an AAC either under section 28 or section 31 of 1922 Act, is appealable to the Tribunal. The latter can substitute its own order of assessment for the one passed by the appellate income-tax authority. This very widely expressed power, however, shall not be immune from such limitation to which ordinarily an appellate authority or tribunal is subject in the disposal of its duty.

sar (SMC) Bench, in the case of the Nangal Khurad Co-operative L & C Society Ltd. v. AO, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was set aside and the Assessing Officer was directed to compute the income for the assessment year 2001-02 by applying net profit rate of 6 per cent instead of 8 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer. The appeal for the assessment year 2001-02 was partly allowed. In the case of ‘D’ for the assessment year 2002-03, the contract receipts were Rs. 10,21,919 and in the case of ‘U’, the contract receipts for the assessment year 2002-03 were Rs. 14,25,627. Thus, in both the cases, receipts were less than Rs. 40 lakhs. The provisions of section 44AD are applicable to the contracts of civil construction or supply of labour for civil construction for contract receipts below 40 lakhs. Explanation to section 44AD further provides that the expression ‘civil construction’ includes the construction or repair of any building, bridge, dam or other structure or of any canal or road. It was not clear from the orders of the lower authorities whether, the activities undertaken by the assessees were contracts of civil work, supply of labour to civil contractors or the contracts falling under Explanation to section 44AD. If the activities of the assessees fell in the above categories, the provisions of section 44AD would be applicable and the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) for upholding the net profit rate of 8 per cent would not warrant any interference. However, if the activities of the assessees did not fall in those categories, the income would require to be computed by applying net profit rate of 6 per cent. In the light of those facts and circumstances of the cases, it was appropriate to set aside the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) and same were restored to his file with a direction to modify the earlier orders only if it was found that nature of contract work done by the assessees was other than supply of labour for civil contracts or the cases falling under Explanation to section 44AD. Otherwise, the earlier orders would stand confirmed.

In the result, the appeal was partly allowed.

HELD: It is true that there is no res judicata in the income-tax law and that the ITO has authority to take a different view from what has been taken in an earlier year. But neither he can exercise this authority in caprice, nor has he an unrestricted, unlimited, unconditional or absolute right in this matter. It was undisputed that the ITO had completed the assessments of the assessee’s income for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 on a flate rate basis observing, inter alia, that in the absence of maintenance of vouchers and receipts for the expenditure incurred by the assessee, the books of account were not acceptable. Now to examine whether the books of account kept in all the years inclusive of the year under appeal were maintained in the same manner or not, the trading and profit and loss accounts were the best available guide on which one should rely. There was no difference in the manner in which they had been kept in any of the assessment years inclusive of the assessment year under appeal. However, it was strange that though the assessee was a big contractor and executions of many of the contracts were spread in these years, no work-in-progress or closing stock had been recorded in the trading account. In view of the circumstances, it was not possible for the ITO to presume that the true profit could be computed on the basis of the books of account. He had overlooked the orders for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 framed by his predecessors. As a matter of fact, his finding was not very much different. He had also overlooked his own letter dated 16-2-1985 addressed to the assessee. Again, there was no whisper in his order as to what were the defects in the earlier years, which were not present in the relevant assessment year. He failed to prove his finding. Accordingly, the reasoning of the ITO to change the mode of assessment could not be accepted and the estimate of profit at a flat rate method as adopted in earlier years in the same circumstances should also apply in the assessment year under appeal, except that, in view of the finding that a large amount of expenses claimed was unestablished, the profit rate to be applied should be 12½ per cent instead of 10 per cent adopted for the earlier years.

It was evident from the terms and conditions of the contract that the assessee had not simply sold the sand to the civil contractor. The sand was available at the site on payment of royalty to the State Government. The assessee had to engage labourers for loading and unloading of the same. The assessee had to engage vehicle for carriage of sand up to the site. The sand was to be unloaded from the vehicle. The assessee was also required to pay octroi in respect of the said supply of sand. It was evident from these facts that the assessee was not engaged in the retail business of trading of goods. The price fixed by ‘U’ Ltd. was inclusive of all the above charges. Section 44AF is applicable in respect of retail traders. The assessee was not engaged in any retail trading - buying or selling of goods to customers. The assessee was neither a retailer nor a wholesale trader. The only business conducted by the assessee was the work executed by the assessee on account of contract for supply and transportation of sand, etc., to U Ltd. for construction of road. No other income had been disclosed. Therefore, the assessee could not be said to be engaged in the retail business of trading of goods. The assessee had engaged himself in the execution of contract with U Ltd. only. Hence, provisions of section 44AF were not attracted in the instant case. In the instant case, the assessee had executed the work of supplying and transportation of sand from a particular area to a civil contractor. In other words, the assessee was a sub-contractor to the civil contractor for execution of part of the work involved in the construction of the road. In view of Explanation 3 to section 194C, execution of work includes the carriage of goods by any mode of transport of goods other than by railways. Therefore, for the purpose of section 44AD, the execution of any works contract would include carriage of goods by any mode of transport other than by railways. In the instant case, the assessee had engaged himself in the supply and transportation of sand from a particular area to the civil contractor. If one were to go by the composite contract, then the entire payments made to the assessee would fall within the ambit of section 44AD being the payment received for the execution of works contract in the construction of a road. In this view of the matter, the entire payment would fall within the ambit of section 44AD. However, the contractor had made payments to the assessee in two parts - one for supplying of material, i.e., the sand at specified rates and the other for transportation charges including loading and unloading, octroi, etc. In case the contract was divisible in two parts - one for the supply of material and another for transport of the same, then section 44AD would be applicable only in respect of transportation charges and for the supply of material it would be reasonable to apply a net rate of profit of 5 per cent as applicable in the case of retail transfers, notwithstanding the fact that the assessee’s case might not strictly fall within the ambit of section 44AF in respect of the supply of the material. In the absence of relevant material, it would be just and reasonable to restore the issue to the file of Assessing Officer for the purpose of determination of the net profits after verification of the nature of payments to the assessee. In case there was a composite contract and there was no basis for bifurcation of transportation charges and cost of material, then the profit of the assessee should be computed at the rate of 8 per cent as provided under section 44AD. However, if there was a reasonable basis for bifurcation of payments, for the cost of material separately and for transportation charges, then the profit should be computed at the rate of 8 per cent in respect of payments made for transportation charge and at the rate of 5 per cent for the supply of the material. The Assessing Officer should decide the issue accordingly.

Assessee's books of account stand rightly rejected by Assessing officer

The assessee is admittedly not maintaining any stock register, so that there is no basis to verify the material consumption, which constitutes a very significant part of its operating cost. Not only that, it is admittedly following the 'method' of writing off its purchases for the year to the operating statement, treating the same as consumed. Now there is no basis to state that the material is actually consumed as soon as it is purchased, or that the assessee maintains no inventory thereof. The accounts as maintained are thus admittedly inconsistent with the actual, obtaining state of affairs, which the books of account of any entity or enterprise are supposed to reflect. There is no basis whatsoever, either in law or in accountancy; the law only upholding the accepted principles of commercial accounting, for the said concocted and/or arbitrary method of accounting being followed by the assessee. That the method has been followed from year to year, does not in any manner mitigate the defect, or justify its adoption. The assessee's books of account, as maintained, are thus not amenable to yielding correct operating results, so that the same stand rightly not accepted by Assessing Officer, applying section 145(3). [Para 3.1]

Continuing further, there is no basis in the Assessing Officer's estimation of material consumption at 36 per cent. Equally unjustifiable is his separate addition toward closing stock, which arises as a by-product to the finding of an actual lower material consumption. In fact, neither any separate addition can be sustained nor there is any warrant for allowing the assessee, as claimed by it, credit for the closing stock. The assessee would also have, similarly, opening stock, which has to be necessarily taken into account in determining the profit of the year. In fact, the opening stock being taken at nil, i.e., the value of the closing stock as reflected and accepted for the immediately preceding year, no opening stock for the year could be taken without first sustaining an addition toward the same under section 69/69A. [Para 3.2]

Section 145(3) mandates for making the assessment in the manner as provided in section 144, i.e., according to the best judgment of the assessing authority, taking all the relevant material into account. The assessee has relied on case law, i.e., Kesharbhai Ghamarbhai Chaudhary v. ITO [2012] 23 taxmann.com 273 (Ahd.), to the effect that under the circumstance of rejection of books of account, the prescription of section 44AE; the assessee in that case being a transport operator, is a good guideline for the purpose of estimation of income. The presumptive provision in the case of civil contractors is section 44AD, which provides for a net profit rate of 8 per cent. The matter is purely factual, though the prescribed presumptive statutory rate, applicable for assessees with a turnover of up to Rs. 40 lakh, without doubt provides a good guideline. The Apex Court in Brij Bushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524 approved a profit rate of 10 per cent. The Tribunal has in such cases upheld profit rates varying from 8 per cent upwards to as much as 20 per cent, or even higher. A net profit rate of 10 per cent on the assessee's contract receipt of Rs. 360.86 lakh, i.e., involving material consumption, would be a reasonable estimate. Qua its labour receipt of Rs. 82.95 lakh, a net profit rate of 20 per cent, in view of a much lower base, as appropriate under the given facts and circumstances of the case. The Assessing Officer is directed to work out the assessee's income for the year by applying the said percentages. No other addition is sustainable. [Para 3.3]

Further, the Assessing Officer had also not indicated any defect in the system of accounting regularly followed by the assessee, or its correctness, nor was there any change in the method of accounting during the year under consideration as compared to the earlier years to indicate any intention of the assessee to show low profit. While examining the books of the assessee, the Assessing Officer has to consider the following aspects : (i) whether the assessee has regularly employed a method of accounting; (ii) even if regular adoption of a method of accounting is there, whether the annual profits can properly be deduced from the method employed; (iii ) whether the accounts have been correctly maintained; (iv) whether the accounts maintained are complete in the sense that there is no significant omission therein. If the answers to above four questions would be in the affirmative, then the assessee's profits would be computed on the basis of his accounts. In such cases, proviso to section 145(1) or section 145(2) cannot be invoked. On the perusal of the materials placed on record in the instant case, it was found that the answers to all the above four questions were in the affirmative. No finding had been recorded by either of the lower authorities as to the unacceptability of the method and to the irregularity of the accounts kept by the assessee. It is well-settled that in the absence of such a finding recorded by the authorities, the book results cannot be ignored or brushed aside.

In the instant case, the assessee had been regularly maintaining the percentage of profit between 1 per cent to 2 per cent. Such profit had actually been worked out at higher figure, if one took only labour charges as a contract receipt insofar as the material was supplied by the Government, on which there was no question of any profit being earned by the assessee. From the record, it was also found that out of total contract receipts of Rs. 3.64 crores, the material used, supplied by the Government amounted to Rs. 1,60,35,409 as per the certificate of chartered accountant placed on the record. There was no question of any profit being earned by the assessee on the amount of Rs. 1.60 crores of materials being supplied by the Government/'contractee' to the assessee-firm for being used in the contract assigned to the assessee by the Government departments. It was also not the case of the Assessing Officer that any part of the contract receipt had not been entered in the books of account or that the assessee had accounted for expenses more than what had actually been incurred.

In view of the above facts and circumstances of the case and the materials placed on record there was no valid reason and justification for rejection of audited books of account and the method of accounting regularly and consistently followed by the assessee for accounting for the contract receipts. Thus, there was no justification in estimating the profit at 8 per cent by disregarding the book results.

There were certain discrepancies in the books of account maintained by the assessee. Therefore, the provisions of section 145(3) were applicable. Hence, the Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting the books of account and in applying net profit rate.

In most of the cases of civil contractors, net profit rate applied is 10 per cent, but those cases are of the direct contractorship. The assessee was sub-contactor. Therefore, it was not comparable with the cases of the main contractors. When the main contractors allocate the work to another sub-contractor, they keep the profit for themselves also and, as such, the net profit rate of 10 per cent considered to be fair and reasonable for the work done by the main contractor, cannot be applied to the case of sub-contractor. In the instant case, the Commissioner (Appeals) after keeping in mind that the assessee was a sub-contractor of the contractor who earned some profit, rightly applied net profit rate of 7 per cent. Therefore, the net profit rate of 10 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer on the basis of some cases of main contractor was not reasonable and fair in the assessee's case because it was a sub-contractor and not the main contractor.

It is well-settled that the depreciation is to be allowed when net profit rate is applied.

Therefore, the impugned order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified and deserved to be upheld.

The established law now is that in the case of works contracts, if the contractor has exclusive control over the materials supplied by the Department, then the profit must be calculated on the basis of the gross receipts. If on the other hand, the Department is in exclusive control of the materials supplied to the contractor (assessee), the rate of profit must be calculated on the basis of the net receipt of the assessee. In the instant case, the matter had not been enquired into with an eye on the law laid down in the assessee's own case in CIT v. Azad Builders [1986] 162 ITR 643. In that view of the matter, the instant reference was to be remanded to the Tribunal for reconsidering the entire matter with an eye on the law laid down in assessee's own case (supra).

Note: The case was remanded to the Tribunal.

FACT: ■

The assessee, a contractor executing works for Government departments/PWD, was flagged in NMS for contractual receipts of about Rs. 17.27 crores and interest income of about Rs. 0.24 lakhs during FY 2012-13 relevant to AY 2013-14 but did not file a return of income. On appeal, CIT(A)/NFAC dismissed appeal in limine on account of delay of 957 days and, on merits, upheld AO’s estimation of net profit at 15%.

Before the Tribunal, by an application the assessee referred a comparable case of another dealer who was also on assessee, whose disclosure of 2 per cent was accepted. The Tribunal mentioned that most of the sales were ‘invoice sales’, which meant outstation sales, and the inference was that such sales usually carried a larger margin of profit than local sales. No attempt also appeared to have been made at any time before the Tribunal to split up the turnover of the business on commission basis and the turnover on own account so that different rates might be applied to such turnover. In these circumstances, the question as to the consideration of comparable case mentioned by the assessee did not really arise nor did the question regarding the splitting up of the turnover arise out of the order of the Tribunal.

In any event, it was well settled that, once a proviso to section 13 of the Act 1922 applied, it was for the ITO to determine fairly and not arbitrarily the basis on which the income will be estimated. In estimating the income the conditions of trade obtaining and the average margin of profit in the particular line of business are to be borne in mind. It was clear that these factors in the present case have been kept in view and, therefore, it was not possible to say that the estimate of income was arbitrary or capricious to justify holding that some error of law had been committed by the Tribunal in confirming the flat rate of 5 per cent applied by the departmental authorities. It was again well settled that an estimate can be made by applying a flat rate and, so long as the ITO had exercised his judgment reasonably and not arbitrarily or capriciously, the finding given by him will be one of fact and not of law.

For the reasons given above the application of the flat rate of 5 percent was justified and the income-tax authorities were not liable to split up the total estimated turnover of Rs. 1,50,000 into turnover of business on commission and turnover of business on own account and applied a lower rate of turnover from business on commission.

It was also noticed that the sales tax was mentioned in the profit and loss account and the interest was also mentioned which was reduced from the profit. The assessee had also shown interest on security deposit in the income of the assessee in the balance sheet. The Tribunal on various dates directed the assessee to file details of the length of road, quantity of store and grit and basis of evidence for consumption of the raw material and the details of the sales-tax and TDS certificate issued on that account. Though the assessee had not filed the evidence with regard to consumption of the raw material and length of the road, but he had filed reply on all the abovesaid points. [Para 12]

Section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Civil construction business - Assessment year 2001-02 - Assessee had entered into a contract with a civil contractor ‘U’ Ltd. for supply of sand for construction of roads from specified zones - For said purpose, assessee had to pay royalty to Government, engage labourers for loading and unloading and arrange for transportation of sand up to site for construction of road - Contractor had made payments to assessee in two parts, one for supplying of material, and other for transportation charges - Whether since assessee had executed work of supplying and transporting sand from particular area to a civil contractor, assessee was to be considered as a sub-contractor and in such circumstances, section 44AD would be applicable  - Held, yes - Whether  however, if there was a reasonable basis for bifurcation of payments, for cost of material separately and for transportation charges, then profit should be computed at rate of 8 per cent in respect of payments made for transportation charge and at rate of 5 per cent for supply of material and if there was a composite agreement, then entire receipts would be subject to 8 per cent under section 44AD - Held, yes [Matter remanded to Assessing Officer for purpose of calculating net profits after verification of nature of payments to assessee]

In the case of ‘U’, the contract receipts for the assessment year 2001-02 exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs i.e., Rs. 41,20,790. Therefore, the provisions of section 44AD were not applicable to case of ‘U’ for the assessment year 2001-02. Following the decision of the Tribunal Amritsar (SMC) Bench, in the case of the Nangal Khurad Co-operative L & C Society Ltd. v. AO, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was set aside and the Assessing Officer was directed to compute the income for the assessment year 2001-02 by applying net profit rate of 6 per cent instead of 8 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer. The appeal for the assessment year 2001-02 was partly allowed.

In the case of ‘D’ for the assessment year 2002-03, the contract receipts were Rs. 10,21,919 and in the case of ‘U’, the contract receipts for the assessment year 2002-03 were Rs. 14,25,627. Thus, in both the cases, receipts were less than Rs. 40 lakhs. The provisions of section 44AD are applicable to the contracts of civil construction or supply of labour for civil construction for contract receipts below 40 lakhs. Explanation to section 44AD further provides that the expression ‘civil construction’ includes the construction or repair of any building, bridge, dam or other structure or of any canal or road. It was not clear from the orders of the lower authorities whether, the activities undertaken by the assessees were contracts of civil work, supply of labour to civil contractors or the contracts falling under Explanation to section 44AD. If the activities of the assessees fell in the above categories, the provisions of section 44AD would be applicable and the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) for upholding the net profit rate of 8 per cent would not warrant any interference. However, if the activities of the assessees did not fall in those categories, the income would require to be computed by applying net profit rate of 6 per cent. In the light of those facts and circumstances of the cases, it was appropriate to set aside the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) and same were restored to his file with a direction to modify the earlier orders only if it was found that nature of contract work done by the assessees was other than supply of labour for civil contracts or the cases falling under Explanation to section 44AD. Otherwise, the earlier orders would stand confirmed.

In the result, the appeal was partly allowed.

Sudhir Sehgal for the Appellant. Achal Sharma for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with  section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee- firm was carrying on business of Civil contractors - In course of assessment, Assessing Officer took a view that net profit rate declared by assessee was very low in civil contractual business - In absence of compliance by assessee to various notices issued, Assessing Officer by taking recourse to provisions of section 44AD, applied rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts to calculate assessee's taxable income - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) found that Assessing Officer had not given any basis for adopting the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts to work out the net income of the assessee even after accepting the plea of the assessee that its business was adversely affected on the death of the working partner - He thus estimated income at rate of 5 per cent of gross receipts - Whether since assessee had failed to file evidence in respect of material purchased and other expenses, impugned order of Commissioner (Appeals) adopting net rate of 5 per cent of gross receipts for working out assessee's income was to be upheld - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was carrying on business of civil contractors. In the course of assessment, the Assessing Officer was of the view that the net profit rate declared by the assessee was very low in the line of civil contractual business. The Assessing Officer issued various notices to the assessee but there was no response from assessee's side. The Assessing officer thus took note of fact that as per provisions of section 44AD, the rate of 8 per cent was applicable to gross receipts, and there was no requirement of maintaining books of account. The Assessing Officer thus applied the GP rate of 8 per cent to the gross contractual receipts after deducting the value of material supplied by the Government and sales-tax from the gross receipts. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the Assessing Officer had neither rejected the books of account nor passed an order under section 144 but had estimated the income at rate of 8 per cent of the gross receipts while passing the order under section 143(3). The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the Assessing Officer had not given any basis for adopting the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts to work out the net income of the assessee even after accepting the plea of the assessee that its business was adversely affected on the death of the working partner. In the circumstances, the Commissioner (Appeals) estimated the income at the rate of 5 per cent of the gross receipts.

On revenue's appeal :

HELD: On the facts of the case, there was no merit in adoption of rate of 8 per cent to the book results for working out the income for the relevant assessment year. However, as the assessee had failed to file evidence in respect of the material purchased and certain expenses and in the absence of the assessee filing the same on record, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) adopting rate of 5 per cent to the gross receipts for working out the income of the assessee was to be upheld.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 1959-60 - Assessee was a contractor who had undertaken construction of houses under a project for relevant assessment year - Assessee showed expenditure incurred on jobs during year at 
Rs 4,45,904 which was treated by assessee as work-in-progress and showed a sum of Rs 3,21,358 as received against contracts from executive engineer - Assessee did not show any profit or loss from jobs and claiming overhead expenses at Rs 12,764 a net loss was returned - ITO considered that a profit had to be calculated on basis of receipts from authorities and he accordingly computed gross profit of Rs. 40,169 at 12½ per cent of receipts - Before AAC, assessee claimed that since accounts were maintained on completed job basis which was recognised system of accounting, proviso to section 13 of 1922 Act could not be invoked - AAC did not accept assessee’s contention and upheld order of ITO in invoking provisions of section 13 of 1922 Act for computing assessee’s income - However, he computed gross profit by applying rate of 12½ per cent on gross value of work done and not on net payments received by assessee - Tribunal upheld order of AAC - Whether order of Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a contractor. In the year in question, the assessee had undertaken the construction of houses under a project. The expenditure incurred on the jobs during the year was shown at Rs. 4,45,904 and that was treated by the assessee as work-in-progress and a sum of Rs. 3,21,358 was shown as received against the contracts from the Executive Engineer. The assessee did not show any profit or loss from the jobs and, claiming overhead expenses at Rs. 12,764, a net loss was returned. The ITO considered that a profit had to be calculated on the basis of the receipts from the authorities and he had, accordingly, computed the gross profit of Rs. 40,169 at 12½ per cent of the receipts. The assessee appealed before the AAC. The assessee claimed that the accounts were maintained on what was known as the completed job basis which was the recognised system of accounting and that the accounts having been maintained in a proper manner, the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act could not be invoked. The AAC did not accept the assessee's contention. According to the AAC, the tax had to be levied on the total income of the previous year and not on the total income of a period of 2, 3, 4 or more years, the period that would be required for completing any contracted work. Accordingly, he upheld action of the ITO in invoking the provisions of section 13 of the 1922 Act, for computing the assessee’s income, however, the AAC, held that the rate was to be applied on the gross value of the work done and not on the net payments received by the assessee and accordingly computed the gross profits at Rs. 1,04,926 by applying the rate of 12½ per cent on Rs. 8,29,412 as the gross value of the work done during the previous year. On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the AAC.

On reference:

HELD: In the instant case, the assessee contractor had not been able to satisfy the lower authorities as to what were the terms of the contract with the contractee and in what terms and consideration the materials were supplied by the contractee to the contractor. Furthermore, in the instant case the total amount of profit had to be computed by applying the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act. The rate of profit had also to be determined by applying the proviso to section 13 of the 1922, Act. As the Tribunal had pointed out that if the normal experience and expectation of a contractor as to how the profit would vary, were taken into consideration and in the circumstances where the contractor had not been actually able to satisfy the terms of the contract and where the estimates were to be based by applying the provisions to section 13 of the 1922 Act, it could not be said that the Tribunal was not justified in upholding the decision of the AAC in the manner as it did. In cases where there was clear and unambiguous evidence that there was contract which provided sufficient limit, beyond which the tender could not be quoted and there was a stipulation that the contract was to be quoted at a particular rate, excluding the cost of materials, to be supplied by the contractee, other considerations might apply.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

The next point taken by the Commissioner for revision was based on the CBDT instruction whereby scrutinizing of the case in which the net profit rate disclosed is less than 5 per cent has been made compulsory. But it does not mean that every civil contractor should at least earn net profit rate of 5 per cent on its turnover. This instruction enables the authorities to scrutinize the return and nothing more. Therefore, that objection of the Commissioner was also baseless. The third point taken by the Commissioner to carry out proposed revision was that the Assessing Officer had not conducted any enquiry to verify the genuineness of purchases, particularly when the assessee could not produce the complete bills and vouchers relating to purchases and sales. That objection of the Commissioner could not be agreed with. The Assessing Officer had definitely made proper enquiries from the assessee which was evident from the assessment order itself. The assessee had filed its return of income alongwith audited trading and profit and loss account and balance sheet. A detailed questionnaire was served on the assessee. The notices under sections 143(2) and 142(1) were also issued and served on it. The books of account, bills and vouchers produced were test-checked by the Assessing Officer. The assessee had filed various replies and details and the same were examined by the Assessing Officer. The only discrepancy having worth was with regard to the bills and vouchers issued for supplies, etc., which were stolen and against which FIR had been lodged by the assessee. The documents appended in the paper book of the assessee contained a copy of the detailed reply of notice under section 263, in which entire enquiries made by the Assessing Officer after the assessee filed reply of the notice under section 142(1), copy of reply sent to the Assessing Officer, etc., which were on record were also examined. In fact, it was not the case, where the Assessing Officer had not made proper enquiries and had simply passed the assessment in haste. The Assessing Officer had made ample enquiries, which were evident from the assessment order itself. The Assessing Officer, after considering all the replies of the assessee and in the interest of the revenue, proposed to the assessee an addition of Rs. 7 lakhs which was accepted by the assessee to avoid further litigation. Insofar as, the application of 8 per cent net profit rate in view of the provisions of section 44AD was concerned, the same was against the intention and purport of the Act. Insofar as, the CBDT circular was concerned, which said that the net profit rate being below 5 per cent in civil contractor's case, scrutiny could be ensued, was entirely on different footing. The Assessing Officer had made the scrutiny in the instant case and it did not mean by any stretch of imagination that the said circular meant that 5 per cent net profit rate had to be adopted in all such cases. The Assessing Officer had definitely made enquiry regarding purchases but obviously entire bills could not be produced and that was why the Assessing Officer made the proposal which was accepted by the assessee. It was not correct to say that the assessment had been made and completed in a hurry without making proper enquiry, to ascertain the actual income and verify the expenses claimed in the trading and profit and loss account. The Allahabad High Court, which was jurisdictional High Court in the instant case, while deciding another case, had given a clear verdict by holding that merely because the ITO had not written a lengthy order, it would not establish without bringing on record specific instance that the assessment order passed under section 143(3)/148 was erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. In the instant case, the Assessing Officer had made all the enquiries by issuing questionnaire and asking for entire details. The Assessing Officer had even mentioned all the details examined by him. The books of account of the assessee were audited and it had filed audited trading and profit and loss account and balance sheet. The assessee replied to different notices and questionnaire issued to him. The case was discussed with the advocate and the accountant of the assessee from time-to-time. Various replies and details were produced and examined. The books of account, bills and vouchers were produced and test-checked. The assessee was required to produce complete bills and vouchers for purchases and supplies made during the year under consideration. It was also required to produce the vouchers for expenses debited under various heads. It had produced various papers and vouchers, but complete vouchers for entire expenses could not be produced. Some of the vouchers could not be made available, but entries in their accounts were found to be made. From the above, it was clearly established that the Assessing Officer had made complete enquiry. It was clearly perceived by the Assessing Officer that the assessee had done contract work and had also made supplies of sand, morag, mitti, gover, plants, tractor, trolley, JCB machines and labours, etc. Thus, total receipt was not only from civil construction. It was brought to the notice of the Bench that in the immediately preceding year, i.e., 2004-05 in similar nature of business, the assessment was made at Rs. 6,10,070 by making ad hoc addition of Rs. 4,50,000 on the turnover of Rs

FACT: During the assessment year 1989-90 the assessee, an individual doing construction work, received payments on which he declared a net profit rate of 0.58 per cent after allowing claim for interest and depreciation. HELD: Engaging of employees to carry out the work was not a very special feature which should weigh heavily while determining the income on the basis adopted by the department. The facts of the case showed that at the time of assessment, the assessee was not possessed of full verificatory vouchers as necessary proof by which the expenses entered in the books of account could be vouched and verified. Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c ) which was amended with effect from 1-4-1976, goes to show that to discharge ‘the revenue of its initial burden it has to be established that there was concealment of particulars of income, when additions are made in the income or any disallowance of expenses claimed by the assessee’ has been made. It was to be noticed, in the instant case, that the result of the business as disclosed in the books of account having not been accepted, instead the assessing authority accepted and adopted gross receipts by the assessee as basis for applying flat profit rate, for making the assessment. That resulted in addition of Rs. 28,520 in the income of the assessee and the ITO was justified initially for holding satisfaction that the assessee had concealed particulars of his income in respect of said additions made in the income and initiated penalty proceedings for that purpose.

However, it is settled that Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c ) only provides a rule of evidence for raising a rebuttable presumption in favour of the revenue and does no more. It can be rebutted by leading new material as well as from existing material on record. The presumption is not carried to height of a conclusive proof. Once jurisdiction has been assumed, matter has to be decided in terms of evidence that has come before the assessing authority and it must depend upon dealing with such matters by the Assessing Officer thereof.

In the instant case, while presumption had been raised in respect of additions made in the returned income of the assessee by applying flat profit rate on gross receipts by the assessee, the assessment order revealed that the enquiry had proceeded on the basis of finding whether the claim of deductions against the income had rightly been disclosed in the books of account and the same had been rightly rejected.

The Tribunal had misdirected itself in considering the ambit and scope of the said Explanation and also in dealing with the case where additions had been made not on any specific count but by applying a gross profit rate while rejecting the result shown in the books of account, that is to say, not on the basis of entries made in the books of account. Once books of account are rejected and income is assessed by applying gross profit rate which results in addition of income, though the provisions of Explanation 1 to section 271(1)(c) may be attracted for the purpose of initiating penalty proceedings by raising presumption under the Explanation 1, the same by itself cannot take place of conclusive proof so as to discard the evidence and attending circumstances on that basis alone.
Revision u/s 263 quashed as AO rightly accepted civil contractor’s voluntary 6% profit estimate, no error found: ITAT

In view of the unvouched and unverifiable nature of expenses/payments, particularly when the assessee was a labour contractor, coupled with the fact of steep fall in the gross profit rate of instant year as compared to the last year, the rejection of books of account was upheld. As from the books of the assessee, due to reasons detailed by the Assessing Officer in his order, correct income of the assessee was not deductible, so in view of the decision in CIT v. British Paints India Ltd. [1991] 188 ITR 44/ 54 Taxman 499 (SC), the application of section 145 was upheld. The Assessing Officer himself had not taken guidance from the results of the past year. The gross profit rate declared by the assessee in the assessment year 2002-03 was 7 per cent. Nevertheless, the Assessing Officer had adopted gross profit rate of 6.5 per cent instead. Meaning thereby, the Assessing Officer had found some force in the reasonings tendered by the assessee in relation to decrease in the gross profit rate of the instant year. A perusal of the Tribunal's order in the case of Hanuman Construction Co. for the same assessment year revealed that under identical facts and circumstances, the Bench had adopted a gross profit rate of 3 per cent as reasonable while the assessee had claimed 2.65 per cent as against 7 per cent in the previous year. From the facts of the instant case, it transpired that it was pari materia with the case of Hanuman Construction Co. In that case also, the similar price hike of diesel and the cut throat competition in the line of business was considered by the Bench to be a reasonable explanation for the fall. The gross receipts of the relevant year had experienced tremendous increase and the assessee had accepted the transportation contract below the tender rate, but in the earlier year the position was just opposite. Keeping in view, the topsy-turvy happened between two consecutive years, there was no other option but to follow said order given in exactly similar facts and circumstances. Therefore, by following the above Tribunal order and keeping in view the facts in totality, gross profit rate of 3 per cent was to be adopted.

Section 145, read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1964-65 and 1965-66 - Assessee manufactured sweets and other eatables and also sold confectionery articles which he purchased on wholesale from another merchant-Tribunal rejecting assessee’s books of account acting under section 145 and, on basis of data available, adopted flat rate for calculating profit - Whether, question relating to flat rate was pure question of fact and thus, no question of law arose from Tribunal’s order - Held, yes

a very material question, not only in estimating the total turnover of the business but also in computing the profits, because it was quite possible that profits, if the cloth was dyed and printed in the assessee’s own karkhana, might be different from the profits if the cloth was dyed and printed outside. It was not the case of the department that the assessee got its cloth dyed and printed by outside professionals with the help of the dyes and chemicals, it itself supplied. From the original assessment order, it appeared as though that the ITO was proceeding on the assumption that the dyes and chemicals purchased by the assessee were only used by him for dyeing and printing the cloth in its own karkhana. If, therefore, these unaccounted dyes and chemicals were used in the assessee’s own karkhana, then the turnover in the karkhana itself would be of large proportions, while the ITO stated, evidently on the basis of the private enquiry, that the manufacture and sale of dyed and printed cloth done through professional dyers and printers constituted the major portion of its business and that the manufacture in the karkhana was of a negligible extent. If the unaccounted chemicals and dyes of the value of Rs. 4,533 were also to be taken as used in the assessee’s own karkhana, then the insignificant portion of the business (as opined by the ITO) done in the karkhana itself would be Rs. 2,35,000, the figure arrived at by the ITO on the basis of the chemicals used. If that were to be case, the turnover resulting from the manufacture done outside the karkhana which was bound to be the major portion should be much higher and the estimate of Rs. 2,35,000 would not fit into the calculations. Thus, no proper nexus or connection was made out between the unaccounted chemicals and the estimate of the total turnover. Judged from any angle, this estimate of Rs. 2,35,000 on the basis of the unaccounted chemicals and dyes appeared to be unwarranted.

Equally unwarranted in Court’s view the adoption of the rate of profit at 50 per cent of the total turnover. The assessee estimated his profit only at 18 per cent while the department put it at 50 per cent. This was done by the department on the basis of the disclosed gross-profit rate in some comparable cases. Even in that section of the business of the assessee, which deals with dyeing and printing of cloth and selling it, there were different ways of manufacture adopted by the assessee. The assessee purchased koras, mulls and handloom cloth, got them bleached, dyed and printed through professional dyers. It also purchased dyes and chemicals, dyed some cloth in its own karkhana by engaging dyeing coolies and sold the same. It also purchased the dyed cloth from other merchants and got it printed by professional printers. It also carried on purchase and sale of dyed and printed cloth. It was also quite possible that the profit in the method of manufacture of dyed and printed cloth might be different from the profit in another method of manufacture. A scrutiny of the record did not disclose any consideration by the department as to the possible rates of profit from these different methods of manufacture. No material or data had been place which could have formed the basis of the decision of the department in that behalf. It was not known whether the comparable business on the basis of which 50 per cent rate of profit was fixed by the department were doing dyeing and printing trade in all the methods which the assessee adopted during the year under assessment. There was no basis for the department to reject the assessee’s contention that the total turnover should be analysed into different types of trade and different rates with reference to different types should be adopted. In the absence of any material or data connecting the comparable businesses with the different methods of manufacture adopted by the assessee or indicating that the same rate of profit, viz., 50 per cent was uniformly derived by the assessee in all the different types of manufacture, the conclusion was irresistible that the department was not justified in importing the rule of thumb into the matter and imposing a flat and uniform rate of 50 per cent in all the classes of manufacture. Therefore, the Court was not satisfied that there was any legal and acceptable basis for fixing the rate of profit at 50 per cent of the total turnover.

In view of these conclusions, it was held that the information collected by the department was not completely disclosed to the assessee and it was not afforded an adequate opportunity of rebuttal as directed by the High Court and that there was no material which could form the basis of an order under section 13 of the Act 1922.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

In the next assessment for the assessment year 1985-86 completed on 29-3-1988, there was a mention of the said statement and also of the fact that he purchased the shop in 1983 and the assessee had asked Rs. 33 lakhs as on money. Thereafter, the affidavit of ‘I’ was filed. Hence, it could be inferred that the ‘on money’ was being paid right from the year 1983 and that the deponent ‘I’ should have retracted from that statement not only because of his relationship with or influence of the assessee but mainly because he should have been told that if he did not retract, he might also be required to explain as to from where he paid that amount of black money. Hence, the argument of the assessee attacking the statement of ‘I’ could not be accepted.

As regards application of rate of net profit on receipts, as per the assessee’s own admission if the ‘on money’ was taken into account, the net profit rate for the assessment year 1988-89 worked out to 21 per cent and if the total receipts of the project were taken at Rs. 3.77 crores plus Rs. 66 lakhs ‘on money’, i.e., total Rs. 4.43 crores, the net profit worked out to Rs. 6.66 lakhs as disclosed by the assessee in the books and Rs. 66 lakhs as ‘on money’ This totals up to Rs. 72.66 lakhs and will give a net profit rate of 16.40 per cent. In this view of the matter, case relied upon by the assessee, where net profit rate of 5 per cent was accepted by the Tribunal, could not be relied upon as a comparable case.

In the facts and circumstances of the case, the following conclusions could be arrived at:

(1) It could not be said that the assessee’s books of account were correct and complete and, therefore, the income of the assessee in each of the assessment years had to be assessed according to provisions of section 145(2) and (2) it could not be accepted that the assessee had received the ‘on money’ as its income only in the last two assessment years as it had been earning ‘on money’ from the beginning of the project although the percentage might have increased in the later years.

Therefore, the view taken by the Assessing Officer to the effect that assessee should have earned profits at the rate of 25 per cent of gross receipts was reasonable. This was because even as per the assessee own submissions and disclosure, it had earned ‘on money’ at the rate of 17.5 per cent of Rs. 5.77 crores. As no builder can be expected to be selling the shops and flats without charging some profits, a rate of 7.5 per cent might be considered to be reasonable rate of net profit. This net profit was in addition to the ‘on money’ and must have been earned even from those parties from whom no ‘on money’ had been charged, such as banks, BMC and other institutions. This would mean that the total profit rate would be 17.5 per cent plus 7.5 per cent which is equal to 25 per cent. This rate would be applied on the total receipts and not on the receipts after deducting the profits. It was, therefore, to be held that the Assessing Officer was justified in applying the profit rate of 25 per cent on the gross receipts and in allocating the profits in different years. Further, the Commissioner (Appeals ) was not justified in taking the view for the assessment years 1985-86 and 1988-89 that assessee’s profits should be computed on the basis of project completion method. Therefore, the order of Commissioner (Appeals ) to that effect was to be reversed with direction to Assessing Officer to assess the profits on each year starting from the assessment years 1981-82 to 1988- 89 separately.

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits (Gross profit rate) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Where assessee-firm derived income from work contracts, net profit of assessee should be estimated at 8 per cent as against 10 per cent adopted by Assessing Officer [Partly in favour of assessee]

The books of account regularly maintained in the course of business which are duly audited under the provisions of the Act and are free from any qualification by the auditors should be taken as correct unless there are strong and sufficient reasons to indicate that they are unreliable. For rejecting the books of account, it is the revenue's onus to prove that either the books of account maintained by the assessee are not correct and complete or the method of accounting adopted by the assessee is such that true profits cannot be deduced therefrom. In the instant case, while rejecting the books of account, the adverse observation of the Assessing Officer was with respect to delay in payment of labour charges for the month of January, 1998. That was not sufficient cause for rejecting the audited accounts wherein no adverse comment had been made by the auditor, nor any specific defect had been pointed out by the Assessing Officer. It was not the case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee had recorded excess payment of labour charges, nor there was any allegation that labour charges were disproportionate to the nature of contract work executed. On the other hand, even as per the Government manuals, the percentage of labour expenses as a percentage of total value of contract, in respect of civil contract, is 25 per cent whereas in the instant case, the expenses claimed under labour charges worked out to 20.67 per cent (total contract receipts Rs. 364.54 lakhs, labour charges Rs. 75.37 lakhs.) Thus, it was not a case of excess payment of labour charges to reduce the profit, but, on the contrary, as against the standard norm of 25 per cent labour charges amounting to Rs. 91.13 lakhs, the assessee had actually incurred only Rs. 75.37 lakhs, which worked out to be at 20.67 per cent. Income-tax provisions nowhere either authorize the Assessing Officer or cast an obligation on the assessee to prove the negative result, i.e., to prove as to why he had failed to make a profit at a particular rate.

The accounts may be rejected as unreliable if important entries and transactions are omitted therefrom or if proper particulars and vouchers, bills, etc., are not forthcoming or if they do not include entries relating to particular class of business transaction. Reasons for rejecting wages record as commented by the Assessing Officer related to full address of the labour, which was not given on the muster roll register. The wages record had been kept by the assessee as per regulation known as 'Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970. The addresses of the labourers to whom wages had been paid were not mentioned, since the labourers stayed in the Jhugi Jhoperies at a work site itself and to that effect the assessee had already replied to the Assessing Officer vide its letter dated 23-3-2001, through which site of construction where labourers resided was given which was, however, not taken notice of by the Assessing Officer and the same was sent to him by courier and was found to be duly received by the Assessing Officer. The Assessing Officer had also alleged that the actual date of payment was not mentioned by the payee receiving the wages. The date on which the entry had been made in the wages register was the actual date of payment. As per the nature of the contract work executed by the assessee, he had got a contract to carry out a particular job or a contract for which the material was supplied by the CPWD/DOT and the labour was provided by the assessee-contractor. The assessee used to make payments to the labourers on the basis of mandays put in by the labourers and not on the basis of work performed by them on each day. Therefore, there was no merit in the allegations of the Assessing Officer that work performed by the labour was not mentioned on the payment vouchers and in making them as basis for rejection of books of account. The payment to the assessee-contractor was also made on the basis of work completed which was measured by the department itself and not on the basis of what the labourer had done. The bills for such a contract were prepared, which were not verified by the engineers of contractee before making payments. On the basis of those bills which were finally approved by the Government engineers/contractee, the payment was given to the assessee-contractor after deducting TDS. Thus, it was humanly not possible to provide the details as to what work a particular labourer had done at the site. Further, the Assessing Officer had also not indicated any defect in the system of accounting regularly followed by the assessee, or its correctness, nor was there any change in the method of accounting during the year under consideration as compared to the earlier years to indicate any intention of the assessee to show low profit.

4.10]

The Assessing Officer has taken the rate of 10 per cent from section 44BBB, which is a special provision for computing on presumptive basis income of foreign companies engaged in the business of civil construction etc. in certain turnkey power project. [Para 4]

In the instant case, the assessee is engaged in providing consultancy for various projects including construction, power projects etc. Section 44BBB was exactly not applicable over the facts of the instant case. Once books of account are rejected for estimating the profit of the assessee , the Assessing Officer may apply profit rate of any comparable case. The profit in the case of the assessee should be estimated at a value that the other assessees in similar circumstances could earn. There cannot be a wild guess while estimating the profit of the assessee. In the case of consultancy, major expenses are on human resources whereas the construction or other business of erection etc. of turnkey power projects involves materials and wages etc. and hence cannot be compared with consultancy business. Since the Assessing Officer has not cited any case comparable to the assessee and no opportunity has been granted to the assessee on this issue. In the interest of Justice, it would be appropriate to restore the matter to the file of the Assessing Officer to apply the net profit rate on the basis of comparable cases. Nevertheless to mention that the assessee shall be afforded reasonable opportunity of hearing. [Para 4.2]

, such an impost has to be regarded as unreasonable restriction on the freedom to carry on trade or business. In the instant case, the legislative policy of fixing the rate of profit as has been done in section 44AC had to be regarded as in the nature of unreasonable restriction on cases of some of the assessees. Therefore, section 44AC has to be regarded as violative of article 19(1)(a) in the cases of some of the petitioners before the Court. The further question to be considered was whether anything can be done by the Court to uphold the validity of section 44AC though, as it is, it is violative of articles 14 and 19(1)(g). The Andhra Pradesh High Court found a way out and the same was to be read down. The reading down by the Andhra Pradesh High Court was to the extent that section 44AC shall be read not as an independent provision but as an adjunct to and as explanatory to section 206C; and that it does not dispense with regular assessment altogether with the result that after the tax is collected in the manner provided by section 206C, a regular assessment would be made where the profit and gain of business in goods in question would be ascertained in accordance with sections 28 to 43C. The reading down was resorted to by the Andhra Pradesh High Court, having come to the view that section 206C serves the purpose which the Legislature had in mind, i.e., to take care of tax evasion. lt was observed that once tax is collected at the source as visualised by section 206C, the contractor cannot run away; probably only in cases where the profit is higher than 40 per cent (in case of liquor traders) would he make himself scarce. In all other cases, he would come to the department for assessment of his income and there is no reason, as to why regular assessment should not be made in his case. Thus, the overall object underlying the provision would be subserved by section 206C. Following the view taken by the Andhra Pradesh High Court, although section 44AC violated articles 14 and 19(1)(g), instead of being struck down, it should be read down as above, as this reading down takes care of all the complaints made by the petitioners inasmuch as if during the course of regular assessment it were to be found that any particular assessee had not earned the profit at the rate specified in section 44AC, the same would be duly taken care of section 44AC would, therefore, cease to be arbitrary and would not be unreasonably restrictive of the freedom to carry on trade or business.

Court for decision, viz.h (1) whether the Assistant Commissioner was legally justified in assessing the petitioner's profits at a standard rate of 10 per cent, on the advances received during the calendar year 1923 on the ground that the accounts for that year could not be separated; (2) whether the Assistant Commissioner has erred in law in holding items of expenditure amounting to Rs. 31,864 as inadmissible merely because no details were given in full in the cash book. It will appear from the order of the Assistant Commissioner referred to above that the second point does not really arise at all. It is true that the Assistant Commissioner was inclined to consider items of expenditure aggregating to Rs. 31,864 as suspicious, but he did not base his decision to assess the profits at the standard rate of 10 per cent, on that ground. The decision was merely based on the ground that the accounts for the year 1923 could not be separated. So the only point which requires decision is No. 1 stated above. The Commissioner of Income-tax apparently treated this as a question of accountancy and not of law. On behalf of the petitioner it is urged, on the other hand, that the question is one of law and not merely of accountancy. The following authorities were cited in support of the contentions : In re, Bishnu Priya Chowdhurani 1 ITC 261 and M. Sankar Iyer v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras 1 ITC 395 . In the former case the assessee had declared that he had no bastu income, but his statement was disbelieved and his bastu income was assessed at Rs. 1,528-6-4, at the rate of 2½ per cent, on the gross rental, without there being any evidence to show that the assessee had, as a matter of fact, derived any bastu income. It was held that when the assessee had declared that he had no bastu income at all, it was for the Income-tax Officers to prove that he had any such income, but not for him to prove the reverse. The question whether, in the absence of any reliable data as to the income of an assessee from a certain source, the Income-tax Officer is justified in making an assessment based on a formula which had been found in practice generally applicable was referred to the High Court, but no opinion was expressed on it as the other point was considered sufficient for disposal of the reference. In Sankar Iyer v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras 1 ITC 395 , the assessee's accounts were held to be unreliable and his income was assessed at a certain figure by the Income-tax Officer without any materials before him. On application by the assessee, the High Court directed the Commissioner to state a case for the determination of the following question :

"Whether in cases where the Income-tax Officer is not prepared to act on the accounts produced or the statement or evidence of the assessee, he can assess without any evidence on the record, or whether he is bound to inform the assessee as to how he proposes to assess him and the information on which he proposes to act and to call evidence so as to allow the assessee an opportunity of showing that such information or evidence is incorrect and ought not to be acted upon."

It will appear from the, above that the facts in both the cases are distinguishable. In the present case the assessee does not allege that he derived no income at all from any contracts, nor does the assessment proceed definitely on the ground that the accounts were unrealiable. The Assistant Commissioner adopted a standard rate for the assessment merely because no separate accounts were available for the accounting year. This was apparently due to the manner in which the accounts were kept. The Income-tax Officer has pointed out, for instance, that expenditure in respect of certain items for two years was lumped together (for example, motor hire, cartage, etc.) in a single item. As the assessee failed to produce correct and complete accounts for the accounting year, it seems to me that it was open to the Income-tax Officer to make an assessment to the best of his judgment : vide section 23 read with section 11, Income-tax Act.

The Assistant Commissioner, however, gives no reasons for adopting what he calls the "usual" rate of 10 per cent. For the purposes of the assessment, and it is not known how that rate was arrived at. The ruling in Sankar Iyer v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras 1 ITC 395, referred to above, seems to support the contention that the petitioner ought to have been given an opportunity of rebutting the evidence or information on which the rate was based. On behalf of the Commissioner of Income-tax the decision of this Court in In re, Ishar Das Daram Chand 2 ITC 12 was referred to in support of the assessment at a flat rate; but in that case the flat rate was apparently based upon a consideration of the dealings. In my view, the following point of law emerges for decision in the circumstances of this case. Whether in the case of a contract spread over a number of years when accounts for the year under assessment cannot be separated, the Income-tax Officer is legally justified in assessing profits at a flat rate without informing the assessee of the information or evidence on which the rate is based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal.

In the instant case the assessee did not allege that he derived no income at all from any contracts, nor did the assessment proceed definitely on the ground that the accounts were unreliable. The Assistant Commissioner adopted a standard rate for the assessment merely because no separate accounts were available for the accounting year. This was apparently due to the manner in which the accounting were kept. As the assessee failed to produce correct and complete accounts for the accounting year, it was open to the Income-tax Officer to make an assessment to the best of his judgment: vide section 23, read with section 11, of the 1922 Act. The Assistant Commissioner, however, gave no reasons for adopting what he called the usual rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of the assessment, and it was not known how that rate was arrived at. In the circumstances of the case, the point of law emerged for decision was whether in the case of a contract spread over a number of years when accounts for the year under assessment could not be separated, the ITO was legally justified in assessing profits at a flat rate without informing the assessee of the information or evidence on which the rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal.

Accordingly, the petition was accepted and the Commissioner was directed to state the case and refer the point of law to the High Court for decision.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

On writ:

HEADNOTE: Section 143, read with section 256, of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 33, read with section 66, of Indian Income tax Act, 1922] - Assessment - General - Assessment year 1924-25 - In respect of contracts spread over a number of years, assessee produced accounts but accounts for relevant accounting year could not be separated - ITO assessed profit at a standard rate without informing assessee of information or evidence on which rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal - Whether question of law arose out of order of ITO - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a contractor, was assessed to income-tax for the relevant assessment year in respect of certain contracts which commenced in 1922 and were finished some time in 1924. The assessee produced his accounts, but the accounts for the relevant accounting year could not be separated. The ITO considered the accounts to be unreliable. He, therefore, assumed profit at the standard rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of his assessment. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner concluded that in any case it was impossible to ascertain from the assessee’s accounts what the income had been for one year and, therefore, the only way of ascertaining it was to apply the usual rate of 10 per cent on the total payments received. On application under section 66(2) of the 1922 Act, the Commissioner declined to make any reference.

On application under section 66 (3) of the 1922 Act.

HELD: In the instant case the assessee did not allege that he derived no income at all from any contracts, nor did the assessment proceed definitely on the ground that the accounts were unreliable. The Assistant Commissioner adopted a standard rate for the assessment merely because no separate accounts were available for the accounting year. This was apparently due to the manner in which the accounting were kept. As the assessee failed to produce correct and complete accounts for the accounting year, it was open to the Income-tax Officer to make an assessment to the best of his judgment: vide section 23, read with section 11, of the 1922 Act. The Assistant Commissioner, however, gave no reasons for adopting what he called the usual rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of the assessment, and it was not known how that rate was arrived at. In the circumstances of the case, the point of law emerged for decision was whether in the case of a contract spread over a number of years when accounts for the year under assessment could not be separated, the ITO was legally justified in assessing profits at a flat rate without informing the assessee of the information or evidence on which the rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal.

Accordingly, the petition was accepted and the Commissioner was directed to state the case and refer the point of law to the High Court for decision.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Sardha Ram for the Assessee .

Jagan Nath Aggarwal for the Crown.
