FACT: The assessee was a contractor undertaking project of Indian Railways on turnkey basis. A search action under section 132 was carried out at the assessee's premises. As the assessee, at the relevant point of time, was not able to collect information about such contracts or produce relevant personnel, it proposed for fixing net profit rate at 11 per cent. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, applied net profit rate at the rate of 11 per cent on the total contract receipts on estimate basis which however, was reduced to 8 per cent by the Tribunal. A penalty under section 271(1)(c) was also levied upon the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the penalty on the ground that the estimation of income by applying flat net profit ratio did not tantamount to concealment or filing inaccurate particulars of income.

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: The issue of disparity between the assessed income and the returned income is not sustainable as the addition was purely on ad hoc estimation of net profit ratio. The Assessing Officer applied a particular flat rate of 11 per cent against the declared profit rate of 3 per cent by the assessee. The Tribunal has reduced the estimated income by adopting 8 per cent of profit rate which is also based on ad hoc estimation. Ultimately, the addition sustained or survived is ad hoc estimation of income by applying flat rate of 8 per cent of the profit which cannot be held either as concealment or filing inaccurate particulars. The Tribunal, in the quantum appeal, has also observed that suppression of the profit had not been established and the allegations have not been proved. On the basis of the explanation submitted by the assessee, the Tribunal has found no justification in applying and confirming the net profit rate of 11 per cent which has been reduced to 8 per cent on ad hoc basis subject to the allowability of depreciation and interest thereon. For levying penalty under section 271(1)(c), there has to be concealment of particulars of income by the assessee or the assessee must have furnished inaccurate particulars of income. Ultimately, in assessee's case, addition sustained was based on ad hoc estimation of income by applying a flat rate of 8 per cent of profit which can neither be held as concealment of income nor filing of inaccurate particulars of income. Further, the assessee's offering of the profit rate was a conditional proposal as the assessee was not able to collect the whole information about the context and produce the same. Thus, offer made by assessee was to buy peace and not to enter into dispute with revenue authorities. To purchase the peace and avoid any dispute with the revenue authorities in the quantum of income, assessee offered the estimated rate of profit. Considering all these facts and circumstances, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in deleting the penalty levied under section 271(1)(c ). [Para 5]

On reference : HELD: Contracts for building construction or of similar type can be divided into two broad categories. Category No. (1) will cover contracts where, at the time of entering into the contract, the contractor is told that some of the materials required for construction work will be supplied by the person or authority who entrusts the construction work to him and it is on that footing of such construction materials being supplied by the authorities or the other party to the contract, that the contractor enters into the contract for the construction quoting a particular figure for the entire contract. A sub-category of this first category of contract is the type of contract where, for notional purposes, a total figure is mentioned for the construction contract inclusive of materials and on the footing that the contractor is to supply all the materials for the construction work. However, at the time when the contract is entered into, it is clearly agreed between the contracting parties that some of the building materials will be supplied by the other party to the contract, that is, the person or authority entrusting the construction work to the contractor, and that credit will have to be given by the contractor for the materials, thus, received and the rates at which the credit is to be given is also agreed upon between the contractor and the other party to the contract. It was designated as a sub-category of category No. (1) because though notionally and on the face of it the contract has been entered into for a much larger amount and on the footing that the contractor is to supply all the materials, because of the clear agreement between the parties about the materials to be supplied by the other party to the contract and also about rates at which those materials are to be supplied, it is clear that in fact and in substance the parties have entered into the contract where certain specified materials are to be supplied not by the contractor but by the other party to the contract and the contractor right from the beginning enters into the contract on this footing and puts forward his quotation and ultimately gets the contract for the amount where he does not take into consideration supply of those particular materials or rates for those materials. Category No. (2) of contracts is the type where, right from the beginning, the contractor enters into the construction contract on the footing that he has to supply all the materials but while the contract is being executed, the other party to the contract supplies some of the materials and when the bill is finally paid, the other party to the contract claims credit for the price of the materials supplied to the building contractor. In that eventuality, it is really the total figure of the original contract or figure worked out in accordance with the terms of the original contract which will constitute the original receipts of the building contractor and the fact that, instead of going into the market and purchasing the materials for himself, the contractor gets these materials for himself, the party to the contract, does not enter into the picture so far as this aspect of the case is concerned. The question as to under which particular category, category No. (1) or category No. (2) set out above, a particular contract falls, will have to be decided looking to the substance of the transaction between the parties in each individual case. If the case falls under the first category, then it is obvious that the cost of the materials supplied by the other party to the contract cannot be taken into consideration in arriving at the figure of the total receipts of the contractor in respect of the particular contract for building construction. On the other hand, if the case falls, on the facts and circumstances of the particular case, in the second category, then the total receipts of the building contractor in respect of that particular contract will be the total amount of the contract notwithstanding the fact that the other party to the contract has supplied some of the materials required for building construction work.

It is, therefore, clear that in matters of this kind, when deciding whether a particular amount should or should not be considered to be trading receipt, it is the true nature and quality of the receipt, either actual or deemed, which has to be considered and not the outward form or the head under which the amount is entered in the account books of the assessee concerned.

It is thus, substance of the contract which matters and if, the agreement between the parties right from the beginning is that certain materials are to be supplied by the other party to the contract, that is, the Government department, or the authority concerned, then it is obvious that the contract was entered into on the footing that no profit would be made by the building contractor in respect of the supply of those materials.

After coming to the conclusion that the trading results were not prone to verification, the Assessing Officer was left with only one alternative to estimate the income of the assessee in the most appropriate and reasonable manner. In such type of cases, the net profit rate or gross profit rate could be applied or the Assessing Officer could adopt any method of estimation and work out the income from profession or business. But the method adopted must be reasonable and logical. In all civil contract cases, if accounts are not maintained or defective accounts are maintained, a net rate of 10 per cent is applied which was admitted by the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order. In those cases neither depreciation nor interest nor any other expenditure debitable to profit and loss account are separately allowed. By allowing depreciation and interest, net profit rate of approximately 3.5 per cent had been applied consequent to the order of the Commissioner (Appeals). The rate itself was absolutely abnormal. There was no evidence on record whatsoever that there were abnormal conditions prevailing with the assessee to earn such a low net profit by executing the contract. Once net rate was applied it was not open to the Assessing Officer to allow any other claim debited to profit and loss account. Depreciation and interest were definitely items which were debited in profit and loss account before the net profit was arrived at. It could have been the case of the appellant to justify the net profit rate shown as .27 per cent or to justify the net profit rate applied by the Commissioner (Appeals) at 3.5 per cent approximately. But no such discussion was available on record. The logical conclusion of the circular of the CBDT regarding claim of depreciation that in case profits were estimated, the same should be made subject to the allowance of depreciation and the assessee should file complete details of the claim of depreciation. One has again to look into the power given by the statute to the Assessing Officer when he invoked proviso to section 145(1). The first proviso to section 145(1) gives power to the Assessing Officer to decide whether or not income can properly be deduced from the accounts maintained by the assessee, even if the accounts are correct and complete.

[1991] 188 ITR 44/ 54 Taxman 499 the Assessing Officer has to adopt rationale and reasonable method in arriving at the estimate of income, after he gives finding that the accounts maintained by the appellant are neither prone to verification nor reliable. In regard to the legal aspect, whether in a case where the best judgment assessment is made on rejection of books of account, deduction as permissible under the provisions of the Act otherwise would not be available to such assessee, has to be seen in the light of the provisions of the Income-tax Act and the scheme laid down therein.

9. Sri Rajan Roy, appearing for the assessee, has drawn our attention to the provisions of sections 144 and 145 of the Act and also section 139 to rebut the submission of the learned counsel for the revenue in a case of best judgment assessment, statutory deduction would not be available to him where flat rate is to be applied.

10. Section 144 of the Act prescribes the procedure for best judgment assessment, whereas section 145 is the method of accounting and reads as under :

"145(1) Income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" or "Income from other sources" shall, subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), be computed in accordance with either cash or mercantile system of accounting regularly employed by the assessee.

(2) The Central Government may notify in the Official Gazette from time to time accounting standards to be followed by any class of assessees or in respect of any class of income.

(3) Where the Assessing Officer is not satisfied about the correctness or completeness of the accounts of the assessee, or where the method of accounting provided in sub-section (1) or accounting standards as notified under sub-section (2), have not been regularly followed by the assessee, the Assessing Officer may make an assessment in the manner provided in section 144."

11. The aforesaid provision gives power to the Assessing Officer, if he is not satisfied about the correctness or the completeness of the accounts of the assessee, or where no method of accounting has been regularly employed by the assessee to make an assessment in the manner provided in section 144. The provision in sub-section (1) with regard to the income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" or "Income from other sources" has been made subject to the provisions of sub-section (2). This has to be computed with either cash or mercantile system of accounting regularly.

In the instant case the assessee had not maintained any books of account and the revenue applied a rate of profit of 12.6 per cent on the gross amounts of bills received by the assessee. The assessee had tendered for the contract as a whole including the cost of materials which were subsequently supplied by the Government. There was no evidence on record to show that the assessee did not know about the supply of materials by the Government to be made or at what price. Furthermore, the gross profit had been computed on the total gross bill of the assessee. In the aforesaid background the Tribunal had come to the conclusion that the assessee, though tendered the contract as a whole, it must have included the cost of materials which were supplied by the Government as an element of profit in respect of cost of materials also. In the aforesaid background, it could not be said that the Tribunal was indulging in any surmise or acting without any proper evidence. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in holding that a net profit rate as applied by the departmental authorities on the gross amounts of bills without deducting the cost of materials supplied by the Government was legally justified for the assessment years 1964-65 and 1965-66.

In its income-tax return, the assessee showed its total receipts from the two sets of contract businesses as Rs. 12,45,000 resulting in a net profit of Rs. 42,209. The Income-tax Officer proceeded to make the assess­ment under section 143(3) of the Income-tax Act. He thought that the amount of profit disclosed by the assessee, which came to slightly more than 3.3% of the total receipts, was very low. Accordingly, he scrutinized the books of the assessee and found that neither the cash book had been written from day to day, nor had the daily balance been struck. Although the assessee had mentioned that it had furnished the particulars of its closing stock in its trading account, yet that had not been done. Subsequently, the assessee estimated its closing stock at Rs. 1,549, but did not disclose the basis for estimating or valuing the same. The expenses claimed by the assessee were mostly unvouched and they had not been debited correctly. Some of the car expenses which should not have been debited in the material account were found debited therein. He, accordingly, found the account books of the assessee to be unreliable and after rejecting them proceeded to make the assessment on the basis of the material available on the record.

In respect of the business relating to the Kanpur set the assessee showed its total receipts as Rs. 6,29,554 which included a sum of Rs. 5,72,621 in respect of two contracts and some miscellaneous receipts, resulting in a net profit amouting to Rs. 27,765, i.e., about 4% of the receipts. In the opinion of the Income-tax Officer, the profit disclosed was too low. The assessee attempted to explain the low rate of profit by stating that ever since the contracts in question had been entered, the price of material and wages had increased. In this connection the Income-tax Officer observed :

"Assessee's condition of accounts, however, as disclosed above is very unsatisfactory. In view of this, however, a net rate of 8% will be applied so as to give an income of Rs. 50,364. The assessee received raw material of Rs. 27,766 on which a not rate of 5% will be applied so as to give an income of Rs. 1,388. Income from this set thus comes to Rs. 51,752 subject to depreciation."

While dealing with the business relating to the Lucknow set, the Income-tax Officer found that the assessee had disclosed its total receipts and net profit as Rs. 6,18,145 and Rs. 14,444. The rate of profit thus came to about 2% which, in his opinion, was absurd. Again, the assessee attempted to explain the low rate of profit by alleging that the contracts in question had been entered into in the year 1962. It was expected that the work under those contracts would be completed within one year. However, the work continued right up to the year 1964 by which time the cost of material and wages had shot up. While dealing with this point of the case the Income-tax Officer observed:

"There is some force in the assessee's contention. Looking, however, to the fact that this remains unproved in the absence of proper account net rate of 8% will be applied on payments of Rs. 6,18,145 so as to give a profit of Rs. 49,452. A net rate of 5% will be applied on raw material received on Rs. 39,400 so as to give a profit of Rs. 1,970. The income from this set comes to Rs. 51,422."

A bare perusal of the findings recorded by the Assessing Officer would indicate that he had applied the principles determining the profit vide section 44AD, whereas the aforesaid provision was not at all applicable in the case of assessee in the relevant assessment years. This factual position was not being disputed by either of the parties. That being so, the question arose as to what should be the profit rate for the purpose of determining the profit accrued or gained by the parties. Since the Assessing Officer, had not dealt with this question independent of section 44AD, the rate of profit could not be upheld. [Para 3]

So far as the determination of profit of 5 per cent by the Commissioner (Appeals) was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) had also not given any reason nor any material was placed before the Commissioner (Appeals), or for that matter before the Assessing Officer for arriving at a conclusion about the rate of profit. Merely on assumption that since the assessee was performing the work for the PWD and as the contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under supervision of the PWD authorities, the rate of profit would be low or merely because the turnover exceeded Rs. 10 lakhs, it would incur more expenses, the aforesaid rate of profits could not have been arrived at. Neither the Commissioner (Appeals) nor the Tribunal had taken into consideration the relevant material or facts which might be necessary for arriving at such a conclusion. [Para 4]

The rate of profit cannot be assumed merely on assumptions or surmises and conjectures. It is the first liability of the assessee to produce such records, evidence and material so as to substantiate his plea about the rate of profit that he claims and in case the books of account have been rejected , the onus shifts on to the Assessing Officer to determine the rate of profit on consideration of the material which may be brought before him or even on making such inquiry, which may be necessary and which may include the requirement of having any information from the assessee also during the course of determination of such rate of profit, namely, during the assessment proceedings. In no case, simply because the turnover was more than Rs. 40 lakhs or the assessee was performing civil construction work for Public Works Department, neither the rate of profits could be determined nor it could be taken to be less nor it could be reduced nor could be arrived at any presumptions. [Para 5]

Since the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) as also the Tribunal had not recorded any finding based on any material, and the findings recorded were merely based on surmises and conjectures or on purely guess work and imagination of the authorities, as it had not been brought to the notice of the High Court that any such rate of profit could be assessed under the rules or any law in that manner, the findings of rate of profit could not be sustained and were liable to be set aside and the matter deserved to be remanded to the assessing authority for re-determination thereof. [Para 6]

As per provisions of section 158BB, the block assessment is to be made based on evidence before the Assessing Officer. The word 'Evidence' has to be construed in a comprehensive manner and it includes all circumstantial evidence also. The material or evidence with the Assessing Officer on which assessment may be based is not confined to direct testimony by witnesses. Such evidence need not only be evidence found during the course of search but also material gathered by him. The Assessing Officer was not fettered by the Technical rules of evidence and the like and he may act on material which may not strictly speaking, be accepted as an evidence in the Court of law. It may be circumstantial evidence or assessment based on the preponderance of probabilities judged by human conduct. For this purpose, the past history of the case, and general market conditions will constitute relevant material for the purpose of assessment. For the purpose of block assessment under Chapter XIV-B, in view of amendment by Finance Act, 2002 to section 158BC(b) of the Income-tax Act which is effective retrospectively from 1-7-1995 wherein there is insertion of section 145 for the purpose of determining the undisclosed income. As per amendment to section 158BC(b ), the section 145 could also be invoked by Assessing officer for determining the undisclosed income. [Para 37]

However, it is to be made clear that if no material was found during the search which could show suppression of income, no estimation of undisclosed income of block period by resorting to section 145 could be made. In other words, where there is a material, such an estimation of income can be made. It is not necessary that addition should be limited to what is found during the search. [Para 38]

Income-tax provisions nowhere either authorize the Assessing Officer or cast an obligation on the assessee to prove the negative result, i.e., to prove as to why he had failed to make a profit at a particular rate. The accounts may be rejected as unreliable if important entries and transactions are omitted therefrom or if proper particulars and vouchers, bills, etc., are not forthcoming or if they do not include entries relating to particular class of business transaction. Reasons for rejecting wages record as commented by the Assessing Officer related to full address of the labour, which was not given on the muster roll register. The wages record had been kept by the assessee as per regulation known as 'Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970. The addresses of the labourers to whom wages had been paid were not mentioned, since the labourers stayed in the Jhugi Jhoperies at a work site itself and to that effect the assessee had already replied to the Assessing Officer vide its letter dated 23-3-2001, through which site of construction where labourers resided was given which was, however, not taken notice of by the Assessing Officer and the same was sent to him by courier and was found to be duly received by the Assessing Officer. The Assessing Officer had also alleged that the actual date of payment was not mentioned by the payee receiving the wages. The date on which the entry had been made in the wages register was the actual date of payment. As per the nature of the contract work executed by the assessee, he had got a contract to carry out a particular job or a contract for which the material was supplied by the CPWD/DOT and the labour was provided by the assessee-contractor. The assessee used to make payments to the labourers on the basis of mandays put in by the labourers and not on the basis of work performed by them on each day. Therefore, there was no merit in the allegations of the Assessing Officer that work performed by the labour was not mentioned on the payment vouchers and in making them as basis for rejection of books of account. The payment to the assessee-contractor was also made on the basis of work completed which was measured by the department itself and not on the basis of what the labourer had done. The bills for such a contract were prepared, which were not verified by the engineers of contractee before making payments. On the basis of those bills which were finally approved by the Government engineers/contractee, the payment was given to the assessee-contractor after deducting TDS. Thus, it was humanly not possible to provide the details as to what work a particular labourer had done at the site. Further, the Assessing Officer had also not indicated any defect in the system of accounting regularly followed by the assessee, or its correctness, nor was there any change in the method of accounting during the year under consideration as compared to the earlier years to indicate any intention of the assessee to show low profit.

While examining the books of the assessee, the Assessing Officer has to consider the following aspects : (i) whether the assessee has regularly employed a method of accounting; (ii) even if regular adoption of a method of accounting is there, whether the annual profits can properly be deduced from the method employed; (iii ) whether the accounts have been correctly maintained; (iv) whether the accounts maintained are complete in the sense that there is no significant omission therein. If the answers to above four questions would be in the affirmative, then the assessee's profits would be computed on the basis of his accounts. In such cases, proviso to section 145(1) or section 145(2) cannot be invoked. On the perusal of the materials placed on record in the instant case, it was found that the answers to all the above four questions were in the affirmative. No finding had been recorded by either of the lower authorities as to the unacceptability of the method and to the irregularity of the accounts kept by the assessee. It is well-settled that in the absence of such a finding recorded by the authorities, the book results cannot be ignored or brushed aside.

The AO should not make his best judgment assessment on mere suspicion, impulsively or arbitrarily. If the unaccounted chemicals and dyes of the value of Rs. 4,533 were also to be taken as used in the assessee’s own karkhana, then the insignificant portion of the business (as opined by the ITO) done in the karkhana itself would be Rs. 2,35,000, the figure arrived at by the ITO on the basis of the chemicals used. If that were to be case, the turnover resulting from the manufacture done outside the karkhana which was bound to be the major portion should be much higher and the estimate of Rs. 2,35,000 would not fit into the calculations. Judged from any angle, this estimate of Rs. 2,35,000 on the basis of the unaccounted chemicals and dyes appeared to be unwarranted.

Equally unwarranted in Court’s view the adoption of the rate of profit at 50 per cent of the total turnover. The assessee estimated his profit only at 18 per cent while the department put it at 50 per cent. This was done by the department on the basis of the disclosed gross-profit rate in some comparable cases. Even in that section of the business of the assessee, which deals with dyeing and printing of cloth and selling it, there were different ways of manufacture adopted by the assessee. The assessee purchased koras, mulls and handloom cloth, got them bleached, dyed and printed through professional dyers. It also purchased dyes and chemicals, dyed some cloth in its own karkhana by engaging dyeing coolies and sold the same. It also purchased the dyed cloth from other merchants and got it printed by professional printers. It also carried on purchase and sale of dyed and printed cloth. It was also quite possible that the profit in the method of manufacture of dyed and printed cloth might be different from the profit in another method of manufacture. A scrutiny of the record did not disclose any consideration by the department as to the possible rates of profit from these different methods of manufacture. No material or data had been place which could have formed the basis of the decision of the department in that behalf. It was not known whether the comparable business on the basis of which 50 per cent rate of profit was fixed by the department were doing dyeing and printing trade in all the methods which the assessee adopted during the year under assessment. There was no basis for the department to reject the assessee’s contention that the total turnover should be analysed into different types of trade and different rates with reference to different types should be adopted. In the absence of any material or data connecting the comparable businesses with the different methods of manufacture adopted by the assessee or indicating that the same rate of profit, viz., 50 per cent was uniformly derived by the assessee in all the different types of manufacture, the conclusion was irresistible that the department was not justified in importing the rule of thumb into the matter and imposing a flat and uniform rate of 50 per cent in all the classes of manufacture. Therefore, the Court was not satisfied that there was any legal and acceptable basis for fixing the rate of profit at 50 per cent of the total turnover.

In view of these conclusions, it was held that the information collected by the department was not completely disclosed to the assessee and it was not afforded an adequate opportunity of rebuttal as directed by the High Court and that there was no material which could form the basis of an order under section 13 of the Act 1922.

While discussing the second question, factors required to be taken into consideration for determination of the net profit rates, it was observed as under:- "The second question of law namely factors required to be taken into consideration while applying a net profit rate has come up for consideration, as on the same set of facts the Assessing Officer, the Commissioner of Income-tax and Income-tax appellate Tribunal have applied different rates of net profit, the discretion to determine on adequate net profit rate undoubtedly vests with authorities under the Act by the discretion so vested is neither unbridled nor unguided as it must be guided by reason i.e. should be preceded by reasons which, in turn, should be preceded by a perceptible process of reasoning based upon due consideration of all relevant facts. However, authorities under the Act appear to construe their jurisdiction as a discretion to apply a thump rule dependent almost entirely on the whims of a particular officer.

The discretion to determine a net profit rate must necessarily be exercised on the basis of relevant factors which we shall enumerate but before doing so, would clarify that these factors are neither exhaustive nor a final word on relevant factors that may be considered while determining the net profit rate. A few significant factors are the past tax history of the assessee, if available, assessment order that may have been passed and accepted by the department, the nature of the assessee's business, an appraisal of the value of the contract, prevailing economic conditions vis a vis the assessee's business, the price of raw material, labour etc. the rice in price index as notified by the Central Government from time to time if applicable and if the Assessing Officer proceeds to rely upon assessments of other assessees engaged in similar business to do so only after determining points of similarity etc. "

In the instant case there was material before the Tribunal on which its finding could be based: the assessee's representative had admitted before the AAC that full quantitative details in respect of the stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of that contract might not be available. In the circumstances, recourse to estimating the profits on the contract was inevitable. He, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 10,000 as against Rs. 26,434 added by the ITO. If the assessee wished to displace the AAC's estimate it was open to him to adduce evidence in support of its claim that the consumption of stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 was fully justified. This the assessee apparently did not do. For the subsequent year 1960-61 the assessee itself declared a net profit rate of 9.9% as against 9% declared in the assessment year in question. It could not be disputed that this was additional material which the Tribunal could take into consideration as it did. There was thus material before the Tribunal on which its estimate was based. The Tribunal's decision was, therefore, in conformity with the decision in the case of CIT v. Maharajadhiraj of Darbhanga [1933] 1 ITR 94 (P.C.).

The Tribunal was therefore justified in holding that the proviso to section 13 was applicable and there was material before it to sustain the aforesaid addition.

HELD: A bare perusal of the findings recorded by the Assessing Officer would indicate that he had applied the principles determining the profit vide section 44AD, whereas the aforesaid provision was not at all applicable in the case of assessee in the relevant assessment years. This factual position was not being disputed by either of the parties. That being so, the question arose as to what should be the profit rate for the purpose of determining the profit accrued or gained by the parties. Since the Assessing Officer, had not dealt with this question independent of section 44AD, the rate of profit could not be upheld. [Para 3]

So far as the determination of profit of 5 per cent by the Commissioner (Appeals) was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) had also not given any reason nor any material was placed before the Commissioner (Appeals), or for that matter before the Assessing Officer for arriving at a conclusion about the rate of profit. Merely on assumption that since the assessee was performing the work for the PWD and as the contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under supervision of the PWD authorities, the rate of profit would be low or merely because the turnover exceeded Rs. 10 lakhs, it would incur more expenses, the aforesaid rate of profits could not have been arrived at. Neither the Commissioner (Appeals) nor the Tribunal had taken into consideration the relevant material or facts which might be necessary for arriving at such a conclusion. [Para 4]

The rate of profit cannot be assumed merely on assumptions or surmises and conjectures. It is the first liability of the assessee to produce such records, evidence and material so as to substantiate his plea about the rate of profit that he claims and in case the books of account have been rejected , the onus shifts on to the Assessing Officer to determine the rate of profit on consideration of the material which may be brought before him or even on making such inquiry, which may be necessary and which may include the requirement of having any information from the assessee also during the course of determination of such rate of profit, namely, during the assessment proceedings. In no case, simply because the turnover was more than Rs. 40 lakhs or the assessee was performing civil construction work for Public Works Department, neither the rate of profits could be determined nor it could be taken to be less nor it could be reduced nor could be arrived at any presumptions. [Para 5]

In the case of ‘D’ for the assessment year 2002-03, the contract receipts were Rs. 10,21,919 and in the case of ‘U’, the contract receipts for the assessment year 2002-03 were Rs. 14,25,627. The provisions of section 44AD are applicable to the contracts of civil construction or supply of labour for civil construction for contract receipts below 40 lakhs. Explanation to section 44AD further provides that the expression ‘civil construction’ includes the construction or repair of any building, bridge, dam or other structure or of any canal or road. It was not clear from the orders of the lower authorities whether, the activities undertaken by the assessees were contracts of civil work, supply of labour to civil contractors or the contracts falling under Explanation to section 44AD. If the activities of the assessees fell in the above categories, the provisions of section 44AD would be applicable and the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) for upholding the net profit rate of 8 per cent would not warrant any interference. However, if the activities of the assessees did not fall in those categories, the income would require to be computed by applying net profit rate of 6 per cent. In the light of those facts and circumstances of the cases, it was appropriate to set aside the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) and same were restored to his file with a direction to modify the earlier orders only if it was found that nature of contract work done by the assessees was other than supply of labour for civil contracts or the cases falling under Explanation to section 44AD. Estimation of net profit from the business is one of the accepted method of determination of income from business. But, there is no hard and fast rule for estimation of income.

The department is following estimation of net profit on various rates depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. But, while estimating net profit from the business, there should be a basis for adopting a particular rate of net profit, either based on comparable cases of similar nature of business or assessee's own book results for earlier years. The provisions of section 44AD provide for estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on gross receipts, in case where the assessees are involved in specified businesses and turnover from the business does not exceed specified limit. (1) It could not be said that the assessee’s books of account were correct and complete and, therefore, the income of the assessee in each of the assessment years had to be assessed according to provisions of section 145(2) and (2) it could not be accepted that the assessee had received the ‘on money’ as its income only in the last two assessment years as it had been earning ‘on money’ from the beginning of the project although the percentage might have increased in the later years.

This was because even as per the assessee own submissions and disclosure, it had earned ‘on money’ at the rate of 17.5 per cent of Rs. 5.77 crores. As no builder can be expected to be selling the shops and flats without charging some profits, a rate of 7.5 per cent might be considered to be reasonable rate of net profit. This net profit was in addition to the ‘on money’ and must have been earned even from those parties from whom no ‘on money’ had been charged, such as banks, BMC and other institutions. This would mean that the total profit rate would be 17.5 per cent plus 7.5 per cent which is equal to 25 per cent. This rate would be applied on the total receipts and not on the receipts after deducting the profits. The books of account regularly maintained in the course of business which are duly audited under the provisions of the Act and are free from any qualification by the auditors should be taken as correct unless there are strong and sufficient reasons to indicate that they are unreliable. For rejecting the books of account, it is the revenue's onus to prove that either the books of account maintained by the assessee are not correct and complete or the method of accounting adopted by the assessee is such that true profits cannot be deduced therefrom. In the instant case, while rejecting the books of account, the adverse observation of the Assessing Officer was with respect to delay in payment of labour charges for the month of January, 1998. That was not sufficient cause for rejecting the audited accounts wherein no adverse comment had been made by the auditor, nor any specific defect had been pointed out by the Assessing Officer. It was not the case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee had recorded excess payment of labour charges, nor there was any allegation that labour charges were disproportionate to the nature of contract work executed. On the other hand, even as per the Government manuals, the percentage of labour expenses as a percentage of total value of contract, in respect of civil contract, is 25 per cent whereas in the instant case, the expenses claimed under labour charges worked out to 20.67 per cent (total contract receipts Rs. 364.54 lakhs, labour charges Rs. 75.37 lakhs.) Thus, it was not a case of excess payment of labour charges to reduce the profit, but, on the contrary, as against the standard norm of 25 per cent labour charges amounting to Rs. 91.13 lakhs, the assessee had actually incurred only Rs. 75.37 lakhs, which worked out to be at 20.67 per cent. Income-tax provisions nowhere either authorize the Assessing Officer or cast an obligation on the assessee to prove the negative result, i.e., to prove as to why he had failed to make a profit at a particular rate.

The accounts may be rejected as unreliable if important entries and transactions are omitted therefrom or if proper particulars and vouchers, bills, etc., are not forthcoming or if they do not include entries relating to particular class of business transaction. Reasons for rejecting wages record as commented by the Assessing Officer related to full address of the labour, which was not given on the muster roll register. The wages record had been kept by the assessee as per regulation known as 'Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970. The addresses of the labourers to whom wages had been paid were not mentioned, since the labourers stayed in the Jhugi Jhoperies at a work site itself and to that effect the assessee had already replied to the Assessing Officer vide its letter dated 23-3-2001, through which site of construction where labourers resided was given which was, however, not taken notice of by the Assessing Officer and the same was sent to him by courier and was found to be duly received by the Assessing Officer. The Assessing Officer had also alleged that the actual date of payment was not mentioned by the payee receiving the wages. The date on which the entry had been made in the wages register was the actual date of payment. As per the nature of the contract work executed by the assessee, he had got a contract to carry out a particular job or a contract for which the material was supplied by the CPWD/DOT and the labour was provided by the assessee-contractor. The assessee used to make payments to the labourers on the basis of mandays put in by the labourers and not on the basis of work performed by them on each day. Therefore, there was no merit in the allegations of the Assessing Officer that work performed by the labour was not mentioned on the payment vouchers and in making them as basis for rejection of books of account. The payment to the assessee-contractor was also made on the basis of work completed which was measured by the department itself and not on the basis of what the labourer had done. The bills for such a contract were prepared, which were not verified by the engineers of contractee before making payments. On the basis of those bills which were finally approved by the Government engineers/contractee, the payment was given to the assessee-contractor after deducting TDS. Thus, it was humanly not possible to provide the details as to what work a particular labourer had done at the site. Further, the Assessing Officer had also not indicated any defect in the system of accounting regularly followed by the assessee, or its correctness, nor was there any change in the method of accounting during the year under consideration as compared to the earlier years to indicate any intention of the assessee to show low profit.

In the case of ‘U’, the contract receipts for the assessment year 2001-02 exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs i.e., Rs. 41,20,790. Therefore, the provisions of section 44AD were not applicable to case of ‘U’ for the assessment year 2001-02. Following the decision of the Tribunal Amritsar (SMC) Bench, in the case of the Nangal Khurad Co-operative L & C Society Ltd. v. AO, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was set aside and the Assessing Officer was directed to compute the income for the assessment year 2001-02 by applying net profit rate of 6 per cent instead of 8 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer. The appeal for the assessment year 2001-02 was partly allowed.

In the case of ‘D’ for the assessment year 2002-03, the contract receipts were Rs. 10,21,919 and in the case of ‘U’, the contract receipts for the assessment year 2002-03 were Rs. 14,25,627. Thus, in both the cases, receipts were less than Rs. 40 lakhs. The provisions of section 44AD are applicable to the contracts of civil construction or supply of labour for civil construction for contract receipts below 40 lakhs. Explanation to section 44AD further provides that the expression ‘civil construction’ includes the construction or repair of any building, bridge, dam or other structure or of any canal or road. It was not clear from the orders of the lower authorities whether, the activities undertaken by the assessees were contracts of civil work, supply of labour to civil contractors or the contracts falling under Explanation to section 44AD. If the activities of the assessees fell in the above categories, the provisions of section 44AD would be applicable and the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) for upholding the net profit rate of 8 per cent would not warrant any interference. However, if the activities of the assessees did not fall in those categories, the income would require to be computed by applying net profit rate of 6 per cent. In the light of those facts and circumstances of the cases, it was appropriate to set aside the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) and same were restored to his file with a direction to modify the earlier orders only if it was found that nature of contract work done by the assessees was other than supply of labour for civil contracts or the cases falling under Explanation to section 44AD. Otherwise, the earlier orders would stand confirmed.

In the result, the appeal was partly allowed.

While examining the books of the assessee, the Assessing Officer has to consider the following aspects : (i) whether the assessee has regularly employed a method of accounting; (ii) even if regular adoption of a method of accounting is there, whether the annual profits can properly be deduced from the method employed; (iii ) whether the accounts have been correctly maintained; (iv) whether the accounts maintained are complete in the sense that there is no significant omission therein. If the answers to above four questions would be in the affirmative, then the assessee's profits would be computed on the basis of his accounts. In such cases, proviso to section 145(1) or section 145(2) cannot be invoked. On the perusal of the materials placed on record in the instant case, it was found that the answers to all the above four questions were in the affirmative. No finding had been recorded by either of the lower authorities as to the unacceptability of the method and to the irregularity of the accounts kept by the assessee. It is well-settled that in the absence of such a finding recorded by the authorities, the book results cannot be ignored or brushed aside.

In the instant case, the assessee had been regularly maintaining the percentage of profit between 1 per cent to 2 per cent. Such profit had actually been worked out at higher figure, if one took only labour charges as a contract receipt insofar as the material was supplied by the Government, on which there was no question of any profit being earned by the assessee. From the record, it was also found that out of total contract receipts of Rs. 3.64 crores, the material used, supplied by the Government amounted to Rs. 1,60,35,409 as per the certificate of chartered accountant placed on the record. There was no question of any profit being earned by the assessee on the amount of Rs. 1.60 crores of materials being supplied by the Government/'contractee' to the assessee-firm for being used in the contract assigned to the assessee by the Government departments. It was also not the case of the Assessing Officer that any part of the contract receipt had not been entered in the books of account or that the assessee had accounted for expenses more than what had actually been incurred.

In view of the above facts and circumstances of the case and the materials placed on record there was no valid reason and justification for rejection of audited books of account and the method of accounting regularly and consistently followed by the assessee for accounting for the contract receipts. Thus, there was no justification in estimating the profit at 8 per cent by disregarding the book results.

It was evident from the terms and conditions of the contract that the assessee had not simply sold the sand to the civil contractor. The sand was available at the site on payment of royalty to the State Government. The assessee had to engage labourers for loading and unloading of the same. The assessee had to engage vehicle for carriage of sand up to the site. The sand was to be unloaded from the vehicle. The assessee was also required to pay octroi in respect of the said supply of sand. It was evident from these facts that the assessee was not engaged in the retail business of trading of goods. The price fixed by ‘U’ Ltd. was inclusive of all the above charges. Section 44AF is applicable in respect of retail traders. The assessee was not engaged in any retail trading - buying or selling of goods to customers. The assessee was neither a retailer nor a wholesale trader. The only business conducted by the assessee was the work executed by the assessee on account of contract for supply and transportation of sand, etc., to U Ltd. for construction of road. No other income had been disclosed. Therefore, the assessee could not be said to be engaged in the retail business of trading of goods. The assessee had engaged himself in the execution of contract with U Ltd. only. Hence, provisions of section 44AF were not attracted in the instant case. In the instant case, the assessee had executed the work of supplying and transportation of sand from a particular area to a civil contractor. In other words, the assessee was a sub-contractor to the civil contractor for execution of part of the work involved in the construction of the road. In view of Explanation 3 to section 194C, execution of work includes the carriage of goods by any mode of transport of goods other than by railways. Therefore, for the purpose of section 44AD, the execution of any works contract would include carriage of goods by any mode of transport other than by railways. In the instant case, the assessee had engaged himself in the supply and transportation of sand from a particular area to the civil contractor. If one were to go by the composite contract, then the entire payments made to the assessee would fall within the ambit of section 44AD being the payment received for the execution of works contract in the construction of a road. In this view of the matter, the entire payment would fall within the ambit of section 44AD. However, the contractor had made payments to the assessee in two parts - one for supplying of material, i.e., the sand at specified rates and the other for transportation charges including loading and unloading, octroi, etc. In case the contract was divisible in two parts - one for the supply of material and another for transport of the same, then section 44AD would be applicable only in respect of transportation charges and for the supply of material it would be reasonable to apply a net rate of profit of 5 per cent as applicable in the case of retail transfers, notwithstanding the fact that the assessee’s case might not strictly fall within the ambit of section 44AF in respect of the supply of the material. In the absence of relevant material, it would be just and reasonable to restore the issue to the file of Assessing Officer for the purpose of determination of the net profits after verification of the nature of payments to the assessee. In case there was a composite contract and there was no basis for bifurcation of transportation charges and cost of material, then the profit of the assessee should be computed at the rate of 8 per cent as provided under section 44AD. However, if there was a reasonable basis for bifurcation of payments, for the cost of material separately and for transportation charges, then the profit should be computed at the rate of 8 per cent in respect of payments made for transportation charge and at the rate of 5 per cent for the supply of the material. The Assessing Officer should decide the issue accordingly.

, such an impost has to be regarded as unreasonable restriction on the freedom to carry on trade or business. In the instant case, the legislative policy of fixing the rate of profit as has been done in section 44AC had to be regarded as in the nature of unreasonable restriction on cases of some of the assessees. Therefore, section 44AC has to be regarded as violative of article 19(1)(a) in the cases of some of the petitioners before the Court. The further question to be considered was whether anything can be done by the Court to uphold the validity of section 44AC though, as it is, it is violative of articles 14 and 19(1)(g). The Andhra Pradesh High Court found a way out and the same was to be read down. The reading down by the Andhra Pradesh High Court was to the extent that section 44AC shall be read not as an independent provision but as an adjunct to and as explanatory to section 206C; and that it does not dispense with regular assessment altogether with the result that after the tax is collected in the manner provided by section 206C, a regular assessment would be made where the profit and gain of business in goods in question would be ascertained in accordance with sections 28 to 43C. The reading down was resorted to by the Andhra Pradesh High Court, having come to the view that section 206C serves the purpose which the Legislature had in mind, i.e., to take care of tax evasion. lt was observed that once tax is collected at the source as visualised by section 206C, the contractor cannot run away; probably only in cases where the profit is higher than 40 per cent (in case of liquor traders) would he make himself scarce. In all other cases, he would come to the department for assessment of his income and there is no reason, as to why regular assessment should not be made in his case. Thus, the overall object underlying the provision would be subserved by section 206C. Following the view taken by the Andhra Pradesh High Court, although section 44AC violated articles 14 and 19(1)(g), instead of being struck down, it should be read down as above, as this reading down takes care of all the complaints made by the petitioners inasmuch as if during the course of regular assessment it were to be found that any particular assessee had not earned the profit at the rate specified in section 44AC, the same would be duly taken care of section 44AC would, therefore, cease to be arbitrary and would not be unreasonably restrictive of the freedom to carry on trade or business.

It is noted that the audited financial statements were available before the Assessing Officer but without disputing the sales turnover during the year he disallowed the total expenses including the purchase of material towards contract work undertaken by the assessee during the year. When the matter travelled before the Commissioner (Appeals) he observed in the impugned order that the net profit rate for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 disclosed by the assessee in its regular audited books of account is 0.22 per cent, 0.17 per cent and 0.25 per cent. Even during the course of scrutiny proceeding for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 net profit rate applied by the Assessing Officer was 0.16 per cent, 0.93 per cent and 0.18 per cent. Though the Commissioner (Appeals) appreciated the fact that undisputed revenue just could not have come without incurring an expenditure, but based on his observation that the purchase made by the assessee in the past were in dispute and genuineness of the same had not been proved, the Commissioner (Appeals) computed the net profit applying the rate of 8 per cent on the total revenue for the year of Rs. 87.46 crores.[Para 9]

The revenue has challenged the relief given by the Commissioner (Appeals) and the assessee is agitating for the higher net profit rate applied by the Commissioner (Appeals) and ignoring past net profit track of the assessee.[Para 9.1]

It is found that the net profit rate of 0.4 per cent has been accepted by this Tribunal in one of the sister concern of the assessee. It is also found that the net profit declared by the assessee for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 was within the range of 0.2 per cent to 0.29 per cent and even in the scrutiny proceedings the revenue authorities in assessee's own case have estimated net profit below the rate of 1 per cent so by no means estimating the net profit at the rate of 8 per cent could be justified, looking to the fact that there is no change of business during all these years, books of account are duly audited, no specific error has been pointed out by both lower authorities.[Para 9.3]

One more important fact which is relevant in the instant appeal is that subsequent to the assessment proceeding search and seizure operation was carried out at 'B' Group on 27-4-2017 and subsequent to search notice under section 153C were issued to the assessee company also and the assessments were framed under section 143(3) for assessment years 2012-13 to 2014-15 on 27-12-2019 assessing the income only to the extent of additions confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals). In other words the grounds raised by the revenue will have no merit in these cases because revenue authorities have themselves accepted the income determined by the Commissioner (Appeals) giving part relief given in the grounds raised by the assessee. Certainly another fact which cannot be ignored is that there was a complete non-compliance on the part of the assessee, thereby, not allowing the Assessing Officer to examine the documents of sales, purchase and expenditure thoroughly.[Para 9.4]

Therefore, under the given facts and circumstances of the case, respectfully following the decision of this Tribunal in the case of ITO v. B.B.C. Project Services (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No.1669 (Kol.) of 2016, dated 30-11-2018] consistent business of contract work carried out by the assessee and the net profit rate offered in the financial statements and being fair to both the parties, it is viewed that application of net profit rate of 0.6 per cent on the turnover of contract business during the year i.e. Rs. 87.46 crores will meet the end to justice. It is accordingly ordered and the revenue is directed to compute the net profit for the year at the rate of 0.6 per cent. Further, it is made clear that this net profit rate of 0.6 per cent will take care of all the business expenses including interest and depreciation incurred for the purpose of running contract business and related to the turnover of Rs. 87.46 crores. Accordingly assessee will get part relief on this common issue and revenue fails to succeed.[Para 9.5]
IT : Enhancement in profit rate was not justified where revenue failed to point any special circumstances for estimation of high profit
